aa699d11d00c.text: By — Michelle Price, Associated Press Michelle Price, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-launches-new-attacks-on-iranian-targets-days-after-netanyahu-pressed-trump-for-more-strikes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. launches new attacks on Iranian targets days after Netanyahu pressed Trump for more strikes World Nov 3, 2026 10:07 AM EST The United States launched strikes on Iranian targets, a U.S. official said, in what appeared to be a limited operation on the eve of Tuesday's crucial midterm elections. Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Unlike earlier in the war, the strikes were not publicly announced. President Donald Trump previously said the U.S. wouldn't launch strikes on Iran before the midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress. READ MORE: Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year A U.S. official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. The move came as Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the critical waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply flowed during peacetime, and resume nuclear talks with the United States. Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement Back-channel negotiations have also been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran. Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday that he and Trump "both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East. The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes are likely to renew concerns. Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports. They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity. Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies. "The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children," said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei. He said he hopes for changes that will "bring about peace and stability, not just for Americans, but for the whole world." One woman was less optimistic. "It doesn't really make much difference who comes into power," said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. "The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I'm not talking about the American people, mind you. I'm talking about their policies." Iran's chief negotiator says it's up to the US to prevent renewed war Iranian state television quoted the country's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had "delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America's court to prevent war." It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to. Qalibaf also warned that Iran's armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness. "If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today," he said. Iranian authorities announce plans to train 1 million paramilitary volunteers Iran opened its third military training center in Tehran on Monday as authorities announced plans to train 1 million paramilitary volunteers nationwide, amid fears of renewed conflict. Members of the Basij, a paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guard, attended the inauguration, the semiofficial ISNA news agency reported. "Starting this week, across the country 1,500 training bases will start working in all cities and towns, and will aim for training 1 million sacrificial volunteers," said Ali Kows

7e7a9372225c.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/listen-live-supreme-court-hears-case-on-catholic-preschools-and-lgbtq-families Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LISTEN LIVE: Supreme Court hears case on Catholic preschools and LGBTQ families Politics Nov 3, 2026 10:00 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court will hear arguments Tuesday in a case brought by Catholic preschools that say it's unconstitutional to exclude them from a state-funded program over their admissions policy for LGBTQ+ families, the latest religious-rights case before the conservative-majority court. Arguments begin at 10 a.m. EST. Listen live in the video player above. Colorado says their refusal to admit kids from those families violates the state's anti-discrimination law. But St. Mary Catholic Parish and the Archdiocese of Denver argue that the policy is based on religious teachings about same-sex marriage and that excluding them violates their free-exercise rights. WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage President Donald Trump's administration is supporting the Catholic institutions. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. A win for the preschools could further narrow a landmark 1990 Supreme Court decision that found religious practices don't create exemptions from laws that otherwise apply broadly. Written by conservative icon Justice Antonin Scalia in a case over the spiritual use of peyote, a cactus containing mescaline that's sacred to many Indigenous people, the decision has nevertheless long been a target of the conservative legal movement. In the Colorado case, the high court could be sympathetic to the schools. The justices have sided with religious schools in similar disputes before, ruling in recent years that they can't be excluded from programs in Maine and Montana that provide public aid to private schools. In 2025, though, the court deadlocked over a plan to establish a publicly funded Catholic charter school after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself. The Colorado universal preschool program was created by a 2020 ballot measure. It provides public funding for preschool at schools chosen by parents. The plaintiffs, represented by the group Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, say the state has allowed other preschools to prioritize children with disabilities or those from low-income families, so admission based on religious beliefs about gender and same-sex marriage should be allowed, too. The Catholic preschools say their enrollment has dropped 20% since the program started. Colorado argues that the other admissions decisions are in line with the state's anti-discrimination rules. Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.
The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.
It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.
Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.
The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.
It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.
The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.
The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.
The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.
Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.
The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.
Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.
The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.
In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.
The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.
The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.
Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.
Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.
In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, an increase over just two Democratic ads mentioning those topics from 2020 to 2024, according to a new analysis from the Tech Oversight Project shared first with Semafor.
Democrats used these messages four times as often as Republicans, the report says. The ads appeared in nearly every battleground state, as well as three toss-up governor races.
Ads cited by the report blame AI for price-gouging, harm to children, and even healthcare denial, while data center-focused ads press Republicans on water use and threats to farmland.
âDemocrats have potentially found a winning message. Now is the time to step on the gas and reject a return to business as usual in Washington, Silicon Valley fundraisers, and light-touch approaches,â the group, which is mostly funded by eBay founder Pierre Omidyarâs philanthropic network, writes in the report.
âIt would be a betrayal of their campaign promises, and not only would it squander our victory ââ it would create resentment in the base that will cost us in 2028,â it continues.
Groups that are pushing for stricter rules on AI and social media, like the Tech Oversight Project and other anti-AI organizations, see a huge opportunity to push Democrats in Congress and 2028 presidential contenders further on AI safety and data centers. They argue conservatives have already lost credibility on it thanks to President Donald Trumpâs cozy relationships with billionaire tech executives.

6d7d6558c6cf.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/election-day-underway-after-a-surge-in-early-voting-as-trump-sows-on-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:48 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The final day of voting in this year's midterm elections arrived Tuesday against a backdrop of uncertainty after a year in which President Donald Trump has tried to interfere in how states run their elections and sown doubts about the outcome should Republicans lose. Millions of Americans already have cast their ballots, with early voting turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections. In contrast to the president's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump has spent months trying to use the power of the presidency to put his thumb on the scale of this year's elections, which will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress. His Justice and Homeland Security departments have been involved in a massive hunt for voters who are not U.S. citizens, at one point engaging in a made-for-the-cameras predawn operation that led to more than two dozen arrests in California. The Department of Justice was planning its largest-ever effort to monitor Election Day polling places, countered by an even larger effort among Democrats and allied groups, and at the president's urging had sued to block certification of Alaska's results if the outcome of the Senate race favored Democrats. At the same time, Trump's constant false claims about widespread voter fraud led election officials and Democratic groups across the country to plan for the possibility of immigration agents at voting sites or federal officers seizing voting machines. His administration has insisted that no armed federal officials would be guarding the polls on Election Day. Courts have blocked the Trump administration's efforts to influence elections In the run-up to Tuesday, none of the steps Democrats most feared had come to pass, and the Republican administration's legal maneuvers had been largely blocked by the courts. One of the Trump administration's most high-profile attempts to interfere in state elections was turned away Monday night by the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected its push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots as part of its search for noncitizen voters. In another Monday night ruling, a federal judge said the Trump administration must stop sending voter lists of alleged noncitizens to election officials. Even the administration's own record of arrests and charges has demonstrated what research and state investigations have made clear for years — that instances of noncitizens casting ballots are extremely rare. Monday's rulings followed another defeat for the president at the Supreme Court less than two months ago, when it rejected his attempt to limit mail balloting through changes at the Postal Service. That directive was included in one of two executive orders Trump has signed during his second term that attempted to federalize certain aspects of elections, even though the Constitution gives the states, and sometimes Congress, the authority to set election rules. Voting begins smoothly with some weather disruptions in the Southwest The first polling sites were open Tuesday morning across much of the East Coast, with few disruptions so far. In New York's suburban Westchester County, where some voters are casting ballots in a competitive U.S. House race, election officials said an issue with voting machines accepting paper ballots was requiring ballots to be placed in emergency bags for later counting. But they stressed that the ballots would remain secure and monitored, that they would later be counted and that voters could continue casting ballots while they worked to resolve the issue. You can also follow the NewsHour's live coverage on YouTube, Twitter, Facebook, and TikTok, and see highlights on our Instagram. Heavy rains and flash flooding in a swath of the Southwest were expected to make it harder for some voters to reach polling places in parts of Colorado, Arizona, Utah and New Mexico. Election administrators in the Navajo Nation announced changes to several of its polling locations, and in Utah's rural San Juan County, voters were being allowed to vote electronically on Tuesday because some of them may not be able to reach polling places. Election administrators and voting rights advocates have been advising voters casting late absentee ballots to use drop boxes or deliver them to polling places in person rather than mail them. The advice came after concerns emerged that recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations could result in postmarking delays that would mean mail ballots could not be counted. Late-arriving ballots or late postmarks disenfranchised tens of thousands of voters in California, Oregon and Washington, which mail ballots to all voters, during this year's primaries. Trump hasn't committed to accepting the election results The most significant disruptions ahead of Election Day were the Trump administration's attempts to interfere. Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged noncitizen voters, federal election monitors, federal intimidation of election officials and other concerns. They reveal how Trump's attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections — combined with high-stakes races — are resulting in court battles that could extend past Election Day into ballot counting an

22c06f963c77.text: Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-florida-senate-midterm-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Results: Florida Senate midterm election Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:30 AM EST WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage WASHINGTON (AP) — Florida Republicans will try to extend their dominance in statewide elections Tuesday as voters decide races for Senate, governor and other state and legislative offices. The election will mark the first under a new congressional map adopted by Republicans to boost the party's chances of keeping control of the closely divided House. Once the nation's most evenly divided swing state, Florida has shifted steadily to the right in the last quarter century. At the time of the 2000 presidential election, Democrats had held a voter registration advantage over Republicans for decades. That advantage would erode until 2021 when registered Republicans overtook registered Democrats. Today, there are 1.5 million more Republicans in Florida than Democrats. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News In the race for governor, Democrats have nominated a former Republican to lead them out of the electoral doldrums. Former Rep. David Jolly defeated five other candidates in the Aug. 18 primary with 61% of the vote. Jolly took an unlikely path to running for governor as a Democrat, joining the party in 2025 after leaving the GOP in 2018. He has tapped former Democratic Rep. Gwen Graham as his running mate. Graham is the daughter of the late Bob Graham, the longtime Democratic senator and governor. The Republican nominee is Rep. Byron Donalds, who won the 11-candidate primary with the help of an endorsement from President Donald Trump. Donalds received about 48% of the primary vote, almost double that of the runner-up, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. Donalds backed Trump over Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis in the 2024 presidential primaries and was considered as a possible Trump running mate that year. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have each campaigned for Donalds in Florida since the president launched his midterm campaign push last month. READ MORE: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida Six other independent or third-party candidates are also on the ballot. In this year's Senate race, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody defends her seat against Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon as well as an independent candidate. Moody was state attorney general in January 2025 when DeSantis appointed her to fill the seat vacated by Marco Rubio, who was tapped by Trump to be secretary of state. She is now running to complete the final two years of Rubio's term. Nixon, a democratic socialist, received 56% of the August primary vote against retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman, who received about 44%. Vindman, a former National Security Council staff member, was a key witness in Trump's first impeachment in 2019. His brother, Eugene, was elected to Congress from Virginia's 7th District in 2024. WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran If elected, Donalds would become Florida's first Black governor and the nation's first elected Black Republican governor. Nixon would become the state's first Black U.S. senator. Florida Democrats have faced a drought in statewide elections, particularly for governor. A Democrat last won the governorship more than 30 years ago. DeSantis was reelected in 2022 with a 19-point margin over former Gov. Charlie Crist, another former Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat. Democrats last won a Florida U.S. Senate seat in 2012. The new congressional boundaries Republicans enacted in May essentially eliminate four congressional districts most recently represented by Democrats. Three Democratic incumbents face tough challenges in newly drawn districts: Kathy Castor in the 14th District around Tampa, Darren Soto in the 9th District near Orlando and Jared Moskowitz in the 25th District in South Florida along the Gold Coast. The redrawn 22nd Congressional District in South Florida also has a competitive race. It contains almost all of the current majority-Black 20th Congressional District, which had been represented by Democrat Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick before she resigned in April. It also includes large portions of the current 26th and 18th Congressional Districts, which are both heavily Republican. In statewide elections, Democrats usually perform best in the Orlando and Tallahassee areas and in South Florida along the Gold Coast. Republicans usually post their strongest numbers in North Florida and the panhandle. They also do well in Central Florida and along the Gulf of Mexico. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties around Tampa Bay are key state battlegrounds. Trump narrowly won both counties in 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden narrowly carried both in 2020. Trump and Democrat Hillary Clinton split the counties in 2016. Duval County, home to Jacksonville, is another swing area. Trump narrowly carried it in 2024 and 2016, while Biden carried it narrowly in 2020. Miami-Dade County in South Florida will also be a key county to watch. In 2024, Trump made significant inroads with Latino voters and became the first Republican presidential candidate to win the county since George H.W. Bush in 1988. Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied: When do polls close? Polls close at 7 p.m. local time, which is 7 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET. Most of the state is in Eastern time, and polls there close at 7 p.m. ET. A few counties are in Central time, and polls there close at 8 p.m. ET. What's on the ballot? 2625fce6fa4a.text: Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-nebraska-senate-midterm-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Results: Nebraska Senate midterm election Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:30 AM EST WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans in the ruby-red state of Nebraska have found themselves on the back foot this midterm season as their opponents have made surprising gains in key races. Losing a Nebraska seat in the U.S. Senate or House could set up Republicans to lose control of Congress. Even if Republicans hold onto their seats, a near-loss could signal an erosion of Republican power in a state that has not voted for a Democratic presidential candidate since 1964. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Sen. Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent who took office in 2023, is running against Independent candidate Dan Osborn, a union organizer. Cindy Burbank, the Democratic nominee, dropped out of the race in July. Osborn has insisted he will not caucus with Democrats or Republicans, though he has received funds from Democratic donors, which Republicans contend is evidence that he will align with Democrats, if elected. Ricketts was appointed in 2023 to the Senate to fulfill the term of Sen. Ben Sasse, a Republican who left Congress to become president of the University of Florida. The next year, Ricketts won the same seat in a special election by a margin of more than 25 percentage points, even more than President Donald Trump's 20 percentage point margin of victory in the state. READ MORE: Here's when polls are closing in your state this midterm election But the optics of this midterm race have been challenging for Ricketts, as they have been for many Republicans on the ballot this year. The president's tariffs and rising fuel prices have hit the state's agricultural and manufacturing industries hard. Ranchers and beef producers in Nebraska have opposed Trump's attempts to address soaring beef prices by importing more beef, saying it would lower their profits. And Osborn has been able to use Ricketts' family history as son of the founder of TD Ameritrade to portray him as political insider who is out of touch with Nebraskans' concerns. The contrast works well for Osborn, who embarked on a political career after leading a 77-day strike at the Kellogg's plant in Omaha, where he worked as a mechanic in 2021. Osborn, who had been an employee of the company for nearly two decades, was fired following the strike and went on to run for U.S. Senate against the incumbent Republican, Sen. Deb Fischer, in 2024. Though Fischer won the race, Osborn came within 7 percentage points of his opponent, a surprising outcome. Ricketts has raised $14.5 million for his campaign as of mid-October, while Osborn had raised $11 million. Millions more in outside spending have poured into the race. READ MORE: When will we know 2026 midterm election results? It may take some time, but that's normal On the congressional map, Democrats are once again targeting Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, where Democrat Denise Powell is up against Republican Omaha City Councilor Brinker Harding. They are running to fill the seat of retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon, a moderate Republican who has criticized the Trump administration over Ukraine and tariffs. Democrats have zeroed in on the district, which includes the state's largest city, Omaha, and is sometimes called the "blue dot," as a possible opportunity to flip a seat. In June, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced it had added Powell to its "Red to Blue" program, which supports Democratic candidates running in competitive districts. The 2nd Congressional District was the only district in the state to vote for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. The gubernatorial race in Nebraska has also become competitive. Republican Gov. Jim Pillen, who took office in 2023, is being challenged by Democrat Lynne Walz, a former member of the state Senate. Nebraska's governorship has been held by Republicans since 1999, but the national political environment has prompted Trump to travel in and campaign. "When I'm on the ballot, people show up and you always win," Trump said at an early October rally in Grand Island, appearing on stage with Ricketts, Pillen and Flood. "Pretend I'm on the ballot, please. We gotta go and win this." Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied. When do polls close? Polls close at 7 p.m. MT and 8 p.m. CT, which is 9 p.m. ET. What's on the ballot? The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in races for U.S. Senate, governor, U.S. House, attorney general, secretary of state, statewide ballot measures, state Legislature, state auditor, state treasurer and Workers' Compensation Court judge. How many people voted in the last midterm election? About 667,000 votes were cast in the 2022 race for governor in Nebraska. How much of the vote is cast by absentee ballot? About 39% of all ballots cast in Nebraska's 2022 race for governor were cast early or by absentee ballot. The latest advance vote totals for Nebraska can be found in the AP's advance vote tracker. When are early and absentee votes released? Most of Nebraska's 93 counties are expected to release all or nearly all of their early and absentee vote results in the first vote update of the night, often before any results from in-person Election Day results are available. About half of counties are expected to release no or relatively few in-person Election Day results in their first report, including the most populous counties of Douglas and Lancaster. Voters in the Lone Star state will cast ballots in a hotly contested U.S. Senate race and elect U.S. House representatives to districts newly redrawn to favor Republican candidates in contests that could be decisive in Democrats' bid to retake control of Congress. Voters will also elect a governor, state and local representatives and judges, and decide on ballot measures. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Facing off in the race for Senate are Democratic state Rep. James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, the state's embattled attorney general and an ally of President Donald Trump. Paxton beat out the seat's incumbent of over two decades, Sen. John Cornyn, for the Republican nomination in a tight primary runoff race after Cornyn lost favor with the president and Paxton received Trump's last-minute endorsement. Trump's support for Paxton, who has promised to champion the president's priorities if he wins the election, has been both a crucial asset and a liability for the candidate. The candidate's website says he is "running to help President Trump finish the border wall" and states that he plans to help the president deport "criminal illegal aliens." But Texas shares over 1,200 miles of border with Mexico, and the rising number of arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement risks alienating Latino voters, who make up over 30 percent of the state's electorate. Talarico has stressed the need for border security but also called for legal immigration to be made easier, saying in campaign materials, "our border should be like a front porch — it should have a welcome mat out front and a lock on the door." Both candidates have made affordability central to their campaign messaging. Talarico has promised to cut taxes for the middle class, increase taxes on billionaires and repeal Trump's tariffs on imports. Paxton has said he plans to cut taxes, reduce federal spending and remove regulations on energy companies that harm the economy. Trump carried Texas in the last three presidential elections, defeating Democratic nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris by over 10 percentage points in 2024. The state has not elected a Democratic senator since 1988. Yet recent polls suggest a tight race. The Texas race could become the most expensive Senate race in the country's history. As of mid-October, Talarico had raised more than $146.3 million, eclipsing Paxton's $22.3 million. But hundreds of millions more in independent expenditures have given Paxton the advantage in total spending. Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a Texas resident, gave $158 million to the Republican-supporting Senate Leadership PAC, which donated the same amount to Texas PAC, a group supporting Paxton. Musk also gave $10 million to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton. Among the most competitive House races in the country is the one for Texas' 34th Congressional District on the state's southern Gulf Coast. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez is running for reelection against Eric Flores, a Republican and Army veteran endorsed by Trump. In the 2024 election, Gonzalez won the district by a thin margin of less than 3 percentage points, and its boundaries were redrawn in 2025 to advantage Republicans. In a possible sign of growing wariness of associating with the president, Flores' campaign appeared to remove a reference to Trump from a section of his website. Democrats are hoping to reclaim Texas's 15th Congressional District, an inland strip in the southern part of the state and the only part of the Rio Grande Valley represented by a Republican in the U.S. House. Monica De La Cruz, the incumbent Republican, is facing Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano musician and political newcomer, in a newly redrawn version of the district that favors Republicans. De La Cruz won her 2024 reelection by a margin of nearly 15 percentage points. Another race that has become increasingly competitive is the Texas governor's race between Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who has held office since 2015, and Democratic state House Rep. Gina Hinojosa. Texas has elected only Republican governors since 1994, and Trump endorsed Abbott. But the most recent polls show a tight race, making the current contest one of the most vulnerable in Abbott's career. AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.
Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?
In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.
Episode 5 transcript
Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?
Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.
Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.
Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.
Sanders: Snoop has partnered with a company called Speechify. If you subscribe, you can get famous voices like Snoop’s, Gwyneth Paltrow, MrBeast to read whatever you want. It turns out people are doing this in all sorts of ways. Here’s Snoop in a marketing video.
Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.
Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.
Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.
Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.
Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.
MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.
Sanders: And even back to themselves.
Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.
Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.
Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.
Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.
Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.
Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.
Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.
Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.
Farid: My bread and butter is developing technologies to distinguish real from fake. And we work with media outlets and law enforcement and courts, et cetera. But one of the questions you always want to ask when you’re in my business is, well, do you need the mathematics and the computation? Just let somebody listen to it or look at it. And can they tell the difference?
Sanders: It turns out they cannot. In laboratory tests, people can’t reliably say whether a voice they hear was created by a machine or by a real living, breathing person.
Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.
Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.
Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?
Sanders: Okay, give it a try yourself. Is this the same person?
[Sanders voice clone] And how about now? Is this the same person?
Farid: And when you ask them, is it the same person? They say yes, which means the AI has figured out with roughly 20 seconds or so of your voice how to make their AI sound like you, which is mind-blowing.

4f1f7a6f6fab.text: By — Ben Finley, Associated Press Ben Finley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/trump-says-u-s-will-stop-giving-4-billion-in-aid-to-israel-next-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump says U.S. will stop giving $4 billion in aid to Israel next year World Nov 3, 2026 9:28 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump says the U.S. will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East. The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Tuesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple years. Trump says Israel doesn't need the aid and it's a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also says that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. "You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash," Trump said. "Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money." There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office. The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years. An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict. Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years. While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East. c4a90b067f33.text: By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/midterm-elections-come-to-a-close-in-referendum-on-trumps-presidency Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Midterm elections come to a close in referendum on Trump's presidency Politics Nov 3, 2026 9:20 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters struggling with high prices and angry over an unpopular war with Iran will decide Tuesday whether to drastically shift power in Washington in midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term. Democrats were cautiously optimistic as they watched Republicans spend the campaign's final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago. They're betting that discontent over Trump's failure to deliver on his promise to tackle rising costs and perceptions that he has focused more on gilding the nation's capital than their pain at the pump will depress Republican turnout and drive their own voters to the polls. Republicans held out hope their money advantage would help stem the tide, but they were bracing to lose control of the U.S. House and fighting to hang onto the U.S. Senate — an outcome that seemed unlikely earlier this year, given a map widely seen as favoring their party. Please check your inbox to confirm. Still, margins are tight in both chambers; one or two seats could tip the balance. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the 100-member Senate to win the majority, an uphill climb because many of the most competitive races are in historically red states. In the 435-member House, they need only three. More than 57 million people had already cast ballots as of Monday, with turnout surpassing the early vote four years ago in many closely watched states. Trump, whose party has struggled when he's not running to turn out the low-propensity voters who've fueled his victories, has told voters to act as though he is running, even as many Republican candidates have tried to keep their distance. "I really want you to pretend I'm on the ballot," he told the crowd in Salina, Kansas, on Sunday at the final of several dozen rallies in the campaign's closing weeks. On Tuesday, Mark Barker, of Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, said Trump was very much top of mind as he voted. "I've just been following Trump the whole time. I really think he's doing an awesome job," said Barker, noting the president's promise of $5,000 for every U.S. adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, border policy and war in the Middle East. "Everything he's done has been outstanding." In Raleigh, North Carolina, 57-year-old librarian James Moore said he voted for Democrats to push back on Trump's big tax breaks and spending cuts bill. "I'm paying more taxes. I'm paying more for my healthcare. I'm paying more for everything," he said. "We need more representatives in Congress that are going to stand up to Trump." Trump's aggressive schedule had stops in the reddest states, including Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, underscoring his party's challenges. He also has continued to make false claims about voting fraud, such as insisting noncitizens are casting ballots en masse. His administration has filed lawsuits in Alaska and California, and Democrats fear interference and voter intimidation as his Justice Department threatens to prosecute local election officials. The election could reshape the political landscape The results will shape the final two years of Trump's second term after the Republican-controlled Congress acted as a rubber stamp to much of his agenda. While Trump has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats taking control of even one chamber of Congress would open the floodgates to investigations and possible impeachments. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets. An especially strong showing for Democrats would also boost potential presidential candidates, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. It could also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may be looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum. Republicans tried to buck historical precedent — a president's party almost always loses seats during the midterms — with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But the plan may fall short as new districts drawn in Florida and other states to be safely red may not vote that way. Other Trump choices could prove costly. In Texas, Trump worked to oust longtime incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in favor of scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton, setting the stage for an extraordinarily expensive race against Democratic nominee James Talarico, who Democrats hope may finally help them realize their dream of flipping the state. In North Carolina, Sen. Thom Tillis retired after clashing with Trump. The president's chosen replacement, former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, has struggled to gain traction against the Democrats' candidate, former Gov. Roy Cooper. "Everything depends on turnout. If we turn out our voters, we win, and that's what we've been planning for," said Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters, expressing optimism on the eve of the election. The money crunch that has hit AI in recent weeks is coming for the space industry, which shares DNA, investors, and market vibes with artificial intelligence.
âIf youâre a high-quality, well-run company with a good balance sheet and a good business model, you are very well positioned because everyoneâs paying attention,â Dylan Taylor, CEO of Voyager Technologies, said on this weekâs episode of Compound Interest. Everyone else is âbeing cast aside.â
Voyager builds space infrastructure for the Pentagon and defense contractors, and is working on a commercial space station, Starlab, to replace the International Space Station when it is retired in 2030. The company is publicly traded, which last month allowed it to raise $400 million on terms roughly in line with a hot convertible-debt market.
âLow cost of capital [is] a secret weapon,â Taylor said, âbecause the first question is, âhow do you compete with SpaceX?ââ
Even Elon Muskâs behemoth is feeling the squeeze: It throttled usage of its Grok AI bot this week because, as Musk said in an X post Sunday, it was getting too expensive. Taylor, like most space executives today, counts Musk as both a competitor (for contracts and capital) and collaborator (Voyagerâs hardware hitches a ride on SpaceXâs rockets).
The space and AI trades are increasingly twinned, tapping into similar pools of capital, riding similar national-security vibes, and carrying similar potential of catastrophic escalation. âItâs the same thing,â Taylor said of the two, but for a different reason: their potential to reshape every corner of the economy. âEveryone is in the space industry,â he said. âThey just donât know it yet.â
We also talked to Taylor about building data centers in space, which would sidestep the energy needs and political backlash back on Earth. And if they break? Just âbuild more,â is Taylorâs quintessentially American answer.

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.
In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.
Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.
The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.
The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.
And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”
Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.
Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.
Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

Timâs view
Todayâs US election is a test of how much voters will want to punish the president for soaring gasoline and power prices.
Energy costs are always an important factor in elections; gas prices are the only economic indicator displayed in big bold numbers at major intersections. But between the war in Iran and the data center power rush, thereâs rarely been an election in which energy prices â and the policy decisions pushing them up, from the White House to local zoning boards â are so much in the headlines.
The average gas price during US President Donald Trumpâs two years back in office is the highest itâs ever been halfway through a presidency, according to a Financial Times analysis. Since the oil embargoes of the 1970s, US presidents have been keenly aware that Americans have a very limited willingness to tolerate pain at the pump in the service of foreign policy objectives. And in many of the key congressional battlegrounds, AI-linked increases in household power bills are a central point of tension, making the votes a kind of referendum on how hard to hit the brakes on data center development, too.
If Democrats succeed in regaining a majority in one or both houses of Congress, the US energy story is in for big changes over the next two years. The partyâs leaders will face an immediate challenge, needing to decide how much hardball theyâre willing to play with Republicans and the White House over permitting reform. Federal budget fights will likely resurface arguments about tax incentives for EVs and other clean tech. Investigative committees will demand answers from the administration about everything from offshore wind lease pullbacks to the diesel deal with Moscow. Meanwhile, a new cohort of state and local leaders will grapple with what kind of pressure to apply on the power demands of Big Tech.
These are the storylines Iâll be focused on here until 2028. Happy voting!

A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland, 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe BÃ¼sken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal, the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven IntermarchÃ© stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland, irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

d3bbfb8b554c.text: There's a lot at stake for energy in the midterms, from the fate of the bipartisan permitting deal to the growing backlash against data centers and electricity prices. Why it matters: The results could spotlight which energy topics resonate with voters — and which have become political liabilities. Gasoline and diesel prices have been big on the campaign trail, offering a chance to see how much voter frustration over energy costs matters at the ballot box. Data center politics: There are sharp differences between the parties, even though data centers aren't especially popular with either party's slate of candidates. Why it matters: The pace of the AI buildout affects power demand and emissions. State of play: 32.4% of Democratic candidates support moratoriums at the federal, state, or local level, compared to just 3.4% of Republicans, per Data Center Watch, which tracked hundreds of races. Zoom in: Meanwhile, Ballotpedia is tracking dozens of ballot measures on data centers, many of which would impose new restrictions. Ohio is a hot spot. Control and permitting: The outcome will affect the politics of the lame-duck session — and that means the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal. What they're saying: If Democrats take both chambers, "leaders might opt to wait until they hold the gavels next year to renegotiate compromises," the research firm ClearView Energy Partners said in a note. Yes, but: A reminder that backers of the current bill think it's folly to expect political space to write a more liberal bill that President Trump would sign, or that could even pass the Senate. Threat level: What if the results are very close? ClearView notes that if Trump and allies contest the results, "weeks of post-election skirmishing could complicate passage of any bill." Political lessons: The results could offer clues about where energy and climate policy are headed. State of play: Exit polling is not famously precise, but it could provide a barometer of how much voters truly care — or not — about data centers. It's also worth watching how candidates who made high gas and diesel prices central to their campaigns fare tonight. My thought bubble: Keep an eye on the performance of progressive vs. centrist Democrats. If the latter overperform, it could be another sign that aggressive climate policies won't return to vogue with Dems. Zoom in: Let's say, for instance, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro's (D) victory is even more of a blowout than expected. That could bolster more centrist, oil and gas-accepting candidates in the 2028 cycle (when he might run for president). The next Congress: Regardless of chamber control, don't look for many opportunities for big new energy laws if permitting goes kaput. Yes, but: There will be no shortage of messaging bills and positioning for the 2028 White House race. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has pledged to bring back clean energy tax credits killed in the 2025 GOP budget law. What we're watching: Limited chances for common ground around nuclear power and geothermal. For instance, the wide-ranging Senate permitting bill contains several bipartisan geothermal bills that already cleared the House. Oversight power: If Democrats take control of either chamber, expect aggressive investigations of White House energy policies and investments, a topic we recently explored. State utility bosses: A number of states have elections for electricity regulators, who often exert powerful control over power prices and planning. Zoom in: One place to watch is Georgia, where two Democratic victories would flip party control of the state's Public Service Commission for the first time in decades. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has more. Governors: The winners of governors' races will have a big say in everything from oil and gas development to electricity prices. Zoom out: S&P Global has a nice look at energy differences in several governors' races, though a number of the contests are not especially competitive. Friction point: One place to watch is Texas, where oil and gas interests favor incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in his surprisingly tight race against Gina Hinojosa. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

Investcorp, one of the Gulfâs largest asset managers, is preparing for a spree of infrastructure deals in the region as governments look for new ways to finance massive investment plans to reduce their reliance on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Gulf states will be more open to partnering with investment funds to pay for new infrastructure projects in the future as they look to preserve cash, Investcorp chief investment officer Rishi Kapoor told Semafor.
These funds have become more active in the Gulf in recent years as governments and state-owned companies seek to raise money by selling stakes in oil pipelines and other assets that for decades have been kept under state control. The scale of the buildout in new infrastructure needed in the wake of the Iran war is set to open up a bigger role for private investors.
âOne of the really attractive investment themes unfolding in the Gulf in coming years will be the renewed focus on building resiliency into essential infrastructure,â Kapoor said. Investcorp already has several deals to acquire Gulf infrastructure assets in the works and could look to raise a new infrastructure fund in the next year or two to help it boost dealmaking.

e56fffe30b8b.text: The Justice Department said Tuesday it will deploy about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states for the first time ever to watch the polls. Why it matters: The unprecedented effort comes after courts repeatedly rejected the DOJ's efforts to force states to restrict voting for alleged noncitizens. It comes amid a long-running Trump administration push to fight voter fraud , which studies say isn't nearly as prevalent as the administration suggests. Driving the news : The department, in a statement early Tuesday, said one of its most important goals was to protect election integrity. "Today, the DOJ will further this mission by engaging in its largest monitoring effort in history—with approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers deployed, and, for the first time, in all 50 states," the department said. The department said observers would come from the DOJ, U.S. Attorney's offices, and staff from the Office of Personnel Management. What they're saying: "I am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner," assistant attorney general Harmeet K. Dhillon said in the statement. The intrigue: Some local election officials have already expressed concerns that such a massive wave of observers could intimidate or otherwise interfere with voters. What to watch: The DOJ is still pursuing legal efforts in multiple states to have ballots segregated or otherwise impact counting.

2f9a19141953.text:
Saudi Aramco reported a 9% rise in profit and increased dividend payments, most of which go to the Saudi state, as a jump in crude prices more than made up for lower production. Profit rose to $31.2 billion in the third quarter, driven by a 35% increase in the average selling price of its oil, even as the company tackled repeated attacks on its facilities from Yemenâs Houthis and Iranian strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Despite Aramcoâs ability to export oil at higher prices, its stock has lagged the global majors that mostly operate outside the Gulf.
Although lower than prewar levels, Aramco reported higher oil production than the previous quarter as it embraced more risky ship-to-ship transfers to get crude out through Hormuz and boosted shipments through the Red Sea.
Aramco is looking to maximize production through the end of the year, âutilizing all the routes that we have,â and sees buoyant demand lasting for several years, CEO Amin Nasser said on an earnings call. It could take two years to refill depleted global oil storage reserves even if the Iran war was resolved today, Nasser said.

4c84fe5de61d.text:
Mohammedâs view
Abu Dhabiâs annual energy exhibition is buzzing, tangible proof that the UAE has absorbed the blows of the Iran war and has its eye on the future. Most conversations Iâve had at ADIPEC, one of the biggest events on the global calendar, have focused on opportunities: oil above $100 a barrel, a new unconventional oil play being unlocked in the UAE, fusion, AI, and infrastructure upgrades. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke at the opening ceremony, a symbol of the close relationship between energy and technology.
Thereâs plenty to be excited about in the industry that remains the Gulfâs economic lifeblood. But this ADIPEC isnât like its predecessors, and itâs not just because of the war.
The UAEâs decision to leave OPEC has changed the gatheringâs makeup. This event previously brought together the groupâs energy ministers, with major decisions made on the sidelines. This year, Saudi Aramco doesnât even have a booth, a sign of increasingly fractured Gulf business relations.
While the biggest Saudi, Kuwaiti, Omani, and Qatari companies stayed away, the rest of the world is here, with participants from more than 170 countries. Yet the absence of top executives from ExxonMobil and Chevron, as well as US government representation, has been noticed.
Amos Hochstein, a former senior energy and national security adviser to President Joe Biden, was forceful in his critique: âI think they should be here,â he said of US officials. âThe United States and UAE are close allies, you have to be here when it counts.â
The war is transforming everything in the region, from trade flows to alliances, but the conflict itself may, in hindsight, seem temporary. The bigger shift will arguably come from AI, determining the future winners and losers. Hochstein said the UAE is a âcritical partner for the US when it comes to AI buildout,â and Sultan Al Jaber, UAE minister of industry and advanced technology and managing director and group chief executive of ADNOC, stressed the point by having Altman as the guest of honor.
ADNOC agreed to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, part of a partnership with OpenAI and G42 to improve operations, strengthen resilience, and increase productivity. âFrom the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI,â Al Jaber said. âAnd now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.â

Separating signal from noise on whether the US-Iran war will escalate has been difficult for months, and now itâs a cacophony. Oil prices plunged on Monday on hopes of a deal with Tehran before jumping almost 2% Tuesday after the US struck Iranâs Qeshm Island, reportedly in response to Iranian fire at an American plane. Yemenâs Houthis are still attacking Saudi Arabia and have advanced toward Aden, threatening to outflank Yemenâs Saudi-backed government forces and potentially extend Iranâs influence to Bab el-Mandeb, the Gulfâs other maritime chokepoint.
Then thereâs diplomacy. US President Donald Trump told Axios heâs in âno rushâ to resume strikes and repeated that Tehran wants a deal. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks are also returning to Abu Dhabi next week, with Trumpâs envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner expected to attend, making an escalation during their visit seem less likely.
The US midterm elections Tuesday are perhaps the noisiest indicator. Democratic control of either chamber could complicate Trumpâs agenda in his last two years, potentially accelerating military plans before the new Congress takes office in January. But the president will still have considerable foreign policy powers.
The final signal probably matters most: Where are the bombs and planes? Three US aircraft carrier strike groups are expected to arrive near Iran within two weeks, with the USS Theodore Roosevelt the last one to make its way from Japan.

In recent weeks, weâve chronicled a rush of companies staffing up with Democrats in anticipation of a blue wave on Tuesday. But on Monday, OpenAI bucked the trend, hiring former US Army secretary Dan Driscoll for a new national security role just two months after he resigned after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
While tapping a top Republican operative close to the vice president defies conventional wisdom, itâs a good reminder that Trump remains president for another two years â an eternity in AI time â and that OpenAI sees value in advancing its priorities while it still holds executive favor. Regardless of what happens in Tuesdayâs midterm elections, OpenAI knows that Trumpâs national security apparatus remains a powerful force in deciding which new models get approved for use and who can access them.

81cb13115edb.text:
Lizâs view
Todayâs US midterm elections are a race to see who gets blamed for a host of economic problems coming down the pike. Democrats are favored to take the House, with control of the Senate still a toss-up.
Whoever wins Congress inherits a stack of problems due to detonate over the next two years â just in time to crater 2028 ambitions â and few have obvious fixes.
Inflation is running around 3.7%, rising in six of the past eight months, and the Fed has gone back to unpopular tightening. That a Trump-picked Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, is leaning hawkish into a midterm election underlines how stubborn the problem is.
The labor market is no better. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September; July was revised into negative territory. Companies too uncertain about whatâs ahead â and unsure of exactly how AI is muddying the employment picture â are neither hiring nor firing, leaving things in what Jerome Powell earlier this year called âan uncomfortable kind of balance.â
Then there are the outside shocks. Reports that the White House is planning post-midterm strikes on Iran may push political fallout from an unpopular war outside the election window, but the economic weight of high gas and diesel prices lands on whoeverâs nominally in charge come January.
Those are the known unknowns. AI brings another set of unknown unknowns: A financial squeeze waiting to happen, as investment shows no signs of slowing down even as the returns on that investment appear even further out than we thought. A leaking AI bubble is likely to burst on the next Congressâs watch (as always, look to the jittery credit market, not the booming stock market, for signs of whatâs to come).
The second problem is political, and Congress has punted on it. Lawmakers left town in September with no movement on AI guardrails. Dozens of data-center moratoriums and AI referendums appear on the ballot today, with more than 20 in Ohio alone.
Even some of President Donald Trumpâs media allies concede that he owns the narrative on the economy no matter what happens on Capitol Hill. But a Democratic Congress would give the White House a foil it hasnât had since the back half of Trumpâs first term, and every stalled bill, shutdown, and soft jobs report could be pinned on the people holding the legislative pen â and subpoena power (more on that below in todayâs newsletter).
Either way, the winners tomorrow arenât claiming a prize so much as signing for a package.
Notable
- Who controls Congress will make little difference to the economy, analysts argue. âA lot of voters head to the polls Tuesday hoping for a fix for affordability,â The Wall Street Journalâs chief economics commentator wrote. âThey are going to be disappointed.â

The witness-prep business is about to take off for Washington law firms. As Democrats appear poised to take the gavel, at least in the hearing-happy House of Representatives, the task of helping corporate executives prepare for their turn in the chair â a DC practice known as âmurder-boardingâ â will be in high demand. Democrats have been plotting for months about how to go after corporations that have courted Trumpâs approval, Semaforâs Nicholas Wu reported earlier this year, citing missives sent to companies over things like ballroom funds, antitrust suits, and business deals involving the Trump family and one-time âfirst buddyâ Elon Musk.

Peter Donald, a former spokesman for the FBIâs New York field office and assistant NYPD commissioner who now advises companies in tight spots. âEverything will be on the table. CEOs should be ready to explain their decisions under oath.â Itâs a good time for companies to prepay any outstanding law firm bills and book some time on CEOsâ calendars for mock grilling.

5c753a1323f0.text:
Tech companies are turning over the couch cushions in their hunt for money to fund the AI buildout. Meta is prepping a big bond offering that includes its first-ever euro borrowing for up to $15 billion, people familiar with the matter tell Semafor, while Alphabet closed its second euro deal of the year.
The tech giants that have run through US markets are now turning to other pools of capital. Alphabet this year issued its first-ever British sterling bond â a rare âcentury bondâ that comes due in 2126 â along with deals that tapped Swiss and Japanese debt markets. For most companies, broadening lender bases is a test-the-pipes exercise to ensure that diverse funding is available if itâs needed. For hyperscalers today, itâs a globe-trotting bush-beating thatâs crucial to funding the AI buildout thatâs propping up their stock prices.

52482429b6ca.text:
Investors voiced growing worry the AI bubble will burst, as concerns mounted over eye-popping capex plans, debt issuance, and expansion. Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle all either issued new bonds or reportedly planned to do so, with interest rates on the rise. Separately, institutional investors have urged Anthropic â which expects to spend nearly $900 billion on AI infrastructure in the coming years â to lower its IPO valuation target, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Demand has meanwhile surged for options and credit-default swaps that help protect against what is now the biggest market bet in history. âAt some point in time, thereâs going to be a downturn,â the CEO of bond giant PIMCO warned, âand then things are going to break.â
