The News
OpenAIâs attempt to rebrand data centers and set a new tone for AI policy discourse after the midterms is landing with a thud in some circles, including with members of Congress.
The companyâs latest policy push is multi-pronged. It involves calling data centers âcompute campusesâ and seeking community input on their buildouts. It likens AI rules to speeding limits for cars, arguing that AI helps people in their daily lives, and pushing for global AI standards, as Axios first reported.
If initial reactions from AI safety advocates are any indication, AI and tech companies have a long way to go to convince both voters and Democrats, who will likely hold more power in Washington after Tuesday, that their efforts are sincere and not just an attempt at face-saving.
âIf they think they can change the AI debate with Orwellian name changes, they are setting themselves up for failure,â said Brad Carson, former Oklahoma Democratic congressman and co-founder and president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group pushing for AI guardrails.
âAI will be the number one issue in 2028,â Rep. Greg Casar, D-Tex., posted on X. âAnd anyone looking to OpenAIâs lobbyist for advice will lose.â
Still, OpenAIâs top lobbyist, Chris Lehane, is betting the companyâs refreshed positions â on data centers and AI policy that puts people in control of the technology â will be âdurable,â even if itâs in a âlonely position,â he told Semafor in an interview.
âPeople are going to wake up in November and December and January, and thereâs going to be hundreds and hundreds of state bills out there. So does Congress and the White House want to cede control of all of this?â he said, adding that OpenAI plans to push for a mandatory AI testing bill that can get 60 votes by connecting members across the aisle.
OpenAI still supports certain state AI laws as well, recently endorsing two frontier AI safety bills in California, he said.
He also said OpenAI spoke with Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif. on the AI âkill switchâ bill the Democrat proposed in July, and said he would soon have ânext stepsâ on making OpenAIâs products safer for teen users.
Lehane said OpenAIâs views are meant to offer an alternative to extremes around AI. He argued that embracing a middle path would avoid the US ceding ground to China by being outright opposed to data centers, echoing the White Houseâs argument for a light touch on AI regulation.
His argument isnât doing much to win over skeptics.
â[Lehane is] trying to get the best deal out of the Trump administration that he can before Democrats take over,â Alex Bores, the New York State assemblyman who became a top target of the AI industry in his run for Congress, told Semafor. âBut itâs nice to see him say this debate is about control, and that the American people need a stake in whatâs happening.â
Room for Disagreement
If Democrats want to get anything done on AI policy next year, theyâll need to work with Republicans â regardless of control of Congress. And that will inevitably involve moderation and compromise, as well as working with AI firms.
âIâd expect others to follow [OpenAIâs lead],â Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at Monument Advocacy, told Semafor. âThis is where the political calculus is inevitably heading. The industry had a good run making the case for a lighter touch, but the polling shows the limits of that strategy â¦ and a hands-off message gets harder to sustain when voters are asking whoâs in control.â
Hoefer said that for AI companies looking to buoy continued AI sector growth, âthe goal is to give lawmakers a case for AI investment they can defend back home.â

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.
The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican party.
When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.
Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.
The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.
The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.
But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.
“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”
In its Oct. 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.
“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”
Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”
Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.
“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”
Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”
Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”
The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The U.S. livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.
And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.
Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.
Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.
He made his closing pitch on Monday in front of the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".
But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.
His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.
"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.
"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.
At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."
Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?
The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.
Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.
Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."
Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.
There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.
"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.
"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."
"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.
When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.
"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."
"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.
"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."
That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.
But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.
Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.
In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, external, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.
Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.
"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.
"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."
The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
A lower-league player with an eye for goal
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

A spending watchdog has strongly criticised the lack of progress made by public sector organisations in tackling climate change.
Audit Wales says since a Welsh government "climate emergency" was declared, external in 2019, "decarbonisation" has become a lower priority for public bodies.
It says there are many examples of positive changes but the "collective ambition" for a net zero public sector in Wales by 2030 is unlikely to be met.
It has been estimated that it would cost at least Â£2.3bn to decarbonise Welsh council buildings alone.
The Welsh government said its 2030 ambition had "driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do".
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
In its new report, the spending watchdog said public bodies in all sectors recognise decarbonisation is important.
But it said: "Since 2022, financial and political pressures have caused decarbonisation to fall down the priority list.
"Public bodies told us their overall financial pressures mean they are struggling to invest in decarbonisation."
It criticised the Welsh government for not defining the "collective ambition" for net zero by 2030 as a "target".
"There are also no penalties or incentives to drive compliance. Some public bodies told us this had added to uncertainty around the level of priority to attach to carbon reduction."
On spending, it added that public bodies had made "limited progress" overall in understanding how much it will cost to decarbonise in the near or longer term.
"Where public bodies have estimated the longer-term cost, some described it as unaffordable."
Ann-Marie Harkin from Audit Wales said: "We can list positive examples, but not enough progress has been made overall, and we owe it to future generations to do better."
In 2017, the then-Labour Welsh government called for a net zero public sector by 2030, saying that public bodies were "uniquely placed" to influence emissions in areas such as buildings and transport.
The thinking was that if government-backed bodies made the switch and invested in infrastructure like electric vehicles and charge points, renewable power and heating systems, it would make it easier and cheaper for the public to follow suit.
The "collective ambition" does not require every public body to reach net zero individually by 2030 but it is meant to provide a shared direction of travel and an expectation that all public bodies contribute towards reducing emissions.
Responding to the report, a spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "A net zero public sector is a priority for Welsh government.
"We want to continue to support the decarbonisation of the public sector to lower emissions, energy bills and strengthen energy security.
"The 2030 ambition has driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do on decarbonisation across and beyond the public sector in Wales."
The current Plaid Cymru government's ambition is for Wales, as a whole, to reach net zero by 2040 - which is ten years sooner than the current legally binding target for Wales and UK.

Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured.
He announced his decision in Congress, where he had appeared to give the circumstances of last Wednesday's crash near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said, also referring to a deadly crash in January in Andalusia, southern Spain
The latest tragedy in Urda happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
Puente announced his decision at the end of a congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and been grilled by the opposition.
He said he had taken the decision immediately after the 28 October disaster.
Puente had been under mounting pressure as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.
Three tapes between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".

1201cf121c45.text: By — Josh Kelety, Associated Press Josh Kelety, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/escaped-tennessee-inmate-convicted-of-co-workers-murder-is-recaptured-in-missouri-officials-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of co-worker's murder is recaptured in Missouri, officials say Nation Nov 3, 2026 3:54 PM EST A man convicted of murder who escaped from a Tennessee prison was recaptured on Tuesday in Missouri after troopers used roadside cameras and a helicopter to track him down after more than a week on the run, authorities said. READ MORE: Florida executed a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence. It's the state's 17th execution of the year Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was apprehended at around noon near Kansas City, Missouri, officials said. The Missouri State Highway Patrol says it learned Tuesday morning that Morley was possibly traveling west on Interstate 70. The vehicle was located using automated license plate readers and undercover officers traveling on a state highway in western Missouri. A Kansas City police helicopter also followed the vehicle, which made it into Carroll County, a small county in northwest Missouri, before it traveled off the road, getting stuck. Troopers took Morley into custody without incident ending a weeklong hunt. Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee's far northwestern corner on Oct. 25, after he slipped through a fence in his prison clothes. Surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned last week in Marion, Illinois. That is about 120 miles (193 kilometers) north of the prison. Morley was serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee. When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. After his escape, law enforcement agencies searched buildings and other structures near the prison, which is in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in flat farmland near a bend in the Mississippi River. Prison officials offered a reward of up to $17,500 for information leading to Morley's arrest. Morley's escape is the latest blemish for Tennessee's prison system. Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate killings and other violent acts. Following the failed execution of Christa Pike in September, Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada resigned after less than three years on the job. Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".
In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".
"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".
A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.
Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.
Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
In a separate development, a bomb alert triggered the evacuation of 1,537 passengers and crew from an Israel-bound cruise ship in Greece, media reports from both countries say.
Initial checks of the Panama-flagged Crown Iris vessel currently docked at a port on the Aegean island of Syros found no explosives, they said citing the Greek Coast Guard. A second inspection is expected shortly.
Tuesday's aircraft incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.
Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".
Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".
Additional reporting by Thomas Copeland, BBC Verify

77457cd9bde5.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press By — Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/man-charged-with-mailing-hundreds-of-letters-containing-powder-to-officials-ahead-of-the-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man charged with mailing hundreds of letters containing powder to officials ahead of the election Politics Nov 3, 2026 3:37 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check Federal authorities charged an Oklahoma City man with sending hundreds of letters containing white powder and ominous warnings about treason to public officials ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections. The powders turned out to be nonhazardous — yeast or flour — though not all letters have been fully tested, the FBI said in a court filing made public Tuesday. READ MORE: Election Day underway after a surge in early voting, as Trump sows doubt on results Robin Martin is charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications. He was arrested Monday and was expected to make an appearance Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Online records do not list an attorney who could comment on his behalf, and several relatives didn't immediately respond to social media messages seeking comment. The investigation stretched back to 2024 when election officials in multiple states reported mail with a white substance and a three-page letter declaring war, the FBI said. Some bore warnings that could only be read under ultraviolet light, such as, "Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it!!" READ MORE: Midterm elections come to a close in referendum on Trump's presidency The sender wrote a return address as "U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD." Investigators believe more than 700 mailings this fall appeared to be associated with the same sender but with a different return address. They were addressed to election officials, members of Congress, pollsters, news media and federal law enforcement, FBI agent David Cole said in an affidavit. A common message in the 2024 and 2026 mailings was a warning to recipients about upcoming arrests for treason "or worse!!" "The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election," Cole said. READ MORE: Trump faces prospect of impeachment if Democrats gain control Federal authorities announced last month that they were investigating letters with "suspicious substances" that had been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and urged recipients to treat the mailings as potentially hazardous. The packages led to the evacuation of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Numerous states, from Idaho to Florida, said they either received letters or had them intercepted by the Postal Service. The FBI said it has video evidence of Martin's car stopping in October at mailboxes at Postal Service sites in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio. Investigators also gleaned his fingerprints from a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel, whose first name was written as "Kashyap." Walmart records show Martin purchased common household goods, such as turmeric and vinegar, to create invisible ink that could be read with ultraviolet light, the FBI said. The Democratic Socialists of America apparently assisted the investigation. The FBI said it believes Martin, posing as someone using the name George Livingston, posted a message to a DSA email list in October, warning that members were traitors and eligible for arrest for treason if they vote in the Nov. 3 election. bdf10d5d2510.text: Voting is underway across the country Tuesday in a midterm election that could decide whether President Trump gets two more years of unified Republican rule — or faces a potential Democratic check on his power. Why it matters: The results will be the clearest national test of Trump's second presidency , following war abroad, economic anxiety at home and sweeping changes in Washington. Trump, facing all these challenges, has made himself the face of the Republican campaign for control. State of play: As voters head to the polls, the Trump administration is zeroing-in on the Alaska Senate race. The Department of Justice has sent more than a dozen target letters as part of its investigation into the Dan J. Sullivan campaign, which has been the subject of Trump's ire for several days. It's an escalation into the Trump administration's push for answers in the race where Democrats reportedly conducted an organized effort to recruit another "Dan Sullivan" to join Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) on the ballot. The Justice Department's move comes as the White House is circulating Election Day talking points across the administration, touting Trump's accomplishments as the GOP braces for a tough evening that could see them lose both the House and the Senate, according to some forecasters. Trump has been a massive force on the campaign trail, rallying in several states for his Republican picks. The president has claimed to voters that he is on the ballot this year, making the election about his policies and actions — despite his dismal polling ratings, plagued by the Iran war and economic anxiety. Trump spent the morning of Election Day criticizing Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and the Daily Mail in various social media posts. Zoom in: Voting machine glitches and hiccups popped up in various spots of the country Tuesday, including in the high-profile New York House race between Rep. Mike Lawler (R) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley. Otherwise the temperature was rather low despite the power of Washington hanging in the balance. The big picture: Republicans have largely given Trump a free hand in Washington since his return to the White House. Democratic control of even one chamber of Congress would open the door to investigations, subpoenas and even more legislative gridlock. Voters are weighing the Iran war and rising energy costs , broader affordability concerns, and intensifying debate over AI's economic impact, among other issues. An unprecedented mobilization of election monitors and legal battles involving the Trump administration have raised concerns about potential disruptions and challenges to the results. Trump has said he'll respect the election results if "they're honest elections." What's at stake: Republicans enter Election Day defending narrow congressional majorities, with a number of battlegrounds and traditionally GOP districts and states shifting into toss-up territory during the campaigns' final weeks. The House: All 435 seats are on the ballot. Democrats need a net gain of three seats to reclaim the majority. Redistricting has reshaped the battlefield. The Senate: 35 seats are on the ballot. Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats. Some scenarios: Democrats flip the House: They gain greater investigative power, control of committees and leverage over spending — but Trump retains his veto and executive authority. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) could become the first Black speaker of the House, or face an opponent from his left. Democrats take Congress: Democrats' oversight power expands, while Trump's agenda faces major obstacles. A third Trump impeachment could be on the table, although being convicted in a Senate trial would require a two-thirds vote. Republicans retain Congress: Trump and GOP leaders get another two years to advance his agenda, though narrow margins could complicate plans. Between the lines: Beyond control of Congress, the results will test whether Trump's gains among young, Black and Latino voters in 2024 have endured — or if those voters are moving back toward Democrats who are trying to rebuild a winning coalition for 2028. What we're watching: Whether close races, outstanding ballots and legal challenges delay a clear verdict.

Tenerife's largest shareholder Rayco García told reporters that De Miguel's body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel's teammates and club officials would be present for a "final farewell." On Saturday, fans will gather at the team's stadium to honor the player, García said. "We will all join forces and get through this together," García said. Club president Felipe Miñambres said players and their families would likely need help to cope with De Miguel's death. "We will need professional help and the help of all of our fans," he said. "They will be feeling the same way that we are feeling today." The club asked for its league game at Granada on Saturday to be postponed. The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach. De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides. Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel. The goalkeeper's Instagram account, which had nearly 30,000 followers, had been deactivated on Tuesday. Another player with the same last name of Owono, Michel Owono, who plays for sixth-division Spanish club Can Vidalet, denounced a wave of racist insults against him by people thinking he was the Andorra goalkeeper. Fans pays tribute to CD Tenerife's Jesus de Miguel on Nov. 3, 2026, who died after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match. He joined Tenerife last year. There were no local media reports about De Miguel having a pre-existing health condition. The precise medical cause of death was not immediately disclosed. Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter. "There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community." Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Piqué, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga. "We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement. Piqué said on X: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús." The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach. Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: "So much sadness. There are no words." Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends." English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media. The Spanish soccer federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches scheduled on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. 133cbb4ca5c8.text: North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations to steal $6.3 billion from Binance, the crypto exchange said Tuesday. Why it matters : The country's hackers are weaponizing both sides of the job market , posing as recruiters and job applicants to infiltrate companies and steal billions. Driving the news : Binance said one of its software engineers was contacted in September through a "legitimate job-hunting platform" by someone posing as a project director at a fictitious company. During the first-round interview, a fake HR representative conducted a live video call with the engineer and showed off a seemingly legitimate social media profile featuring personal photos and videos. The hackers waited until the second round — after building trust with the employee — to ask them to download an infected code repository as part of an interview assignment. Separately, another software engineer also downloaded a "tampered Homebrew installation" in June to install a popular AI coding tool onto their device. Binance's security team detected the installation and replaced the device, as well as rotated all credentials, but the engineer and colleagues were all exposed to the hacker. The intrigue: The fake interview was just one of several suspected North Korean attempts to compromise Binance employees. So far in 2026, Binance said it has detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber incidents, including attempts involving fake job interviews and compromised software packages. Between the lines: North Korean hackers have spent years exploiting both sides of the hiring process. As job applicants, North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT workers to land high-paying jobs at American companies. Those salaries are then funneled back to Pyongyang. Operatives are also increasingly posing as recruiters and prospective employees to lure in people who work at cryptocurrency firms in the hopes of tricking them into downloading malware. Data from Pindrop Security shows that IT worker fraud has been rampant in 2026: Last year, North Korean job applicants made up 1 in every 343 applications. This year, across Pindrop's customer base, those applicants now make up 1 in 47. The big picture: North Korea has found an opening in a difficult job market, where companies are eager to find qualified workers and job seekers are anxious for their next opportunity. Hiring managers have struggled to find qualified candidates , while job applicants have been anxious for years about their ability to find new roles in a tough market. Go deeper : How North Korea perfected the crypto heist

9680058e2c7f.text: Voting machines across New York's Westchester County are rejecting paper ballots on Election Day , raising concerns about potential delays in one of the nation's most competitive House races. Why it matters: Results could be delayed for one of the country's most prominent House races, between Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Democratic nominee Cait Conley, as officials address a problem with paper ballots. Catch up quick: The Westchester County Board of Elections said Tuesday it was aware of a problem preventing voting machines from accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county. The Board of Elections said it is speaking with New York State officials and the Westchester County government "to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible." New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. The intrigue: Election officials initially blamed the thickness of paper ballots but later removed that explanation from their statement, per reports. The latest: On Tuesday afternoon, the New York State Board of Elections said the malfunction was linked to "an update to the county's election programming" released after initially testing Election Day equipment. Officials said the software update wasn't installed on all machines, leaving them unable to recognize and accept ballots. Officials are still working to restore the machines while voters continue casting emergency paper ballots, which will be counted once scanning resumes. What they're saying: Lawler said officials were working with vendors to resolve the problem, while Conley reassured voters that their ballots would count. Westchester County government wrote on its website: "Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted." What we're hearing: Voters in the county told Fox 5 NY that they had to fill out paper ballots instead of using the machines. Voters said their ballots were placed in a security box. Other voters shared discontent with the ballots issue on social media . Katie Miller , wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller, claimed on X: "This is how the Left steals elections. Mike Lawler's competitive district and they are turning away voters." Context: The county covers roughly 30% of New York's 17th District, which Lawler represents. The contest has emerged as a key battleground race in Democrats' push to gain control of the House. Zoom out: The ballot-scanning problems come as technology vulnerabilities have been a key issue heading into the midterms, with researchers saying some vulnerabilities remain in plain sight. Officials in Broward County, Florida, reported a computer glitch that disrupted voting at polling locations early Tuesday, CNN reports. The malfunction reportedly caused systems designed to stop voters from receiving the wrong ballots to reject all ballots. Officials said the issue was resolved. What's next: Voters at affected polling locations were urged to remain in line and cast their ballots. Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about polling glitches in Broward County, Florida.

5ff060bf9bd6.text:
This article was first reported by The Examination, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates global health threats.
When Rachel Curtis visited her 86-year-old grandmother in Odessa, Texas, last summer, the putrid odor of hydrogen sulfide hit her as soon as she got out of the car.
She could smell the toxic gas, which is often compared to rotten eggs and is fatal in high concentrations, inside her grandmother’s house. Her grandmother has lived about 50 yards from an oil pumpjack for decades and was used to the smell, but she was suffering from frequent headaches—a common effect of exposure to hydrogen sulfide, or H2S.
Worried about her grandmother’s health, Curtis grew even more upset when she found out who operates the pumpjack and other oil equipment nearby: Aghorn Operating. The company had recently pleaded guilty to criminal health and safety violations related to the 2019 deaths of an employee, Jacob Dean, and his wife, Natalee—who were killed by a cloud of hydrogen sulfide inside a nearby Aghorn pumphouse.
After the deaths, Curtis felt both Aghorn and authorities should be keeping better tabs on all of its facilities.
“It just really ticks me off because, I mean, she’s an 86-year-old woman who’s lived across the street from this for how many years,” said Curtis, a high school teacher who had been friendly with the Deans before she moved across the state. “I feel like something should have been done.”
Aghorn and its president, Frosty Gilliam, didn’t respond to calls, emails and detailed questions.
In a court filing last year, Aghorn stated that since the 2019 deaths, the company had hired a full-time safety manager, established written safety policies, conducted hydrogen sulfide safety training and upgraded monitors and alarms for the gas in various facilities. “Aghorn has substantially improved the safety of its facilities and instituted measures to ensure the safety of its employees and the general public,” it said.
Often called “sour gas,” hydrogen sulfide forms naturally underground in some oil-rich regions of the world and can get released into the air during oil production. It can also escape from badly sealed equipment. Low levels of the gas can irritate the eyes and respiratory system and chronic exposure has been associated with neurological problems like fatigue, impaired memory, headaches and dizziness.
As The Examination and the Houston Chronicle detailed in a 2024 investigation, tens of thousands of Texans live near hydrogen sulfide hotspots, but despite community complaints of exposure, state regulators have largely failed to hold companies accountable. When investigators find the gas seeping into the air, companies usually get what amounts to a fix-it ticket, often without any penalty. Problems can persist for years.
That pattern has continued with Aghorn, despite the deaths in the heart of the Permian Basin.
In 2019, Dean was checking on some malfunctioning equipment inside an Aghorn facility when he collapsed in a cloud of hydrogen sulfide. Natalee went looking for him and died next to him. Their kids, then 6 and 9, were sitting in the car outside.
Federal prosecutors charged Aghorn with willfully violating worker safety laws, causing the death of an employee, as well as obstruction and false statements. They added a conspiracy charge, alleging a widespread practice, continuing to 2024, of putting profits and convenience above human health and safety.
Prosecutors documented a pattern of chronic leaks and unsafe practices that continued years after the Deans’ deaths. “At Aghorn,” they wrote in a 2024 filing, “placing workers, contractors, and the public at risk was a way of doing business that was deeply ingrained in the corporate culture.”
The company pleaded guilty last year to the more limited charges of negligent endangerment and willful violation of safety laws, paying a $1 million fine. As part of the plea deal, Aghorn admitted its failure to implement workplace protections was a cause of Jacob Dean’s death and that its representatives “had neglected to control H2S emissions and provide adequate safety systems, which negligence placed Natalee Dean in imminent danger of death.” The company’s vice president, Trent Day, was sentenced to five months in prison.
Industry consultant Jim Kirksey, who reviewed the evidence for prosecutors, wrote in a report filed in the case that Aghorn mostly ignored health and safety complaints, and that the state’s oil regulator, the Texas Railroad Commission, was slow to act.
“The residents who live or work near Aghorn Operating facilities are the innocent victims of Aghorn Operating non-compliance with H2S safety regulations,” Kirksey wrote in his 2024 report, noting that complaints of headaches and nausea were commonplace. Aghorn objected to Kirksey’s qualifications in court filings.
Shortly after that report was written, Adrianna Yanez, a mother of four who lives about 11 miles west of Curtis on the outskirts of Odessa, complained to regulators about hydrogen sulfide leaks wafting toward her home that she said caused bad headaches and bouts of vomiting.
Inspectors from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality found gas leaking from an Aghorn pumpjack just over 100 meters from her house. The company patched it, and TCEQ resolved the complaint with no penalty, records show.
The Railroad Commission then found gas leaking from storage tanks and an unlit flare about a third of a mile away and told Aghorn to fix it. Investigators came back twice and found gas still leaking. On the fourth visit, in early 2025, they didn’t see any leaks and closed the investigation.
The smell went away for a few months, Yanez said, and then it came back.
“It’s really sad because I guess they see us as the poor people who live out here on the west side of Odessa and they could care less about our health or our children,” Yanez told The Examination recently.
The Railroad Commission didn’t respond to questions about its oversight of Aghorn. Commission spok

1ac9c9efb113.text: State officials have largely taken securing the 2026 midterm elections into their own hands after nearly two years of federal program and funding cuts during the second Trump administration. Why it matters: The reduction in federal support has come as AI tools threaten to make it easier for hackers to uncover software vulnerabilities, launch cyberattacks, and spread disinformation that undermines trust in election results. Reality check: Just because a security flaw exists doesn't mean hackers can exploit it to manipulate election results. Nearly all U.S. elections maintain paper records that can be used to verify electronic tallies. Threat level: Election officials are preparing for everything from cyberattacks and AI-generated disinformation to physical threats, logistical disruptions and legal challenges. The big picture: State election officials relied on homeland security agencies, fusion centers, police, National Guard units and private cybersecurity firms to prepare for the midterms, John Milhofer, a spokesperson for the National Association of Secretaries of State, told Axios. That group and the National Association of State Election Directors are helping states exchange threat intelligence and connect with federal agencies and private sector experts. Catch up quick: State resources have become more important after the Trump administration scaled back federal election security assistance. CISA cut election security personnel and services in 2025, while federal funding for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a key information-sharing network for election officials, ended that year. Election officials are receiving fewer election-specific threat briefings and less direct technical assistance, even after CISA outlined plans to restore some services in September. Zoom in: Michael Moore, chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office, told Axios that the state has been without a dedicated CISA cybersecurity adviser since March 2025. The Arizona Department of Homeland Security has helped fill the gap, providing security tools and monitoring services to smaller counties. On Election Day, Arizona is bringing together its state cybersecurity team, National Guard, the FBI and a representative from CISA's Region 9 office to coordinate responses to potential threats, Moore said. Moore's team has spent years conducting tabletop exercises covering cyberattacks, AI-generated impersonations of election officials, suspicious packages and other disruptions. Between the lines: Arizona is also getting threat intelligence from former CISA personnel who work in the space, election security nonprofits and officials in other states. Moore said his relationship with New Jersey's election security officials is particularly useful because his East Coast counterparts can warn him about threats hours before they might emerge in Arizona. What they're saying: A CISA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency will provide state and local government officials, including election officials and election vendors, "no-cost voluntary services" like vulnerability scanning and technical expertise, when they request it. "We are committed to supporting state and local elections officials to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy," the spokesperson added. Yes, but: Moore said he still wants CISA to return to its 2024 staffing levels — and then double them. "If we are literally experiencing a cyberattack from a nation-state, it shouldn't be Arizona versus that nation-state," Moore said. "We're the United States of America. It should be a unified response." David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, told reporters during a briefing Thursday that states have hired vendors and built their own networks to compensate for the federal retreat. "They might not be able to replace everything," Becker said. "They're not going to get the same bird's-eye national-level view of potential disinformation or potential cyber events." The bottom line: Election officials said they're prepared for disruptions, even if they can't prevent every attack. "The goal is prevent as much as we can, detect and recover," Moore said. "We're going to have some amount of disruption.... We're going to recover."

Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-decide-key-ballot-measures-on-abortion-rights-congressional-redistricting-and-voter-id-laws Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters decide key ballot measures on abortion rights, congressional redistricting and voter ID laws Politics Nov 3, 2026 12:30 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check WASHINGTON (AP) — A battle over abortion rights is playing out in several states Tuesday as voters decide 145 proposed laws and constitutional amendments, including some that could affect voting for future elections. The ballot measures provide a political undercard for a high-profile midterm election that will determine which party controls Congress, state legislatures and gubernatorial offices in many states. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Some measures put President Donald Trump's priorities to a public test by gauging support for his attempts to reshape congressional districts, limit transgender athletes in sports and strengthen voter identification requirements. Abortion ban faces an unusual redo in Missouri Two years ago, Missouri voters became the first in the nation to pass a ballot measure undoing an existing ban on most abortions. Now voters are deciding whether to repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment and replace it with a new prohibition — this time allowing exceptions for medical emergencies and fetal anomalies, and in cases of rape or incest up to 12 weeks of pregnancy. The proposed ban was placed on the ballot by the Republican-led Legislature. Abortion rights advocates, led by national progressive groups, have greatly outspent abortion foes in a bid to defeat the measure. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump In three other states, ballot measures would create a right to abortion using standards similar to what was in place nationally before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and opened the door to state bans. Ballot measures in Idaho and Nevada would block bans on abortion before fetal viability, usually considered after 21 weeks. Nevada voters already approved the measure once but have to do so a second time for it to become official. In Virginia, an amendment would ensure abortion is allowed for the first two trimesters. Redistricting measures could affect 2028 elections Nine states are using new congressional districts in the midterm elections after a rare spate of mid-decade redistricting encouraged by Trump. Missouri's Republican lawmakers also had adopted new House districts designed to help the GOP win an additional seat. But courts ruled they cannot be used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. If passed, the districts would take effect for the 2028 election. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate Voters in Democratic-led Maryland are deciding on a constitutional amendment that also could pave the way for new congressional districts in the 2028 election. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have urged a "yes" vote as way to "stop Trump." Some Democrats also want to redistrict in Colorado. But a citizen initiative on the ballot would prohibit any potential 2028 redistricting from favoring one political party and require approval from both an independent commission and the state Supreme Court. Transgender restrictions are proposed in several states Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington are considering measures restricting transgender athletes or medical procedures. That comes as Trump's administration has been pushing for restrictions impacting transgender people, especially youth. Most Republican-led states already bar transgender women and girls from female school sports teams. Citizen-led ballot initiatives propose similar restrictions in the Democratic-led states of Colorado and Washington. The Arizona measure would extend public school sports restrictions to private schools. And Nebraska's measure would add existing restrictions to the state constitution. A second ballot question in Colorado would ban some transgender medical treatments for minors. The Missouri abortion amendment also would add existing transgender medical restrictions to the state constitution. A scrutiny panel has heard Jersey is in a "biodiversity crisis", amid concerns the government is not focusing on the environment enough.
Willie Peggie, government Director of Natural Environment, said the Environment Department needed time and resources for a state of nature report.
Piers Sangan, who runs Sangan Island Conversation, said a biodiversity crisis included more invasive species, fewer native species, and a decline in the ecosystem. He said the government had responsibility to ensure the environment did not "fall by the wayside" because it was a "fundamental part of our island".
The environment minister said policies were being worked on to further protect the environment.
Peggie said any state of nature report should be similar to those in the UK, external, Guernsey, external and Alderney, external.
Sangan said Jersey's biodiversity strategy had been "put on the shelf" since the early 2000s, and the island had lost animals including stoats.
He said there had been a "woeful lack of investment" in ecology.
"The environment is becoming quieter and, as someone who's been looking at this day in, day out for the last 15 years, it's becoming horribly noticeable."
He said several bird species were struggling to increase numbers.
"Even though they're still here, they're still breeding, they're not increasing in number... They are more or less extinct already and are likely to go extinct in the next few years," he said.
Environment Minister Senator Mary Le Hegarat said the countryside needed to be managed properly with a rise in invasive species.
She said: "Everybody needs to manage the countryside together, and we'll do the work and set out the policies and strategies in order to do so."
Government officials are expected to release a state of nature report in 2027, which would inform a new biodiversity strategy.
Joshua and Benjamin Voak work for the Jersey Grazing Project, which uses cows and sheep to improve and restore habitats.
Joshua Voak said it was concerning the environment had not been discussed much in the summer's election as "there are so many economic advantages to having a healthy environment".
Benjamin said biodiversity was "super important" for the island's air and water quality and the retention of habitats.
'Caution' needed over spending
Concerns around biodiversity come as questions have been raised about the government's commitment to the environment.
Deputy Hilary Jeune, who chairs the environment scrutiny panel, said ministers' draft Common Strategic Policy, external did not take the natural environment into account.
The panel worked with Le Hegarat on an amendment to address that, external.
Jeune said biodiversity needed to be "front and centre".
Professor Liz Bentley was part of the Jersey Climate Council, which suggested Jersey need to spend Â£10m per year to reach net zero by 2050, rather than the Â£4m in the Climate Emergency Fund.
She said the council recognised the financial pressure on the government, but delayed action to tackle climate change would cost more in the long-term.
"We need to consider it over decades, not over a four year budget... It's about that long-term investment."
Le Hegarat said ministers needed to be "very cautious" about spending.
She could not say how much it would cost to reach net zero by 2050, but thought investing the money in the fund was a good way forward.

Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as a "truly remarkable, immensely talented and inspirational human being" in a tribute read out at her funeral.
Hundreds of people have paid their respects to the runner at her funeral on Tuesday.
The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner died on Sunday after she was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.
Among those in attendance at the funeral in Portaferry, County Down, were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, as well as fellow Olympian Rhys McClenaghan and 1972 gold medallist Lady Mary Peters.
Mageean's funeral cortege was given a guard of honour by Portaferry GAC and her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch.
Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
Mourners began arriving at around midday for the 2:00 GMT requiem Mass at St Patrick's Church.
Family, friends and those wishing to pay their respects followed the funeral cortege the short distance along the Ballyphilip Road from Mageean's family home to the church.
Others in attendance included representatives for Irish President Catherine Connolly and the Irish Government, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna, GAA President Jarlath Burns and former boxer Paddy Barnes.
The Mass booklet included an image of Mageean's greatest achievement on the track, the moment she crossed the line at the 2024 European Championships.
In his homily, Father Martin Kelly, who knew Mageean from her childhood, spoke of her accomplishments, her love for her husband and the joy and pride she had brought to her hometown.
Kelly recalled visiting her in hospice shortly before her death, when she suggested they go for a walk.
Despite her illness, Mageean noticed he was struggling and offered to link arms with him.
"On the way down, she knew I was struggling and she said, 'Let me link you'," he told mourners.
"One of my happiest moments and memories is that of Ciara Mageean linking my arm as we walked back to her room."
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
What are bowel cancer symptoms?
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP, external.
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

67cb3704ebeb.text: By — Sophie Austin, Associated Press Sophie Austin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/california-voters-consider-proposition-to-tax-billionaires-wealth Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter California voters consider proposition to tax billionaires' wealth Politics Nov 3, 2026 12:04 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California could become the first state in the nation to tax the net worth of billionaires Tuesday under a ballot measure that has divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history as the ultra-rich scramble to figure out whether they would pay the tax or flee. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders has framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warns it would prompt the state's wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The "no" side has raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who have poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Billionaires are already bracing for its approval. Some of them, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state after the measure was unveiled. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, say it's needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years. "It's time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe," said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition opposing it. They're concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state's budget if there's a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California's budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state's richest residents. Californians are divided on the measure. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump Likely voters were slightly more likely to oppose the measure than support it in a poll conducted in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California, with 52% saying they would vote "no" and 46% saying they would vote "yes." That's an apparent shift from a PPIC survey conducted in early September, when 52% of likely voters said they'd vote for the tax and 46% said they'd vote against it. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who's politically independent, said he planned to vote against it. "Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don't believe taxing them out of existence is going to work." Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation's largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support "anything that is a positive for healthcare." Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it, which are also on this year's ballot, passes and receives more "yes" votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee has raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin. Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator's focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree." Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said. "We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on," she said.
