Hi, I’m Kate Waxman, and this is my first edition of Today’s Climate. I’m taking this newsletter over from my colleague Kiley Price, whom I admire for her sharp coverage. I’m a Florida native and was a fellow at Inside Climate News this summer, where I covered climate and environmental justice in my home state. That meant following fights over AI data centers, the homes least prepared for the super El Niño and water quality aid. Across all of that reporting, climate change kept showing up in power bills, insurance premiums and hurricane recovery, but rarely by name. That gap is what this week’s edition is about.
Many candidates in this year’s midterm elections have faced a dilemma heavily romanticized in literature and cinema: “Is it better to speak, or to die?” The choice between speaking up or letting silence take over has a literal, existential meaning when applied to “climate hushing.” Candidates have opted not to discuss climate change in order to protect themselves from political backlash or polarization.
The case for hushing: The logic for this is simple—talk about what voters say they care about the most. In the Environmental Voter Project’s survey of battleground voters, 66 percent ranked cost of living among their top issues, while 16 percent said the same of climate change and pollution. (You can hear more on this survey and climate hushing in the latest episode of our Inside Climate podcast.) Even a University of California, Santa Barbara, team that set out to test the hushers’ claims conceded the point on priorities: Climate ranked 12th of 15 issues. Strategists also argue the word “climate” itself is a liability. Democratic pollster Jonathan Voss told E&E News that “many Republican voters have been conditioned to feel a certain way” when they hear the word.
At a rally against a data center this summer in my home state of Florida, nobody I spoke with used the word “climate.” They talked about water, noise and their power bills. And continuing with the theme, my colleagues Claire Barber and Marianne Lavelle reported on a paper from the Searchlight Institute with a perplexing title: “The First Rule About Solving Climate Change: Don’t Say Climate Change.”
Candidates have listened. My colleague Peter Aldhous found that mentions of climate change in Democrats’ congressional press releases plummeted after 2025, giving way to energy affordability once the Iran war sent oil prices soaring. Faced with the choice to speak or hush, Syracuse University geographer Matthew Huber chose hush. For now, he wrote in The New York Times this spring, “it might be better to say nothing at all.”
The case for speaking: Despite these claims, many voters have said they want to hear more. Likely voters in eight Senate battleground states want politicians to talk more about climate and pollution, not less, by 59 percent to 17 percent, according to the Environmental Voter Project. Last week, I reported on a poll that showed that Florida likely voters chose protecting the environment over economic growth 61 percent to 26 percent. Registered Republicans agreed, 48 percent to 35 percent, and the pollster, Sean Freeder, called it “a blowout.”
Yet in the state’s Senate race, that sentiment isn’t coming through as directly as you might imagine. Rather, it’s showing up in fights over data centers, power bills and hurricane recovery. These all connect back to climate change, but people aren’t talking about that. As Sara Peach writes at Yale Climate Connections, voters take their cues from leaders. When candidates mirror the polls and stay quiet, it can create “a vicious cycle,” teaching the public the issue matters less than it does.
On one hand, it’s hard to blame the candidates for wanting to protect their political image. On the other hand, choosing silence structurally ensures the very outcome we are trying to avoid. Did candidates in your area mention climate change by name? Email me to share your observations.
The Latest on Earth
- Yerevan: The United Nations biodiversity summit, COP17, closed Saturday with the “Yerevan Pathway,” a pledge to speed up cuts to nature-harming subsidies and strengthen national plans for oceans and freshwater, but its fund for paying Indigenous and local communities left nearly empty. The Guardian’s verdict: The agreements need to be fast-tracked to make a real difference.
- Atmosphere: A new report shows that the Trump administration’s cuts to satellite weather forecasting will set the country back by a decade, according to CNN. The cuts began in spring 2025, when the administration directed NOAA to scale back its next generation of weather satellites, dropping planned instruments that would have tracked air quality, wildfire smoke and monitored water quality.
- Mediterranean: The European Union has blocked an extension of the Mediterranean deep-sea trawling ban. According to Oceanographic Magazine, this decision leaves deep-sea habitats vulnerable to the impacts of fishing.

If you want to know where climate went this election season, ask Marianne Lavelle. ICN’s Washington bureau chief has been covering national elections for over 30 years, and she reported last week that candidates and climate advocates alike have traded talk of climate risk for issues that are closer to home, like data centers and sky-high energy bills. I asked her whether climate has really gone quiet, or just changed its name.

bc2789664f14.text: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former GOP Sen. John Sununu in the New Hampshire Senate race, AP projects. Why it matters: Pappas' victory keeps the seat in Democratic hands and could boost the party's chances of taking control of the Senate. Driving the news: Pappas led Sununu 61% to 38% with 20% of the votes counted. He'll replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in January. Catch up quick: Republicans saw New Hampshire as a top pickup opportunity, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune campaigning for Sununu in the competitive race, despite polls showing Pappas ahead. Most polls compiled by the New York Times in the weeks before Election Day showed the Democratic Pappas leading Sununu by 5 to 8 percentage points. Zoom in: Although President Trump endorsed him, Sununu has shown daylight with the president, criticizing his trade war with Canada and his so-called anti-weaponization fund — and he backed Trump's primary opponents in 2016 and 2024. Still, prominent New Hampshire Republicans — including Don Bolduc , the Trump -endorsed 2022 Senate nominee — endorsed Pappas in mid-October, accusing Sununu of being too beholden to the president. Between the lines: Republicans welcomed Sununu's entry into the race because of his family's long ties to New Hampshire politics. Sununu served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 before losing to Shaheen in 2008. His brother Chris served as governor for eight years. Senate GOP Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) posted on X in October 2025 that Sununu's decision to run catapulted New Hampshire to "a top-tier U.S. Senate race." The bottom line: Pappas' win reflects a preference New Hampshire voters expressed in pre-election polling : They wanted a check on Trump's power. Price, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Elena Becatoros, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-strikes-strait-of-hormuz-hours-before-tuesday-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. strikes Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday midterms World Nov 3, 2026 8:15 PM EST What appeared to be a limited strike by the United States on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz hours before Tuesday's midterm U.S. elections is raising questions about what's coming next. For weeks now, U.S. President Donald Trump has said he was considering launching a new wave of strikes on Iran after the elections. Just days ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump for renewed military action, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The Middle East and beyond have been on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months. READ MORE: Iran says 7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, and other Middle East news Talks aimed at avoiding that are ongoing, and other American allies in the region are pressuring the U.S. not to resume the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled the global economy and wreaked havoc on Iran. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for his Republican Party as it tries to keep control of Congress. Strikes were targeted in Strait of Hormuz Iranian state media reported explosions being heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. A U.S. official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Monday that the strikes targeted Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against the U.S. in the strait. Iran official says US must resolve its conditions The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said Tuesday that the U.S. response to Tehran's demands to end the war was not convincing. Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei wrote on social media that the strait won't reopen until the U.S. addresses Iran's conditions. Iran has offered to reopen the strait, and resume talks on its nuclear program if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, and observes a ceasefire including in Lebanon. Vice President Vance buoyed hopes for a negotiated settlement Back-channel negotiations have been playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump. Speaking before the U.S. official confirmed strikes, U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump "both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September. But thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East. READ MORE: Iran war renews concerns about lasting toll of traumatic brain injuries to American troops Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a call with Trump over the weekend, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress and that mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the strait in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, was not authorized to comment publicly and also spoke on the condition of anonymity. Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi has called on Iran and the U.S. to engage in dialogue and reach an agreement to resolve their ongoing conflict, warning against further military escalation in the region. Iranians keeping watch on U.S. elections Some people in Tehran were hopeful that the midterm elections would bring a shift in U.S. policies. "The American people need to make a fundamental decision and bring about real change. They need to put an end to the leadership of someone who is so extreme and who runs things through lies, someone who supports Israel, a country that is literally killing children," said 69-year-old Reza Rezaei. READ MORE: How Iran war votes in Congress became a focal point for campaign ad attacks One woman was less optimistic. "It doesn't really make much difference who comes into power," said Raheleh Movahhed, also of Tehran. "The American government and its policies have always had a problem with us. I'm not talking about the American people, mind you. I'm talking about their policies." Iran's chief negotiator says it's up to the US to prevent renewed war Iranian state television quoted the country's chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, as saying on Tuesday that Iran had "delivered a firm and rational response to the American side. The ball is now in America's court to prevent war." It was not immediately clear what response he was referring to. Qalibaf also warned that Iran's armed forces remained at the highest level of defensive readiness. "If Washington makes another strategic miscalculation, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will find itself even more desperate than it is today," he said. cd73225ff082.text: By — Brittany Peterson, Associated Press Brittany Peterson, Associated Press By — Savannah Peters, Associated Press Savannah Peters, Associated Press By — Mead Gruver, Associated Press Mead Gruver, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/receding-floodwaters-leave-a-sea-of-mud-and-shattered-homes-in-the-u-s-southwest Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Receding floodwaters leave a sea of mud and shattered homes in the U.S. Southwest Nation Nov 3, 2026 8:06 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check PAGOSA SPRINGS, Colo. (AP) — Skies began to clear Tuesday, but while floodwaters from almost two weeks of on-and-off heavy rain still inundated parts of the U.S. Southwest, other areas left mud-caked by receding torrents presented homeowners and businessowners with the filthy work of cleanup. Jack Ellis, a retired schoolteacher, surveyed damage along the San Juan River in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, which has suffered through multiple rounds of severe flooding in recent weeks. "This is quite a disaster for everybody, especially in the low-lying areas," Ellis said. "We dig in and dig out, and that's what it's going to take." In all, more than 20 trillion gallons (76 trillion liters) of rain — 10 months of the flow over Niagara Falls — have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News After rain atop rain, flood risk persists The U.S. Southwest has endured two recent major rounds of storms, with rain falling on ground already saturated from an especially wet fall. One person died in floodwaters, and police suspect a second death was weather-related. Skies were clearing after some rivers crested at levels lower than forecasted overnight, offering a measure of relief to areas that were bracing for more catastrophic flooding, including Shiprock and Farmington in northwestern New Mexico. Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan County, New Mexico, said major rivers in the area remained above flood stage. "Now it's a waiting game for the waters to recede," Neeley said, adding that the county would likely soon lift evacuation orders impacting at least 20,000 residents and begin to focus on recovery. Flooding in Florida, too, complicates voting The situation wasn't unique to the region. As downpours swamped eastern Florida, at least 20 polling places were changed in at least eight counties after Gov. Ron DeSantis issued an emergency declaration. Flooded areas included Brevard County on the east-central coast, where over 2 feet (61 centimeters) of rain has fallen since Sunday. In Palm Beach County in southeast Florida, over 20 inches (51 centimeters) fell, cutting off access to condominiums and submerging cars in parking places. Some communities in Colorado and Utah, too, had to make alternative Election Day voting plans because of the flooding. Alyssa Gallegos, a contract mail carrier for the U.S. Postal Service, spent Tuesday morning helping get mail-in ballots from mailboxes to the post office in time for a 7 p.m. deadline for counting. "Regardless if we're in a crisis and having a hard time, the world doesn't stop turning," Gallegos said. "They're not gonna wait for us, so we just gotta stay with it." In Rock Point, Arizona, in the Navajo Nation, officials were forced to relocate a polling place because of flooding impacts. Valinda Shirley, vice president of the Rock Point Chapter, the local seat of tribal government, said hundreds of voters are still unable to cast ballots in both the U.S. midterms and the Navajo Nation presidential election because a major bridge closure and washed-out dirt roads have left them stranded on election day. "I have people that are still texting me asking how I can get them out so they can vote," Shirley said Tuesday afternoon. Another blow for Colorado hot-springs tourist town An eighth-generation Pagosa Springs local, Gallegos said her ancestors went through a catastrophic flood in 1911 but no one alive in her family expected anything like it in their lifetimes. She was watching videos of the devastation on social media Monday when she spotted her stepfather's home swept off its foundation by raging floodwaters. Inside, she knew, were old photographs and other treasured possessions from her childhood. "My heart's crushed," Gallegos said. "And it's not just him, it's all the people." Cleanup and repairs could take weeks or more in Pagosa Springs, a tourist town famous for hotels with riverside hot springs. The downtown area remained closed to traffic Tuesday while workers used heavy equipment to clear mud, water and debris from roads. Walkways and bridges collapsed or were heavily damaged. Outside a resort entrance stacked with sandbags, a sign read "Love Pagosa." Basement becomes 'soup bowl' in Durango In Durango, about 60 miles (96.5 kilometers) to the west, Willow Bradner's ranch-style home was surrounded by about 2 feet (60 centimeters) of mud. Nearly 5 feet (1.5 meters) of water from an overflowing creek poured inside at one point. "Our basement became a soup bowl," she said. The basement had been a selling point when she bought the property in 2024. Bradner said she and her husband once asked if they needed flood insurance and were told they were not in a flood zone. They and their teenage daughter had been offered a place to stay through the end of the year. But the loss of their home and uncertainty about the future were overwhelming, Bradner said. "The majority of our savings is in this house," she said. "We have to dig deep, and we have to rebuild." Peters reported from Santa Fe, New Mexico, and Gruver from Fort Collins, Colorado. Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control, CBS News reports.
Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia, a key swing state, voted for Donald Trump in 2024.
Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.
With polls suggesting Ossoff held a solid lead in the race, Republicans had diverted resources from Georgia to other contests.
Brian Kemp, Georgia's term-limited Republican governor, was the favoured candidate to run against Ossoff, but he declined.
Political pundits suspected that Kemp had avoided running, wary of Ossoff's rising star power, with rumours swirling that the Democrat could be mulling a run for president in 2028.
Throughout his campaign, Ossoff downplayed such rumours, saying on multiple occasions that he has "zero interest" in a presidential bid.

The first polls have closed in the US midterm elections, which will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. The outcome determines which party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.
It is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.
When will we know the results and who controls Congress?
Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.
To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.
The first results to come in won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).
Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.
There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.
Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.
This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.
The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.
When did we know the results in 2022?
In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.
While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.
The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.
Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.
Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.
The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.
What are the key races to watch in 2026?
There are six Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external - Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas.
Of these, six are currently held by Republicans. The Democrats would need to win three of those seats, plus five classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
Polls have suggested Democrats have a chance in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
Democrats also need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent in a closely-observed race. The state was initially classified as a "toss-up" by Cook Political Report, but was reclassified as "leans Democrat" the day before the vote.
The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, plus one independent who votes with them.
Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.
When do polls close?
The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.
Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the key battleground states:
- 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold
- 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Kansas and Texas
- 21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa, as well as in Kansas and Texas. In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats
- 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska, the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot
How does the vote-counting work?
Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.
Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.
Local election officials verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.
Most states require a post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.
Every state and locality has rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, includ

0d249f7629f5.text: By — Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Martha Bellisle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/authorities-release-911-call-from-the-man-who-killed-a-shooter-inside-an-oregon-elementary-school Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities release 911 call from the man who killed a shooter inside an Oregon elementary school Nation Nov 3, 2026 7:32 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check A frantic 911 call from the man who fatally shot a 16-year-old shooter who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school last month was released Tuesday to The Associated Press through a public records request. In a tense call lasting a little more than a minute, Kaylub Giamanco told the 911 operator there's "someone with a gun" at the school his daughter attends. "I have a gun and I will shoot them right now," said Giamanco, who was driving home for lunch and saw the shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School. WATCH: Oregon school shooter attacked special education classroom, police say The operator implores him "don't do anything, let me get an officer there." They talk over each other and Giamanco sounds increasingly frustrated by the exchange. "I'm about to go kill this kid," he said. A few seconds later he says the shooter is entering the building. The operator asks if the shooter is firing and Giamanco says yes. The operator tries to get more information but the call ends. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News A 16-year-old had shot his way through locked doors to get into the school in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher in a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized. A teacher tried to stop the shooter, Griffin J. John II, before Giamanco entered the school through an open window, opened the door of the classroom and fired his gun, dropping the shooter to the floor. Teacher tried to stop shooter before father arrived As Giamanco was racing toward the building, a teacher inside the school confronted the shooter in an effort to stop his progress. She threw her phone at the attacker, tackled him and wrestled with him for control of the weapon. Giamanco's arrival stopped the struggle. He said the teacher was "a real true hero" because her actions gave him an opening to shoot the attacker. The teacher, a certified learning specialist, had not been previously identified, but last week, Bend-La Pine Schools identified her as Cassidy Schutz and shared her statement. She said there were no words to describe the sadness she feels following the shooting. "This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives," Schutz wrote. "My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you." Schutz said her focus is on the families, the school "and my own healing." A second teacher in the classroom, Becky Drury, previously released a statement saying she never had a chance to shelter the children inside. She had tried to shut the door behind her, but the shooter was already there. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground," Drury said. She was shot in her left hand and right arm. Unable to get up, she said she pretended to be dead in the hopes he would not shoot her again. Father said he was the 'last line of defense' Giamanco said in a Oregon Public Broadcasting interview that he regrets not arriving soon enough to save everyone who was killed and injured. After imploring the 911 operator to send help, Giamanco climbed into the school through a window and peeked into a nearby classroom. He saw Schutz and the shooter in profile, giving him an open shot. "I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children," Giamanco said. He stepped into the room and fired his gun. The teacher ran from the room and the shooter reached for his shotgun. "I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn't move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else," he said. "If I wasn't there, I just don't know what would have happened." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. ee56edd11d38.text: By — James Brooks, Associated Press James Brooks, Associated Press By — Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press By — Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press Kostya Manenkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/greenland-approves-trilateral-deal-with-denmark-and-u-s-following-pressure-from-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Greenland approves trilateral deal with Denmark and U.S. following pressure from Trump World Nov 3, 2026 7:21 PM EST ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenlandic lawmakers on Tuesday voted to approve an agreement between the Arctic island, Denmark and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic after months of pressure by U.S. President Donald Trump seeking to control the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally. The trilateral deal paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump's repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States. The agreement's goal is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence. WATCH: What's in the Greenland agreement between U.S. and Denmark Greenlandic lawmakers voted 16-0 for the agreement, with seven abstentions, in the capital city of Nuuk. Some 570 kilometers (350 miles) north of Nuuk, Nukaaka Lund-Mathaeussen hoped that the deal's approval means the Trump administration "got what they wanted." "Hopefully after this we won't be getting underhanded threats from the American government," the 28-year-old Ilulissat resident told The Associated Press in Ilulissat after the vote. William Tukula, a 34-year-old chef in Ilulissat, said he'd seen posts on Facebook from older Greenlanders who were "a little bit scared about Trump and soldiers." The U.S. president had previously said he would not rule out the use of military force to seize control of Greenland because he declared U.S. control of it to be vital to American national security, though he also underlined his support for Greenlanders determining their own future. He later backed down from any threat. READ MORE: Why Trump wants Greenland The White House had no immediate comment on the vote, but the State Department said it "marks another major victory for American national security." "This administration is securing America's strategic interests in the Arctic, strengthening our national defense and ensuring this critical region remains free of adversarial threats," it said in a post on X. Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the security agreement in September on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. Nielsen, in a post on Facebook after Tuesday's vote, said Greenlanders stood united over the last few months despite the geopolitical tensions to show the world that the island decides its own fate. "We must be able to cooperate with other countries," he wrote, adding that the cooperation must respect "our people, our country and our rights." He added: "Greenland is our country. Greenland will always be our country." WATCH: Denmark and Greenland say sovereignty is not negotiable after Trump's meeting with Rutte Danish lawmakers are set to debate it later this month. The deal will "enter into force" once the "necessary parliamentary processes of the Kingdom of Denmark, in conjunction with Greenland, have been completed." Despite the Greenland parliament's approval, Lund-Mathaeussen said some residents on the island felt worried and powerless. "What can a regular guy like me do about the diplomatic engine?" the municipality worker said. "It's a big machine, and being a small person here in Greenland — it's hard to have any influences on those things." Nukaaraq Thomsen, a 43-year-old incineration plant worker from Ilulissat, said the trilateral deal still won't benefit Greenlanders. "My opinion is it's safe for Greenland. But not for the people — only for the land," Thomsen told the AP on Tuesday. In expanding its military presence on the island, the agreement says Washington is to award contracts for goods and services related to setting up, maintaining or dismantling such bases "to Greenlandic sources to the maximum extent possible." But Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of Avannaata Municipality, is not convinced that Greenlanders will see any advantages. "It's a good deal for Denmark, NATO. Not a good deal for us," he said. "There are no benefits, no money to our society. Zero." Dazio reported from Berlin and Manenkov reported from Tallinn, Estonia. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The first midterm votes counted on Tuesday night suggest a tough night for Republicans, in line with polling that has put Democrats well ahead in the battle for Congress on the strength of public frustration with President Donald Trumpâs agenda.
In Indiana and Kentucky, where most polls closed at 6 pm ET, Democrats ran well ahead of their early vote totals two years ago. They were competitive in Indianaâs 5th Congressional District, outside of Indianapolis â where Trump won by 17 points in 2024 â and in Kentuckyâs 6th District, which went for Trump by 15 points.
Neither of those seats was a Democratic target at the start of this election cycle, but both races saw later investment as the environment appeared to degrade for Republicans.
Indiana Rep. Victoria Spartz, an erratic candidate in the 5th District who has underperformed the party before, faced a last-minute spend from the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a green energy PAC working to beat Republicans who voted to revoke energy credits last year. House Majority PAC, the Democratsâ super PAC, spent nearly $400,000 for their candidate, JD Ford.
The Kentucky seat became a target after Rep. Andy Barr left it to run for Senate. Republicans nominated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado, while Gov. Andy Beshear campaigned for Democratic nominee Zach Dembo, a federal prosecutor. Republicans expected their numbers to improve as Election Day votes came in, but in both Indiana and Kentucky, the partyâs vote share has universally fallen since 2024. Indiana Democrat Beau Bayh, the son and grandson of former senators, led in the early count for secretary of state, the one statewide race his party was competing for.
Yet Democrats remain wary about overreading the meaning of early votes, recalling that they banked votes for Kamala Harris two years ago before getting overwhelmed on Election Day.

The letter to attorney Marc Elias, who for years has represented Democratic presidential campaigns and the party itself in election-related challenges — and has himself been a target of President Donald Trump — is among numerous ones that have been issued, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Target letters are sometimes issued to people the department intends to indict, but they do not necessarily mean someone will be charged. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest. Recruiting spoiler candidates to siphon votes from the other major party is a practice that has been used by Republicans and Democrats alike for decades without drawing criminal scrutiny. But Trump's Justice Department says it takes the matter seriously. "Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn't want to run, that doesn't expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News. "And so that's why the Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process." Blanche declined to discuss the target letters, saying he was not going to " confirm anything that has to do with an ongoing investigation." South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's former ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.
The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.
Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.
A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".
"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.
Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.
The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos pre

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.
But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.
“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.
The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.
But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.
The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.
Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.
Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.
These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.
Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”
The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.
But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.
“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

54d5802999c0.text: Top party strategists may hate seeing one of their candidates gutted by a brutal ad. But they can still admire the hit. Why it matters: A record $11.6 billion has plastered political ads across screens of every size in the country during the 2026 midterms . Only a handful of those earned the grudging respect of operatives on both sides. 📺 Zoom in: Multiple Republican strategists singled out the "brutal" series of ads attacking Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.) over lawsuits against patients with overdue medical bills — some of whom were later arrested . Against the advice of his own team, Marshall released a self-directed ad answering the attacks. In Nebraska , an ad highlighting a past vote by former Gov. Pete Ricketts to pardon a man convicted of rape was singled out by both parties as one of the cycle's most damaging. Ricketts is expected to win re-election to the Senate. In Maine, an upbeat jingle hit Democratic nominee Troy Jackson for having children with his second cousin. "If he'll f**k his own family, he'll f**k yours too," the radio ad said (among other things). Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called for the ad to be taken down. And in Florida , Rep. María Salazar (R-Fla.) turned on her own party leader, criticizing President Trump over ICE's aggressive enforcement tactics, saying some immigration policies had "gone too far." The intrigue : Even hardened operatives are dealing with a new frontier: AI-generated attack ads that can make up scenarios and put words in an opponent's mouth. In Michigan , a Republican-aligned super PAC used AI-generated imagery to depict Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo and playing a game with cards referencing "Death to America" and 9/11. In Texas, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton's team used AI to depict Democratic candidate James Talarico defacing a Bible with a crayon and saying: "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." 🤺 Between the lines: An attack ad helped spark this weekend's blowup in the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens' (D-Mich.) shocking decision to withdraw support from El-Sayed grew out of their public dispute over an ad she called antisemitic. El-Sayed ultimately disavowed the ad but said Stevens wasn't welcome at his events, and she endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Sunday. The other side: It's hard to imagine a bigger backfire than Vivek Ramaswamy's (R) ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent for Ohio governor, Amy Acton (D). It could prove fatal for his gubernatorial bid, and Republicans worry it could hurt Sen. John Husted's (R) re-election chances too. The ad sparked immediate bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy doubled down before pulling it off-air. One internal GOP poll had Acton's lead grow by 6 points after the ad ran.

'I'm not a quitter': Kim Kardashian on retaking the bar exam
Kim Kardashian has said she will retake the California bar exam with the aim of becoming a lawyer in real life, after playing one in the legal drama All's Fair.
The reality TV star and actress discovered she had failed the exam after the first series of the Hulu programme aired last year. She had previously studied law for six years.
"I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," Kardashian told the BBC's Annabel Rackham, adding: "I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there."
She was speaking alongside co-star Naomi Watts ahead of the second series of All's Fair, which was roundly panned by critics despite breaking streaming records.

The economy and the state of democracy have been named as the top issues for US voters, according to an election day poll.
The survey - officially called the Voter Poll - asks tens of thousands of the American electorate their opinions and motivations, and providing a breakdown by age, gender, education and other demographics.
Polling company SSRS collects data on behalf of a consortium of news companies, and the survey is a representative sample of American voters in the run up to the election, and includes exit polling of both early and on the day voters.
Here are some of the breakdowns from the 2026 voter poll. Like all surveys they are estimates; the numbers are also likely to be updated as more data arrives.
Economy ranked as top issue
Some 39% of those asked in the poll of more than 79,000 people said the economy was the most important issue, while 32% put the state of democracy top.
Following that, immigration was named most important by 14% of voters while healthcare, foreign policy and crime were ranked first by a lower share.
Data suggests the majority of US voters have a negative view of the state of the national economy.
Some 75% of those asked said the economy was in a "not so good or poor" state with 25% saying it was "excellent or good".
Looking at their own family finances, 44% of people said they were in a worse situation than two years ago, 38% said about the same and 18% said better.
Majority say Trump's policies 'worsened economy'
Almost two thirds (65%) of voters surveyed say US President Donald Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the US.
By contrast, 28% say Trump's policies have improved conditions and only 8% say the president has had no impact.
People were also asked whether expressing support or opposition for Trump was one reason for their midterm vote.
Some 43% said expressing opposition was a reason but a similar proportion (41%) said he was not a factor. Only 16% of those asked said expressing support was a reason for their vote.
Nearly 40% unhappy with state of the US
Almost four in ten of those asked (38%) said they were angry at the way things are going in the US at the moment, with a further 37% saying they were dissatisfied.
Only 18% said they were satisfied, and 7% of respondents felt enthusiastic.
So taken together, there is a majority telling pollsters SSRS they are not happy about the current state of the country.
Inflation has caused hardship for most Americans
As well as broader issues, pollsters also asked about inflation and the impact of rising prices on people's lives.
Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year. A fifth (21%) of those answering said it had caused them no hardship at all.
A majority of voters (59%) said they were "very concerned" about the cost of petrol and diesel and a similar proportion (58%) gave this answer about the cost of food and groceries.
More than six in 10 respondents (62%) said they thought that higher than usual prices were more because of Trump's policies.
And 38% said it was more due to factors beyond his control.

Geoff Bennett:

Amna Nawaz:

Amy Walter:
Right.
Amna Nawaz:
What are we hearing from voters so far about what's driving them to the polls?
Amy Walter:
Not surprisingly, the economy is driving everything; 39 percent of voters saying this was their top issue that they were voting on.
We have known now throughout the last two years that voters have been telling us over and over again that the economy, especially inflation, is something that continues to frustrate them. Geoff Bennett:

Voters are now saying Democrats are better able to handle the following issues, the economy, foreign policy, health care, and government corruption. If that happens, if this wave plays out that way, that has a chance to fundamentally change the way we govern ourselves, at least for the next couple of years.
Amna Nawaz:
Doug.
Doug Heye:
Yes, look, I go back to 2010 when, I was at the RNC. Our magic number for Obama was 46 percent. We thought if he was at or below that, we'd take back the House.
There's not been a number that's shown Donald Trump that starts with a four in a long time. And it's why you have seen some candidates, certainly Ashley Hinson and Mike Rogers being two, trying to create separation.

722db43ca2ea.text: In recent months, the Trump administration and the Department of Justice have led an extraordinary effort to exert federal control over state-run elections. Nearly all of those efforts, so far, have been blocked or rejected by the courts. To discuss election security and the prospect of potential election interference, Geoff Bennett spoke with Rick Hasen and Juliette Kayyem. Amna Nawaz: This election cycle has been compared to the midterms of 2006, when Democrats won back control of Congress and, in an historic first, elected Nancy Pelosi to be the first female speaker of the House. That was 20 years ago. Today, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi is in the final months of her political career. And like she's done every election night since 2016, Speaker Pelosi joins us now. Madam Speaker, welcome back. Thank you for continuing this tradition with us. I want to begin, of course, with your predictions. How big a majority do you think Democrats can win in the House tonight? And will you win control of the Senate? Rep. Nancy Pelosi(D-CA): Well, thank you, Amna, for the opportunity to share some thoughts with you once again on election night. One thing I will say, following up on your previous guests, be not afraid to voters. Just go out and vote. Hakeem Jeffries has worked very hard to do three things, one, to win the election, two, to protect the election, and, three, to show the people what will happen once we do. So, your vote is protected, go vote. Whether it's litigation, whether it's legislation, whether it's communication or mobilization, we're ready. We're ready for anything they might come up with. Amna Nawaz: Always good to underscore that. You're absolutely right. What will you think will happen tonight now? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: I think, tonight, we will have a big victory. It will be many seats in the House of Representatives. I put -- I want 30. But the fact is, they will be very slim victories. So I don't want anybody to think, oh, well, you have won, so let's move on to other things. No, we -- every race will be close, but there will be many of them. You mentioned 2006. And, in 2006, he who shall be nameless was at 44 percent favorable. Now it's -- 45 percent favorable. Now it's 38, a seven-points difference. And, in 18, we won 40 seats, 31 of them in Trump districts. So now he's down to 38. We expect to have a big Democratic victory in the House and hopefully also in the Senate. In my own district, I'm supporting Connie Chan. And, for me, what is interesting is, when I went to Congress, there were 12 women, Democratic women out of 435 people, 12 Democratic women. So my passion over the years has been to increase that number. And I'm so happy to still be in Congress for the election, but we will go over 100, and hopefully Connie Chan will take us there as well. So, we're prepared for victory. Amna Nawaz: We have certainly seen some big changes on that front. You're absolutely right. I do want to ask you about some specific races, though, because Democrats have been sort of reeling from some late-breaking stories in Michigan, in particular, in the Senate race. I'm sure you were tracking Haley Stevens on Sunday stepping in after she lost the Democratic primary to actually endorse the Republican candidate there, Mike Rogers. He's running against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee. What do you think -- or how do you think, rather, that impacts the race? Will that hurt El-Sayed? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: By all reports that I have from Michigan -- and we have races there too in the House -- of course, we're concerned about the Senate and the governor's race -- it's going to be a landslide in Michigan. We will win that Senate seat in Michigan. Unfortunately, and with all the respect in the world that I have for my former colleague Haley Stevens, this distraction from what we should be talking about is, what are the Democrats going to do when they win, rather than why did Haley Stevens change her support in that race? So let's not be distracted by that. That was then. This is now, today. The Democrats will win big in Michigan, and it will not -- it will not affect whether we win the House -- excuse me -- the Senate and the House, as a matter of fact, as well. Amna Nawaz: So, to that point... Rep. Nancy Pelosi: It's a pretty exciting night. It's going to be a big victory for us. Amna Nawaz: To that point, as you mentioned, what Democrats should prioritize if they do win control of both chambers -- rather, in the House especially, I know you have supported Hakeem Jeffries to be the eventual speaker if the Democrats do win the majority there. I'm sure you have seen a number of sort of anti-establishment candidates, though, reserve their judgment and say they're not ready to support him to be speaker. They say they're frustrated with the status quo. They say Democrats and leaders aren't fighting hard enough. Are there concerns valid, in your view? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: Hakeem Jeffries will be a very strong speaker of the House, and he will be the speaker of the House. And with all due respect for all members, they represent their district. Their job title and their job description are one and the same, representative. So we respect that. But we also respect the consensus of the House Democrats, again, respecting everybody's point of view, but with enough votes, just win big, baby. And that's the answer to all this. I always had that. Everybody -- I was always fighting. But, nonetheless, we always prevailed and we got our votes and we won, even when we were down to like two- or three-vote majority. So Hakeem will be fine with that. I think that more is made of those differences. Those people are wonderful. They're welcome to Congress, but they're not going to hold up a Democratic agenda to reduce the cost of living, to make sure that people have access to health care and overturn what Trump did to take a trillion dollars out of Medicaid, half-a-trillion out of Medicare, hundreds of billions out of food

36cb11f7cd41.text: Ronna McDaniel served as chairwoman of the Republican National Committee during President Trump’s first term. Now, she’s a surrogate for Mike Rogers’ Senate campaign in Michigan. McDaniel joined Geoff Bennett to discuss the race. Geoff Bennett: And now, for a Republican perspective, we're joined tonight by Ronna McDaniel. She chaired the Republican National Committee for seven years, including throughout President Trump's first term. She's now a campaign surrogate for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan. And she joins us tonight from Lansing. It's good to see you. Welcome to the "News Hour." Ronna McDaniel: Great to be with you. Thanks for having me. Geoff Bennett: And we should say you chaired the RNC during President Trump's first midterm back in 2018. House Republicans then lost a net total of 41 seats. In your view, how does the political environment right now compare to then, eight years ago? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I would also add that we picked up Senate seats in that first midterm, which was unprecedented to pick up Senate seats in a midterm. Listen, in the first midterm of a sitting president, you typically lose seats in the House or flip a chamber. That's been the precedent for over 100 years. And when I was RNC chair in 2022, we actually flipped the House and won that back for Republicans under Biden. So that's what happens in midterms, and I think this is something that we're seeing this midterm. I do think that the House probably will flip to Democrats this cycle. Geoff Bennett: Let me ask you this, though. As you look across the electorate, where do you see the greatest opportunities for Republicans? What are you watching most closely tonight? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I'm in Michigan, so I'm looking at Mike Rogers. This is a Democrat seat that they have held. We haven't had a Republican in the Senate here since 1994. Mike has run a very good race. He has made inroads in traditionally Democrat constituencies, the Jewish vote, the Black vote. He actually has a whole Democrats for Rogers coalition. And then we saw the endorsement of Haley Stevens, a sitting Democrat congresswoman come out and endorse Mike Rogers. So I think this is a seat that we're looking at very, very closely. Geoff Bennett: And looking nationally, you said recently that Republicans shouldn't be spending hundreds of millions of dollars defending a Texas Senate seat. How did the party find itself fighting for seats that should have been safely Republican? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I don't know if I said they shouldn't be. I said it's concerning to have to spend that much, because that means you're not spending in races where you can pick up, right? Like, if you're spending in a safe -- in a safe seat in a safe state, that takes away resources from potential gains. But, of course, we are battling in red areas right now. I do think we're going to hold the Senate. I do think Texas comes through, Kansas comes through. These are states that Donald Trump won by double digits. And so, while I think we may lose the House, I think the Senate stays in Republican hands. Geoff Bennett: Republicans are asking to give -- asking voters, rather, to give President Trump two more years of unified Republican control. What would Republicans deliver that they haven't already? Ronna McDaniel: Well, the Big Beautiful Bill did provide no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security. I think getting out of this Iran war, you will see gas prices go down, which I know is heavy on the minds of many voters across this country. Affordability is a huge issue. And as you see the policies of deregulation come forward, things that Trump has enacted, I think you will see a better economy in the next two years. And he wants to complete that with Republicans. He may not have that opportunity. I hope the Democrats don't go in and just go into lawfare and trying to attack Republicans in retribution, which we have heard our own Senator Elissa Slotkin say is on the agenda for them. I actually hope that we can work together and find ways to help the American people, because that's what they want. Geoff Bennett: President Trump will not be on the ballot again. Is the Republican Party prepared for a political future without him? Ronna McDaniel: I think he will have a lot of say in the nominee for 2028. I -- he's not somebody who fades to the background very easily. The Democrats look like they're going to have something like 20 candidates running for president. I don't think our field has shaped up yet. And I think whoever our nominees are or whoever's running, they're probably going to go and talk to President Trump first, and he will have a lot of impact in that primary because he does have huge sway with our base, specifically in primaries, and we saw that across this cycle as well. Geoff Bennett: President Trump, his approval rating is underwater. His numbers on the economy are even worse. They're in the 20 percent range. When he tells voters to act as if he's on the ballot, is he helping Republicans or hurting them, in your view? Ronna McDaniel: Yes, there are Republicans that just don't turn out, or there are Trump voters that just don't turn out unless he's on the ballot. So him saying that to his voters is key, because we have seen in past midterms -- and I know this personally as former RNC chair -- those Trump voters sit out without his name on the ballot. So those are the people he's talking to. And Republicans are going to need those voters to turn out, traditional Republicans to turn out, and we are certainly going to need independents if we're going to win in states like Michigan, Maine, some of these battleground states. In Kansas and Texas, I think him saying that does mean a lot to those Republican voters because he did win those states by double digits, and that is where he can really help. Geoff Bennett: Ronna McDaniel, former RNC chair, great to have your perspectives as part of our coverage. Thanks for being

365cc6777796.text: On Election Day, candidates, campaigns and analysts are looking for more than the total number of voters. They also want to know who showed up to the polls and what issues were on their minds. Traditional exit polls are evolving as the way people vote has changed. Deema Zein takes a closer look at some of the data behind the election. Geoff Bennett: Well, on this Election Day, candidates and campaigns and all of us watching closely are interested in more than just how many people voted. We want to know who turned out, what motivated them to vote, and which issues mattered most as they cast their ballots. Amna Nawaz: Traditional exit polls are evolving, as the way people vote has changed. Deema Zein takes a closer look at some of the data behind the election. Deema Zein: To know exactly who showed up to the polls and why they voted for a particular candidate, you have to ask the voters. This year, "News Hour" is getting some of that information from the voter poll. It's a new collaboration between the Associated Press and other news outlets to survey voters directly by phone, Internet, and in person. To explain how it works, I'm joined by David Scott, V.P. of election services at the Associated Press. David, thanks for joining us. David Scott: Glad to be here. Deema Zein: So this is a new system this year, joining forces with broadcast networks after about a decade of developing and using your own system to measure the vote. Why? David Scott: We wanted to reach voters where they are. That's the most important thing. So if you're conducting a survey as Americans are casting their ballot, you need to be in all of the places where they cast a ballot. We needed to be able to interview voters who are casting their ballots in person on Election Day. But, at the same time, most Americans vote in advance. And so we look at the voter file and look at who's cast a ballot, and then we try to interview them either online, by mail, by phone. Whatever way that they would like to interact with us once we see that they have cast a ballot, then we're able to interview them, ask them questions about who they voted for and why. Deema Zein: So people are familiar with this term exit poll. This is different. Can we talk a little bit about how exactly? David Scott: Well, part of it is an exit poll, right? We are going to have thousands of people who are out in the 50 states interviewing people as they cast their ballot on Election Day. But we also will interview people before Election Day, because people cast their ballots before Election Day. Really, what we have tried to do with our colleagues at the broadcast networks is design a methodology that reaches Americans. No matter how you cast your ballot, you have the opportunity for us to ask you questions, so we can understand the fullness of the American electorate. Deema Zein: And how many people are you talking to as part of this new process? David Scott: Yes, it's an enormous survey. So, like a normal political poll that you might see in a state about a Senate race might be based on 500 interviews. We're going to aim for somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 interviews taking place leading up to Election Day and then on Election Day itself. So it's an enormous survey. And it's one of the things that we think is really important, that we're going to have results in every state where there's a statewide election this year. It's not just about the battlegrounds. Deema Zein: What does this help tell you guys at the AP? David Scott: We're looking for insights in the data about who has voted, what they cared about, what issues were resonating. We know which issues each candidate was talking about in a race, and so which ones were most important to voters. We look at the demographics of a state and we look at the demographics of the electorate and see how that matches up. One of the things that we saw in 2024 was some of those demographic shifts that pointed early in the night to success for President Trump. You could see in the data about who was voting that he was poised to have a good night. We were able to get a sense that this is where the election was going, and so those are the types of things that we will be looking at. Deema Zein: David Scott, vice president of election services at the Associated Press, thanks again for joining us. David Scott: Happy to be here.

e1ce6b4c85b2.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ap-voter-poll-the-economy-and-the-state-of-democracy-are-voters-top-issues Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP Voter Poll: The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues Politics Updated on Nov 3, 2026 7:55 PM EST — Published on Nov 3, 2026 6:26 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check Voters overwhelmingly feel frustrated with the way things are going in the U.S. today, according to The AP Voter Poll, which points to a midterm electorate that is deeply unhappy with the country's direction and pessimistic about the future. About three-quarters of voters say they feel "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the country's current trajectory. Only about one-quarter feel "satisfied" or "enthusiastic." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states like California and Massachusetts, but even in deep-red states, a majority of voters were at least "dissatisfied." Voters are also displeased with the condition of the economy, with roughly three-quarters saying it is "not so good" or "poor." That's in line with what U.S. adults have said in recent months in AP-NORC polling. The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues Voters say the economy and the state of democracy are the top issues facing the country, with high costs and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections. READ MORE: A guide to the key ballot measures voters will decide on Election Day About 4 in 10 U.S. voters nationally say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, as most express concern about gas prices and the cost of groceries. About 3 in 10 say the state of democracy is the top issue. Only about 1 in 10 say the same about immigration or health care, and few name foreign policy or crime. Roughly half of U.S. voters say government corruption and the cost of living are "crucial" to their vote for Congress, much higher than the share who say that about immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran or AI data centers. Most voters believe Trump's policies have harmed the U.S. economy Relatively few voters have positive things to say about Trump's economic leadership. About two-thirds of U.S. midterm voters say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 say they've improved things, The AP Voter Poll found. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters said Trump's tariff policies have hurt the national economy. READ MORE: AP Voter Poll: Voters want Congress to impose more checks on an unpopular president Views of Trump's priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — are also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than the country's interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country's interests. Voters express severe concerns about inflation About 8 in 10 voters say inflation has caused a "severe" or "moderate" financial hardship on their households, according to The AP Voter Poll. The drag caused by prices rising faster than wages over the past year has made it harder for many voters to afford basic essentials such as gasoline, groceries and their utilities. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate The persistent concern is a carryover from the 2024 presidential election when voters specifically tasked Trump to solve the problem, but inflation is now higher than it was when he returned to the White House. More than 8 in 10 voters say they are "very" or "somewhat" concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and healthcare. Capitalism viewed more positively than socialism The AP Voter Poll found that more than half of voters strongly or somewhat favor the free market principles of capitalism. Only about 3 in 10 feel similarly positive about socialism, in which the government plays a greater role in economic activity. Trump and other Republicans campaigned on the idea that many Democratic candidates with their plans for universal healthcare were socialist. Democrats countered that the Trump administration had taken ownership stakes in dozens of private companies.
