"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.
Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.
The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.
"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.
The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.
Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.
She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.
Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.
Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.
Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.
Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

f25174120b66.text: Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) will announce his bid to lead House Republicans on Wednesday, a person familiar with his plans told Axios, as his party begins to regroup from stunning midterm losses that cost them their congressional majorities. Why it matters: Scalise's announcement sets up a potentially bruising battle for the minority leader post, with Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) also being floated as a potential contender. It's Scalise's second attempt at the top House Republican job. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff that he will not run for minority leader on a Wednesday morning call, a person familiar with his plans said. Driving the news: Scalise pitched himself as a leader positioned to bring Republicans back into the majority "He is a proven and tested leader who is ready on day one. He's spent his career unifying Republicans and he is prepared for the big legislative and oversight battles ahead. The conference knows him, how he fights, and that he's a trusted leader," the person familiar with his plans said in statement. Catch up quick: Scalise defeated Jordan in the Republican conference's secret-ballot vote to nominate a speaker in October 2023, but withdrew a day later after failing to secure enough support on the House floor. Johnson ultimately emerged as speaker after weeks of Republican infighting. State of play: A Scalise-Jordan race would pit two of the House GOP's most prominent figures against each other. Scalise enters the contest with more than a decade of experience in leadership, while Jordan could draw support from the party's conservative wing. But the scale of the loss on Tuesday night has prompted calls for an entirely new leadership slate — a potential stumbling block for Scalise. Three House Republicans previously told Axios that a major midterm defeat could fuel calls for an entirely new leadership team The intrigue: Majority Whip Tom Emmer, meanwhile is making calls to lock down support from him to stay on as whip in the minority, a person familiar with his plans told Axios. Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios in September that he intends to remain in his current role rather than seek a higher leadership position. That could leave the losing candidate in a Scalise-Jordan matchup without an obvious fallback spot in the top leadership ranks. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to elect their next leadership team on Nov. 10, with candidates facing a Friday deadline to declare their intentions. The winner needs a majority of House Republicans in a secret-ballot vote. Trump could play a pivotal role in determining the next top House Republican, and GOP lawmakers are watching closely to see whether he throws his support behind a candidate.

The Scoop
As soon as Republican Sen. Darline Graham won the GOP nomination to replace her late brother in August, Democrat Annie Andrews made her move.
Andrews immediately began spending more than $5 million on advertising in South Carolinaâs Senate race at a moment when she largely had the airwaves to herself as her new opponent struggled to raise money. At the time, Republicans were racing to prioritize other competitive races across the country â and most people in both parties still saw South Carolina as a pipe dream for Democrats.
But by October, when the rest of the country began tuning into South Carolina â and spending money â Andrews quietly became the frontrunner, according to internal campaign details shared with Semafor following her victory on Tuesday.
On Oct. 5, the Andrews campaign received a poll showing her with a 3-point lead over Graham. But the Democratâs campaign decided against publicly releasing the poll â or any subsequent internal poll â showing Andrews with a lead over Graham, wary of drawing too much attention from national Republicans and jeopardizing a peak at the right time, according to Chas Goldman, a strategist for Andrews.
That Republican attention did come, but not in time to save Graham in a state where Democrats hadnât won a Senate race since 1998. On a Senate map filled with shocking GOP losses, South Carolina stands out: Itâs the home of the National Republican Senatorial Committee chair, Tim Scott, and territory on which Democrats tried to compete statewide in 2020 â and lost handily.
Former GOP Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., told Semafor on Wednesday that he could feel the anti-Graham sentiment building on the stateâs coast but that most Republicans still felt that Graham could ânose it outâ elsewhere. Ultimately, though, he said President Donald Trumpâs backing of Graham in a crowded primary which included Sanford and Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry ânever sat well with folks.â
Sanford said Andrews did a good job appealing to disaffected Republicans but also said the rejection of Graham amounted to âa Waterloo moment for Trump.â
âThe fact that a state as red as South Carolina would go the other way on his hand-picked candidate? This is a person who said: âClose your eyes and pretend youâre voting for me.â OK, they did,â Sanford told Semafor. âThey just didnât like Darline as a candidate and felt it had been forced down their throats by Trump. And theyâre like: âWeâre not doing this.ââ
Andrews outran her partyâs gubernatorial nominee by 4 percentage points, evidence of both her strength and Grahamâs weakness as a candidate. Graham ran behind Alan Wilson, the Republican governor-elect, by roughly 100,000 votes.
In an interview with Semafor in early September, Andrews said she welcomed help from national Democrats and âanyone who wants to help me win this race, but I am confident I can do it without investment from the national party.â
âIâm on TV, sheâs not up yet, and thatâs a huge advantage,â Andrews said of Graham at the time. âAll of the ingredients are in place, and Iâve been gifted with what is frankly an incredibly weak opponent. Iâm ready.â
turning the red tide
Andrews exploited divisions in the Republican Party over Trumpâs endorsement of Graham, reaching out to supporters of Norman and former GOP Gov. David Beasley, according to details shared with Semafor.
She ran an ad with her Republican dad to appeal to former supporters of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham R-S.C., and worked with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and other Black leaders in the state to juice turnout. Beasley ended up cutting a joint endorsement ad with former Democratic Gov. Jim Hodges while Normanâs son, Warren, warmed publicly to Andrews.
By traditional campaign metrics, Andrews swamped Graham. She raised more than $25 million, according to her campaign, and was largely able to keep her own campaign afloat into October, when both national parties began spending in the race. Graham raised nearly $2 million, a sum that meant she would need outside support to win.
Ultimately Democrats joined Andrews in the fray. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quietly spent $500,000 there and Senate Majority PAC spent $750,000. Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, said that âGraham brought significant negatives and baggage to the race, thatâs undeniable, but Andrews won this race as much as Graham lost it.â 
Sen. Raphael Warnock, from neighboring Georgia, campaigned for Andrews, but she mostly sought to keep the campaign local. Her coattails extended to a House pickup in the stateâs lowcountry as she targeted Republicans and independents in her campaign events.
âFor 18 months, she traveled all 46 counties, earning votersâ trust one conversation at a time. She worked just as hard to raise the resources to go up on TV early and stay there. Those relationships and that early investment built a lead that she never gave up,â said Brexton Isaacs, Andrewsâs campaign manager.
Burgessâs view
I interviewed Andrews throughout this saga: Once when she launched, once earlier this year when it appeared Lindsey Graham would be her opponent, and once after Darline Graham replaced her brother on the ticket. Each time she explained to me why this wasnât like 2020, when Jaime Harrison raised gobs of money but lost to Lindsey Graham.
I was as skeptical as anyone else that South Carolina was ready to elect a Democrat to the Senate. But over the last couple weeks, the whole country tuned in as national Republicans and Democrats alike poured money in. At the moment itâs the biggest surprise on the Senate map â perhaps until we find out what happens in Mississippi.

French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
'Hybrid warfare' claim
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.
Additional reporting from Chris Vallance

dcc2ec2b63bd.text: By — Josh Boak, Associated Press Josh Boak, Associated Press By — Hyojin Yoo, Associated Press Hyojin Yoo, Associated Press By — Humera Lodhi, Associated Press Humera Lodhi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-trump-and-republicans-lost-the-2026-midterm-elections-according-to-ap-voter-poll Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to AP Voter Poll Politics Nov 4, 2026 11:19 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U.S. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of midterm voters in all 50 states. LIVE RESULTS: 2026 Midterm Election Map The president's failure to deliver on key promises — most prominently, his vows to tame inflation, which has worsened instead — clearly weighed on his fellow Republicans in Tuesday's midterm elections for the House and the Senate. The polling shows that voters generally saw Trump as being more focused on his own fortune and gold-leafed existence than their needs. The president also helped elevate candidates with obvious flaws, amplifying their struggles in an already challenging year. He suggested in a Tuesday evening interview with Fox News Channel that Democrats "fought hard" and that the Republican base "didn't like the candidates" he had endorsed because some of his picks were not fully loyal to him. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News But the poll also contains a serious note of caution for Democrats. Many voters dislike the party — and while Democrats hold an advantage on key issues such as the economy, their edge is relatively slim. About 7 in 10 voters said Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the president, setting the bar for Democrats who won back the Senate and the House. Inflation crushed Republicans It was impossible for GOP candidates to hide from inflation. Voters could see it clearly in their receipts from grocery stores and gasoline stations. The financial blow of an auto repair or a utility bill after a sweltering summer was inescapable. And even in Republican strongholds such as Texas, the drag caused by inflation helped Democrats. WATCH LIVE: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions About 2 in 10 Texas voters said inflation had imposed "severe" hardship on them and their family — and about three-quarters of this group backed Democrat James Talarico for the Senate. An additional 6 in 10 voters, roughly, said inflation had led to "moderate" hardship, and Talarico won the majority of these voters, too. That same pattern repeated in state after state. Nationally, voters who said they were "very concerned" about everyday costs — including groceries, healthcare and gas — overwhelmingly said they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race. READ MORE: The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues But it wasn't just the inflation itself that mattered. Voters nationwide pinned the blame on Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices. Asked about the impact of Trump's policies, about two-thirds of voters nationwide said they had made the economy worse. And out of this group, about 8 in 10 said they backed the Democratic candidate. Corruption was a major concern Demonstrators gather near the White House to cheer for midterm election results on Nov. 4, 2026. Photo by Evan Vucci/ Reuters More than half of voters nationally said government corruption was "crucial" for their vote for Congress. That was a little higher than the share who said the cost of living was "crucial," a striking finding in a year when about 6 in 10 voters said they were personally "very concerned" about the cost of food and groceries. Meanwhile, despite Republicans' suggestion that voters cared little about Trump making more than $1 billion last year from meme coins and cryptocurrency, most voters saw Trump as obsessed with his own interests. During his second term, Trump solicited donations from powerful companies to build his desired White House ballroom after having surprised the country by rapidly demolishing what had been the building's East Wing. That tenor set at the top spilled over into business deals for his family and other deals by his associates involving pardons and federal policies. Ultimately, about two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates. Voters want an assertive Congress For much of the past two years, Trump acted on his own. Much of the Republican-controlled House and Senate barely objected to his whims. He laid off federal workers, imposed sweeping new tariffs, launched the war with Iran, remodeled Washington in gold paint, threatened the Federal Reserve, the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian Institution and bullied a bevy of longtime allies. Voters made it clear that they want more congressional oversight. READ MORE: Voters want Congress to impose more checks on an unpopular president About 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the presidency, including about 4 in 10 Republicans. Swing voters don't really love Democrats, even if they voted for them Despite Democrats' victories, voters did not deliver a ringing endorsement of the party as a whole. Many voters expressed frustration with both parties: On the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, taxes and immigration, roughly 2 in 10 voters said "neither" party was better equipped to handle these issues. An even larger share of voters said neither party would be better at addressing government corruption or artificial intelligence. Those skeptical voters generally broke for Democrats. Israel's President Isaac Herzog has begun consultations with political parties on whom to task with forming a new coalition government, after he received the official results of a general election last week he said had no clear winner.
Herzog told party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid a new election.
Neither the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his rival Gadi Eisenkot secured a majority in parliament.
Earlier, electoral officials said there was no evidence of irregularities and that unsubstantiated claims by Netanyahu's camp of Arab-led parties "stealing" the election did not justify delaying the results' certification.
The Shin Bet security service is investigating allegations of foreign interference in the election, but the head of the Central Elections Committee stressed that they would not fundamentally change the outcome.
In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.
The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem.
"In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said.
"One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."
Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening.
"In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.
The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.
But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared".
"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.
Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.
It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.
Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".
On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".
His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.
Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

House Speaker Mike Johnson privately told staff he is not planning on running for minority leader or any other leadership role in the next Congress, according to people familiar with the comments.
His decision will kick off a scramble among House Republican leadership contenders in the aftermath of their sweeping losses Tuesday night. Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, and current Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., are launching leadership bids on Wednesday. Some progressives have threatened to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, though itâs unlikely to derail his ascension.
Meanwhile, Republicans could see other shakeups further down their leadership chain. Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, currently the Republican Study Committee chair, announced in a letter to GOP colleagues Wednesday that heâd run for the second-ranking position.
âWe need fresh ideas and a leadership team committed to rebuilding a culture with a clear game plan to win in 2028,â he wrote. That sets up a clash with Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., currently the House majority whip. And leading up to Election Day, Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., had received encouragement from other Republicans about running against Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., for conference chair.

Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk.
According to the Financial Times, external, the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (Â£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September.
The money was not enough to stop the seat from turning Democrat for the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokingly wrote on X, external.
While stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning following the election outcome, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively. Many Democrats had been vocally outspoken against the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres on the campaign trail.
Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US.
Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.
As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.
"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.
On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall, contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.
Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.
Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.
Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.
Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign.
A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around.

Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.
Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.
The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.
"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity," Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.
"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.
In the ensuing decades, conservative, Socialist-Liberal, and Fidesz-led governments have all contemplated, but ultimately refused to open the files.
Since 1998, it has been possible to apply for your own file, and for historians to research those of others. But many names were blacked out, and many files withheld by the post-communist secret services for their own use.
Over the past 36 years, there were frequent leaks of data from the files, as successive governments tried to damage their opponents. Many files were also shredded, as the Communist party lost its grip in 1988-89.
From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services have become available on the nyitottaktak.hu website, external.
A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.
Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.
These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.
Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.
Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.
Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.
Krisztian UngvÃ¡ry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.
"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna BorvendÃ©g, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.
Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

The mother of a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was fatally shot in the United States last week has left Ghana for America after being granted an emergency visa by President Donald Trump.
"I want justice for my son," Doris Adu Gyamfi told the BBC at the airport before her departure.
She said he had dreamt of becoming a medical doctor.
Her son, Javits Frimpong, who had only been in the US for a year, was chased down and shot on Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx, New York.
He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection with the shooting.
His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited the debate about gun violence in America.
His mother was escorted to the airport by relatives and Dr Erieka Bennett, Head of Mission of the African Diaspora Forum.
"I'm going to America to plan my son's funeral," Gyamfi said.
She thanked the government and well-wishers for their support and prayers following her son's death.
In a social media post on Saturday, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said Trump had agreed to grant a visa to Gyamfi so she could mourn her son in person.
Mamdani said the murder of a child was a pain no parent should endure, "let alone from thousands of miles away.â
"Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," he said.
"All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," he added.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it was following the case closely to ensure justice.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators are brought to justice.
Police are searching for three teenage suspects who fled the scene, captured on surveillance footage.
The shooting has sparked concern among Ghanaians about the safety of children sent to study in America.

f4afcb1df036.text: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) plans to step down as the House's top Republican after his party's epic midterm election losses wiped out their majority, according to a person familiar with his plans. Why it matters: Johnson's exit touches off a potentially contentious scramble to replace him with Republicans days away from choosing their next leaders. Johnson told staff on a Wednesday morning call that he will not run for minority leader, the person familiar with his plans said. Driving the news: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) have been floated as potential successors, setting the stage for a bruising leadership battle. Johnson's political future remains uncertain, with questions swirling over whether he will remain in Congress or leave the House altogether after three years as speaker. The Louisiana Republican had spent months traveling across the country and raising millions of dollars in a last-ditch effort to preserve the GOP's majority. Flashback: Johnson ascended to the speakership in October 2023 as a little-known lawmaker after weeks of GOP turmoil following Kevin McCarthy's historic ousting . Johnson spent much of his speakership navigating razor-thin Republican majorities, managing persistent GOP infighting and repeated conservative rebellions that brought legislative business to a standstill. But he also emerged as a prolific fundraiser and close Trump ally, helping shepherd the president's legislative agenda through a fractious Republican conference. Yes, but: Johnson had publicly insisted he intended to remain in Republican leadership even if the GOP lost control of the House. After suggesting to Fox News that he could return to Shreveport and start a lawn care business if Republicans lost the majority, Johnson told CBS News in October that he planned to remain the top House Republican regardless of the election's outcome. His political future had become the subject of private speculation among Republicans, with many lawmakers skeptical he would run for minority leader after a GOP loss. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to hold leadership elections Nov. 10, with candidates facing a Friday deadline to declare their intentions. The race will be decided by a secret ballot of Republican members, requiring only a majority of the conference to win. Trump could play a pivotal role in determining Johnson's successor, and Republicans are watching closely to see whether he throws his support behind a candidate.

0c3eadf7373f.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-u-s-political-map-anyones-guess-after-democratic-wave Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The U.S. political map? Anyone's guess after Democratic wave Politics Nov 4, 2026 10:14 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Voters took a wrecking ball to the traditional map of political battlegrounds, electing Democrats in states that were long considered reliably Republican. LIVE RESULTS: 2026 Midterm Election Map Kansas, South Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Iowa, all states Republican Donald Trump easily won two years ago in the presidential election, backed Democrats for the U.S. Senate and occasionally governor, too, on Tuesday. Now the question is whether the results represent a durable tectonic shift — one that could reshape the path to the presidency — or a fluke stemming from Trump's deep unpopularity and voters' unhappiness with the rising cost of living. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Either way, Republicans are reeling from losses they never expected at the start of this election year. Kansas backed a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932 as Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. WATCH LIVE: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions South Carolina rejected Republican Sen. Darline Graham in favor of pediatrician Annie Andrews, the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there since 1998. Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called it a "generational remake of the Senate map." The Democratic victories went even deeper in Texas. James Talarico beat Ken Paxton for Senate, Gina Hinojosa ousted Gov. Greg Abbott, Vikki Goodwin dislodged Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, and Nathan Johnson defeated Mayes Middleton for attorney general. Until Tuesday, no Democrat had won a statewide race in Texas since 1994. WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know "This was a wave election in Texas and across the country," Patrick acknowledged in a statement. Democrats also swept to power in states that were once battlegrounds but were more recently viewed as out of reach. Iowa chose Rob Sand for governor and Josh Turek for senator, and Ohio backed Amy Acton for governor and Sherrod Brown for senator. Brown is a former senator who lost his seat just two years ago, defeated by Republican Bernie Moreno. This time, he beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Most of Qatarâs gas remains trapped in the Gulf, but Doha is finding ways to export more of it while securing US supplies to meet some of its commitments. QatarEnergy has adopted the âHormuz shuttleâ tactic used by regional crude exporters, lifting LNG shipments from almost nothing in March to around a third of pre-war levels last month. Itâs also on pace to become the biggest buyer of US LNG by 2033, the Financial Times reported, citing research firm Wood Mackenzie.
To recover roughly $4 billion in lost monthly revenue, Jim Krane and Alex Munton argue in a Baker Institute paper that Qatar should pursue a âstrategic hedging strategy,â focused on improving commercial relations with Iran and Oman, attracting Chinese equity investment, and reinforcing security ties with Washington through Al Udeid Air Base.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump.
The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, was awarded to Melania Trump for her "significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine", according to the presidential decree.
It comes after the end of ceasefire in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, which allowed for the evacuation of several hundred people from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Russian and Ukrainian delegations - made up of ombudsmen who were involved in the evacuation mission as well as senior officials - are due to meet at the White House on Thursday on Melania Trump's invitation.
The White House said that Melania Trump had "independently initiated engagement between the two warring nations and successfully secured a ceasefire".
"This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady", it added.
Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides repeatedly thanked Melania Trump for brokering the ceasefire, though neither elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement.
The delegations travelling to the White House on Thursday will include Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian senior official Kirill Dmitriev.
Lubinets and Lantratova travelled together into Oleshky last week, in an unusual show of cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament, has previously been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team during peace talks with Russia.
He was responsible for informal contact between the White House and Moscow during the ceasefire, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Ukrainian media, and has confirmed he will take part in Thursday's talks.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian delegation will be made up of Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian businessman close to the Kremlin who has frequently taken part in US-brokered ceasefire talks.
Dmitriev and Arakhamia are veteran participants in high-level peace negotiations, and it is unusual for meetings involving such senior representatives to be convened through an initiative led by a US First Lady.
No details of what the White House event will entail have been shared. "There are important meetings ahead," said Lubinets in a social media post while announcing he was on his way to the US.
On Thursday Melania Trump will also deliver remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at 11:00 (16:00 GMT), the White House website said.
Zelensky's decree also cited Melania Trump's wider humanitarian work, including her efforts concerning Ukrainian children affected by the war, as reasons for giving her the Princess Olga award.
Melania Trump has largely remained discreet on foreign policy matters, but in 2025 she said an "open channel of communication" had been established with Russian President Vladimir Putin, allowing for Ukrainian children displaced in the war to be reunited with families.
Earlier this year the UN said the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime.
According to Ukraine, almost 20,000 children have been illegally sent to Russia and Belarus since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are also going to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral meeting since February. The talks will be focused on postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.
The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.
Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.
Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.
Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.
The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.
Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”
Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

DR Congo ordered an investigation into suspected illegal mining, after authorities seized thousands of tons of copper and cobalt. The probe could mark the start of a tougher response to illicit operators occupying sites, following years of complaints from some of the worldâs biggest mining companies. The justice minister said police, soldiers, and mining officials confiscated more than 500 trucks and machinery at several sites in the countryâs southeast.
DR Congo, the worldâs largest cobalt producer and a major copper supplier, is courting investment in metals used in electric cars and electronics and seeking greater economic benefits from its mineral wealth. But the government faces pressure to protect investorsâ mining rights, while safeguarding nearby communities, following repeated reports of harm to residentsâ health and livelihoods.

Nigeriaâs state oil company NNPC could float up to a 10% stake in a Lagos initial public offering and follow it up with a secondary listing in London or New York, its CEO told Reuters. The listing would be the second major energy IPO in Nigeria after that of the Dangote refinery, which sought to raise $1.6 billion.
NNPC manages Nigeriaâs joint venture agreements with oil producers such as ExxonMobil, Shell, and TotalEnergies and has subsidiaries that operate petrol stations and own the countryâs currently dormant refineries. Africaâs biggest oil producer has recorded an uptick in hydrocarbon investments in the past three years. NNPC plays a key role in the countryâs revenue generation because of its multibillion-dollar interests in oil and gas assets, but critics say it is emblematic of Nigeriaâs decades-old mismanagement of its oil earnings.

Kenyaâs growth prospects are being undercut by corruption and other governance challenges, the World Bank said in a report. The bank warned that graft could raise Kenyaâs borrowing needs, adding pressure to an already strained debt servicing burden that swallows roughly 60% of government revenue. It estimated that the country could incur a cost of 2% of GDP a year through higher fiscal deficits.
President William Ruto, who is seeking reelection next year, is looking to assuage frustrations about his governmentâs handling of the economy and the cost of living, which have spurred street protests in recent years. Kenyaâs economy grew 5.1% in the first half of 2026, a higher rate than the same period last year. But persistent deficits and rising debt service costs still leave the economy vulnerable, the World Bank said.

Senegalâs parliament rejected a revised budget on Tuesday, complicating the heavily indebted West African countryâs efforts to restore financing from the International Monetary Fund. A long-standing row over spending policies and relations with the IMF has created instability at the top of Senegalese politics, threatening to undermine creditorsâ confidence and delay IMF approval.
The governmentâs $13 billion plan included a cut to public investment in order to cover extra costs after high oil prices made energy subsidies more expensive. But Pastef, the majority party led by parliament speaker and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko, argued that households and essential public services would bear too much of the burden.
The country is seeking final approval for a three-year, $2.2 billion IMF loan program intended to ease budget pressures and unlock other financing. The deal, agreed in principle in September, would replace a program frozen after billions of dollars in unreported government debt emerged in 2024.

CVS Health confirmed Tuesday night that it would split in two, reversing the 2018 deal that brought together insurance behemoth Aetna and the 9,000-store retail pharmacy chain into a $117 billion empire.
That deal ushered in a new era of healthcare consolidation, lacing together huge swaths of a highly regulated industry into a conglomerate critics said led to less competition and higher prices for consumers. Now, these companies are facing increasing regulatory scrutiny and political pressure in Washington, which is only expected to grow after Democrats regain control of Congress in January.
âWe believe based off of where we are and how weâre performing, the businesses are best served by splitting,â CVS Chief Executive David Joyner told The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.

American voters roundly rejected data centers nearly anywhere they were on the ballot Tuesday, a rebuke sure to rattle investors already growing skittish about the AI buildout. Residents in more than 30 localities across nine states voted for moratoriums, outright bans, and other measures, some in direct response to specific projects underway. Edgewater, Fla. overwhelmingly voted to embed a data-center ban in the cityâs charter, and voters in Perry, Ohio passed a measure placing financial and operational constraints on hyperscalers seeking tax breaks. Democrats running in more than 130 federal and gubernatorial races aired anti-tech or anti-data center ads this cycle, one analysis showed. The pressure pushed some Republican candidates including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, an AI booster just a few months ago, into promises of tougher regulation; he lost anyway.
Banks and asset managers financing the buildout have already begun treating local opposition as a credit risk, while hyperscalers are rushing to hire community liaisons. Meanwhile, tech companies bracing for the vibe shift are trying to rebrand the data centers as âcompute campusesâ with mixed results, Semaforâs Ashley Gold reported.

Prediction markets emerged as big winners of the midterms. Kalshi and Polymarket correctly called the Democratic sweep of Congress by wider margins than most polling models, as well as key battleground races, though they missed surprises like Texas Gov. Greg Abbottâs loss and Democratic Senate victories in Iowa and South Carolina.
Trading volume on down-ballot elections grew nearly fivefold from the 2024 cycle to this yearâs midterms to $1.8 billion, according to a Semafor analysis of the sitesâ public data feeds. Sports and crypto bets still dwarf election contracts across both platforms, and the 2026 midterms attracted less trading interest than the presidential race.
Prediction markets have been racing to win over the sports-betting and gambling industriesâ customers, executing aggressive ad campaigns to expand their influence. Kalshi has struck business partnerships with media outlets including CNN and Dow Jones, and its ad campaign on Meta rivals super PAC spending; Kalshi and Polymarket have also aired a slew of star-studded ads. But itâs one thing to bring in revenue, itâs another to do what the prediction markets say they do well: predict.

b03dab954375.text:
Lizâs view
After the presidential election exactly two years ago, Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy rode into Washington as protagonists of a new type of politics, running the short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. Last night, both suffered the worst defeats of their political careers.
Musk had moved many of his businesses to Texas and spent more than $200 million to hold the state for Republicans â part of a 2026 blitz that dwarfs any political spending by a single donor in a single election cycle â with returns that were diminishing, if not outright negative. Senate candidate Ken Paxtonâs numbers faded the more Musk spent. Ramaswamy lost his bid for Ohio governor, where his Republican predecessor won four years ago by 25 points, a bigger swing than can be explained by Trumpâs unpopularity and the blue wave that crested nearly everywhere.
The two seemed to embody a new type of hard-edged conservative politics that lives at the intersection of Twitter and money, driven by wealthy and successful businessmen who believed their wealth and success would translate into political victories and personal popularity.
I watched last nightâs results from Ramaswamyâs gloomy election night party at an upscale Marriott in Columbus, Ohio, where a prayer circle was going in the womenâs bathroom by 9:45 pm. The outcomes suggest that money and its purest embodiments will be forced to slip politely back behind the curtain, to support more relatable public figures. Ramaswamyâs fellow anti-woke traveler and fringe Wall Streeter, James Fishback, lost even earlier, in the primaries for Florida governor.
The biggest money in American corporate history â the huge new investments in AI â also had a hard night, as Trumpâs embrace of the technology helped doom his party. Now they have to find new ways to recast their projects as pro-worker and community-friendly to make sure the AI buildout actually happens â and to find spokespeople more appealing than the DOGE twins.
Notable
- Shares in Muskâs Tesla and SpaceX slide about 5% in pre-market trading Wednesday after Democrats won in Texas, where both companies are headquartered.

3985f505255f.text:
Yinkaâs view
Last nightâs sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections heralds a shift in vibes rather than policy.
As John âJTâ Tomaszewski, the National Endowment for Democracyâs senior director for Africa, told me, African countries will âstill struggleâ to get on the agenda because of the competing domestic priorities battling for lawmakersâ attention following a chastening electoral rebuke to President Donald Trump. There will, however, be more scope for congressional scrutiny of his administrationâs policies. Democrats will likely be keen to use hearings and investigations to revisit the dismantling of USAID and the human costs of cuts to foreign assistance.
Some of that would be welcomed because there are still key questions about the administrationâs decisions that probably deserve public answers. They will certainly embarrass the White House, which is kind of the point, says Cameron Hudson, a George W. Bush-era official. But I am less convinced that the theater of hearings will translate into meaningful changes in US-Africa policy.
Veteran Democrats understand this challenge. A former US ambassador under Joe Biden told me he would like to see â but doesnât expect â a more assertive Democratic agenda setting out what the US relationship with Africa should actually look like. But, this person suggested, there isnât any political appetite left for restoring traditional development assistance: âEverybodyâs moved on from that.â
Meanwhile, African governments have more immediate concerns. One African ambassador, who asked not to be identified, noted visa bans and restrictions currently affect more than half of sub-Saharan African countries, questioning how Washington can keep promoting âcommercial diplomacyâ while making it harder for African business leaders to travel to the US. âHow can the US keep talking about moving to do commerce with Africa when its business leaders canât visit?â the ambassador asked.
There may be a new mood in Washington, but for now, African governments will have to judge Washington by what it does, not what Democrats say about what Trump has done. As the ambassador said: âWeâll welcome the changes so we can have more soberness.â
Notable
- South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the outcome of the US midterm elections signals a shift in the geopolitical landscape that could open the way for a reset in Pretoriaâs strained ties with Washington.

Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.
After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.
"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."
Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.
But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.
"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.
"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".
The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.
Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.
But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.
The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.
"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".
Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.
He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.
Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.
Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.
Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.
Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."
Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.
"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.
That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.
Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."
Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.

Tennis great Rafael Nadal is set to join the board of Spanish football giants Real Madrid.
Nadal won 22 Grand Slam titles, two Olympic gold medals and helped Spain claim five Davis Cups before retiring in 2024.
Real's members will be asked to approve the 40-year-old's appointment to the board at a meeting later this month.
In a statement announcing the move, external, the club said Nadal was "one of the greatest legends in the history of sport and one of the most admired and recognised Spanish athletes in the world".
"It is a great source of pride that a figure of his sporting and human stature, a benchmark of Spanish and world sport, will become part of our board of directors and contribute, from this position of responsibility, to the present and future of our club," Real added.
The tennis legend - a boyhood Real fan who holds member's number 67,778 - included a photo of himself as a child in a club kit in his response to the news.
"I want to thank president Florentino Perez and the board for proposing that I join the board of directors of Real Madrid," Nadal said in his post on X, external.
"I have accepted this proposal with great excitement, a desire to learn, and a willingness to contribute everything I can."
It is currently unclear as to what responsibilities Nadal would hold on the club's board.
Perez was re-elected to serve a new four-year term as Real president in June, having held the office since 2009.
He swiftly appointed Jose Mourinho to a second spell as head coach, hoping to improve the club's fortunes after they went a second season without a trophy in La Liga, the Champions League or the Copa del Rey.
Real are currently third in the league after 11 games - three points behind defending champions Barcelona.

74c38403bbe9.text: Democrats' big night gives them a chance to turn voter anger over high energy prices into legislative action and congressional oversight, but divisions within the party could complicate their plans. Why it matters: This was an energy election . High gasoline prices, record diesel costs, and rising power bills fueled discontent with President Trump and his party. Voters' rebukes of data centers could slow the buildout of power-hungry AI infrastructure. The latest: Stunning Senate wins in red states and House wins nationwide propelled Democrats to control of both chambers, and flipped several governor's mansions. Energy costs were prominent in key races, such as Democrats hitting GOP rivals over farmers' bills in Iowa, Kansas and Ohio. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) bashed Greg Abbott (R) over his prior embrace of data centers in the state where developers are planning big projects. The data center backlash also featured in Ohio and Pennsylvania, where Sherrod Brown defeated Sen. Jon Husted (R) and Paige Cognetti unseated Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R). Both Republicans faced criticism over their support for data centers. State of play: A detailed Democratic energy agenda hasn't emerged, but there are early clues. Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer tied Republicans to electricity costs in his first comments after returns came in. Likely Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has vowed to quickly push an affordability agenda, with energy as a key pillar. He tasked Reps. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.) and Mike Levin (D-Calif.) with leading a "Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group" that crafted ideas, though they remain under wraps. Another potential source of ideas: Hundreds of proposals backed this year by the 100-plus member House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition. Some could gain bipartisan backing, like support for advanced nuclear power. But other areas would be largely symbolic, like restoring some IRA tax credits. Catch up quick: In the Senate, Schumer has offered broad areas of focus around grid development, affordability and consumer protections, and clean energy. He has vowed to restore clean energy tax credits, while pledging "systematic protection for consumers from rising prices." Other ideas include more support for energy efficiency and greater transparency in utility bills. The intrigue: Democrats did not make climate change a midterm messaging focus. Watch whether progressives push to revive an explicitly climate-focused agenda. My thought bubble: Don't expect Democrats to bring back their select committee on climate change, which Republicans disbanded after winning House control in 2022. There has not been a decision announced. But the party's shift away from messaging focused on climate is reason to be doubtful, even as global warming marches on. What's next: The most immediate thing to watch is how the results may affect the politics of the bipartisan permitting deal in the lame duck. Some House progressives have argued that Dems could get a permitting deal more to their liking next year. But backers of the current bill see almost no chance of a political opening to craft a more liberal bill that Trump would sign or could even clear the Senate. The permitting fight has also opened rifts within the Democratic coalition, with multiple unions and the clean energy industry backing the bill, while many environmentalists are undecided or flatly opposed. The debate also highlights broader divisions between the "abundance movement" and progressives who want a harder line against fossil fuels Those divisions could extend well beyond the lame duck permitting fight, influencing future legislative priorities and the policy agendas of presidential hopefuls as 2028 jockeying begins in earnest. The bottom line: One thing already clear is that Democrats are lining up energy-focused oversight of Trump's diesel agreement with Moscow, offshore wind policies and much more.
