Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El NiÃ±o weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El NiÃ±o, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El NiÃ±o, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El NiÃ±o also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El NiÃ±o predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El NiÃ±o.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El NiÃ±o is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El NiÃ±o is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El NiÃ±o tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

dae6394b592a.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/pope-leo-xiv-welcomes-bob-dylan-to-the-vatican-in-a-brief-visit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo XIV welcomes Bob Dylan to the Vatican in a brief visit Arts Nov 4, 2026 6:06 PM EST VATICAN CITY (AP) — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy. The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One." READ MORE: Kennedy Center names 2026 honorees as Trump renovation battle moves show offsite Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled." Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano. Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music. He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for the 1967 album John Wesley Harding. Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head. It wasn't Dylan's first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy. Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like "Gotta Serve Somebody" and "Saved." In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays. Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven" that contains the lyric, "I've been all around the world, boys/Now I'm trying to get to heaven before they close the door." AP reporter Scott Bauer contributed from Madison, Wisconsin. Democrats’ historic sweep of Texas on Tuesday raises new possibilities of environmental reform after more than 30 years of Republican rule in the home of the nation’s oil and gas industry.
That includes opportunities to cement safeguards for data center development, lower energy costs and, over time, appoint new commissioners to the state’s regulatory agencies and boost environmentally protective standards.
“We have a generational shift in leadership here,” said Adrian Shelley, state director of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group. “I think there’s going to be a real appetite for reform.”
Both the U.S. Senate and governor races were called before midnight Central Time, quickly crushing the longheld skepticism of the potential of a Democrat-led Texas. Democrats also took the House in the state Legislature.
The blue wave in Texas resulted, in part, from an upswell of public outrage over the state’s booming buildout of data centers for artificial intelligence that are gobbling massive amounts of electricity and failing to disclose their water use, experts said Wednesday. When the Democratic administration takes office in January, data centers will sit at the center of its political crosshairs.
“The new state leadership has a clear mandate to rein in the data center industry,” Shelley said. “I think the days of Texas being unequivocally open for business are over.”
Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative who was largely unknown earlier this year, unseated three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was backed by some of the richest and most powerful forces across the country.
Hinojosa will be the first Hispanic politician to lead the state, where Latinos make up the largest population, and will preside over the second-largest state economy in the country, after California.
The victory of James Talarico against Attorney General Ken Paxton ends decades of Republican rule in the U.S. Senate, with the last Democratic senator elected in 1988. It was also the most expensive Senate race in history, with the richest man on earth, Elon Musk, contributing more than $160 million to secure Paxton’s victory.
Democrat Jon Rosenthal defeated a former Tarrant County GOP chair with a storied record of extremism, Bo French, for one of three seats at the state’s oil and gas regulator, the Railroad Commission.
“Pretty much everyone who won the statewide level is a champ on the environment,” said Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas. “That’s really exciting.”
Midterm Shift Signals Big Risk for Data Centers in Texas
Hinojosa’s election has panicked the data center industry over its future in one of the largest markets in the U.S. While Abbott switched from issuing an enthusiastic invitation for data centers to invest and develop in Texas to a list of stringent directives, Hinojosa has campaigned on calling an immediate moratorium on new data centers.
Voters clearly want the data center industry to be held accountable, said the Lone Star Chapter of the Sierra Club’s legislative director, Cyrus Reed.
“For a long time, they’ve had not only a seat at the table, they’ve actually been creating the table with some of the laws that have been passed,” Reed said.
Hinojosa’s election signals a significant shift in Texas’ data center policies, global analysis firm Wood Mackenzie said Wednesday.
Even so, the state will remain a leading market for data center investments, given its renewable resources, natural gas infrastructure and regulatory autonomy from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Wood Mackenzie added.
Jess Heck, the director of Texas government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s largest trade group, said its members will continue to engage with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities and ensure the growth of digital infrastructure delivers clear benefits for Texans.
“Enhancing affordability, creating jobs, and keeping the state’s economy strong are top priorities for Texans,” Heck said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Data centers can continue to play a crucial role in advancing those priorities by bringing investment to local communities and generating critical tax revenue to support local governments and school districts across the state.”
The Dallas-Fort Worth region has the largest concentration of data centers in the state. The most rapid expansion of the industry is in Ellis County, some 30 minutes south of downtown Dallas.
On Election Day, Lacey Hamel, 39, and Jazmin Villegas, 44, stood outside the Red Oak Municipal Center waving at voters driving in and out of the building’s lot. The two wore bright yellow shirts that said, “No More Data Centers.” They’re members of Save Our Red Oak, a group tracking and trying to slow down the expansion of data centers across seven campuses in the city.
As in other rural Texas counties with swaths of land, data centers emerged as a critical issue for the election in Red Oak.
Members of the Red Oak group had asked Abbott to call a special legislative session over the industry’s rapid growth. “That ship has sailed,” Hamel said.
Among their data center protest group, set in a staunchly Republican county where nearly two-thirds of residents voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, several people crossed party lines over frustrations on data centers, Hamel said. It informed how she voted, too.
“This is one of those issues where it’s affecting our air, it’s affecting our land, it’s affecting our water, it’s affecting our kids,” Hamel said.

An international team of lawyers on Wednesday filed a coordinated battery of lawsuits against JBS, the world’s largest meat company, and its financiers, accusing them of money laundering in connection with the destruction of the Amazon rainforest.
The 14 legal actions, filed in four European jurisdictions, accuse JBS and its affiliated banks, asset managers, accountants and lawyers of criminal complicity in connection with the meat giant’s purchase of cattle from deforested land, in violation of Brazilian law. JBS, a historically Brazilian company, is now officially headquartered in the Netherlands, though it continues to maintain major operations in Brazil and to source much of its beef from the Amazon and neighboring ecosystems.
The lawsuits are the latest attempts by advocacy groups to open up new legal avenues to challenge JBS, which recent research has found emits as much planet-warming methane as oil giants ExxonMobil and Shell combined.
The Transnational Legal Coalition, a newly formed network of advocacy groups and lawyers that prosecutes environmental crimes and filed the complaints, says the lawsuits are the first in a series of legal efforts that will target deforestation in JBS’s supply chain. Raising livestock is the biggest driver of forest loss in the world’s largest rainforest, a crucial ecosystem for stabilizing Earth’s atmosphere and a massive harbor for biodiversity.
The coalition commissioned a study to support their filings, conducted by the environmental research group AidEnvironment, which found that JBS was linked to more than 16 million deforested acres, both through direct and indirect suppliers.
The complaints focus on European Union anti-money laundering laws, which require financial institutions, attorneys and accountants to do “enhanced due diligence” on businesses that have a high risk of deforestation in their supply chains. They allege JBS makes huge profits off cattle raised on land that is likely criminally deforested, and therefore, the cattle are criminal property.
They argue these institutions, which include the banks Barclays and Rabobank, the asset manager BlackRock and accounting firms KPMG and EY, were all obligated to perform enhanced due diligence but did not. The coalition also filed a criminal complaint with public prosecutors in the Dutch criminal justice system against JBS directly, accusing the company of money laundering.
“If the European enabler complied with its enhanced due diligence obligations, it would have found out about the risk that JBS is engaged in money laundering and would either have stopped working with JBS or reported them to the criminal authorities,” said George Collecott, an attorney with the Global Legal Action Network, one of the coalition members. “As each of the financial institutions have a long-standing relationship with JBS, they haven’t done that.”
The EU’s anti-money laundering law says a failure to report suspected money laundering to authorities is an offense by both the company and company employees, including compliance officers.
“What we’re really asking is for the regulators in the U.K., Germany, Netherlands and Ireland to open an investigation into these financial institutions and investigate whether there has been a failure of these due diligence obligations,” Collecott said. “It’s really making sure the banks can’t plead ignorance.”
In a response to Inside Climate News, a Barclays spokesperson said the company had reviewed the legal complaint but could not comment. The bank said it has conducted enhanced due diligence for clients engaged in beef production since 2021.
JBS did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Rabobank, Blackrock, KPMG or EY.
As part of its long-sought effort to list on the New York Stock Exchange, which it accomplished successfully in 2025, JBS re-incorporated in the Netherlands, where many companies take advantage of Dutch tax exemptions.
Dutch law, however, requires companies to meet a “duty of care” threshold, which includes harms caused by greenhouse gases. That prompted Greenpeace Netherlands in April to file a preliminary letter with the Dutch authorities, indicating its intent to sue the company.
In this case, Greenpeace Netherlands plans to sue because of the company’s expansion into Nigeria. In its letter, the group asked for details about the company’s intended operations there, its first on the African continent. So far, Greenpeace Netherlands says, neither the Nigerian government nor JBS has provided information about its $2.5 billion investment to develop poultry, beef and pork processing facilities there.
As JBS expands its global footprint, it has also pulled back on its climate commitments. In July, the company issued its annual sustainability report, in which it said it would abandon its previous goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2040. It also dropped any mentions of its goal to eliminate deforestation connected to its Brazilian supply chains.

Here's how to fight back Health Nov 4, 2026 5:57 PM EST As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains. The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there's also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it. Please check your inbox to confirm. In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. "I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck," he said. Scientists are trying to understand what causes SAD No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions. In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness. WATCH: What to know about treating Seasonal Affective Disorder Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains' alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier. Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression. When days get shorter, powerful light can help Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University's Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light. Research supports using a light that's about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs. WATCH: What to know about the latest push to make daylight saving time permanent Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said. Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light. If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered. Talk therapy and medication can also help some with SAD Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days. Light therapy's benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said. READ MORE: Daylight saving time causes lower productivity and higher health care costs, studies say CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts. Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee. Carla K. 095de24ca37b.text: By — Danica Kirka, Associated Press Danica Kirka, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ex-prince-andrew-called-to-testify-in-civil-case-1st-royal-in-156-years-to-get-witness-summons Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ex-Prince Andrew called to testify in civil case, 1st royal in 156 years to get witness summons World Nov 4, 2026 5:44 PM EST LONDON (AP) — The former Prince Andrew has been called to testify as a witness in a civil fraud trial, marking what is believed to be the first time in more than 150 years that a member of the royal family has received a witness summons, British media reported on Wednesday. The summons comes after a judge at the High Court in London gave the green light last month for the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, to be called to testify about payments he allegedly received from the parties in the case. Mountbatten-Windsor may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify. The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former adviser Selman Turk misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound ($1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. Mountbatten-Windsor, a younger brother of King Charles III, repaid the money in 2021 and he is not a party to the suit. Turk claims that Isbilen authorized the payment in hopes that Mountbatten-Windsor might be able to use his connections to help her husband, who has been imprisoned in Turkey since 2015. Isbilen alleges that her husband is the victim of political persecution. Isbilen's attorneys said last month that they believed this would be the first time since 1870 that a member of the royal family was subject to a witness summons. At that time, the future King Edward VII, then the Prince of Wales, was called to testify in the divorce case brought by Charles Mordaunt, a baronet and member of Parliament. The prince accepted the summons and denied having improper relations with Mordaunt's wife, Harriet Mordaunt. Mountbatten-Windsor is facing his own legal troubles as several British police forces investigate his links to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. British authorities began their inquiries after the U.S. Department of Justice released millions of pages of documents from its investigation of Epstein earlier this year. Charles stripped Mountbatten-Windsor of his princely title in late 2025 as he tried to shield the royal family from the scandal surrounding his brother's relationship with Epstein. Georgia voters have broken the Republican grip on the state’s energy regulator, giving Democrats control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years.
Their victories come amid growing frustration over rising electricity bills, a data center buildout and calls for greater accountability from Georgia Power.
On Tuesday, Democrat Peter Hubbard was reelected after winning a seat in a special election last year. Democrat Sheila Edwards, a community activist and business owner, also won a seat.
“Thank you, Georgia!” Hubbard said in a Facebook post early Wednesday. “You have spoken, and Shelia Edwards and I are ready to keep fighting for a future that puts Georgians at the center of our energy policy.”
“Throughout this campaign, I’ve talked about putting People Before Profits, addressing rising utility bills, bringing transparency and accountability to the Public Service Commission, and making sure large data centers pay their fair share,” Edwards said in a Facebook post. “Those commitments don’t end with an election.”
The result is a major shift for the PSC, which regulates public utilities, including the state’s largest energy utility, Georgia Power. Commissioners are tasked with regulating utility rates, overseeing utility service and reliability and approving utility resource plans and major infrastructure investments.
Republicans held a 5-0 majority on the commission from 2006 until 2025, when Hubbard and fellow Democrat Alicia Johnson won seats.
During those nearly two decades, Georgia Power customers saw major rate increases in 2007, 2010, 2013, 2019 and 2022. Since 2023, six more have raised monthly bills by about $44.
Much of the increases were driven by costs tied to the troubled expansion of nuclear Plant Vogtle, in Burke County. Construction began in 2009 after commission approval, with the project expected to finish in 2017 before a series of setbacks. In the end, it took 15 years to complete and went more than $17 billion over budget. While customers continue to pay for the project, the costs of building out gas plants to power data centers have been tacked onto their bills.
“The results show that people are very angry about data centers and climate emissions,” said Patty Durand, founder of Georgians for Affordable Energy. She pointed to a series of protests demanding clean energy in 2024 and 2025. “I won’t pretend it’s not about high bills too, but those are tied to gas and data centers as well.”
The election of Hubbard and Johnson in 2025 was the first signal Georgia voters wanted change in the way utilities, and especially rate increases, are regulated. “It was shocking,” said Charles Bullock, a political science professor at the University of Georgia. “It may have been a straw in the wind of the state’s political realignment.”
Johnson won a five-year term, while Hubbard was elected for just one year, due to a special election schedule. His reelection means he will be in office until 2032, with an early stamp of approval from voters. 
Edwards beat first-time candidate Josh Tolbert by 10.6 points and Hubbard beat former Republican Commissioner Fitz Johnson by 12.8 points, the largest margin of any statewide candidate this cycle in Georgia other than U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who beat his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, by about 17 points.
The Democrats’ victories came despite being outspent by Republican candidates and outside groups. The Republican campaigns raised more than $1 million combined, largely driven by Fitz Johnson’s fundraising, compared with less than $600,000 for the Democratic candidates. Democratic fundraising relied more heavily on individual donations, while Republican candidates received substantially more money from corporate donors.

According to an analysis by the Energy and Policy Institute, the two Republican candidates received a combined $214,100 in contributions of $500 or more from donors associated with entities regulated by the PSC, compared with just $6,500 for the Democratic candidates.
Outside spending in the races topped $5 million, much of it going toward television, digital and other campaign advertising. More than $3 million went toward supporting Tolbert, nearly all of it through a group called Powering Georgia’s Future, which is backed by a separate entity, Competence Matters. Competence Matters is not required to disclose donors. Both Powering Georgia’s Future and Competence Matters websites went dark following the election.
Another $1.5 million was spent through Georgia Conservation Voters in support of Hubbard and Edwards. That money came from the group’s national affiliate, the League of Conservation Voters, as well as from entities including the Jane Fonda Climate PAC and Green Advocacy Project.
Grassroots efforts by volunteers, watchdog groups and activists also helped support the Democratic campaigns. A coalition of more than 30 groups, including Georgians for Affordable Energy, Georgia WAND and Young Democrats of Georgia, organized social media outreach and distributed flyers, yard signs and bumper stickers to compete with the better-funded Republican campaigns.
The results reflect growing political attention to energy costs and utility policy. Nationally, Democrats flipped Senate and House seats in deep red states where Americans have been hit hardest by energy prices and data center buildouts. 
The Democratic majority on the PSC will have an opportunity to follow through on campaign promises to increase scrutiny of Georgia Power and strengthen consumer protections. After their election last year, Alicia Johnson and Hubbard opposed a $16 billion grid expansion dominated by natural gas, which ultimately passed 3-2. 3eb9fe28310b.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/whats-next-in-the-investigation-of-the-learjet-crash-in-florida-that-killed-9 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9? Nation Nov 4, 2026 5:37 PM EST Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane. The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people aboard the Bahamas-bound Learjet, and it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause. READ MORE: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says Dramatic bystander videos combined with the the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder would also help if investigators can find it intact. "Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again," NTSB member Tom Chapman said. Here's what investigators are doing now and what comes next: Investigators are gathering critical evidence The NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane's pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact. Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet's cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft. "That will be very important data," Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won't doom the investigation. "Without it, our folks are very, very good. We're still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired." READ MORE: Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters) and she asked them for a better route through the area. It's not clear why the pilots didn't fly around the storms. Torrential rains in Florida over the past week have hindered the investigators' work. The crater filled with rainwater, possibly concealing parts of the wreckage under water, and a utility pole had to be removed. The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report that to investigators to collect. The initial NTSB report will take about a month The agency's findings so far are limited, but its experts will publish a preliminary report describing the facts of what happened about 30 days after the crash. It won't include analysis or cause, which will come in a later more detailed report. The force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane. Any evidence investigators are able to gather will be taken to a secure hangar where they can test or try to reassemble smashed components to better understand what happened. READ MORE: Parts of jet's tail found more than a mile from plane crash site in South Florida, official says Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he doesn't understand why the plane descended from its cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,500 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said. "If I'm looking at thunderstorms, I'd rather be at 41 than at 35. You've got a better view, you're more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it," Cox said. "I don't understand why they came down." Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane's weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services. Investigators will dig deeper Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and the Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered at around 35,000 feet (11,000 meters). Images that overlay the flight path atop weather radar maps show the Learjet flew directly into a small red storm cell that quickly worsened. But the agency will consider a myriad of factors that may have contributed to the crash. Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed. Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect surveillance footage that might show the crash. In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB can hold investigative hearings during which investigators question people, as it did after last year's UPS plane crash. The final report could take more than a year Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. NTSB's roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations. Final reports include extensive details about what happened and identify the probable causes. The NTSB recommends changes to prevent similar crashes and improve safety, but it doesn't have the power to require those changes to be installed or enforced. The responsibility for adopting those falls to the FAA, the industry and Congress

(AP) — Florida authorities said two people were dead, including a suspect, after witnesses reported a shooting Wednesday at Citibank's sprawling business complex that employs thousands in the Tampa area. More than 360 deputies swarmed the campus, the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office said. TV video showed long lines of workers streaming out of the office buildings. The sheriff's office said in a social media post that it had "responded to an active threat and is currently clearing the building." The sheriff's office said a suspect and one other person were dead. It was not immediately known whether anyone else was injured. "We believe this is a targeted incident," Sheriff Chad Chronister posted on the social platform X. The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant's employees. Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from officers who responded to the Citibank complex described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search of the complex's buildings. Officers found people sheltering in locked rooms and closets, and carefully escorted them from the buildings and parking garage. Citigroup said in a statement that it was "aware of an incident" at the complex and was cooperating with authorities. Doug Merritt said he was startled when his son called him from the Citibank campus, saying he had fled after hearing gunshots. "He was very close to it," Merritt told The Associated Press. "He left all this stuff where he was at and he was able to get out of there." For around an hour, Merritt said, he didn't know whether his son was safe as he struggled to get in touch over a bad internet connection. "I wanted him to get to safety," he said. "I was upset." Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story. Dem lawmakers vow inquest into CISA cuts, intel policy
House Democrats will investigate the administration's cyberdefense cuts, while Senate Dems will control confirmation hearings for the officials who lead the nation’s security agencies.
House Democrats plan to investigate how the Trump administration’s cuts to the nation’s cyberdefense agency affected its ability to protect federal networks and help states secure elections, while their Senate counterparts vow to scrutinize whether intelligence agencies can deliver findings that contradict the president without putting analysts’ jobs at risk.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., who is in line to chair the House Homeland Security Committee when Democrats take both houses of Congress in January, said he and his colleagues would examine the department’s use of its powers against Americans, its immigration enforcement practices, and its dealings with contractors.
The party’s wins in both chambers mean Democrats will decide which officials to call before Congress and what records to seek, under subpoena authorities given to whichever party has the majority in a given chamber.
If a permanent director for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is nominated again, Senate Democrats will also have a say in who leads the agency. The same can be said for a nominee to lead the National Counterterrorism Center, whose previous leader resigned earlier this year.
“We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans, its out of control immigration policies, and its blatantly corrupt self-dealing,” Thompson told Nextgov/FCW. “The American people expect nothing less, and we will deliver.”
The panel also plans to examine the department’s surveillance of Americans engaged in protected speech, its handling of whistleblowers and whether federal officials steered contracts to political allies. On cybersecurity, they want to know how DHS is preparing for attacks aided by artificial intelligence and what became of services the department scaled back.
What CISA lost in the cuts
Thompson and Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., who is positioned to chair the Homeland Security cyber subcommittee, have already asked Congress’ watchdog to assess the impact of staffing cuts at CISA, which helps defend civilian federal networks and other frequent hacker targets like water systems and telecom networks.
CISA lost roughly a third of its workforce after Trump retook office, though the agency has made efforts to refill its roster. By September, about 250 prospective hires had tentative offers and were waiting for clearances, acting Director Nick Andersen said, as part of an effort under DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to recant some of the cuts made to the cyberdefense agency over the last two years.
Ramirez, in a June interview with Nextgov/FCW, said she was planning a significant DHS overhaul bill for next year. She also gave positive feedback on CISA’s rehiring plans, though she added it may not be enough.
In a post on X after the election, she had a message for Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House aide Stephen Miller and others involved in immigration enforcement: “Clear your schedule.”
In the Senate, the retirement of Michigan Democrat Gary Peters puts Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., next in seniority among Democrats on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. Hassan and Peters have already asked DHS to preserve records belonging to former Secretary Kristi Noem and her adviser Corey Lewandowski.
Hassan has also pressed CISA on its own security practices after reports that a contractor left agency account information and passwords in a public database.
One issue facing both homeland security panels could come due before Democrats take over. A law protecting companies from lawsuits when they share information about cyber threats is operating under a temporary extension through Dec. 11. Without a longer renewal planted this year, the incoming chairs could inherit a fight over the legal protections companies rely on when communicating with the government about cyberattacks.
When intelligence findings conflict with the White House
Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., and Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., are in line to chair the intelligence committees in their respective chambers after two years of disputes over whether spy agencies can deliver findings that contradict the president without putting analysts’ jobs at risk.
One major dispute centered on Tren de Aragua, the Venezuelan gang Trump said was carrying out an invasion at the direction of Nicolás Maduro’s government.
Most U.S. intelligence agencies assessed that Maduro was not directing the gang’s operations in the United States. Then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard subsequently fired the two leaders of the National Intelligence Council, which produced the assessment.
Warner also challenged Gabbard directly over Iran. At a Senate hearing in March, weeks after the U.S. and Israel went to war, he pressed her on a passage in her written testimony that she skipped in her opening remarks. It said Iran had made no effort to rebuild its uranium enrichment capability after U.S. strikes the previous June, a finding that bore on President Donald Trump’s claim that Iran posed an imminent threat.
A day earlier, Joe Kent, Trump’s director of the National Counterterrorism Center, had resigned over the war, saying he did not believe Iran posed such a threat.
Last June, after Trump said U.S. strikes had “obliterated” three Iranian nuclear sites, a preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency assessment suggested the attacks could have set the program back only a few months.
When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired DIA Director Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse that August without explanation, Warner pointed to the dispute in accusing the administration of “treating intelligence as a loyalty test.”

0f87c4499652.text: By — Scott Bauer, Associated Press Scott Bauer, Associated Press By — Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-win-full-control-of-more-state-governments-and-the-texas-house Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House Politics Nov 4, 2026 4:50 PM EST MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrats in Texas took control of the state House after historic wins for governor and U.S. Senate, part of a series of sweeping gains nationwide in Tuesday's elections that shifted the balance of power across several battleground and Republican-leaning states. It will be the first time Democrats control the House in Texas since Republicans took over after the 2002 election. Republicans are keeping control of the Senate in the state — which also elected Gina Hinojosa its first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In this year's midterm elections, the party took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors' offices — in at least five states where they previously shared power. The wins put pressure on the party to answer to an electorate angry over the rising cost of living, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of affordable housing. State governments shape a wide array of policies affecting everyday lives, including tax rates and abortion rights, school choice and education funding, data center development, and the use of artificial intelligence and law enforcement surveillance cameras. WATCH: Takeaways from the 2026 midterms and answers to your election questions "Now it's time to deliver," said Devin Remiker, chairman of Wisconsin's Democratic Party, which retained the governor's office and successfully flipped both chambers of the state Legislature, breaking a 16-year Republican majority. Democrats prevail in battleground states Democrats also won or retained full control of both chambers of the legislatures in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania and kept the governor's office for trifectas in all three. In Nevada, they gained control by winning the governor's seat and retaining the legislature. There will be pressure on Democrats in Wisconsin and other battleground states to redraw congressional maps, just as President Donald Trump successfully urged eight Republican-led states to do ahead of this election. But that backfired, with Republicans losing most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip and others they had banked on winning. The Republican congressional redistricting in Texas may have mobilized additional Democratic voters in some parts of the state who helped drive gains in the statehouse, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. But "when we're trying to think about why Democrats won, it's one man in the White House and his policies — Donald Trump," Jones said. Even under maps that favored Republicans in Wisconsin, Democrats picked up two congressional seats in Tuesday's races. That means the state will have an evenly divided congressional delegation in 2027. Democrats also break up Republican trifectas and supermajorities Democrats will also hold at least 28 governorships in 2027, with pickups in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states long held by Republicans. And the party broke or prevented Republican supermajorities in nine legislative chambers in eight states: Florida, South Carolina, Indiana, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina. That means Republicans would need help from Democratic lawmakers to override a Democratic governor's veto in Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. The Associated Press has not called the governor's race in Kansas. The wins come after Democrats lost nearly 1,000 state legislative seats during President Barack Obama's tenure, a slide they've been trying to reverse for several cycles. READ MORE: Democrats win governorships in Texas and other GOP-controlled states in rebuke to Republicans It's the biggest single-election change of partisan power in state governments since 2010, said Katie Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures. Lawmakers who will soon be in the majority say the change brings expectations. "We know that people will be counting on us to deliver, and we take that incredibly seriously," said Wisconsin state Rep. Greta Neubauer, currently the minority leader of state Assembly Democrats. Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said the party won "historic levels of power in statehouses." She said they hadn't flipped this many seats nationwide since the 1980s. This time, she said, Democrats will have to focus on issues that matter to middle-class voters such as improving educational opportunities and increasing access to healthcare, particularly in rural areas. "This election is about kitchen-table issues; it's about economic opportunities," she said Wednesday. "That is what the mandate is about." Wins put spotlight on Democratic priorities in 2027 The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, gas and utility bills were campaign talking points after legislative sessions packed with bills aiming to make life more affordable for Americans, while also providing tax relief and reining in data center development and the use of artificial intelligence. The coming legislative session could see major efforts to lighten the tax burden on the middle class, relax housing regulations, expand access to healthcare, and force utilities and data center developers to do more to stop electricity bills from rising. 1c4fccfb4d83.text: Democrats' midterm tsunami obscured a major polling miss: Surveys correctly anticipated a blue wave, but failed to capture its full force. Why it matters: Pollsters appear to have underestimated Democrats by a wider margin than they underestimated Republicans in 2016 or 2024 — even if they got the headline outcome right this time. By the numbers: Democrats are on track to win the national House popular vote by roughly 13 points, compared with a final Silver Bulletin polling average of 8.9 points, according to an initial analysis by The Argument's Lakshya Jain . That roughly 4-point gap is similar to the 2020 polling miss that underestimated Republicans and larger than the average partisan errors in 2016 and 2024, though comparisons to presidential years are imperfect. The big picture: Pollsters entered the 2026 midterms having underrated Trump's support in three consecutive presidential elections. Their central challenge was accounting for Republican voters who might be missing from their surveys. Many polling organizations have sought to compensate by weighting results based on party affiliation or how respondents voted in previous elections. A Pew analysis found that nearly 70% of national polls used such political weighting in 2024. In an October analysis , The Washington Post warned that a collapse in turnout among Trump voters could cause polls calibrated to the 2024 electorate to underestimate Democrats. Tuesday's results raise questions about whether the industry's efforts to correct past polling misses contributed to a new one. Reality check: Some of the pollsters that projected the largest Democratic margins appear to have come closest to the final result. AtlasIntel placed itself first in a ranking of final national House polls based on its projection of the popular-vote margin. It's the second straight election where the pollster stood out for its accuracy. AtlasIntel's final poll showed Democrats leading by 14.1 points, just 0.3 points from the firm's projected final margin of 13.8. Tufts University, New York Times/Siena, Change Research and RMG Research rounded out the top five in AtlasIntel's rankings.

Cancellations, investigations, and even impeachment could be ahead under Democratic Congress
Efforts like Autonomous Warfare Command, the Golden Fleet, and more could crumble without funding.
The Defense Department was already in Congress’s bipartisan bad graces before the midterm elections. In the wake of the Democrats’ overwhelming victory, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration are likely to face even more pushback for their handling of the Iran war and their plans for pricey initiatives like Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and Autonomous Warfare Command.
And that’s if Hegseth sticks around. Some lawmakers have voiced an intention to impeach him, while rumors swirl that he is angling to be appointed to Tennessee Governor-Elect Marsha Blackburn’s vacated Senate seat.
“My read is that nearly all Democrats and an increasing number of Republicans still want to remove Hegseth,” Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, told Defense One. “He has done nothing to improve his position with members of Congress since the House adjourned over this issue back in September, and it will be at the top of the docket when they get back next week.”
In the meantime, it doesn’t appear that Donald Trump intends to fire him. On Wednesday, the president told reporters that he thinks Hegseth is “doing a very good job.” Trump said he hadn’t heard that Hegseth was being considered for the Senate job, but said he’d be “very popular” in the office.
If Trump does change his mind, Harrison said, now would be the time to push him out and still have time to get a replacement nominated and confirmed.
Once the new Congress is seated in the new year, he added, “they will have a hard time getting anyone confirmed.”
Lawmakers will likely face pressure to investigate Hegseth and his administration for their handling of the Iran war, Harrison said, as well as “potentially improper access and contract awards for Trump’s political allies” like Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey.
Whether Hegseth stays or goes, much of his work reshaping the Defense Department is unlikely to stick, Harrison said. Anything that requires new funding is likely to hit a brick wall, and even initiatives that don’t cost anything may be undone by law.
“I think AUTOWARCOM is something they can do without Congress, but I would not expect it to receive any significant funding of its own,” he said. “The Golden Fleet definitely requires Congress for funding, so that is a dead idea—the battleship in particular.”
Democrats will also have the chance to roll back Hegseth’s culture-war pet projects, by passing laws allowing transgender troops to serve openly, re-renaming Army bases to follow the determinations of a congressionally mandated commission and perhaps even enshrining women’s right to serve in combat roles.
“In general, if it is a Hegseth initiative that requires congressional authorization or funding, it is likely not going to happen,” Harrison said. “If it is something the administration can do on its own, they will probably still try and then the new Congress may try to pass statutes that undo these changes.”
There may also be roadblocks for anything that the administration aimed to fund via a proposed 2027 reconciliation bill, such as billions for autonomous capabilities and critical munitions procurement.
“Assuming the huge increase in munitions funding requested through reconciliation does not pass in the lame duck, that is something the next Congress will have to deal with,” Harrison said.
The jettisoning of a reconciliation bill would also shrink the Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion defense proposal down to a “still substantial” $1.1 trillion, Mark Cancian, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Defense One.
“Many of the major defense initiatives have bipartisan support — drones, munitions, shipbuilding, and missile defense,” Cancian said. “There will be some drone organization, though it may not be a combatant command.”
A rebranding of Trump’s Golden Dome and the Boeing F-47, the Air Force’s six-generation fighter named for Trump’s position in the line of U.S. presidents, could also be expected, he said.
The Defense Department could also face pressure from some familiar faces, including Representative-elect Elaine Luria, D-Va., a retired Navy commander who won back her former House of Representatives seat, and who previously held a seat on the House Armed Services Committee.
In South Carolina, Nancy Lacore, a former Navy admiral that Hegseth forced to retire last year, flipped former Rep. Nancy Mace’s House seat, leaving open another HASC position.
“At this point, I don’t think they have the votes for removal in the Senate,” Harrison said of a Hegseth impeachment. “But it could be enough of an embarrassment to the administration if a decent number of Republicans in the House vote to impeach that they push Hegseth out.”
Help us report on the future of national security. Contact Meghann Myers: mmyers@defenseone.com, meghannmyers.55 on Signal.

4d0135a8d527.text: By — Josef Federman, Associated Press Josef Federman, Associated Press By — Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Natalie Melzer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-takes-first-steps-on-building-new-government-after-accepting-election-results Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results World Nov 4, 2026 4:16 PM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted the certified results of last week's parliamentary elections as legally binding and began consultations with party representatives on forming a new government. The move dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in parliament, known as the Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains. WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock "The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality," Herzog said. Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, possibly with foreign assistance. Herzog began consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night to determine whom to designate to form a government — a process that could bring Netanyahu's opponents to power. Commission finds no fraud in Israel's election Israel's elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties' claims of fraud, it had found "no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results." Netanyahu's Likud party did not respond to a request for comment. A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing. In a private meeting Wednesday of the elections committee's members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states," including from countries hostile toward Israel. READ MORE: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting and requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting. The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened. Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. "At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited," he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog. Sohlberg added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding. Public trust in the electoral process is "easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair," he warned. Consultations kick off coalition-building process In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties. Herzog began a series of sit-downs with political parties on Wednesday. Three factions — all aligned with Netanyahu's religious-nationalist base — recommended Netanyahu be given a chance to form a coalition government, while a fourth — led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival — recommended Eisenkot. Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet Herzog on Thursday, with Eisenkot's Yashar and Netanyahu's Likud speaking last. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election After the consultations, Herzog will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government. He has several days to announce his decision, which will then set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year. Intelligence agency's request to interrogate senior Arab lawmakers is rejected The Shin Bet sought approval from Israel's attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of its separate investigation, including Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported. In a statement rejecting the request, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said: "It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action." WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a "campaign of incitement" by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right ally of Netanyahu, called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no authority, to "arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties" and interrogate them in "basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified." Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet's investigation into possible foreign interference should proceed, but cautioned that Arab Israeli voters "must not be smeared." "I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently," Herzog said. Melzer reported from Nahariya, Israel. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy

1fc13100a110.text: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) formally launched his bid for speaker of the House on Wednesday in a letter to colleagues obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Jeffries is widely expected to secure the speaker's gavel after House Democrats' landslide midterm win. He would make history as the first African American to serve in the role. Jeffries, who was first elected to Congress in 2012, has led the House Democratic caucus since former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) stepped down in 2022. What he's saying: "I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives," Jeffries wrote. "We must now deliver the dramatic change the American people are demanding in the majority," he continued. Jeffries wrote that "every single member of our majority will play a meaningful role" and that his goal is to empower House Democrats to "act decisively in three key areas: (1) Affordability (2) Accountability and (3) American Values." Between the lines: While some incoming progressive and red-district Democrats have declined to commit to supporting Jeffries for speaker, he is not expected to face any serious opposition for the role. The big majority House Democrats won on Tuesday will further help to insulate him from any would-be rebels in his caucus. Zoom out: Jeffries' senior leadership team is similarly expected to run uncontested: Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) for majority leader. Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) for majority whip. Democratic Caucus vice chair Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) for Democratic caucus chair. Assistant Leader Joe Neguse (D-Colo.) for assistant speaker. Read the letter in full, via DocumentCloud : Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

917d978e0699.text: Republicans barely had time to absorb their sweeping midterm losses before President Trump returned to a familiar comfort zone: D.C. construction projects. Why it matters: Voters just delivered an overwhelming rebuke of the administration, demanding that politicians focus on the cost of living, yet the president remains fixed on remaking the nation's capital in his image. Driving the news: Trump hosted reporters at the White House on Wednesday for a previously unscheduled event to update them on the East Wing ballroom's construction, marking his first remarks to the White House press pool since the election. He spent the majority of his remarks discussing planned architectural changes around D.C., including a proposed Triumphal Arch, the National Garden of American Heroes and a planned expansion of a publicly owned golf course that would likely eliminate popular running and biking paths. His remarks came after a pre-election appearance Monday, during which he praised the new pipes installed at the Reflecting Pool and a proposed promenade from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River. What they're saying: Trump addressed criticism he sometimes receives for working on his construction projects, saying he was "doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America, and it's got to be pristine." "It's got to be perfect. And if you take a look at it, that's what it is right now. You have no idea how much work we had to do." He also noted that he spends "very little time" working on the White House, but said he does it because "it's relaxing …I love construction." Catch up quick: Democrats outperformed expectations in Tuesday's midterms, flipping the Senate before the night was over and then the House a few hours later, according to the AP. Democrats have gained complete control of at least five previously divided state governments while ending Republican trifectas in several other states. In ruby-red Texas, the white whale of potential pickups, Democrats flipped the governor's mansion, a Senate seat and now control the state House. Zoom in: "President Trump's commitment to restoring our Nation's treasured landmarks should be celebrated and does not distract from his work to lower costs, strengthen our economy, and improve the lives of American families," a White House spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement. "While making our Nation's capital safe and beautiful again as he promised to do, President Trump remains focused on lowering costs, driving down inflation, creating good-paying jobs, reshoring our manufacturing industry, unleashing American energy dominance, securing new investment, securing our borders, deporting dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and enforcing tough-on-crime policies." Zoom out: Trump also briefly discussed his immigration policies and efforts to lower crime around D.C. during his Wednesday speech. He later took questions from reporters, during which he reiterated that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot. Go deeper: Blue tsunami breaks MAGA: 5 takeaways from a blowout midterm election

9a835dea6b08.text: By — Stan Choe, Associated Press Stan Choe, Associated Press By — David McHugh, Associated Press David McHugh, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/u-s-stocks-surge-and-the-dow-soars-1500-points-as-brent-oils-price-drops-below-95-per-barrel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. stocks surge, and the Dow soars 1,500 points as Brent oil's price drops below $95 per barrel Economy Nov 4, 2026 3:47 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. stocks are soaring Wednesday after President Donald Trump's party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, as of 2:06 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.9% higher. Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump's social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans' midterm losses. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. "Earnings trump elections," according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. A downbeat forecast could be that "Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck" who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies' levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes "a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words." Here's a look at some of the moves rippling through financial markets: Trump Media and Tesla are down Trump's social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market's bigger losers, down 16.6%. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump's postings on the platform. Elon Musk's businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 2.4%, and SpaceX sank 4.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Defense stocks are down A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That helped send down stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military, including drops of 7% for Lockheed Martin, 4.2% for Northrop Grumman and 2.4% for General Dynamics. - Published
As the dust was still settling on the Democratic midterm wave that crashed across America, the official White House account posted a photograph on X of a stern-looking Donald Trump standing behind his desk in the Oval Office.
"Trump is still your president," the caption read.
It's the kind of message Trump surely wants to project â of a president firmly in charge and unbowed despite a dramatic electoral setback.
Left unsaid was that even without control of Congress, American presidents still have broad powers that they can exercise. And Trump has already shown that he is more than willing to push the boundaries of his executive authority.
But also unacknowledged was that the clock is ticking on Trump's presidency â and it will get increasingly more difficult for him to use the powers at his disposal.
Many of his most significant moves have been through presidential orders rather than laws passed by the Republican-controlled Congress.
That includes tariffs imposed on allies and adversaries alike as well as the military operations launched in Venezuela and Iran.
At home, he unilaterally slashed congressionally approved federal spending across government.
Even with the Democrats' majority in the House and Senate, Trump can continue to pursue actions like these â and more â in the final two years of his term. And if the Democrats try to curtail it through legislation, the Constitution provides Trump with a uniquely formidable response â the presidential veto, which can only be overridden by congressional majorities larger than the ones that Democrats will hold.
However, just because some of these powers are still at Trump's fingertips does not mean he retains the political will to do so. There are legions of new Democrats heading to Washington promising to oppose his every move. And the biggest obstacles may come from within Trump's own ranks.
For two years the president has displayed a vice-like grip on the Republican Party, keeping his partisan rank and file in Congress and across the US in line through a combination of political rewards and bare-knuckle threats.
Now, however, there are signs that his hold may be loosening.
Some Republicans have begun showing a willingness to criticise his decisions in a way few would dare even a few months ago. His own vice-president, JD Vance, penned a lengthy post on social media blaming the war in Iran that Trump launched with Israel for Tuesday's sweeping Republican defeat.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Already rumours are circulating that members of Trump's presidential team could be on the chopping block. According to BBC US media partner CBS News, the president is asking close advisers whether he should replace Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, one of the architects of the war. The president denied it.
Such a move would echo George W Bush's move to replace Donald Rumsfeld, a driving force behind the Iraq war, in response to his 2006 "thumping" â the last time Democrats won congressional majorities of Tuesday's scope in a midterm election.
"Republicans who think that they need to pivot away from Trumpism and from the [Make America Great Again] movement are going to either try to emphasise different policy issues, or they're going to try to frame themselves in ways that show some daylight between themselves and Donald Trump," said David Miller, an assistant professor of government at American University.
On Tuesday night, Trump posted on social media and spoke to a series of media outlets, saying in realtime how he would deal with the Democrats â pledging co-operation one moment, and threatening vetoes of liberal legislation in the next.
Then on Wednesday, as construction workers raised the final beam for the White House ballroom he is building despite a lawsuit attempting to halt its progress, he responded to a few questions about the political future.
"I'll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive," he said. "But I have the power of the veto."
In 1995, months after Republicans took control of Congress in a wave election that left Democrats similarly reeling, an isolated and defensive President Bill Clinton insisted that he still mattered and that he had powers left to wield.
"The president is still relevant here," he said, plaintively.
Clinton, still in his first term, had time to rebound politically â and he won re-election the following year.
Time, however, is not on Trump's side.
With Republicans licking their wounds, he may try to make a similar argument to the powers in Washington and the American public.
But with each passing day, the man who loves to dominate the spotlight in US politics may find his powers â and, more importantly, his authority to wield them â slipping through his fingers.
