Democrats’ Election Rout Is Poised To Dramatically Reorder Federal Health Policy
Democrats’ decisive sweep of the U.S. House and Senate in Tuesday’s elections will reshape the direction of federal health policy — setting the stage for oversight investigations, a legislative push to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, and a focus on lowering costs such as insurance premiums and drug prices.
The conclusive string of victories sets up Democrats to argue that voters — who said in preelection surveys that healthcare affordability was a top concern — have given them a clear mandate to overturn historic cuts President Donald Trump and Republicans made to public healthcare programs.
The breadth of success, including wins by Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and other progressives, is likely to embolden some Democrats to forge ahead with ambitious policy proposals such as expanding Medicare, the federal insurance program for people age 65 and older, to cover all Americans. Their plan is to be positioned as the party that prioritizes lowering healthcare costs for the 2028 presidential election.
Party leaders, though, will need buy-in from Trump to advance any healthcare agenda. While he has veto power, he may be interested in brokering legislative deals as he seeks to cement his legacy and deflect fallout from investigations into his administration’s handling of the war against Iran, mass deportations, contracting scandals, and other controversies.
Democrats were projected to win at least 237 of 435 seats in the House and at least 54 Senate seats as of Wednesday afternoon, according to The Associated Press. Several key races remained unresolved, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi.
As election results continued coming out into early-morning Wednesday, Trump said in a phone interview with Politico that he had spoken with Democratic Party leaders and that voters had sent a message he must work with them “to make sure things go well for our country.”
“I don’t want to just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” Trump said. “They want to see things happen, too.”
But how Trump’s new conciliatory position plays out in undoing GOP-led changes, such as new work requirements for many adults enrolled in Medicaid, the state-federal program for low-income and disabled people, remains to be seen. Republicans touted their overhaul of Medicaid and other changes to health programs wrought by their One Big Beautiful Bill Act as signature achievements in midterm campaigns.
Democrats, however, will have to carefully balance their policy moves against their desire to investigate a host of concerns surrounding the nation’s top health official, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has dismantled U.S. vaccine recommendations, gutted the staff of federal health agencies, and cut public health funding.
“Democrats will put forward an expansive healthcare agenda, including reversal of cuts to Medicaid and the ACA, but achieving all of that will be impossible with President Trump still in the White House,” said Larry Levitt, an executive vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
New Year, New Congress, New Majority
An early order of business for Democrats in 2027 will likely be a legislative push to restore enhanced subsidies that reduced the price millions of people paid for Obamacare health plans. The larger subsidies were created during the covid-19 pandemic, as part of economic relief programs, but ended last year after Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress declined to extend them.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the current Democratic House leader widely expected to become speaker of the House, told CNN on Wednesday that the party should bring back the subsidies to help struggling families.
“My guess is it would be rolled into a broader budget negotiation or package that may or may not involve other healthcare priorities, like restoring Medicaid cuts or other things that are priorities for Democrats,” said Sabrina Corlette, a co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
If they act decisively, said Leslie Dach, who chairs the Democratic-aligned advocacy group Protect Our Care, Democrats could both renew the ACA’s expired subsidies and extend the enrollment period for 2027 coverage, which ends in most states on Jan. 15, shortly after the new Congress is scheduled to be sworn in.
They would need to act within days of assuming control, Dach said.
“Congress will be sworn in during open enrollment, at a time when people will be having to make difficult and horrific choices about their healthcare, given the further increases in premiums due to the Republicans,” he said.
Premiums for Affordable Care Act benchmark plans are set to increase by an average of 13% for 2027, according to KFF researchers.
With Congress likely to pass another short-term government funding bill in December, the stage will be set for incoming lawmakers to also fight a battle over Medicaid spending cuts in the spring, said Rodney Whitlock, a healthcare consultant who previously worked for Republicans in Congress.
Democrats — many of whom put healthcare affordability at the center of their election campaigns — are now well positioned to place that issue at the center of negotiations with Trump over federal spending.
“If you’ve got the opportunity for a battle in March over fiscal year funding — and Democrats picking and choosing what they want to make this first battle about with a unified, controlled Congress with the president — damn, doesn’t it scream healthcare?” Whitlock said. “Doesn’t it scream repeal or delay all the Medicaid cuts?”
Allison Orris, a partner at Manatt, advised clients before Election Day not to count on anything changing — even with Democrats in control.
“The White House ultimately will have to sign any legislation, and HR 1 was a signature accomplishment. It will cost money to undo or even just delay change

This story was produced in partnership by Inside Climate News and the Texas Newsroom, the state’s network of public radio stations.
Amid a spate of historic political upsets across Texas, voters in the industrial port city of Corpus Christi on Tuesday overwhelmingly approved a citizen-led petition to impose steep fees for water use on the region’s refineries and chemical plants during future droughts.
The measure passed by a two-to-one margin despite heavy spending by industry groups in opposition—a dramatic rebuke of industrial interests in a port city that leads the nation in crude oil exports.
“The people have woken up,” said Sylvia Campos, a member of the Corpus Christi City Council and the Democratic Socialists of America who supported the measure. “We overcame all that money.”
The city’s referendum was part of an earth-shattering election across Texas, a fortress of conservative politics and the seat of the nation’s energy sector, which saw Democratic challengers wipe incumbent Republicans out of every statewide office on the ballot.
The new governor-elect of Texas, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has described her politics as “economic populism.”
“In the past we evaluated politics as right versus left, I just don’t think those labels apply at this moment,” Hinojosa told the New York Times in October. “Things are so stacked against working people in this country.”
In Corpus Christi, a Gulf Coast city of 300,000, partisan lines didn’t mark the political divisions that emerged over the referendum on industrial water fees, according to Paul Gottemoller, a professor of political science at Del Mar College in Corpus Christi.
“It’s kind of a country club, business, chamber of commerce thing versus a populism thing,” Gottemoller said. “You do have populist and business sentiments on both sides of the political aisle.”
The measure, proposed as an amendment to the city’s charter, would levy millions of dollars in surcharges on the region’s largest water users—industrial titans like ExxonMobil, Valero and OxyChem—the next time its main reservoirs drop below 30 percent full.
Refineries, chemical plants and other industrial facilities account for more than half of all water consumption in the Corpus Christi region, where reservoirs almost dried up entirely this year.
“There’s clearly some anger and resentment about the water issue,” Gottemoller said.
For now, the referendum remains a mostly symbolic win for the voters that supported it. The amendment would take effect after a five-year grace period, during which time it will likely face a litany of legal challenges from industry groups, according to Corpus Christi City Manager Peter Zanoni.
“It has significant legal implications that the city will have to address,” Zanoni said.
The city will face big challenges defending the policy in court and before the state’s Public Utility Commission, Zanoni said.
Industry groups spent hundreds of thousands of dollars supporting candidates and policies in city elections that revolved largely around water, Zanoni said.
A Message to Businesses
The charter amendment “raises broader concerns about the message Corpus Christi sends to businesses considering whether to invest, expand, or create jobs here,” wrote Dolly Trolley, a local industry promoter and school board member, in the Corpus Christi Caller-Times this week. “These companies make long-term investments requiring dependable infrastructure and predictable operating conditions.”
Groups including the Coastal Bend Coalition and Coastal Bend Industries Association did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Texas Campaign for the Environment, which helped lead and finance the petition drive, said in a press release after the amendment’s approval on Tuesday, “Its victory is proof that the community is tired of being plundered.”
“Industry will try to block its implementation through legal channels,” the press release said. “TCE stands ready to defend the sovereignty of Corpus Christi voters.”
Early this year, as an unprecedented water crisis loomed, groups including TCE, the Democratic Socialists of America and For the Greater Good gathered almost 13,000 verified signatures of registered voters on a petition for the charter amendment.
Epic rainfall in July refilled local reservoirs above critical levels. In August, the Corpus Christi City Council approved the petition for November’s ballot, against the advice of city staff.
“This victory is bigger than one water policy,” said Armon Alex, director of the petition campaign for TCE. “It is proof that residents can use the democratic tools available to us to take greater control over the resources and decisions that shape our lives.”
Most of the region’s largest water users currently pay about $4.50 per 1,000 gallons of water supplied by the city of Corpus Christi. The charter amendment would increase the price by $3 when reservoirs fall below 30 percent, by $6 when they fall below 20 percent and by $12 if the city declares a “water emergency.”
For companies that use millions of gallons of water per day, that would mean millions of dollars added to monthly water bills. The region’s largest water user, a plastics plant owned jointly by ExxonMobil and Saudi Basic Industries Corp, used 13.5 million gallons per day in 2025, almost as much as all residents of Corpus Christi combined.
Under the charter amendment, that facility would face about $810,000 in additional water costs every day while reservoirs remain below 20 percent, like they recently did for 19 months between December 2024 and July of this year.

It didn't work Politics Nov 4, 2026 3:00 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election. Ultimately, it didn't work. READ MORE: The U.S. political map? Anyone's guess after Democratic wave Republicans lost most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip, lost others they had banked on retaining and got swept out of power by a Democratic surge fueled by voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy and the war with Iran. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped previously Republican-held seats. The Trump redistricting plan "was systematically dismantled," former Attorney General Eric Holder, chair of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in an election night statement. "And given the opportunity, voters instead chose to elect a new Democratic majority." New districts presumed continuing support for Trump Congressional voting districts typically are redrawn after a census at the start of each decade to account for population changes. But Trump spurred an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle last year when he urged Texas Republicans to reshape U.S. House districts to give the GOP a shot at winning five additional seats in the midterm election. A cascade of redistricting followed, spurred along in the South by a Supreme Court ruling that weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for majority Black districts. Republicans hoped their redistricting could net as many as four more seats in Florida, two in Ohio and one each in Alabama, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee. READ MORE: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to AP Voter Poll In all but one of those revamped districts, Trump would have carried over 54% of the vote had they been in place for the 2024 election, according to Associated Press estimates. "In normal times, that sort of district is relatively safe," said Justin Levitt, a professor at the Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who runs the "All About Redistricting" website. But the presumed Republican districts got undercut by shifting viewpoints of Trump. The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. Views of Trump's priorities also were mostly negative. "It's foolish to presume that the electorate in one year is going to look like the electorate in another in a time of radical swings in public opinion," Levitt said. "I think it is likely that some line-drawers got cocky." Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley In Texas, Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs. Though De La Cruz's new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner. The AP Voter Poll indicates a substantial shift in Hispanics moving away from Republicans compared with Trump's victory just two years ago. Nationally about one-third of Hispanics say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. Republicans had "unrealistic assumptions about a shift in Latino voting" remaining in their favor, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston. Democrats retained seats in Florida and Alabama Republicans in Florida tried to tilt four more House seats to the GOP in Trump's adopted home state. Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz was among their targets, but he decided to run anyway in one of the redrawn districts. He won reelection Tuesday. "I've worked across the aisle. I've delivered results for my community, and they spent $26 million trying to beat me," Moskowitz said after his victory in Florida's 25th Congressional District. "They lit that money on fire tonight." He said voters in his new district, like those nationwide, were most concerned about the economy and their ability to afford a good quality of life. But he said that redistricting angered voters, too. After redistricting, about two-thirds of voting-age residents were new to the district represented by Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor. But she also won reelection. Democrat Pia Dandiya won yet another district -- an open seat in southern Florida — that Republicans had reshaped for an advantage. In Alabama, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Republican-led Legislature to revert to what the GOP considered to be a friendlier map. But Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection anyway, defying Republicans' plans. President Donald Trump is known to occasionally seek collaboration with â even offer praise to â his opponents. Newly ascendant Democrats, however, arenât in much of a dealmaking mood.
As Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate next year, they are already plotting out ways to investigate the president, his administration, and its allies. Democratsâ ravenous appetite for investigations â and the White Houseâs hostility towards them â raises serious questions about whether the two parties will be able to work together to any extent, even as administration officials begin floating opportunities for bipartisan cooperation.
âTheyâre going to be out for blood,â one Trump administration official told Semafor.
Democrats have spent Trumpâs second term on the sidelines, trying to learn from the aftermath of the first Trump administration. Even before voters delivered Republicans a generational rebuke, leaders had been methodically mapping out a multi-pronged oversight approach.
Incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Semafor his committee will be âlaser focused on four major lanesâ â the Trump family, immigration, corporations, and convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.
âWeâve been laying the groundwork,â said Garcia, who released a statement after the midterms advising Republicans to âlawyer up.â He predicted that every Democratic committee chair would get in on the action: âThereâs more than enough corruption to go around.â
Prior to the election, returning and incoming House Democrats had expressed âan incredible amount of interestâ in joining the Oversight panel, Garcia said. Now, leaders in both chambers believe voters have given them free rein to take their efforts to the next level.
âAmericans are calling for accountability, not accomodation,â Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday. âWhenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire.â
The administration is already warning them to back off.
âAs the President has said, heâs willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,â White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Semafor.
Its resistance is no surprise to Democrats, who had already begun strategizing how to circumvent Trump by probing the private sector instead. Government officials can invoke executive privilege to avoid providing documents, as they have in the Kennedy Center case; corporate leaders cannot.
âWe are cognizant of lessons learned from Trump 1.0 of how much they use the courts to string out the process,â said Dan Goshorn, Senate Finance Committee Democratsâ chief investigation counsel, said.
âSo from our perspective, private companies have more of a reputational risk and are going to be more willing to cooperate,â Goshorn added. âWeâre going to go wherever the information is.â
a modicum of legislative optimism
After the bruising results, Trump on Tuesday suggested heâs open to collaborating with Democrats on legislation, telling The New York Times that âweâll probably work something out.â
Some administration officials predicted Trump and Democrats could find common ground on changing immigration enforcement and addressing pharmaceutical costs â though one Trump adviser expressed skepticism at the idea of an immigration deal, pointing to exit polls showing that the issue remained one of the few Republican strengths.
That adviser suggested the president and Democrats could also work together on AI â particularly rules around data centers â and other cost-of-living issues. Specific bipartisan ideas could include enacting manufacturing and clean energy tax credits or reauthorizing federal transportation programs.
Trump âat his core does like dealmaking,â one person close to the White House told Semafor.
But itâs unclear how long that goodwill can last amid a torrent of congressional oversight. Trumpâs aides are bracing for impact, with the administration official predicting Democrats would try to tear down Trumpâs new ballroom.
âThereâs going to be a lot more war than peace,â a former Trump administration official said. âThe Democrats feel they have a mandate to torture the administration with subpoenas and lawfare.â
Spending legislation will pose an early first test. Government funding is slated to lapse next month, which Garcia said Democrats will use to finalize their plans for next year.
âItâs going to be very hard for Democrats to look at what happened [Tuesday] and â¦ pass a clean continuing resolution that locks in Medicaid cuts and SNAP cuts and ICE funding and Pentagon funding after youâve just seen the biggest mandate in the history of midterm elections against the Republican agenda,â Groundwork Collaborativeâs Alex Jacquez told Semafor.
Working with Democrats would also inevitably expose Trump to criticism from his own party. The person close to the White House warned a bipartisan immigration deal could âdamage the GOP even further.â
big oversight plans
The Trump familyâs âenormous amount of griftâ is âat the top of [Democratsâ] list,â Garcia said, now that lawmakers in both chambers will be able to schedule hearings and issue subpoenas. He pointed to the money the Trumps have made from cryptocurrency; the Russian oligarch who helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.âs wedding; and Trump Jr. and Jared Kushnerâs business ventures.
Lawmakers also plan to scrutinize âpay-to-play and profitmakingâ at the Department of Homeland Security, including by former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski. And theyâll go after âcorporate corruption, particularly anyone thatâs worked with the Trumps to rip off the American people,â as well as the Epstein investigation.

396a57ec2a1e.text: Data: The Downballot , Ballotpedia , AP ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republican mapmakers thought they were drawing at least a dozen comfortably red districts to protect their House majority. Why it matters: They weren't red enough . In the seven states where Republicans redrew congressional boundaries, the GOP is on track to lose as many as eight seats — rather than gain the 15 it had hoped to pick up. With two exceptions — TX-32 and TN-09 — the pickups Republicans penciled in never materialized. Then there was a bloodbath in North Carolina. Zoom in: At the heart of the GOP's miscalculation was a bet that the 2026 electorate would look like 2024's. Instead, voters behaved more like they had in 2020 — or even 2018. TX-34: Republicans made an already Trump-leaning district significantly redder, shifting it from Trump +4 to Trump +10. Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez still won by nearly 16 percentage points. TX-23: Republicans made an already red district slightly less Republican, shifting it from Trump +16 to Trump +15. Democrat Katy Padilla Stout won by eight points. TX-15: Rep. Monica De La Cruz's district remained essentially unchanged at Trump +18. She lost by 25 points. Between the lines: The GOP's heaviest losses came in Ohio and North Carolina districts that Republican mapmakers barely touched. Rather than shore up districts Trump had won by double digits, Republicans concentrated on making two Democratic-held seats in Ohio and one in North Carolina redder, betting they would flip in a normal election year. But 2026 was anything but normal. The bottom line: Perhaps the clearest example of a dummymander — when mapmakers spread their own voters too thin in pursuit of additional seats — came in Tennessee's 4th District . Republicans redrew TN-04 from Trump +44 to Trump +24, sacrificing much of its enormous GOP cushion. Democrat Victoria Broderick appears to have won by just 280 votes.

Why it matters: Elections have consequences. Wednesday's price drop — around $8 per barrel — deepened after Vance posted on X that "everyone knows" the war is why Republicans got pummeled and "any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." Sen. Chuck Schumer (D), the likely Senate majority leader in the next Congress, vowed that Democrats will push to end the war. "This crude price drop is entirely about the U.S. election and the belief that Trump will de-escalate rather than escalate on Iran. JD Vance's statement amplified that sentiment," Ben Cahill, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, told Axios via email. What they're saying: Pavel Molchanov, an analyst with Raymond James, said in remarks circulated to reporters that Vance's post was a "key catalyst" for today's oil price plunge. "The market is saying that Congress and members of his own administration are likely to start acting as a constraint on President Trump's war in Iran," Seb Barker, a strategist with the hedge fund, Marshall Wace, tells the Financial Times. Catch up quick: Oil prices were already falling to start the week on signs of new U.S.-Iran diplomacy. What we're watching: "[I]t remains unclear whether Vance's comments signal a more dovish stance toward Iran," Molchanov said. "For oil prices to sustainably move lower, a durable off-ramp is needed," he added.

828d02a4fedb.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-previews-ballroom-construction-the-day-after-voters-rejected-gop-rule Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Trump previews ballroom construction the day after voters rejected GOP rule Politics Nov 4, 2026 2:27 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump gave extended comments Wednesday, not about the Republican Party's midterm election wipeout but instead justifying his building a sprawling White House ballroom. Watch Trump's remarks in the video player above. Trump invited reporters into a cavernous construction site and talked about the building project for nearly 20 minutes without mention sweeping Republican defeats around the country the night before. READ MORE: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to AP Voter Poll "This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere," Trump said before watching crews erect what he said would be the project's last beam and even signing what was being built. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The president had no public events on his schedule originally, but called reporters together at the last minute. He also briefly took questions, insisting, "If I were on the ballot I would have won." He said a series of rallies he held leading up the election featured a lot of love from his supporters that "we weren't able to transfer love to the candidates." Trump's continued heavy focus on the building project comes as midterm voters said they thought he was concentrating on the wrong issues during this year's campaign. About two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities, according to The AP Voter Poll survey — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates. Roughly one-third of voters said Trump has the right priorities. Even as Trump evaded blame for the election fallout, he had used a flurry of late campaign rallies to implore supporters to pretend that he was on the ballot. READ MORE: Trump says Democrats 'did a good job,' blames Republican candidates for midterm losses Now he may work just as tirelessly to insist it wasn't his fault. Republican losses swept Democrats into control of Congress with a wave of Senate victories that once seemed far-fetched in GOP strongholds. There were wins in South Carolina and Kansas, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. In Texas, Democrats had been shut out of every statewide race for more than three decades, until Tuesday. Trump was already backpedaling even before the full extent of his party's defeat was known. On election night, he sounded more humble than usual, pledging to work with Democrats and to accept the election results. But he was still seeking to deflect responsibility. "I don't like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn't on the ballot," he told Fox News. Voters, he said, just "didn't like the candidates" on the ballot. In fact, The Voter Poll suggests that Trump was a drag on GOP candidates. Only 4 in 10 voters nationwide approved of how Trump was handling the presidency. In losing Ohio, Iowa, Maine and North Carolina, majorities said the Republican Senate candidates were "too supportive" of the unpopular president. Going further, on his social media site, the president nonetheless insisted that if he had been running, "We would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump usually blames anyone and everyone but himself Trump has a long history of passing the buck, on issues large and small, but especially when there are ballot-box failures. After Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during Trump's first term, he blamed defeated members of his own party. Utah Rep. Mia Love, who had tried to distance herself from him, "gave me no love, but then she lost. Too bad," the president said. He mocked other losing lawmakers for not embracing him — Florida's Carlos Curbelo, Colorado's Mike Coffman, Virginia's Barbara Comstock, and Illinois' Peter Roskam — with the same words he would use eight years later: "My name wasn't on the ballot." Now he's trying to deflect blame once more, despite having urged voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot." An Associated Press analysis of the 39 Trump speeches and rallies Trump staged since Sept. 1 showed the president used a version of the phrase in 30 of them. In some addresses he returned to the subject more than once, though, meaning there were at least 40 instances where he appealed to voters to engage in that bit of make-believe. Presidents usually acknowledge responsibility for midterm losses After their parties take hits in midterm elections, most White Houses engage in some soul-searching, with the president publicly shouldering at least part of the responsibility. A day after big Republican congressional gains in 2010, Democrat Barack Obama said he took "a shellacking." Republican George W. Bush described Democratic victories in the 2006 midterms as "a thumping." But Trump, known for defying all kinds of presidential norms, began laying the groundwork for avoiding blame this cycle well before balloting began. He told Punchbowl News in August that voters were angry at Republicans "but they're not angry at me." Trump posted on his social media site last month that should Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton lose — and he did — "it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove." That's despite Trump's risky endorsement of scandal-marred Paxton in the primary over incumbent Cornyn, who first got to the Senate in 2002 and was considered the safer bet. 1aac0dedf55c.text: Tuesday's election was great for Democrats. It was bad for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and some of the White House's most ambitious national security projects. Why it matters: Surprise wins across the map for Democrats — including in the Deep South — complicate a lot for the Trump administration. Republicans have relied on a simple-majority funding mechanism known as reconciliation to pay for marquee projects like Golden Dome . That option is now a long shot over the next few months, and impossible after that. Outrage over the Iran war, well beyond the half-year mark, is sure to turbocharge a long list of congressional inquiries. And lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, including Reps. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), have suggested impeaching Hegseth. Follow the money: Defense analysts agree prospects for the administration's full $1.5 trillion defense budget look grim. A Wednesday note from TD Cowen's Washington Research Group warned "Trump 'branded' projects are dead." Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and "other signature efforts," it added, "will be curbed." Meanwhile, Todd Harrison, an American Enterprise Institute defense budget expert, said it's unlikely the lame-duck congressional session will pass reconciliation and instead will keep the defense budget operating under a continuing resolution into next year. "They're all at risk," Harrison said of reconciliation-backed programs. "My base expectation is nothing happens on the defense budget." The other side: The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. Between the lines: Some of the most powerful Republican lawmakers on defense matters were defeated or are on pace to lose. Sen. Susan Collins, the appropriations chairwoman, lost to Troy Jackson in Maine . Sen. Darline Graham, also on appropriations, lost to Annie Andrews in South Carolina . Rep. Jen Kiggans, a member of the armed services and veterans affairs committees, lost to Elaine Luria in Virginia . And as of Wednesday afternoon, Reps. Rob Wittman of Virginia, Mike Turner of Ohio, Scott DesJarlais of Tennessee and Jeff Crank of Colorado all trailed their Democratic challengers. What they're saying: Hegseth himself may be on the hot seat. "Secretary Hegseth's chaotic and incompetent leadership has made America weaker and less safe, and now he will be forced to answer for it," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), a member of the appropriations, armed services and intelligence committees, told Axios. "We owe it to our service members, our military families and the American people to make sure that" Hegseth and the broader Trump administration "are held fully accountable," she added. Yes, but: President Trump told reporters he's not considering replacing Hegseth. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," he said. The bottom line: "People do expect there will be investigations and there will be oversight and all that, and certainly that will have an impact," VJ Sahi, a partner at strategic advisory firm Clark Street Associates, told Axios. fde8e92013d8.text: Democrats' sweeping statehouse gains Tuesday have opened a path to effectively replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote in time for the 2028 presidential election — without needing to amend the Constitution. Why it matters: The results could give Democrats the legislative power to fundamentally change how America picks its president, potentially ending the possibility of winning the White House while losing the national popular vote. Driving the news: Democrats have won control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada, enough to push an agreement called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact beyond the 270-vote threshold required to take effect. The compact has been enacted by 18 states and Washington, D.C. since launching in 2006, representing 222 electoral votes so far. The agreement only kicks in when participating states collectively control at least 270 electoral votes. The five new Democratic trifectas could bring the total to 283. How it works: Americans don't directly elect the president. Instead, they actually cast ballots to choose electors, whose votes determine the winner every four years. Nearly every state awards all its electoral votes to the statewide winner. Maine and Nebraska also award electors based on congressional district results. But the Constitution explicitly gives states power to appoint electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." Under the compact, participating states would instead award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once the agreement reaches 270 electoral votes. Yes, but: The five states would still need to enact the compact, and it's not clear if it will be a priority for the new Democratic states. The Electoral College would formally remain in place, and the compact could face constitutional challenges, including over whether congressional approval is required. Michigan failed to enact it during its previous Democratic trifecta from 2023 to 2024, and Nevada's then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact in 2019, warning it could diminish his state's influence over presidential elections. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the compact would be unconstitutional without congressional approval, which he contends is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. What to watch: Whether and how legislators in the new trifecta states move forward. Lawmakers in all five states have previously introduced legislation to join the compact.

Donald Trump deals in superlatives, so there is political karma in the sheer size of the defeat handed to him by a big majority of the voters of America.
But do not expect him to go gentle into the political twilight of his career. Losing both houses of the US Congress limits his capacity to dictate, manoeuvre and disrupt at home.
Abroad it is likely to be different.
As president of the United States and commander-in-chief of its armed forces he retains broad powers to use America's military might.
It is not easy to predict the actions and oscillations of Donald Trump. As president, he has turned policy u-turns into weapons. Some things, though, are constants.
One is his contempt for those he regards as losers, and his determination never to be seen as one.
The president might be tempted to blot out the electoral rout of the midterms by taking actions abroad. He might try to make moves that he can boast about as the decisive and victorious moves of a strong president, undiminished by an election that he insists, despite all the evidence, that was only lost because he was not on the ballot paper.
The Iran war
In the weeks leading up to the midterms the deployment of US forces and Trump's own, often belligerent, statements ramped up talk that the US was getting ready to go back to war with Iran.
On the eve of the elections, the US carried out a limited bombing raid on an Iranian island in the Gulf.
Before he was hospitalised with a stroke, the US Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, went to a classified briefing about potential military options for renewed war with Iran.
Without going into detail, he condemned the plans as "insane", warning that they would trigger a "devastating escalation".
There has been speculation that the Americans have plans to bomb civilian infrastructure.
Not only would that be likely to constitute a war crime, it might also be answered by devastating Iranian strikes on equivalent targets on US allies in the Gulf. Its list of potential targets could start with the United Arab Emirates, which is as close to Israel as it is to the US.
The regime in Tehran watches political developments in the US closely. It has not concealed its satisfaction that the consequences of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have become a domestic political issue in the US.
Tehran is aware of the damage caused to Trump and the Republicans by the sustained rise in the prices of everything (from petrol and diesel to agricultural fertilisers) caused by the war and its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, posted a warning on social media.
He said: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
Benjamin Netanyahu, now acting prime minister of Israel after its election last week, and manoeuvring hard to form a new government, has repeated that he wants to bring down the Islamic regime in Tehran.
Reports in Israel and the US say that he is pushing Trump to go back to war.
Netanyahu does not have the seats to form a new government with his outgoing coalition.
But if a major war restarted and was sustained, and if Israelis came under direct fire, he could have new options of forming a unity government that he would use his considerable political skills to dominate.
War in Ukraine
The other major conflict to which Trump might turn his attention is between Ukraine and Russia, which has now lasted longer than the First World War.
Before the elections he dropped sanctions against Moscow to buy Russian diesel. He might decide to prolong and deepen sanctions relief in the hope of somehow easing the economic pressure on American consumers.
He has not been noticeably concerned about the deadly pressures on Ukrainian civilians who have been targeted by Russian ballistic missiles, now getting through in greater numbers because Ukraine's appeals for more US-made interceptors, funded by European allies, have not been answered in the way Ukraine needs and wants.
The Kremlin spokesman said Russia hoped that the election results would not impact what it called Trump's "peace-making efforts".
Donald Trump has consistently tried to force Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky into making territorial concessions to Russia to produce an agreement that would amount to capitulation for Kyiv.
Trump would add it to his improbable list of wars solved and stopped.
Smarting from electoral defeat, Trump might attempt to redouble pressure on Zelensky to accept the concessions that he has repeatedly rejected.
It is safe to say Donald Trump will continue building monuments to himself in Washington DC.
Beyond that, it is worth repeating that predictions of his next moves at home and abroad risk being wrong. But it is certain that he is not going to sit in a presidential rocking-chair and wait out his time in the White House.
Throughout his time as president, Donald Trump has relished his power and been determined to use it. That is not going to change, and there is every chance that he wants to show that if he can no longer shake America, he can shake the world.

Election night was a fever dream for Democrats. In January, reality will set in.
They had a reason to be giddy on Tuesday night: Next year, Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress after a blowout victory.
"Today begins the great American comeback," an ecstatic Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, declared.
After months of promises on the campaign trail â to investigate corruption; lower the costs of healthcare, groceries and petrol; and curtail the Iran war â they will now begin the much tougher process of putting plans into action.
A shift in the balance of power in Washington doesn't necessarily mean Democrats will immediately get to start checking items off their legislative wish list. Democrats have Congress, but Republican President Donald Trump still has the power to reject legislation.
The Democrats should not consider what just happened "a mandate," US Senator Chris Coons told the BBC, warning that the party was still "deeply unpopular".
"We need to prove we can get stuff done, actually deliver answers to their concerns and questions about low wages and rising costs in particular."
What Democrats may be able to achieve
Congressman Robert Garcia of California will soon lead a powerful oversight committee in the House, with the power to make Trump's last two years in office quite difficult.
"Lawyer up," the Democrat said in a statement as victorious results poured in on election night.
Committees in both the US Senate and House have investigative powers, which they could use to delve into alleged conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him. On Tuesday, Garcia rattled off a list of possible targets: Trump's family, "corporate corruption", alleged abuses by the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the government's handling of the Epstein files.
The Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations.
Should a US Supreme Court vacancy, for example, arise during Trump's term, Senate Democrats could use their new power to block a nomination - or force Trump to choose a more moderate candidate who garners bipartisan support.
The House also has the power to impeach a president - the first step of Congress' process to remove an official from office.
Democrats twice impeached Trump during his first term, though the US Senate eventually voted to acquit him in both cases. But because it takes a two-thirds majority in the US Senate â or 67 votes â convicting a president in an impeachment case likely will remain out of reach for Democrats.
There's an active debate among Democrats about whether impeachment is a good idea. The first impeachment, in 2019, unleashed partisan rancor and allowed Trump to cast himself later as a victim of political persecution, which later helped build support for his second White House run.
Jeffries, who would almost certainly have to greenlight any Democratic impeachment effort, has kept his plans vague.
"Well, we've made clear: We haven't ruled anything in," he told CNN in August. "And we haven't ruled anything out".
What Democrats may struggle to do
Americans' frustration with Congress' productivity was palpable before the election. Only 14% of US registered voters approved of lawmakers' performance, an October Gallup poll suggested.
But with a Republican in the White House and Democrats running Congress, Americans may face even more deadlock.
"If you thought legislating was hard in the last Congress with unified Republican control, that will get much more complicated," said Casey Burgat, professor of legislative affairs at George Washington University.
Because they will control both chambers with a comfortable majority, Democrats will be able to pass legislation through Congress with relative ease.
Getting it enacted into law will be harder.
A president must sign most legislation in order for it to become law. Trump has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress that he does not support, and Congress can only override him with a supermajority from both chambers - margins Democrats alone will not have despite their success on Tuesday.
As his party lost Senate race after Senate race Tuesday night, Trump struck a conciliatory tone with the New York Times.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," he said.
But a few minutes later, Trump posted a picture on Truth Social of his red campaign hat with the word "VETO" emblazoned across the front. That Jekyll-and-Hyde approach to a Democratic Congress could become a theme.
While opposition to Trump led to Democrats' success, lawmakers acknowledged Tuesday night, it might not be enough.
"It is overwhelmingly a rejection of Donald Trump, and his agenda and policies," Coons told the BBC.
"But if we overreach, or if we fight too much internally, we could miss this moment."
Despite the veto threat, Jeffries has said that his party wants to restore significant cuts Republicans made to healthcare programmes like Medicaid, which is used by low-income groups, and the Obamacare marketplace.
"We're committed as a top priority as House democrats to reversing these Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits," Jeffries said at a September event for healthcare workers.
On typically bipartisan issues â such as policies affecting affordability, regulating the AI industry, re-evaluating military funding for Israel and reining in the Iran War â talks could break down as lawmakers try to compromise. As they become the opposition heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, Republicans might not be in the mood to help Democrats achieve too many wins.

In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president's party for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by wide margins in both the House and the Senate. READ MORE: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to AP Voter Poll The results set up a divided government, with Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch ready to challenge Trump and reverse course after two years of unified GOP control. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "We hear you," said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027. "We're going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve," he said. The tally was decisive, at times bewildering, for the staggering scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses. The swelling margins underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy. All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new opportunities and challenges for governing. Vice President JD Vance blamed war in Iran for Republican midterm losses. Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda. "I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything," he told Politico. House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek reelection as House Republican leader following the Democrats' win, according to two people familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to disclose them. Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump House Democrats are promising a 100-day agenda starting with efforts to lower the costs of gas, groceries and other goods, as well as bills to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They're also ready to launch a robust oversight agenda to, as Jeffries says, "hold the crooks accountable." Impeachment — of the president or his Cabinet members — is an option. The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: "Lawyer up." READ MORE: The U.S. political map? Anyone's guess after Democratic wave Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: "Subpoenas." Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for the high gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran and concerns about the direction of the country. For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists. With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to maneuver. "Five words for the American people: Relief is on the way," the New York senator said. A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans For Republicans, their shriveled numbers will create a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong. Johnson had quipped he may return to his Louisiana hometown of Shreveport to start a lawn care company if the Republicans lost power. Rivals seek to replace him. READ MORE: 4 takeaways from election night Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year. Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate another justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority. However, no current justice has announced any intent to step aside. And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running. In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections as members-elect arrive for freshman orientation at the Capitol. The House will choose its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes. Kansas woke up on Wednesday to sunny skies and historic new leadership after days of rain, hail and tornado warnings - amid a tempestuous election battle that ultimately swept a new brand of blue politics into the deep-red state.
Democrat and church pastor Adam Hamilton claimed victory Tuesday night over Republican incumbent and staunch Trump supporter Senator Roger Marshall, marking the first time a Democrat won the seat since 1932.
The 62-year-old leader of the US's largest United Methodist congregation - with 24,000 congregants - had promised voters civility, moderate policy stances and and open ear to their concerns. He'd invoked the state's most famous cultural touchstone, the Wizard of Oz, on the campaign trail, telling Kansans: "What we need in Washington right now is we need senators with a brain who use it, with a heart who feel with it, and who have courage and speak up because of it."
When the race was called in Hamilton's favour, voters all over Kansas - from lifelong Republicans in tiny unincorporated communities to dyed-in-the-wool liberals who'd felt disenfranchised for decades - erupted in cheers and sighs of relief.
In Wichita, a manufacturing city in the heart of the state, around 100 attendees celebrated as TV pundits onscreen spoke of a "blue tsunami" - cheering as Democrats swept not just Kansas seats but also races across the nation.
"I have lived in Kansas for 30-something years, and I have felt all of those years like I voted and my vote was never counted," said Laura Elliott, 71, sitting at a high-top table with three others.
"We did it!" shouted Chuck Schmidt, 76, hugging a younger voter as he credited upcoming generations with the party's success.
"People are fed up with the chaos and the corruption," Schmidt, a former state representative, told BBC. "People in Kansas, for some reason, have gotten conditioned to just vote for the R - and they haven't realised there was another alternative."
Faith has long been a deciding factor for many Kansas voters. A 2025 report from the Pew Research Center ranked the state as the 10th most religious in the US, with 70% of Kansans identifying as Christian and nearly 30% as evangelical Protestants - a group that has overwhelmingly backed Trump and the Republican Party in recent years.
In Great Bend, Marshall's hometown, Navy veteran Richard Elmore listed abortion, transgender issues, illegal immigration and "the gay rights issue" as some of the reasons he backed the Republican candidate.
"Anybody that'd say they were a Christian and not honour those things are lying to themselves and others," said the 77-year-old grandfather, who believes an angel is protecting Trump, otherwise "he'd be dead".
The Marshall campaign had painted Hamilton as a radical liberal whose views contradicted Biblical teachings â but the strategy failed to curb the Democrat's momentum.
In Marshall's concession speech, the outgoing senator quoted scripture â and called the loss "humbling".
"I don't have any answers," he said. "I'll just tell you it's been the greatest honour of my life to serve the state of Kansas for ten years."
As the founding pastor of the United Methodist Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton told voters his faith is what inspires his belief that the government should help care for the poor and vulnerable.
But some took issue with his positions; Richard Friedeman, a lawyer and Republican Party chair of Kansas' Barton County, accused the pastor of being "very, very liberal - and he has the ability that liberal pastors have of telling you one thing and turning right around and telling somebody else the opposite".
Friedeman was cautiously optimistic on election day as he discussed the race from his Great Bend home, saying he believed Marshall, a personal friend and "good Republican voter," had "done a good job" during his time in office.
But he conceded that the Republican party was embattled.
"I think there's going to be a reckoning for the way Trump has alienated so many people... I think it's going to be hard for awhile," he said.
His prediction proved true, as voters in Republican strongholds like Iowa, South Carolina and Texas turned out for Democratic candidates.
Even in Mississippi, the heart of America's bible belt, the race was neck and neck at the time of publication - a feat once thought nearly impossible for the Democratic Party.
Most pundits and pollsters are viewing these historic victories as rebukes of Trump's second-term agenda, such as aggressive immigration policies, a war in Iran and global tariffs that have contributed to the rising cost of living.
The day before the election, on a rainy afternoon filled with squalls and hail, dozens of Hamilton supporters turned out for a last-minute canvas in the university town of Lawrence, Kansas. Among them were retired teacher Sharron Witters, 77, and her husband Lynn, 78, a former forestry professor and pastor of 25 years.
As evangelical Christians, they said Hamilton's candidacy motivated them to put out signs on their lawn and knock on doors for the first time. They set out with maps and lists, as Sharron navigated their silver VW SUV from address to address in a well-heeled Lawrence neighbourhood.
Hamilton, Sharron said, "doesn't sound like a politician".
"What a delight to stand and listen to somebody whose sentences make sense," she said.
"Wouldn't it be wonderful if he actually motivated people to work across the aisle?
She noted how other evangelical Christians had backed Trump "because he said, 'I'm against abortion'".
But she and her husband, "felt, from the very beginning, that [Trump] was a wolf in sheep's clothing".
Hamilton's campaign galvanised a powerful cross-section of Kansas society - from Republicans voting blue for the first time to long-time liberals initially skeptical of his more moderate positions.

Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability".
Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling.
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, says she is "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.
"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.
Human Rights Watch described the ruling as "cruel and unjust".
"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.
The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.
Who is Joshua Wong?
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them...âInstead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature â but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.
Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.
Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England
The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.
Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.
The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.
The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.
However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
- LIVE: Follow latest updates

It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.
The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if â he'd make an endorsement.
The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport, one of several Italian stops on his Rough and Rowdy Ways tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.
The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

As a blue wave washed over Election Day, ballot measures across the country showed voters strongly support environmental protection, with notable early outcomes in California and Colorado.
Democrats swept Congress on Tuesday, winning control of both houses with notable victories in Ohio, South Carolina, Texas, Michigan and Maine.
Results, which are still being tallied Wednesday, represented national disapproval of Donald Trump’s second presidency on issues like the high cost of fuel and food, an unpopular war with Iran and the proliferation of data centers, according to analysts.
The outcome of ballot measures—some of which had industry backing—on a gamut of environmental and energy issues made voter sentiment clear: they want to safeguard the environment.
With more than half of the ballots counted in California, voters appear to be rejecting a measure to fast-track construction of “essential projects” like housing, clean energy and broadband internet access by streamlining the state’s bedrock environmental law.
Proposition 45 would overhaul the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, by limiting the timeline for environmental review of major projects to 365 days and requiring that legal challenges of projects based on threats to air and water quality, tribal cultural resources and other harms be resolved within 270 days.
Proponents of the measure, sponsored by California’s Chamber of Commerce, say these deadlines are needed to speed the building of much-needed housing and infrastructure in the state. But opponents, including some affordable housing advocates, say the new rules would hobble the state’s landmark environmental law by limiting the scope of review as well as the ability of communities and tribes that are not federally recognized to mitigate the harms of polluting developments on their neighborhoods or ancestral lands.
As of Wednesday afternoon, with 58 percent of the votes counted, just over 54 percent opposed the measure and about 46 percent supported it. The measure can pass with a simple majority but would need two-thirds of the Legislature to amend it.
“We’re encouraged by what we’re seeing,” said Woody Little, spokesperson for the No on Prop 45 campaign, which represents more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations.
“We’re seeing folks show up at the polls who represent the really broad coalition that came together against this measure [and] around protecting our core environmental law here in California,” Little said.
Though it’s too early to declare the final result, Little said, “it’s very clear that millions of Californians voted to defend our core environmental protections.”
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for Yes on Prop 45, was not immediately available to comment Wednesday. Matier previously told CalMatters that by allowing for faster, more predictable reviews, the measure would let California build housing and infrastructure at a lower cost.
Prop 45’s likely defeat is encouraging news, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust, an initiative to restore Indigenous knowledge and practices on the Amah Mutsun tribe’s ancestral lands, which cover parts of counties from Monterey Bay to regions southeast of Silicon Valley.
“Meaningful tribal consultation is essential to protecting ancestral lands and cultural resources, particularly for non-federally recognized tribes whose voices are too often marginalized,” Chambers said. Such consultation, she said, is fundamental to advancing the return of Indigenous stewardship to Amah Mutsun homelands.
Polling from the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California showed that support for Prop 45 had dropped considerably, from 73 percent to 46 percent, between July and October, as voters learned more about the measure.

If passed, the measure could cost state and local governments more than $100 million a year, partly to cover environmental damages that emerged from projects built with limited review or public input, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Californians are rejecting a “false choice” between addressing the affordability crisis and protecting California’s air, water, health and climate at the same time, Little said. “They’re seeing through the tens of millions of dollars of misleading advertising from some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the state,” he said. “That should really send a message to the Legislature about which side their voters are on.”
In Colorado, with 81 percent of votes tallied as of Wednesday afternoon, voters rejected Amendment 82—which would have established a constitutional right for consumers in the state to buy natural gas and for distributors and utilities to sell the fuel. The initiative was intended to prevent local and state restrictions or bans on the sale of natural gas, such as through prohibitions on gas infrastructure in new construction, and to overturn existing regulations that curtail use of the fuel.
Environmentalists worried the change would endanger Colorado’s climate goals and—as the first of its kind—set a dangerous precedent.
“It would have made Colorado the first state in the country to put one industry’s profits into the constitution,” said Kelly Nordini, CEO of environmental advocacy group Conservation Colorado.
“That would have been the opposite direction of where Colorado voters have been going for decades, which is for health and safety protections, for clean energy, and certainly not putting a preference for one industry into the constitution,” Nordini said.
Conservation Colorado organizers criticized anonymous donors for trying to convince voters the measure was sensible.
