On a busy election day, the Alabama Public Service Commission requested that Alabama Power voluntarily stop billing customers, effective immediately, for television commercials and other ads it buys to promote various aspects of its business.
Alabama Power is the largest electricity provider in Alabama, with territory covering about two-thirds of the state. Though it is a monopoly, the company spends millions each year on advertising, touting its reliability, customer service and other aspects of its business.
In recent months, the company has launched a series of television commercials touting a rate freeze it announced late last year amid heavy criticism over rising electricity prices.
A state law passed earlier this year will prohibit Alabama Power from including the costs of those commercials in customers’ electric bills, meaning the powerful utility will have to find all of the dollars in corporate profits. But the new law won’t take effect until 2029.
Currently, Alabama Power is allowed to bill customers for half of its non-public safety advertising costs.
During Tuesday’s meeting, PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond moved to “request” that Alabama Power voluntarily begin excluding those costs immediately.
“I don’t see any reason why we shouldn’t go ahead and take steps now to begin that process, rather than waiting until Jan. 1, 2029,” Almond said during the meeting.
Almond then made her motion, which was not on the meeting agenda, but came after the regular report from the commission’s electricity division.
“I move that the commission request that Alabama Power consent to exclude all advertising expenses from retail rate setting until after Dec. 31, 2028, when the new law takes effect,” Almond said. “Assuming Alabama Power consents, this interim measure would be reflected in its [Rate Stabilization and Equalization] filings for 2027 and 2028.”
Commissioners Jeremy Oden and Chris Beeker IV voted yes after a brief discussion.
According to the company filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Alabama Power spent more than $6 million in general advertising last year, roughly $4 per customer. It’s unclear from the federal filing how much of that total was passed on to customers or how much might be impacted by the new prohibition.
Alabama Power did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said the move was a boon to Alabama Power customers, who faced some of the highest electric bills in the country in recent years.
“We are grateful for the leadership of President Almond and the full commission for acting to end customers paying for Alabama Power’s advertising,” Tait said. “Once in place, Alabama will have one of the strongest customer protections in the nation on this front.”
This will be among the last actions of the commission under its current construction before a major overhaul takes effect.
In January, the commission will expand from three members to seven. Outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey has appointed four new commissioners, who will take office in January, including the PSC’s two first-ever Black members.
Oden and Beeker will also leave the commission in January after being defeated in Republican primaries. Cullman County Sheriff Matt Gentry will take Oden’s Place 1 seat, and former state auditor and PSC Commissioner Jim Zeigler will replace Beeker in Place 2.
Zeigler, a perennial candidate in Alabama across several decades, will return to the commission 48 years after leaving the PSC. He served one term from 1975-1979, during an era of skyrocketing energy costs and protracted political battles over electric rates between Alabama Power and then-Gov. George Wallace.
Almond will be the sole remaining member of the current commission.
The new seven-member commission will be overseen by the state’s first secretary of energy, who will be selected by Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville. The new secretary will set the commission agenda, and overruling the secretary will require a vote of five of seven commissioners.
Tuberville has not yet announced his pick for secretary of energy. The only statutory requirement is that the secretary “must have experience in utility regulation or energy policy or a related field.”
About This Story

9dd23295741c.text: President Trump has conceded that the Iran war cost Republicans dearly in the midterms . Now he must decide whether to cut his losses and reach a deal — or double down and go back to bombing. Why it matters: All of Trump's options are problematic: The first is to strike. But going back to war would be highly unpopular — keeping gas prices high and probably not yielding a better military result. Another is to negotiate. But if Iranian officals refuse to make concessions — or, sensing weakness after the president's political loss, up their demands — Trump will have a hard time reaching a deal. The third is to "strangle," as aides put it. This would mean sticking with the status quo — the naval blockade coupled with crippling economic sanctions that leave the Iranian regime to "rot" — while continuing to test its appetite for a deal. This path, however, could take months to show progress. The big picture: The president has said for weeks he would end the war one way or another after the election. One of his former advisers told Axios: "It's one thing to lose the midterms. But Trump doesn't want to look like a loser twice." That's left even his closest aides unsure what he's going to do next. The intrigue: Vice President Vance, in an extraordinary statement Wednesday morning, bluntly blamed the war for the GOP's midterm drubbing. It added a new political calculation to Trump's decision. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote on X . "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. ... But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there." Vance also cited the U.S. relationship with Israel as a serious liability for Republicans. Trump told reporters on Wednesday that Vance's analysis was "largely true" because the war drove gas prices up. But Trump said he'd do it again if he had to: "We had no choice. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Asked when he's going to end the war, Trump responded: "Whenever I wanted to. But it's got to be done right, because they can't have a nuclear weapon." Behind the scenes: In recent months, Vance has led a faction within Trump's inner circle advising him to reach a deal with Iran to end the war. He privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of "being wrong on everything" regarding Iran, sources said. Vance warned that the war was highly unpopular and could cost Republicans the election, the sources said. Most senior officials around Trump have shared Vance's views. But Trump still leaned toward resuming the war. At one point, he considered launching strikes before the midterms, as Netanyahu was pressing him to do. Trump decided to wait. But against the advice of his top advisers, he still endorsed Netanyahu in Israel's election last week. State of play: The U.S. military is finishing preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran, including sending more assets to the region, American officials say. At the same time, Qatari mediators are working to secure U.S. and Iranian support for a draft agreement to head off a return to battle and possibly resume direct talks in the coming days, regional sources say. The mediators asked White House officials before the election what Trump would do if he lost. The president's advisers couldn't vouch either way, a source with knowledge said. "We told everybody that we want to see first how the elections turn out for us," a U.S. official said. The other side: Iranian officials celebrated Trump's electoral defeat, saying it showed they're winning the war. "The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz — and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington," Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X. "Meanwhile, Americans got stuck with the bill for his war. Anyone who takes on Iran will pay the price — from the battlefield to their own doorstep." Diplomats involved in the mediation efforts, Trump advisers and Middle East experts said Iran's gloating could make the president more likely to return to war. "Tehran's temptation is likely to mistake Trump's political weakness for military weakness and overplay its hand, when the smarter move is to bank a deal while Washington still wants one," Ali Vaez , deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Axios. Yes, but: Trump could opt to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo. CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other advisers want Trump to let the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign play out longer, tightening the screws on Iran. The bottom line: There's no tidy way for Trump to "finish the job" in Iran. Go deeper: Oil prices plunge after Vance post on Iran war

The News
In Piqua, Ohio, voters on Tuesday approved a ban on large data centers and recalled the commissioners who backed Metaâs massive project there. In Trenton, less than 50 miles south, a similar ban passed. And outside Columbus, the heart of Ohioâs data center boom, voters in Ashville repealed the villageâs deal with developer EdgeConneX.
These Ohio races were part of a swell of anti-data-center sentiment that echoed across the country in dozens of ballot measures concerning bans, moratoriums, or stricter regulations and oversight. The votes were hyperlocal and often emotional in nature, but they could carry financial consequences, because some of the projects at stake were already in motion.
- Meta bought more than 600 acres in Piqua last year for about $110 million, and signed agreements with the city in January. âWe are proud of our investments in Ohio, and will work with local officials to determine the future of our investment in Piqua,â a Meta spokesperson told Semafor on Wednesday.
- Amazon had proposed a 600-acre campus on land Trenton hoped to annex; the ban effectively blocks that plan, according to local news. An Amazon spokesperson didnât directly comment on the vote but said the company is âcommitted to setting a high bar for responsible data center development in Ohio, and will continue engaging communities early as we build out this important infrastructure.â
- EdgeConneX said its development in Ashville is moving forward despite the vote, given that its permits are secured and construction is underway.
More than 40% of the USâ planned data center capacity is located in states where governors or governors-elect have pledged or already imposed a pause on new data centers, according to a Cleanview analysis. That doesnât mean the data center buildout will grind to a halt, but markets are pricing in a slowdown.
Shares of companies that are directly exposed to the physical buildout of data centers tanked Wednesday, including Modine (a maker of data center HVACs, down about 21%) and Sterling Infrastructure (site prep and electrical work, also down 21%).
Hyperscaler stocks, though, soared, with traders betting they will be forced to rein in the rapid spending that has pushed their free cash flow to negative territory. More restrictions on data center construction also means tech giantsâ compute capacity âpotentially even becomes more valuable,â Morgan Stanley US Equities Strategist Andrew Pauker told Semafor.
The View From Washington
Tech companies are also recalibrating their data center strategies in Washington as they prepare for a Democrat-controlled Congress.
One tech-focused public affairs adviser suggested companies work with Democrats to craft national rules around data center development. Incoming Democrats in the House and Senate say theyâre going into Congress with a mandate to do something about AI data centers, and Republican groups who pushed their party to listen to grassroots concerns about data centers are saying Washington Republicans can only blame themselves for the midterm losses after aligning with AI companies.
Ellen DiMauro contributed to this story.

d3612eb8ffc1.text: House Democrats channeled anti-Trump fury into a landslide victory over Republicans. Now comes the hard part: Figuring out what to do with their huge majority . Why it matters: That question is already igniting a power struggle between Democrats' ideological factions as they lay out contradictory visions for what the next two years of governing looks like. This story is based on interviews with more than a dozen sitting and incoming House Democrats from across the political spectrum. "Last night was a rebuke of the status quo," progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios, adding that "for the left it was an affirmation and a validation that we are on the right track." There is "absolutely no excuse," Ramirez said, for House Democrats not to do "the most over the next two years, and as quickly as possible." Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), a centrist, said Tuesday was a "gigantic night for the middle ground," and that the mandate is far more modest: "We need to crush high costs and corruption." State of play: House Democrats are on track to win more than 250 seats, which would give them a comfortable majority of dozens of votes. That blows up the plans of a cohort of incoming progressives known as the "Bloc" to demand concessions from leadership in exchange for voting with the party. The potential concessions included changes to House rules, plum committee assignments and votes to enact Medicare-for-All , defund ICE and cut off U.S. aid to Israel. What we're hearing: The left's new tactic is to try to convince the Congressional Progressive Caucus to, as one sitting House Democrat put it, "assert its authority in a way it has never done before." "That should definitely be part of the game plan," an incoming Bloc member told Axios, "we've got so many members of the CPC and I think we're adding 25 more." Said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a former CPC chair: "We have certainly used our power many times ... and we will do that again." The CPC is currently around 100 members, though not all are pugnacious ideological brawlers. The new strategy also involves aggressively recruiting incoming House Democrats from battleground districts, a group that hasn't traditionally been at the core of the CPC's membership. The left is hopefully eyeing the "Bernie Dogs": Populist candidates from working class backgrounds who won red districts with support from both progressives and centrists. They are also taking a close look at the "wave babies": Candidates who won upset victories in districts that weren't even on the party's radar and whose politics are largely unknown on Capitol Hill. What they're saying: CPC chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) argued in an interview that it may not be such a fight to pass a progressive agenda, noting that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has called for "dramatic change." "Americans delivered a demand for bold change, and progressives are excited to deliver it," Casar said, adding that Medicare-for-All is "overwhelmingly popular" and that Democrats "should move that kind of legislation forward." Jayapal told Axios: "We will be driving an agenda that truly is big and bold and looking for [Jeffries'] leadership to make sure that is what we deliver." The former CPC chair said she is "100% down" for the items on Jeffries' 100-days agenda but "I just don't think there's any way we can stop there. ... We have to pass a living wage bill, we have to pass universal childcare." The other side: Rep. Adam Gray (D-Calif.), a leader of the centrist Blue Dog Coalition, told Axios, "The most extreme elements ... want to do messaging bills and yell and scream and point the finger." "There's time for that, let's just not make it the majority time," he continued, "and I think you're going to find a lot of people ... agree with me on this." Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas), an ally of Jeffries, said the results were a "victory for common sense, not any extremist ideology" and that Jeffries "understands what last night was all about and he will lead accordingly." Jeffries is being characteristically taciturn about how he will govern. "We're going to have a conversation as a caucus upon our return about what the agenda looks like," he told reporters at a press conference on Wednesday. Asked about marking up Medicare-for-All, Jeffries said House Democrats will have a "family conversation" about what health care measures to pass beyond renewing expired Affordable Care Act tax credits and reversing the GOP's cuts to Medicaid. The bottom line: "Medicare-for-All is not going to happen in the next two years and everybody knows that," said progressive Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), a co-sponsor of Medicare-for-All. "I hear all of this jockeying, and frankly I find it tedious," he told Axios. "We're going to have a huge majority to navigate these issues and it's all going to be fine. ... We're mostly on the same team here." Said another House progressive: "With this big of a majority, honestly, the Bloc has way less influence, but the good news is so do the members who buy Depends by the carton." "On balance, this is a center-left caucus," a third House Democrat said.

- Published
The Democrats have swept to victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress.
While the incumbent president's party generally tends to have a bad night in these elections, the scale of the Republican defeat is being viewed as a resounding rejection of Donald Trump's two years in the White House.
From angry voters to an unpopular president, here are five reasons why the Republicans lost so many seats.
1. Soaring cost of living
From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.
"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.
Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (Â£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.
Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.
And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.
2. Unpopular Iran war
A major factor in surging prices has been the war with Iran which the US and Israel launched in February.
Fuel prices then shot up after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation, strangling a key artery for the passage of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).
US voters have been paying the price at the petrol pump ever since.
The war has proved broadly unpopular with most Americans. For Maga Republicans it also felt like a broken promise in Trump's America First campaign agenda in which he pledged there would be no more wars.
Around six in 10 (63%) of those asked in a voter poll said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.
Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.
The morning after the election, Trump conceded the war had played a role in the defeat but insisted in an interview on Fox that he had no choice but to intervene to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
- RESULTS: How America voted in maps and charts
- EXPLAINER: Five reasons why Trump did so badly
- ANALYSIS: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
- REACTION: Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms 'disaster'
- NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox
3. Disciplined message from Democrats
The scale and breadth of this Democratic wave was made possible by some strong candidates who came across as authentic, especially in traditional Republican heartlands.
They stuck to a disciplined message about the cost of living and healthcare access.
Former teacher James Talarico and pastor Adam Hamilton also talked about their faith in a way that struck a chord in Texas and Kansas respectively.
In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a shock upset. A former paediatrician, her focus on health care affordability resonated in a country where many see the system as broken.
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed in Michigan to keep that seat Democratic, made getting "money out of politics, money in your pocket" a key slogan.
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election in Georgia, made the cost of living and corruption a central message. The 39-year-old's comfortable victory in a state Trump won twice will only fuel rumours of a 2028 presidential run.
Even Trump himself praised the Democrats, telling Fox News they "did a good job".
Conversely, some Republican candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas were criticised for running poor campaigns that were not focused enough on voters' concerns.
4. Trump's unpopularity a drag on Republicans
Two of the issues voters were most unhappy with - rocketing prices and the Iran War - were directly linked to the president.
His approval ratings had even fallen among Republican voters, which made some of these states which backed him in 2024 especially vulnerable.
He urged voters to imagine he was on the ballot in an effort to galvanise his supporters.
But after more than a decade as the central figure in American politics, some see these results as evidence that the glitz may be wearing off Trump's brand.
Against a backdrop of increasing anger, making himself the focus of the Republican campaign was risky and appears to have backfired.
In the months leading up to the vote, polling indicated that many Americans wanted Trump to focus more on their concerns about rocketing prices.
In his final campaign speech on Monday in Washington DC, he talked at length about his controversial renovation project of the Reflecting Pool behind him.
5. Hispanic and black voters shift again
Two years ago a move towards Republicans among some Hispanic and black voters helped Trump secure a decisive win. That seems to have reversed in these midterms.
Democrats claimed all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.
Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to a New York Times analysis.
The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country, data reporter Jeff Adelson said.
The shift comes amid widespread anger at immigration enforcement, with a majority (56%) of Americans saying they have an unfavourable opinion of ICE, according to the Pew Research Center.

NY-17: Last in a series on the environmental stakes behind one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.
Before midnight, and before any official body had called the race, Republican incumbent Mike Lawler conceded to Democratic challenger Cait Conley in New York’s 17th Congressional District. Conley flipped the closely watched toss-up seat, denying Lawler a third term in a district Kamala Harris won in 2024, as a nationwide blue wave promises Democrats a commanding House majority.
It was a district in which energy costs, data center development and nuclear power were central to campaign messaging. Though climate policy was seldom invoked by name, Conley pledged to fight climate change “as a national security priority.”
“When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it’s gonna be pretty clear that we will be short,” Lawler said during a speech to supporters Tuesday evening.
Westchester County experienced widespread problems with ballot-scanning machines on Election Day, delaying results, with concerns that the issues might discourage low-propensity voters. Still, Conley carried the county by a 34-point margin and flipped the seat by roughly 5 percentage points, according to preliminary results Wednesday. The outcome represents an approximately 11-point swing toward Democrats compared with the 2024 congressional race.
Many in the district viewed Conley’s victory as a repudiation of President Donald Trump and Lawler’s alignment with him, despite the congressman’s efforts to portray himself as a moderate. Lawler was formerly head of the New York state GOP, while Conley is a decorated Army combat veteran who served in Iraq and Afghanistan before working on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.
Trump has repeatedly endorsed Lawler, who joined him at what Trump called the 2026 Republican Midterm Convention in September in Dallas. On Tuesday, Trump urged Jewish voters in the district to re-elect Lawler, an appeal that underscored the perceived political influence of the district’s Orthodox Jewish voting bloc.
“VOTE MIKE LAWLER FOR CONGRESS — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” he wrote on X.
Yet Erik Lindberg, a Westchester County resident who voted for Conley, said that while Lawler “ran a really impressive constituent services shop,” he “had no significant ideological principles, other than being a member of the Republican caucus.”
“He lost because he worked in lockstep with Trump,” said Susan Shapiro, an environmental attorney and resident of the district.
William Knox, a veteran and self-described “anti-MAGA Republican” who had been undecided shortly before the election, said he voted for Democrats across the board, not necessarily because he agreed with their policies, but to give those opposing MAGA all the support he could.
A Referendum on Lawler
Throughout the campaign, Lawler sought to make rising energy costs a central issue, blaming Albany Democrats for higher utility bills. But his own record included millions of dollars in contributions from utility-related political action committees, as well as previous work as a registered lobbyist for a natural-gas advocacy group whose backers included utilities and fossil-fuel interests.
While Republicans like Lawler repeatedly sought to shift blame for rising costs onto Democrats, a majority of Americans now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high prices.
“The fact that there has been a Republican trifecta while fuel prices have hugely increased has made it clear to everyone, including the most MAGA Republicans, that this isn’t Democrats’ doing,” said Madalina Vlasceanu, a researcher at Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability.
Lawler continually advocated for reopening Indian Point, the district’s shuttered nuclear power plant, and for expanding domestic oil and gas production. In addition to centering the energy debate, he capitalized on public unease surrounding artificial intelligence and data centers, regularly highlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings.
The result suggests Conley succeeded in distancing herself from accusations leveled throughout the campaign that she was the “AI candidate for the AI industry.”
What’s Next?
The district, in the Lower Hudson Valley, includes all of Rockland and Putnam counties, most of northern Westchester County and portions of southern Dutchess County. For many environmental advocates there, the prevailing sentiment after Conley’s victory was hope.
On her campaign website, and less consistently in campaign appearances and debates, she said she would expand federal investment in clean energy, protect open spaces, hold corporate polluters accountable and pressure the administration to rejoin the Paris climate agreement. She also opposed efforts to reopen Indian Point and pledged to tackle PFAS, better known as “forever chemicals.”
“With Democratic control of Congress, it becomes possible again to begin to reverse the assault on the environment,” said Peggy Kurtz, an environmental activist from Rockland County.

“I’m hopeful we can make some progress. Lawler was a real roadblock to any progressive climate action,” he said.

7053d16d9186.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, top officials in Iran welcomed the results of the U.S. midterm elections, Israeli President Isaac Herzog says he's accepted the results of last week’s election and will consult with party leaders on forming a new government and Ukraine's air force says Russia launched more than 300 drones overnight. Geoff Bennett: Meantime, top officials in Iran welcomed the results of last night's U.S. midterm elections, casting them as a rejection of President Trump's war. That's where we start our day's other headlines. Iran's Parliament speaker and chief negotiator said American voters sent a clear message, no to war. But Iran's supreme leader warned that anyone expecting a change in U.S. policy toward Iran is, in his words, gravely mistaken. The U.S. has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets in recent weeks, while fears of renewed all-out war following the election have kept the region on edge. In Israel, President Isaac Herzog says he's accepted the results of last week's election and will consult with party leaders there on forming a new government. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party nor that of his chief challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority. That means Herzog must now meet with party officials and choose a candidate to form a coalition government, which would likely lead to weeks of talks. He urged all sides to work towards a compromise. Isaac Herzog, Israeli President (through interpreter): I expect the factions and the representatives to understand that, in the current reality, it is not possible to fulfill all commitments and promises. I'm not asking anyone to give up their fundamental values, but, in the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after, I'm asking for originality, creativity, boldness, and goodwill. Geoff Bennett: Earlier today, Israel's election commission said it found no evidence of voting irregularities, despite Netanyahu's attempts to cast uncertainty on the result. He's claimed without evidence that Arab-led parties, as he put it, stole that election. Ukraine's air force says Russia launched more than 300 drones overnight. Most were shot down, but one strike in Western Ukraine set a shopping center ablaze, injuring at least one person. Meantime, rescue crews are still searching for bodies after Monday's attack on a former school that was being used as a shelter in Southern Ukraine. President Zelenskyy says at least 40 people were killed, while 30 more possibly trapped beneath the rubble. It's believed to be one of the deadliest strikes of the war. In Brussels, officials from the U.S., Germany, France and other countries met to discuss Ukraine's postwar reconstruction. The E.U.'s foreign policy chief expressed cautious optimism following the U.S. election results. Kaja Kallas: U.S. voters have made their choice clear. I hope that the new Congress and the new Senate will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia. Let's see what happens now, but elections have results. Geoff Bennett: The talks in Brussels come ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered peace talks set for next week in Abu Dhabi. A federal judge in Boston has dismissed a case against a Russian-born Harvard scientist who was accused of smuggling frog embryos into the U.S. Kseniia Petrova was arrested last year as she returned from a holiday in France with the specimens. She spent four months in detention, during which she spoke with us on this program via video call. Prosecutors agreed to drop the charges after a judge said she could seek evidence to support her claim that she had been unfairly targeted. Petrova has said she did not realize she had to declare the items. One of NASA's most successful space telescopes plunged back to Earth today. The U.S. Space Force says the Swift Observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere near Indonesia. NASA officials believe the 3,200-pound spacecraft likely burned up upon reentry, though a few components may have survived. Its demise came less than three months after a rescue mission failed. Swift was launched in 2004 to study gamma ray bursts and exploding stars and has been pulled back towards Earth ever since. The mission was meant to last for two years, but instead continued for more than two decades. Well, stocks surged on Wall Street today as investors welcomed last night's election results. The Dow Jones industrial average soared more than 1, 500 points. The Nasdaq jumped nearly 1.5 percent. The S&P 500 also ended sharply higher. And we have two passings to report tonight, starting with British celebrity hairstylist and beauty entrepreneur John Frieda. Frieda built a global hair care empire best known for products like Frizz Ease and Sheer Blonde. He started his career in London, styling some of the world's most famous figures, including Princess Diana, Jackie Kennedy Onassis, Madonna, and Sarah Jessica Parker. He opened his first salon in 1976 and later turned his expertise into a multimillion-dollar hair care business, which he sold in 2002 for a reported $450 million. His salon announced that Frieda died peacefully surrounded by family. No cause of death was disclosed. John Frieda was 75 years old. And a founding force of techno music, Juan Atkins, has died. His 1985 single "No UFOs" made "Rolling Stone"'s list of the 200 greatest dance songs of all time. The Detroit native broke out in the early 1980s, inspired by the German band Kraftwerk and George Clinton's Parliament Funkadelic. Over the years, his work as a deejay and producer helped bring techno to a global audience. Atkins is even credited with originating the name techno. His talent agents confirmed his death in Mexico City this past weekend, but did not provide a cause of death. Juan Atkins was 64 years old.

A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.
The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.
He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC, external.
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

8a29289b36ba.text: The results of the midterms have set up a two-year power struggle between Trump’s White House and the incoming Democratic Congress. Lisa Desjardins takes a look at the races and the potential size of the incoming Democratic majority. Geoff Bennett: Turning back now to tonight's top story, last night's midterm results have set up a two-year power struggle between Trump's White House and the incoming Democratic Congress. Amna Nawaz: Lisa Desjardins is back at the Super Screen with more on the races and the potential size of the coming Democratic majority. So, Lisa, let's start with the Senate. Democrats have so far swept the toss-up races, but it's not over yet. Where do things stand? Lisa Desjardins: That's right. Remember, this is where we started last night, a look at the toss-up races all held by Republicans right now. What's happened? Look at all these flips. This is a sweep like you seldom see in politics. And we are still waiting, of course, for results from Alaska and from Mississippi. So, just given what they have already flipped, Democrats have flipped seven seats in the Senate. They could get nine. That total, nine, is something that only comes around for either party in, say, 50 years. Either way, this is quite a tsunami that we see tonight. Now, I want to look at exactly kind of what the numbers are saying, as you see, gaining seven, and you can see all around the country. There's one that stands out here, Mississippi, which is light blue and waiting on. As you heard Liz say, we are waiting on votes because right now there's just a 65-vote difference. Mississippi has 82 counties in it. So think about that. That is fewer than one vote per county difference in this race right now. As they're waiting for provisional ballots, they also have some votes out here in Hinds County. This is a place that has 90 percent counting, and where the Democrats Scott Colom is ahead by quite a lot. We may be waiting for days or weeks on this. And, as well, we could very well be the same for Alaska, where we have a virtual tie right now as well. Geoff Bennett: So that's the Senate. Let's shift our focus now to the House. We know Democrats have claimed control of the House, but the question at this hour is the margin. How are things looking? Lisa Desjardins: That's right. I wanted to look at what the current Congress looks like. First of all, you can see it's a mostly red Congress that we have today. And then if you go to our map of where it stands now, here you can see all of this blue in the center of the country and on the side of the country, more than one blue dot in the center now. You can see Democrats at this moment have gained 28 seats. And what's interesting, as I prepared this segment, I also carefully looked at all the seats where we haven't had race calls yet. There are quite a few. And as I have been standing here, Democrats have picked up in Michigan 10 and in Michigan 4 and in Nebraska 2. The Republican has conceded, Mike Lawler, in New York 17. So remember the numbers, 28 pickups so far. This is another 23 seats where Democrats are leading and poised to flip. That is 51 seats that they could have total gain. That's the kind of number that Newt Gingrich saw in 1994, a huge shift. Amna Nawaz: So, Lisa, those are the numbers. But what do the maps tell you about who or what shifted in this election? Lisa Desjardins: Right. Let's talk about Texas there, because I think that is something historians will study for a long time. James Talarico 55 percent to Ken Paxton, that is a huge margin. Where did it come from? Again, let's compare this to 2024 and the presidential vote. You can see right here the Rio Grande Valley nice and red. I want to pick one county that I think typifies the state a little bit. That's Brewster County, where they happen to be having their famous chili cook-off right now. Happy for all of them. President Trump won this county by 13 points in 2024. What happened with James Talarico? Look at that. It's a complete flip. And this is a plurality Hispanic district. This is all Hispanic territory. I also want to point out we have a lot of close races in the House. So it may take some time to know exactly what's going on. For example, here, Arizona, we have a virtual tie right there in Arizona's Second District. And one we're watching closely, Tennessee's Fourth District right here, again, just 280 votes between Victoria Broderick and Scott DesJarlais. It's going to be a while before we know the exact margin, though we do know the general outcome. Amna Nawaz: All right, Lisa Desjardins still going strong at the Super Screen for us. Lisa, thank you. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

37737cf1b6b5.text: For a deeper dive into the election data and why people voted the way they did, Geoff Bennett and Amna Nawaz spoke with Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report. Geoff Bennett: And for a deeper dive into the data and why people voted the way they did, Amy Walter of The Cook Political Report With Amy Walter is back with us. Hello, Amy Walter. Amy Walter: Hello, Geoff Bennett. I feel like I never left. Geoff Bennett: That's right. (CROSSTALK) Amy Walter: ... I didn't. Geoff Bennett: Yes, we just stayed here under the desk. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: So, look, President Trump urged voters to treat his -- this election as a referendum on him, and in many ways that's what they did. Amy Walter: Right. Geoff Bennett: The economy was a top issue for voters, as we know, with gas prices soaring amid the war in Iran. How much did voters hold the president and his party, the Republican Party, personally responsible for the economic pain they're feeling? Amy Walter: Yes, I mean, that's the real takeaway from this election. It's not just that people thought that the economy was their most salient issue. It's that they believed that it was Trump's policies that had caused the higher prices. In The Voter Poll, the exit poll, 63 percent of Americans who voted said Trump's policies are the cause of higher prices. Only 37 percent said it was for some other reason. And here's really -- the next piece of this is the priority piece. It's not just that they were frustrated about the war and its impact on gas prices and on inflation. The president has mentioned that today, as you noted, the vice president saying it's really the Iran war that's the big problem. But what voters also felt was a real sense that the president was focused much more on his priorities than he was focused on their priorities. Just 36 percent of voters said they believed that Trump has the right priorities; 64 percent said no. And when asked, well, what does he actually prioritize, 62 percent again said his priorities. Just 38 percent said the country's interests. And this, I think, was really typified, Geoff, by the fact that he ended his campaign -- we talked about this a lot going into the election -- ended it at the Reflecting Pool talking about the work he was going to do there, and then the day after the campaign, he's standing in the still-not-completed ballroom. Voters looked at that and said, I just don't understand how he could be more focused on this than on bringing down my costs. And I think the issue of betrayal overall -- it's not -- again, I don't think it's just that people are upset that their prices went up. It's that they believed that, when he came to Washington for a second time, he was not only going to fix the economy, but he was going to focus on them, and he was not, certainly not going to get the U.S. involved in overseas conflict. Amna Nawaz: Amy, let me ask you something about the redistricting push. I know we have talked a lot about the president pushed for that in a number of states over the last two years. All of that was based on the idea that Republicans could recreate the coalition that pushed him back into the White House in 2024. Amy Walter: Right. Amna Nawaz: It didn't work. Where did they fall short? Amy Walter: Yes, with almost every single piece of that coalition that Trump put together in 2024, Latinos a big piece of this, in 2024, Harris only won Latino voters by about 12 points. But Democrats this election won them by 30. Texas is a great example of the swing that we saw there. And then younger voters. Remember, we talked so much about especially younger men, younger men of color; 18-to-29-year-olds only supported Harris by three points in 2024. They gave Democrats 73 percent of the vote in this election. So the real sense, again, of the betrayal of the core promises of a Trump presidency really led to much of this backsliding with this coalition. Geoff Bennett: Amy Walter, thanks so much for your sharp insights this entire election season. Amy Walter: Thank you. Appreciate that. Geoff Bennett: We deeply appreciate it. Amy Walter: You're welcome.

The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift's reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years. NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space's three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September. It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving. Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper. WATCH: How NASA's new space telescope could help solve mysteries of dark energy and dark matter NASA is gauging industry's interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses. The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble's orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032. Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA's science mission chief. "Hubble still has important science ahead of it," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, "and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible." 0cc5efdf4d48.text: In Michigan's 7th Congressional District, progressive activist William Lawrence unseated Republican Tom Barrett in one of the year’s most competitive House races. Lawrence joined Amna Nawaz to discuss the win and what comes next. Amna Nawaz: We want to zero in now on some of the most notable results from last night's election. And we will start with Michigan's Seventh Congressional District. That's in the Lansing area. That is where progressive activistWilliam Lawrence unseated Republican Tom Barrett in one of the years' most competitive House races. Representative-elect Will Lawrence joins me now. Representative-elect, congratulations. Thanks for joining us. William Lawrence: Thank you so much. It's my pleasure to be here. Amna Nawaz: So this race was one of the most closely watched races in the entire nation, also among the most expensive House races in the country. It's a critical swing district in Michigan that Republicans really fought hard to hang on to. So how did you turn it blue? William Lawrence: It was all about the grassroots movement that we built. We knocked on more doors than any House campaign in the entire country. We have got thousands of volunteers who were out there knocking on those hundreds of thousands of doors. And I spent the last 15 months crisscrossing the district, showing up in small towns all over and here in the city of Lansing in the suburbs. And we took nothing for granted, went out to reach every single voter. And people were motivated by our campaign because I didn't take a dime of corporate PAC money, despite going up against $23 million from the other side. More money was spent trying to take me down than any other Democrat in the country. And they saw me speaking out on issues like stopping these wars, saying no to AI data centers, and investing in good housing and health care that we can actually afford. Amna Nawaz: We should mention to folks you co founded the Sunrise Movement. You are a climate activist. And, yes, AI data centers, regulating AI, those were core parts of your message. Why did they resonate so deeply where you are? William Lawrence: You know, it came to me from the bottom up. I started getting calls in the fall that we had not one, not two, but three hyperscale AI data centers proposed in different parts of my district. And in listening to people, it was clear that the pitch from these data center developers was just not persuasive. They're proposing to suck up a lot of our water, jack up our energy bills, cause all kinds of noise pollution and damage people's property values, all for the sake of generating AI, which, to hear them tell it, is going to put tens of millions of people out of work, if it doesn't kill us all by accident. So people just really responded organically in opposition to these bullies from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, and I was proud to stand alongside those residents throughout the campaign. Amna Nawaz: So you were previously endorsed by Bernie Sanders. We should note your primary opponent was actually endorsed by Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, who previously held this seat. She is a moderate. You are a progressive. What does your win say about this district or about the party more broadly? William Lawrence: I think all the results last night show that the American people delivered a striking rebuke to the Trump agenda and are -- have delivered a mandate for change. We have got to get the prices down. We have got to protect the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid. We have got to pass a war powers resolution to end this war in Iran. And people also want to see us stop arming Israel, stop sending money to drop more bombs around the world when our neighbors here in Michigan can't afford basic housing and health care. And I see that similar message was delivered all over the country, and I'm thrilled to be part of this huge majority, and we got to be ready to go in January to pass bills through the House and the Senate to make folks' lives easier. Amna Nawaz: I hear you saying your priorities for wanting to bring prices down, which seems to be the number one reason people voted so broadly for Democrats wanting change. On the accountability front, if I can ask you, where do you think Democrats' priority should be? Where should you go first in oversight hearings or impeachment or some other step? William Lawrence: I think there will be various ideas about how to approach it. But we've got to end this... Amna Nawaz: What is your top priority? William Lawrence: I'm interested to have conversations with my colleagues. We have to put a stop to this elite impunity. I mean, we got to get the Epstein files released. That is one top priority. So there's a bill that it was introduced by Khanna and Massie that was just one signature shy on the discharge petition from getting a vote. We definitely have to vote that bill on the House floor. And when it comes to the rest of the president's corruption and that of his administration, we have to pursue oversight and hearings and accountability and do it in a way which makes sure that we're clear that this is about defending the rule of law and putting to an end this age of elite impunity that, frankly, both parties have been complicit in. So we got to make sure to do it the right way and not allow it to distract from the economic agenda, but we got to continue to defend our economy and our democracy walking hand in hand there. Amna Nawaz: That is Representative-elect William Lawrence from Michigan's Seventh Congressional District joining us tonight. Thank you so much for your time. William Lawrence: Thank you.

15045fda0d84.text: The election led to several historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Black woman governor. And in New Mexico, Deb Haaland will make history as the first Native American woman to serve as a governor. Haaland joined Geoff Bennett to discuss more. Geoff Bennett: As have been reporting, yesterday's election brought a number of historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate. In Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress. And, in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor. Among those making history is Deb Haaland, who will become the first Native American woman to serve as governor of any U.S. state. Haaland previously served as interior secretary under President Biden and was one of the first Native American women elected to Congress. Governor-elect Deb Haaland joins us now. Congratulations on your victory and welcome back to the "News Hour." Deb Haaland: Thank you so much. Thank you. Geoff Bennett: You made history, of course, but voters are also expecting results. So how will you balance the symbolism of this victory with the responsibility now of governing a state that has faced persistent challenges? So many people are dealing with the high cost of living, persistent challenges with poverty, education, access to health care. How are you planning to deliver tangible results in New Mexico? Deb Haaland: Absolutely. Thank you so much for the question and for having me. And, of course, very proud to be the first Native American woman governor in the history of our country. That wasn't why I was running, though, of course. I have so much experience, having served at the highest level of government as the secretary of the interior, where I managed a work force of 70,000, an $18 billion annual budget. And, yes, like the rest of the country, our state is facing steep Medicaid cuts; 89,000 people can be kicked off the Medicaid rolls come the beginning of the year, people losing their SNAP benefits. This is all the result of the Trump bill that passed earlier this year. And so, of course, we want to make sure that we're stepping up, the legislature and myself continuing to fill in the gaps that our governor now has worked to fill in. We know that prices are getting higher due to so many of the tariffs and the war in Iran making gas prices higher. New Mexicans are paying higher costs for everything. And so we want to put more money in the pockets of New Mexicans, enhancing the child tax credit, the working families tax credit, continuing to move our clean energy forward, which we know will lower utility costs. So there's a lot of work to do, but I'm confident that we can get there. Geoff Bennett: Democrats had a strong election night across the country. How much of your victory, in your view, was a rejection of President Trump and his approach, and how much of it was an endorsement of your own vision for New Mexico? Deb Haaland: Thank you so much. Well, we currently have a Democratic governor here in New Mexico. Generally, every eight years -- our governor is termed out the end of this year. Every eight years, the seat flips back to Republican. And New Mexicans realized that yes, we needed to keep going on the trajectory that we are going on. We have universal childcare. We have early childhood education for every child in New Mexico. And those are things that New Mexicans feel have made their lives better. And so I want to ensure that we can enhance those programs, expand them across the state, so that every New Mexico family has an opportunity to participate. Universal childcare, it's an economic driver all over New Mexico. It creates jobs and helps parents to know their kids are safe while they're at work. So it's a win-win for our state and the people of New Mexico, and we will continue down that path. Geoff Bennett: Yes. I wonder, what have you learned from your time in Washington, both in Congress and in the Cabinet, about what government gets right and what it gets wrong, and how does all of that shape your approach to governing? Deb Haaland: Well, I will tell you, I feel like I always do the right thing when I listen to stakeholders, when I have the people at the table whose lives would be affected by the decisions that I make. I did that when I was at the Interior Department, and I will do it again. The most successful projects that we got across the finish line, transmission lines, offshore wind projects, protecting millions of acres of public lands across the country, that was all done with the idea that we need to bring people to the table early, that we should act with full transparency. So I intend to be transparent as the governor of New Mexico. I intend to bring stakeholders together to tell us what they need and what is best for their communities. New Mexico is different anywhere you go. None of our communities are the same, the northeast, the northwest, the north, the south, Central New Mexico. There's so many different communities with different needs. And so we're going to make sure that we're listening and that we can do what's best for our state. Geoff Bennett: Yes. I hear you when you say that you did not run for the sole goal of making history. But you have broken barriers before, as we mentioned, the first Native American woman -- among the first Native American women elected to Congress, the first Native American Cabinet secretary. Does this victory feel different, serving as governor? Deb Haaland: Well, I mean, look, this is my first successful statewide campaign. New Mexico's the fifth largest state, hundreds and hundreds, thousands of miles of rural roads that we drove on all throughout this campaign. So I feel like I worked really, really hard for this victory. We raised the funds to hire organizers. We had them on the ground a

c6efbf1bb649.text: President Trump has sought to deflect blame for the sweeping Republican losses. But within the party, some are beginning to ask whether they have been too deferential to the president — and whether the GOP needs to rethink its identity. Amna Nawaz discussed what comes next with David Holt, the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City. Amna Nawaz: President Trump has sought to deflect blame in last night's sweeping Republican losses. But within the party, some are beginning to ask whether they have been too deferential to the president and whether the GOP needs to rethink its identity. To discuss what comes next for Republicans, we're joined by David Holt. He's the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City. Mayor Holt, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. David Holt: Absolutely. Thank you. Amna Nawaz: So it was a tough night for your party. You posted on X last night this message, writing: "A political party that's morally and intellectually bankrupt deserves the rebuke of the American people." It's very strong language. So what do you think Republicans could or should have done to avoid that rebuke, to mitigate some of those losses? David Holt: Well, how much time do you have? (LAUGHTER) David Holt: We 10 years ago as a party -- I wouldn't say I was a part of this decision and that -- or that I have gone along with it -- that we as a party ultimately ceded our decision-making and our intellectual capacity to one person and really became a cult of personality, instead of what we had been, at least for the remainder of my adult life, which was a party of ideas, a conventional American political party trying to bring together enough people to win an election and build a coalition. It changed 10 years ago. And so I don't think this was a -- like something we could have messaged better in the last two weeks. I mean, I think we made a fundamental decision to really not be the Republican Party anymore, but to be this banner carrier for Trumpism, for a specific individual and his whims and desires, and to be the MAGA party. And what happened last night was such a total rejection of Trumpism and MAGA that really that party now no longer exists as a functional political movement. Amna Nawaz: We should point out your state of Oklahoma was one of the few bright spots for Republicans, right? You still control the governorship, both Senate seats, all five congressional seats. So if this was a referendum on the president, what do those results tell you about where Oklahoma is? David Holt: You're correct. I mean, the Republican nominee for governor did win in Oklahoma last night, but certainly the writing was on the wall that something was shifting even in Oklahoma, maybe not enough to shift all the way over to exchange control. But I have often pointed out, I mean, I'm a student of politics in my part of the country, and Oklahoma always follows Texas a few years later. We did in the '90s and in the 2000s, and so anyone who doesn't take pretty serious lesson from what happened last night in Texas in my neck of the woods is just living on borrowed time, because that's going to happen in Oklahoma. Oklahomans, Texans, Americans, they're ready to move into a different kind of conversation. And they still want, in my view, a center-right party, and this country needs a center-right conservative party. But people are wanting a normal party that's competent, that's talking about the real priorities that are in front of us, the real challenges and opportunities that are in front of us. And, ultimately, that's just not what was being offered. The MAGA movement had exhausted itself. Amna Nawaz: If there is one thing you want to see from your party and party leadership right now that you think could be some kind of a course correction, what's that first step? David Holt: Well, we have to return to being a political party again with a platform and ideas, and we have to be serious. I mean, too much of what you have seen from Republican governance the last few years is really seemed geared more towards entertainment. And we need -- this isn't professional wrestling. This is governance. So we have to be serious. We have to be talking about pocketbook issues, not reflecting pools and arches. We have to be meeting people where they are. I mean, I don't think this is going to be like some quick turnaround. I think this is going to be a multiyear conversation, but it finally began last night, and it needed to. And this country needs two real parties. And I think we're finally going to -- we're finally going to have that conversation that we have needed to have really for the better part of a decade. Amna Nawaz: That is the Republican mayor of Oklahoma City, David Holt, joining us tonight. Mayor Holt, thank you for your time. It's good to speak with you. David Holt: Likewise. Thank you.

2fbcaae40fad.text: A major factor in the midterm elections was the number of Latino voters who headed to the polls and supported Democrats. For perspective on this massive swing, Amna Nawaz spoke with María Teresa Kumar, CEO of Voto Latino, an organization that helps register Hispanic and Latino voters. Geoff Bennett: As we have heard tonight, a major factor in last night's victories were the number of Latino voters who headed to the polls and supported Democrats. Amna Nawaz: For perspective on this massive swing, we turn now to Maria Teresa Kumar. She's CEO of Voto Latino. That's an organization that helps register Hispanic and Latino voters. Good to see you. Thanks for being here. Maria Teresa Kumar, Founder and Executive Director, Voto Latino: Thanks for having us. Amna Nawaz: So Amy mentioned earlier, of course, that there was the shift we saw from 2024 to 2026. We should also just say, to be clear, Latinos are not a monolith. But how do you look at that and what's behind the people who backed Trump in '24 and went Democrat -- Democratic in '26? Maria Teresa Kumar: So it's -- folks are absolutely right. Latinos are not a monolith until you come for our families. And that's basically what we saw last night. It was a repudiation of the ICE raids that have been happening. I can tell you that I can go around the country and there's not a Latino, whether they work in Wall Street or they work in the fields, that don't know someone that's been caught in the dragnet. You marry that with the fact that financially they're not doing well; 36 percent of Latinas that we surveyed in April were skipping meals. All of a sudden, you realize that there is an opportunity for the Democrats to have a real conversation with them that is not talking about who is and isn't an American. What Amy was talking about, I think, is really important. I think it's something that both the Republicans and the Democrats need to take note, is that the Latino vote, because they are so young -- they're about a generation-and-a-half younger than the rest of the American voter. They are oftentimes considered very much independent, but the swingiest of swing voters because they don't have a history of voting even among their families. And so they are very issue-driven. And if you promise that you're going to basically provide for them to be able to actually stretch that dollar, then they will listen to you. But at the same time, if you start criminalizing them, then you're going to see what happened last night. Amna Nawaz: I want to talk to you about Texas in particular, basically a 30-year grip by Republicans broken last night. You have the first Latino governor in the state in Gina Hinojosa. You have the Democrat, James Talarico, winning the Senate race there. How do you look at Latino participation in those races? And generationally also, what are the trends you're seeing in Texas? Maria Teresa Kumar: So, Voto, I tell you, we started investing in Texas almost three cycles ago because we recognized that 54 percent of the kids in classrooms were young Latinos. And when you go down to the Rio Grande Valley, it is one of the poorest zip codes of people who are incredibly resilient. And when they flipped from left to right, it was because of the flood of immigrants coming across the border that was creating real chaos in their communities, and they were having a hard time stretching that dollar. So they took a chance on Trump. And what Trump did was overstep. I spent a lot of time with in the Rio Grande Valley, and I was talking to folks that were -- that voted very heavily for Trump and said, look, I'm a builder. It used to cost me $300 to do a square foot. Now it cost me $630 for a square foot because they're deporting my men. And because of the tariffs, we can't actually be able -- we can't actually try to figure out how to plan for our job, for the work that needs to happen. But I do think that the headline is, is that young Latinos showed up. And, again, when we talk about this idea of affordability versus immigration, for young Latinos, this is where we're going to see a generational shift. For young Latinos, it was absolutely to protect their parents. Amna Nawaz: When you look at this broader picture, this is the question we're asking again and again, do you feel like these votes were solely against President Trump? Or was there something also going for Democrats here? Maria Teresa Kumar: The candidate quality in Texas specifically was through the roof. Gina Hinojosa is from the Valley. Something that I -- when -- during the 2024 campaign that I often reminded the Harris campaign, neither Harris nor Biden went down to the border. Vance and Trump were there all the time. They did the retail politics so well this last week that their closing arguments were all along the Valley. If you look at who swung the most, who in Texas, when you look at the map of all the blue, it was all the southern border of Texas. And it proves the point. This was a community that has been long overlooked, but once you recognize them and you gave them something to vote for, they came out in force. Amna Nawaz: So what do you think Democrats have to do now? They have two years to try to make good on some of the promises that they made. What can they do? What should they prioritize for these voters that they have won back to make sure they don't lose them again? Maria Teresa Kumar: So, Amna, in August, we actually asked this very question, and we came up with a pothole agenda. Latino voters are looking for accountability on ICE, they're demanding for a pathway to citizenship and for the Democrats to say that out loud, and they're trying to figure out economic relief. Talk about SNAP benefits. Talk about raising the minimum wage. Talk about how you actually can identify their taxes, and, believe it or not, how do you actually create term limits for the Supreme Court? That's all top of mind. Amna Nawaz: Maria Teresa Kumar, CEO of Voto Latino, thank you so much for bein

7c90d1378b2a.text: For perspective on how both parties are responding to the historic election wins, Geoff Bennett spoke with two strategists from both sides of the political aisle. Mo Elleithee is the former spokesman for the Democratic National Committee, and Doug Heye is a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee. Amna Nawaz: Well, for perspective now on how both parties are responding to last night's historic wins, we're joined by two strategists from both sides of the political aisle. Geoff Bennett: That is Mo Elleithee, Democratic strategist and former spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee, and Doug Heye, a Republican strategist and former spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. Good to see you, gentlemen. Doug Heye: Thank you. Geoff Bennett: So, Mo, Democrats didn't just win. They won in places, in states and districts that Republicans thought were safe. What did Democrats get right in this cycle and what can they replicate in election seasons beyond this Trump era? Mo Elleithee: Yes. So we talked about this a little bit last night. My party isn't always the best at message discipline. But this cycle, boy, were they solidly on message. Candidate after candidate, the most progressive to the most moderate, from Kansas and Texas to Maine and Michigan, every Democratic candidate was talking about cost of living and corruption, and, in many cases, tying those two things together. All cycle long, Donald Trump did what Donald Trump does, just tossed out a bunch of crazy. And we usually chase it. We usually take the bait. We didn't this time. We stayed focused, and the results showed that. Geoff Bennett: And looking at the scale of the losses, was any of this avoidable for Republicans, or was the environment just too politically toxic? Doug Heye: The environment was too toxic. And, ultimately, if it were going to be avoidable, Trump would have had to be the one to avoid it by telling voters, here's what's important that we're doing for you, not here's what I'm doing that's important to me. So every time he talked about building an arch or reconstructing the East Wing or something about the Kennedy Center, all these things that voters don't really care about, especially when they're going through so much in their lives, is a real -- was a challenge to every Republican on the ballot. And I always start with my home state of North Carolina. Here's the most interesting thing to me about it, is that we have all seen the big losses, right? You have lost the General Assembly. The state Senate is still in question. So many Republican members have lost, and we're still counting ballots. But there were three constitutional amendments on the state ballot last night. All three were fairly conservative. One was voter I.D., and then two were about constitutional amendments limiting and capping taxes on property and income. Those three passed was 60 percent of the vote. So people voted for these conservative initiatives and then voted against every Republican that they could up and down the ballot to send that message to Trump. Geoff Bennett: To include Richard Hudson from North Carolina, who has the job of getting Republicans reelected across the country, congressional Republicans. He also lost his seat. Doug Heye: Sure. And the dean of the delegation, Virginia Foxx, who's the chair of the House Rules Committee, my member of Congress, right now is behind by 99 votes. They will go to a recount, but that's not an optimistic place to be in. Geoff Bennett: The vice president, J.D. Vance, was pretty blunt today. He's saying that the war in Iran was the reason Republicans lost. Here's the tweet. He says: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you would like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so." What do you make of those comments? Mo Elleithee: J.D. Vance is -- has got some real challenges moving forward. The guy clearly wants to be president. He wants to be the Republican nominee. And his entire party got wiped out because of his boss and him. So he's -- really interesting to see him try to put some distance between himself and the war. And look, in fairness, J.D. Vance, it's been reported, wasn't for the war in the beginning. But I don't know that voters who repudiated this administration are going to see that, right? They're repudiating Trump/Vance. He's partly right. It's partly the war, but it is also the long litany of broken promises that both Donald Trump and J.D. Vance have made. It is, as Maria Teresa was talking about, the inhumanity that we saw in the streets. And, remember, just days ago, when Vivek Ramaswamy put out that terrible ad in Ohio that was repudiated by both parties, J.D. Vance was the first guy to go into the state and hug it and embrace it and chastise the Republicans who were complaining about it. So J.D. Vance is going to have a hard couple of weeks trying to figure out how to position himself. Geoff Bennett: And President Trump, his midterm closing argument was at the Reflecting Pool, as you mentioned. Today, the morning after his party sustained these major losses, he was at the site of his reconstructed -- or in the process of being rebuilt here, this -- this future White House ballroom. What does that choice tell you about how the president is processing these results and whether he's prepared or has a willingness to pivot? Doug Heye: Well, it's not where we would want him to be consistent with his messaging, but he's been consistent that what is important to him as a priority of building things is somehow going to be important to voters throughout the country, and it just hasn't been. And if we were having this conversation and there were no Iran war, or we're having it the day before it started, what would we be talking about? Grocery prices. 87ffc4a0a839.text: Republicans woke up "in shock" Wednesday morning after they got hit with the biggest midterms wave in 50 years. Within hours, that shock was turning into rage. Why it matters: The battle for control of what's left of the Republican conference — headlined by Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Oho) — is the first salvo in a quest to bring GOP lawmakers back from the political wilderness. Johnson set the tone Wednesday morning, when he took himself out of the running for leader, citing the toll the job has taken on his family. A key outstanding question is the extent to which Republican finger-pointing leads to a wholesale shake-up of the party's leadership ranks, versus a slight readjustment. Driving the news: The intra-party blame game quickly hit a fever pitch. "Dear Republican Senate and House "Leadership," No, the polls were not wrong. You were. Even with record amounts of money at your disposal, you managed to get absolutely annihilated," Rep. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) wrote on X Wednesday morning. "Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction," Steube added. "When you have the worst defeat in modern history, you need a new playbook," another GOP lawmaker told Axios. State of play: The fallout is rippling across the entire House GOP leadership team, with every top position facing a contested race. Minority leader: Scalise and Jordan are squaring off in a rematch of their bitter 2023 battle for the speakership. Minority whip: Tom Emmer faces a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas). NRCC Chair: Rudy Yakym and Brian Jack will face off for the post. Current NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) is on track to lose his own reelection bid. Zoom in: Behind the leadership infighting, Republicans are reckoning with what went so disastrously wrong on Election Day, with some blaming the Trump administration's policies for their losses. "Iran, Iran, Iran ... we should have never done the war before the midterms," one GOP lawmaker told Axios. Another pointed to "Iran, ICE, inflation, fuel prices, lack of focus on pocketbook issues" as factors in the defeat. "Iran and the vanity of putting your name on things like the Kennedy Center," another GOP lawmaker said. What's next: House Republicans are scheduled to elect their next leadership team this coming Tuesday. The winner needs a majority of House Republicans in a secret-ballot vote.
