Six people have died after a large fire broke out in a residential building in Brooklyn, New York City, officials say.
Several others were hurt in the blaze, which occurred early on Thursday morning, the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) said in a statement.
More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel were sent to the scene near Sunset Park after the fire was first reported at around 01:40 local time (06:40 GMT).
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was "heartbroken" by the deaths, and has asked New Yorkers to "take a moment to pray for the full recovery of those who were injured".
The cause of the blaze is being investigated.
A crew specialising in hazardous materials was sent to the scene because of the presence of a lithium-ion battery, although it was not clear whether this was linked to the blaze.
The emergency responders reportedly discovered on their arrival that the building's first and second floors had been engulfed by flames.
Four individuals were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY.
A male and female were also taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, the New York City Police Department (NYPD) said.
Six other civilians were injured, two of them critically, along with three firefighters, the FDNY said.

A investigation is underway after "a major fish kill" in a County Down river, the Department for Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) has confirmed.
The pollution caused the death of brown and migratory sea trout in the Gransha, Ballystockart and Inler (also known as Enler) Rivers.
Glenn McKibbin, the secretary of Inler Angling Club, said about 1,000 fish were killed in the incident and it "could not have happened in a worse location on the river or at a worse time".
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) and Daera Inland Fisheries are working to "identify the source of the pollution and to finalise the numbers of fish killed".
The Department said the incident was reported by a member of the public on Tuesday at 09:30 GMT.
Fish stocks 'obliterated'
McKibbin said that "current and future fish stocks obliterated for years to come".
He added that resident and non-resident migratory fish, which only return at this of year to spawn, have been impacted.
"Knock-on effects for other wildlife such as resident kingfishers, herons & otters unavoidable.
"For our members and volunteers who work tirelessly in a bid to improve the river this is soul-destroying, particularly as the river was still in recovery from major pollution incidents / fish kills in 2013 and 2015," McKibbin said.
"Waterways up and down the country continue to be treated like sewers.
"The paltry fines that usually follow incidents of this nature are not a deterrent and the current 'system' is broken."
Many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up smaller tributaries to lay their eggs in cleaner, gravel-bottomed, or cooler waters away from larger predators in the main river.
A tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger mainstem river where many migratory fish, such as trout and salmon, swim up to lay their eggs away from larger predators in the main river.
Inler Angling Club Chairperson David Pyper said: "For those who dedicate so much time and effort to caring for the river, witnessing the sheer loss of fish in circumstances such as these is particularly disappointing.
"The club hopes that the forthcoming investigations will establish the cause of this latest incident and help ensure appropriate steps are taken to protect the river and its wildlife."
The club has encouraged local representatives and authorities to continue to prioritise rivers and direct resources towards improving water quality and preventing further incidents.

Protests are taking place across France after five unions launched a national day of strike action, joining high school students and demonstrators criticising the rising cost of living.
More than 250,000 people had taken to the streets in almost 70 towns and cities by 13:00 (12:00 GMT) on Thursday, and that was "just the start", said Sophie Binet of the CGT union.
The unions have vowed to take the wave of protests that began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycÃ©es (high schools) "to the next level".
They have since spread to include workers and the so-called "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said 70,000 police were being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest has been reported in the cities of Lyon and Rennes.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the RhÃ´ne river in central Lyon, as hundreds of people belonging to the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Meanwhile, there were clashes in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march.
The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, announcing more than 250 separate actions as part of their campaign for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protect public services.
Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
A coalition of unions has urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic, which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.
The head of the CFDT union, Marylise LÃ©on, complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase: "We are asking for a net increase of â¬100 a month."
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycÃ©es, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.
Large numbers are expected on the streets, especially in the capital, and the CFDT leader said she would be happy if 800,000 people turned out.
Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.
Union leaders have complained that recent marches have been kept away from the centre of Paris, because of violence that broke out in towns and cities on 17 October and led to more than 2,000 stores being looted and historic buildings being set on fire.
Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, and the prime minister's residence at HÃ´tel Matignon.
Instead, the march was set to follow another central route from Place de la RÃ©publique to Place de la Nation. The CFDT union complained that getting court approval for the route only on Wednesday evening made organising the march more difficult.

AI companies are racing to lock down clients in the oil industry. A deal announced Monday between ADNOC and OpenAI was the highest-profile example in a broader push at ADIPEC by tech companies to pitch bespoke, AI-driven tools to help operate drilling rigs, refineries, and other oil assets.
Thanks to the breakneck evolution of frontier AI models, âWeâre now really seeing the technology mature to the level where it will make a significant change in the operating processes within the sector,â said Dan Jeavons, president of UK-based Applied Computing. The company, which counts numerous veterans of Shell and other producers on its staff, uses AI to process millions of data points coming from sensors inside oil infrastructure and help the operator work more efficiently, identify malfunctions faster, and reduce emissions. ADIPEC is first and foremost a trade show, with hundreds of vendors selling every imaginable tool and piece of equipment, from simple screwdrivers to entire offshore drilling platforms. Even when oil prices surged, oilfield equipment vendors â which constitute a $250 billion global market â didnât often benefit, since most production companies moved to defend their balance sheets rather than rush to drill more.
Now business is looking up again: âIn the past month or two, thereâs been a surge in orders, and all of them are very urgent,â said Deleen Laxamana, an administrator for hardware producer PressBolt. âPeople are spending money again,â added Shawn Sharp, vice president of Texas International, which manufactures giant wrenches used for manipulating pipes. Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith are locked in a tight race for a US Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic candidate to the upper chamber in more than 40 years.
With 96% of votes counted as of Thursday morning, Colom was leading by just over 1,000 votes.
Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was elected in 2018 and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. The president won the state by more than 22 points in 2024.
If Colom wins the race, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875.
Both campaigns projected confidence as the count continued.
"We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith," the incumbent's campaign said in a statement.
The Democrat's campaign had an "army of lawyers" working to ensure the count continued "ensure the process is followed according to the law," Colom said on Wednesday.
"I am very happy with where we stand," Colom said. "I'm confident once the process plays out, where we are, where the ballots are, we're gonna win."
Counting continues in the Mississippi race after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, scoring victories in deep red states such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which had not elected Democratic senators in decades.
The Democratic Party had sent extra funding to the Mississippi race in recent weeks, seeing an unexpected opportunity to flip the seat.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has dispatched extra legal and campaign resources to the state as the count continues, Punchbowl news reported.
Hyde-Smith led the race early on with about 30% of votes counted, but as more ballots were processed, Colom started to gain a small edge over his opponent.
Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races or allow candidates to request recounts. The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days later.
About 3,600 absentee ballots remained outstanding as of Wednesday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said in a statement.
Several thousand affidavit ballots also remained outstanding, according to Colom. Voters can cast these ballots at polling sites if they say they are eligible but do not appear on the rolls or there is another issue. Election officials then set them aside for extra verification.
That means the race is very likely not to be called until at least 10 November, said Julie Wronski, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi.
"Because the difference between the two candidates is so narrow, really, we're going to have to wait for every single vote received in any capacity to be counted," Wronski said.
On the campaign trail, Colom, a district attorney, focused his message on his Christian faith and plans to address economic concerns. He took aim at Trump's policies including the war in Iran and the rising cost of living in the US.
Wronski said Hyde-Smith, who was appointed to the role in 2018 to fill a vacancy, ran a mostly lacklustre campaign, relying on the state's reliably conservative base to deliver.
"The lack of public appearances was quite striking," Wronski added.
Trump campaigned alongside Hyde-Smith last month, saying he was there "because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance".
Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, at nearly 40%, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and reportedly showed up in large numbers this election.
Charles Taylor, director of the NAACP's Mississippi branch, told the BBC his organisation saw a huge swell in black voter participation leading into Election Day.
"We saw long lines for absentee voting," Taylor said. "We saw long lines in person yesterday. Folks everywhere were motivated across the state."
"So, when the data comes back, I think it's going to tell a story that black voters turned out and turned out big."
Colom told the Washington Post, external in October that Democrats had not typically done well in Mississippi because large wins from Republicans in recent years led them to direct resources elsewhere.
In 2020, Democrats threw their support behind Mike Espy, a former US secretary of agriculture who they believed had captured momentum, but he lost to Hyde-Smith by a wide margin.
National Democrats are "conditioned not to care about Mississippi", Colom told the outlet. "To me, you can't be a party that cares about working people if you don't care about working rural people in Mississippi who are struggling."

Tuesdayâs Democratic sweep shook the energy stock market, boosting clean energy company shares on the expectation of a more renewables-friendly Congress and casting a pall on oil.
Solar companies First Solar and SunRun both rose around 8%; wind companies Orsted and Vestas, and the EV makers Lucid and Rivian also rallied. Chevron and ExxonMobil fell, meanwhile, weighed by the prospect of lower oil prices if Democrats push for a quicker end to the war in Iran. And the likelihood that new state and local-level Democratic leaders could impose restrictions on data center development weighed on companies riding the AI energy demand boom, including fuel cell battery maker Bloom Energy and gas turbine maker GE Vernova.
A Democrat-led Congress is likely to push to resurface tax benefits for renewables, and to push to reinstate other forms of Congressionally allocated clean energy funding. Still, the initial market reactions may overstate how much will change under a split government, TD Cowenâs John Miller told Semafor: Democratic infighting could impede the passage of permitting reform legislation, and pro-renewables legislation is vulnerable to Trumpâs veto.

958acc1e845a.text:
Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.
That advantage has disappeared, clearing the path for more climate and clean energy legislation, according to analysts and advocates.
Democrats swept the vast majority of competitive races at the state level, flipping control of governors’ offices from Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas.
Democrats have a 29-19 edge in governorships, with Kansas too close to call and Alaska likely to take a while to declare a winner.
The party is on track for a net gain of hundreds of legislative seats, potentially giving it control of more nationwide than Republicans for the first time in more than a decade. Going into the election, Republicans had 4,072 seats and Democrats held 3,257, according to MultiState, a research and lobbying firm. Democrats had a net gain of more than 350 seats on Tuesday and are likely to add several hundred more as results continue to be tabulated, according to MultiState.
Democrats won five new trifectas: Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, with Arizona likely to be the sixth once officials finish counting. Those additions would give the party 22 trifectas, with Republicans holding unified control in 18 states and nine with split control. Kansas is yet to be determined.
Republicans lost trifectas in Iowa, Georgia, Texas, New Hampshire and Ohio. Before the election, Republicans had trifectas in 23 states, Democrats had 16 and 11 were under split control.
The implications for climate and energy policy are likely to be profound, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group.
“In the states, we had a generational political window shift to make people’s lives better, to lower costs and to lower climate pollution at the same time,” she said in a conference call.
This was the “affordability election” with concerns about inflation and high energy prices, she said.
Newly elected lawmakers will enter office with energy policy proposals to address voter concerns, she said. She noted that renewable energy is less expensive than fossil fuels and can be developed quickly, promising rapid benefits for consumers. The growth of electric transportation reduces greenhouse gas emissions and shields consumers from the volatility of gasoline and diesel, she said.
Jay Inslee, former Democratic governor of Washington and a prominent advocate for climate and clean energy policies, urged lawmakers to seize this opportunity.
Inslee took a jab at President Donald Trump, calling him the election’s clear loser, even though he wasn’t on the ballot.
“The chief climate denier got his head handed to him,” Inslee said.
John Farrell, co-director of the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a research and advocacy nonprofit, said in an interview that he is excited to see what comes next with the new trifectas.
“There is this growing sense that more accountability measures are needed in order to rein in [utility] rates, and that utility companies are central to that problem,” he said.
Farrell sees an opportunity for Wisconsin to catch up with neighboring states that have already established climate and clean energy agendas. He’s pleased that Democrats’ legislative majorities in Minnesota are large enough to give the party leeway to propose more ambitious policies. In Michigan, he is encouraged by residents calling for publicly owned utilities and pushing back against the influence of large utilities.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
In the past, Farrell might have worried that utilities would stave off consumer-friendly policies by showering newly elected Democrats with campaign donations. But he thinks scenarios like this are less likely now because the public is wary of candidates they view as puppets for large companies. And some candidates have shown it’s possible to win without accepting money from utilities.
“We’re in a moment right now where there is enough scrutiny to make it harder for that sort of check-writing strategy to be successful,” he said.
More on the six states that attained trifectas or are on track to do so:
Arizona: Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs cruised to re-election and her party was on track to win majorities in the state House and Senate, although officials are still counting ballots in many races. Analysts said a Democratic trifecta is likely based on available results.
Michigan: Democrat Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state, won the governor’s race. Democrats expanded their majority in the state Senate and gained a majority in the state House, with some races still being counted.
Minnesota: Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar was elected governor by a wide margin. The party expanded its majority in the state Senate and turned an even split with Republicans in the state House into a comfortable majority, with counting still underway.
Nevada: Democrat Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, defeated the incumbent Republican governor, Joe Lombardo. Democrats also retained control of the state House and Senate.
Wisconsin: Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, was elected governor. Democrats flipped control of both chambers of the Legislature, with an 18-15 majority in the state Senate and a 53-46 majority in the state House.
Pennsylvania: Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro easily won re-election. His party gained a 26-24 majority in the state Senate and expanded its majority in the state House to 111-88, with four races still being counted.

eb38cf964cb2.text: Democrats' blowout win further complicates the fraught path to passing a permitting deal in the lame duck. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the Senate plan unacceptably weakens environmental protections and tribal input. The big picture: Dems' looming control of Congress "worsens the outlook" for the bill this year, the advisory firm Capstone said in a note. The firm sees Democrats as "further emboldened" to punt the bill into 2027. President "Trump is likely to put pressure on House Republicans to support the package, but with his standing diminished in the wake of the midterms, his political capital may be limited," it states. Analysts with Jefferies also see reduced odds of lame duck support for a package that makes it easier to build gas pipelines. Yes, but: The bipartisan bill's Democratic co-authors argued on Wednesday that now remains the time, with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) calling it a "bird in the hand" and saying "we'd be fools not to take it." "Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises," he said in a statement. State of play: Rapidan Energy Group now sees a 20%-25% chance in the lame duck, down from 30% pre-election. Yet Rapidan's rather bullish on a permitting deal with Trump in 2027-2028. That challenges the view of many bill supporters who see a fleeting opening right now. Rapidan's logic: Trump struck first-term deals with Dems on the debt limit, government funding and more — at times against the will of GOP congressional leaders. "Democrats need only five or six Republican votes to reach 60 on a bill Republicans helped write, and Trump's first-term precedent ... suggests he may be willing to make deals with Democrats to reduce the veto risk," their note states. Catch up quick: TD Cowen analysts quickly dropped their assessment of lame duck passage from 40% to 25%, while the firm ClearView Energy Partners also argues that Dems' bicameral win could weaken the prospects. What they're saying: American Clean Power Association head Jason Grumet told reporters on Wednesday the bill reflects voters' interest in cheaper energy. "I think that the understanding in Congress is that this is a really unique opportunity, and if you don't move forward in the next three or four weeks, it's hard to imagine a bipartisan effort over the next couple of years," said Grumet, whose group represents renewables, storage and transmission companies. The other side: Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to helm the Natural Resources Committee, is arguing that Democrats should show that the days of Trump's "supplicant Senate" are over. Huffman, who wants to wait until next year, said Dems should demand hearings and amendments on the bill he currently opposes. The bottom line: The White House is still pushing for lame duck action, but did not directly say whether it would be open to a deal on an altered bill next year. "The White House supports the bipartisan deal worked out between Republicans and Democrats and agrees that the time to get permitting reform done is now," a White House official said. Amy Harder contributed reporting. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

HPâs new chief executive, Emma Walmsley, is the latest in a parade of CEOs who have done the job before. Nearly 30% of incoming S&P 500 CEOs over the past year had already been a chief executive, double the historical average, according to data from Russell Reynolds.
Many are switching industries, too, as companies favor experience over expertise. Sector expertise matters less than outward-facing skills: navigating tariffs, export controls, and an unpredictable Washington. âSomeone whoâs âbeen-there-done-thatâ gives boards a sense of security, regardless of the industry,â Constantine Alexandrakis, who runs CEO search firm Russell Reynolds, tells Semafor.

39d9b210e83f.text:
Matthewâs view
For decades, Gulf oil and gas companies boasted of their reliability. But recent deals point to a new recognition: The region can no longer guarantee energy security for the world. Instead, Gulf producers will spend the next decade investing internationally, enmeshing themselves in global energy supply chains so the region is ready when the next disruptions hit.
In the early days of the Iran conflict, as oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz virtually ground to a halt, their focus was on rerouting. New pipelines, railways, and ports were discussed as ways to get around the chokepoint.
Saudi Arabiaâs East-West pipeline proved to be a crucial lifeline, both for energy markets and the kingdomâs financial health, as did Abu Dhabiâs pipeline to Fujairah. Both are now being expanded. But as Houthi attacks on the Saudi pipeline have shown, Plan B isnât enough. The problem isnât just a couple of narrow waterways, itâs the inability to ensure the security of Gulf energy facilities in a crisis.
This yearâs conflict has shown the relative ease with which cheap drones can slip past some of the worldâs most expensive air defense systems and hit pipelines, ports, and ships. Pouring billions more into new pipelines may achieve little more than creating a longer target list and spreading defensive systems more thinly. The outcome of the US midterms makes it more likely the Iran conflict remains unresolved from the Gulfâs perspective â with President Donald Trump possibly facing constraints on his ability to pursue âfinish-the-jobâ strikes and a track record of failed diplomacy that may not get any better faced with Iranâs famously tough negotiators. That ensures fundamental animosity in the region will continue to fester.
But even if the Iran war is settled today â bringing to an end Houthi threats to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Iranian attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz â the Gulfâs reputation as a reliable supplier of oil and gas has been irreparably damaged.
To avoid losing market share, the Gulf is readying itself for when instability next hits.
QatarEnergy is buying up international LNG shipments as a hedge against any future closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi had already launched an international investment plan before the war and is now accelerating its ambitions.
Saudi Arabiaâs latest deal, to store oil in underground caves in Singapore, may not be big enough to sway global markets. But it, too, is a statement of intent â in this case to build reserve capabilities around the world, ready for a worst-case scenario.
Expect to see many more similar deals in the months ahead. Unable to ensure the security of domestic infrastructure, Gulf energy companies will increasingly hedge by going global.

2db34d5b79cb.text:
Jihadâs view
Resilience or luck? At the recent IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, this question was on every policymakerâs mind. There were good reasons for relief: despite a succession of shocks, the global economy had held up better than many feared. So too has the Middle East and North Africa.
When hostilities erupted in the Gulf at the end of February, provoking the largest oil and energy shock in history, many feared the regionâs economies would be overwhelmed: Shipping lanes would close, energy prices would soar, and the more vulnerable economies would struggle to stay afloat. Eight months later, those worst fears have not materialized. Activity has slowed sharply in some places, but it has not collapsed. In many economies, it has continued to expand.
Economies have adjusted, while existing buffers and policy responses have helped absorb the shock. But pressures are building, particularly in import-dependent, low-income, and fragile states.
The IMFâs latest Regional Economic Outlook for the Middle East and Central Asia projects output in the Middle East and North Africa to contract by 1.3% in 2026, 2.7 percentage points below our April forecast. Yet that headline figure conceals considerable differences in a region that spans more than 20 countries.
Several Gulf economies face deep contractions this year as disrupted energy production and trade take their toll. A sharp rebound is expected in 2027, assuming the conflict abates and trade gradually normalizes. But it will not erase the losses: Gulf output is projected to remain below pre-conflict expectations in the medium term.
Major oil importers like Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco have shown surprising resilience, with growth expected to exceed 4% this year. Remittances, tourism, investment, and favorable financial conditions have helped sustain growth, while policy measures have cushioned households from higher food and energy costs. But pressures are building, with inflation expected to decline more slowly than forecast in the spring.
The risks will grow the longer conflict-related disruptions persist. Low inventories and tight spare capacity could magnify further energy price spikes. Prolonged uncertainty could weigh on investment, tourism, and trade. The poorest economies are especially vulnerable: food accounts for a large share of household spending, and declining aid leaves less room to cushion another shock. A global market correction, whether prompted by a reassessment of AI-driven gains or interest rates remaining higher for longer, would add to the strain, particularly where financing needs are already large.
For MENA policymakers, the consensus in Bangkok was clear: In times of turbulence, preserving macroeconomic stability remains the immediate policy priority. As one finance minister put it, âthe policy frameworks and buffers built in good times decide how much room we have in the bad times.â
Policies should focus on containing inflation, preserving fiscal sustainability, and protecting the vulnerable. With food, energy, and transport costs rising, central banks need to guard against renewed inflation. Meanwhile, governments should protect vulnerable households while keeping debt manageable and pursuing the investment and reforms needed for future growth. That means mobilizing revenue, prioritizing spending, and ensuring support is targeted and temporary. Countries with stronger buffers have more room to support recovery and reconstruction. Those with less will face tougher choices to avoid adding to their debt.
But managing this shock is only part of the task. Regional economies need to prepare for the next crisis. Diversifying trade and production would reduce reliance on narrow export baskets and vulnerable transport routes. Better infrastructure and deeper regional integration would cut rerouting costs and strengthen supply chains. Investment in renewable energy would limit exposure to volatile fuel markets.
At the same time, the region needs new engines of growth. Digital technologies, including AI, offer opportunities as Gulf economies invest in data centers and digital infrastructure. Turning that investment into broader prosperity will require better education and skills, stronger governance and competition, and deeper links to global markets.
The experience of the past eight months suggests that resilience has been earned, through adjustment, stronger policy frameworks, and buffers built before the conflict. But resilience is a process. If the Middle East conflict persists and buffers are steadily depleted, todayâs delayed effects could become tomorrowâs larger adjustment.
Governments have an opportunity to act. In an era of recurring shocks, the economies that prepare before the next disruption will be best placed not just to endure it, but to emerge stronger.
Jihad Azour is the IMFâs Director for the Middle East and Central Asia Department

Global oil markets have shifted to a supply surplus, despite months of disruption caused by the war in the Middle East. JPMorgan estimated supply exceeded demand by 1.4 million barrels a day last month, driven largely by Middle Eastern exports returning to prewar levels, while HSBC forecast Saudi output will jump in the fourth quarter as exports recover faster than expected.
Soaring output in Latin America â which is producing around 1.5 million more barrels a day than last year â also contributed to the global glut. The surplus and the US midterm results have pushed crude prices down 20% from this yearâs peak, putting Americans âdays away from enjoying the cheapest retail gasoline since March,â a leading Bloomberg columnist wrote.

b499b22e996b.text:
US tariffs were a drag on Republicans in midterm elections, but President Donald Trump is unlikely to change tack on trade, experts said. Trump has sought to use tariffs to bolster domestic employment and cut trade deficits, but âeach of these goals is wrong-headed, and neither has been met,â one analyst wrote in the Financial Times.
The legislature has limited sway over the imposition of levies, a former Trump administration economic adviser noted, and even if it sought to force his hand, âTrump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool,â an Atlantic Council scholar argued. One country has benefited, though: Canadaâs prime minister said the US is âasking lessâ and âoffering moreâ in once-rancorous negotiations.

7f8bc709f170.text:
French authorities were braced for a nationwide general strike over public services and cost-of-living concerns, demonstrations that showcase growing pressure on Europeâs social-welfare model. Todayâs protests bring together students, labor unions, and the âyellow vestâ movement, whose various demands include improvements to schooling, higher wages, taxes on the rich, and better worker protections.
The litany of grievances underlines the scale of the challenge facing France, which is already grappling with a slow growth and ballooning debt. The country is not an outlier: Spain faces its own strike soon. According to the Brussels think tank Bruegel, a demographic squeeze, labor-market insecurity, and a weakening of traditional family support networks have altogether meant the âpillars underpinning post-war European stability have eroded.â

91d4e8e53596.text:
US President Donald Trump conceded the Iran war was the defining issue that drove a Republican pummeling in midterm elections, though analysts were skeptical that any long-term truce was on the horizon. Oil prices fell for a fourth successive day, with the international benchmark dropping to nearly $93 a barrel on tradersâ bets that Democratsâ sweeping victories reduced the risk of escalation between Washington and Tehran.
Yet Trump nevertheless insisted that âif I had to do it again, Iâd have to do it again,â and one leading expert said the oil selloff âhas been somewhat baffling,â arguing that âthe risk of escalation structurally grows post midterms, and the outcome (a Dem victory) has been the base case for months.â

e176928d6a96.text:
- Published
Protesters claim Google's headquarters in London refused a petition of 54,000 signatories worried about the environmental impact of an Essex development.
The tech giant plans to build four data centre buildings, covering 130,500 sqm, and an office building on the former Arena Essex Raceway near Purfleet which closed in 2018.
The 52 hectares of land became a Local Wildlife Site in 2006 and conservationists said the development would threaten rare bumblebees and endangered broad-leaved cudweed.
Google would not confirm or deny that it refused the petition on Wednesday, but said data centres were "vital" and that the firm was taking its environmental responsibilities "very seriously".
A number of environmental groups claim the development would wipe out more than 80% of its protected habitats, as the site is also home to butterflies and nightingales.
They have called for Google to "search elsewhere", and want it opened up as a green space and the return of the racers.
Jamie Robins, programmes manager at Buglife, said the plan "makes a mockery" of Google's sustainability claims.
"Handing in this petition today is making it clear to Google that their Thurrock Data Centre plans are inappropriate and unwanted," he said.
"During a nature and climate emergency, with our insects in decline, we should be protecting our precious wildlife sites and need powerful companies to lead and make better decisions."
Emily Buttress, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said: "Its loss would be devastating for the local area.
"It would fragment the ecological network even further, putting already at-risk wildlife under an even greater threat."
A Google spokesperson said: "Data centres are vital to the UK, providing the critical infrastructure required to power our digital economy and the online services used by people in every corner of the UK.
"As we work to deliver this critical infrastructure, we share the Essex Wildlife Trust and Buglife's view that development at the former Arena Essex site must be sustainable.
"Our goal is to regenerate the site, bringing long-term investment and jobs to Thurrock while taking our environmental responsibilities very seriously.
"We are working closely with Natural England and ecological experts to guarantee a 10% Biodiversity Net Gain.
"Our proposal also ensures a substantial part of the site is preserved for new public open space, green links, retained habitat, and the long-term enhancement of key woodland corridors."

997f48f1374d.text:
Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

d0dd8285e3ca.text: Vice President Vance stepped out of President Trump's shadow Wednesday, seizing on the GOP's midterm catastrophe to begin the explosive task of claiming MAGA as his own. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in an extraordinary 600-word postmortem on X , blaming Trump's Iran campaign for Republicans' historic collapse. Why it matters: Vance's presidential ambitions are entangled in the wreckage of a war he privately opposed but publicly defended. His path to 2028 demands a delicate political calculation. Vance must convince MAGA's disillusioned voters that he understands their sense of betrayal, even as he remains a central figure in the administration responsible for the Iran war. His maneuvering will take place under the gaze of a president who doesn't seem particularly eager to leave the stage — and who isn't shy about reining in those on his team who overstep. "Today, JD Vance became president — or acted like he wanted to become one," a source close to the administration told Axios. Zoom in: Vance argued that defections from Trump's 2024 coalition — not lack of turnout — drove the GOP's collapse in Tuesday's midterms. Citing polling of disaffected Trump voters, he identified four demands: "End the war." "Focus on cost of living/inflation." "Put America First." "Change our relationship to Israel." Those happen to be the four hottest topics among top MAGA podcasters and activists. So Vance is aligning with those leaders on topics where MAGA anger with Trump is raging. What they're saying: "If you'd like to argue [the war] was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." Trump accepted that challenge Wednesday, acknowledging that the war had hurt Republicans but insisting it was worth the cost. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he told reporters. "As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different." As for Vance's post, Trump said: "I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine. I thought it was good." Behind the scenes: Vance's commentary caught some in the White House by surprise. But insiders said the vice president worked with senior administration officials on the post. "These were his words and thoughts," one insider said. "He's leading." Said another: "It pains me to say this, but Tuesday showed the emperor had no clothes, and Vance knew he should just state the obvious. There are going to be a lot of other Republicans putting a lot more distance between them and the president." One Republican consultant representing a potential rival in the 2028 presidential race offered a blunter assessment: "The VP had to show he's not a dead man walking out there." Zoom out: Trump's second term has been riven by a bitter ideological feud between MAGA's anti-interventionist wing and the pro-Israel hawks who championed the Iran war. Vance privately questioned the war's objectives and duration, then publicly defended the campaign and led peace negotiations with Iran. His postmortem now puts him squarely in the anti-interventionists' camp. That could help him fend off potential 2028 challengers who also are skeptical of foreign intervention. It also gives Vance an opening against more hawkish Republicans, particularly Texas Sen. Ted Cruz. If Cruz runs in 2028, as many expect, and argues that it's time for the party to move on from Trump administration figures, Vance could try to argue that Cruz was on the wrong side of the issue that helped cost Republicans the midterms. The midterm results have unleashed a fresh wave of recriminations, with MAGA influencers blaming Laura Loomer, Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin and other hawks for betraying Trump's America First promises. Those influencers, in turn, have generally accused their critics of antisemitism or disloyalty to Trump. By the numbers: A GOP political group that surveyed 12 key congressional races in January found that a plurality of voters blamed Democrats for inflation. By October, the numbers flipped and Trump and Republicans bore the blame. "What changed? The war in Iran. The cost of gas. It's that simple," a Republican consultant who provided the polling to Axios said. The intrigue: Donald Trump Jr., an influential voice in MAGA's grassroots movement, threw his weight behind Vance's postmortem, writing on X : "Every word of this is 💯 💯 💯." Between the lines: For all his professed straight talk, Vance's postmortem is strikingly selective. He blames the Iran war and acknowledges voters' anger over inflation, but makes no mention of Trump's tariffs, corruption controversies or fixation on White House construction projects as Republicans' political fortunes collapsed. The omissions are revealing: Vance offers a diagnosis of the defeat that validates MAGA's "America First" wing, while shielding Trump from a broader reckoning with his presidency. What to watch: Trump has yet to anoint Vance as his successor, and the Republican collapse is already exposing the contours of a potential succession fight. Asked Wednesday whether he had discussed a presidential run with Vance, Trump said the two talk about "a lot of things," before adding: "Maybe he won't run. I don't know who's going to run." Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), a Trump primary rival in 2024, seized on his state's narrow Republican victories — a rare GOP bright spot amid Tuesday's rout — to offer his own diagnosis of the party's failures. "This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans," DeSantis said at a news conference. "In January, when everyone in office leaves, who were either term-limited or got voted out of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control of their state — the state of Florida."

755f937eaa39.text: Americans made it very clear on Tuesday that health care is too expensive. The challenge for Democrats is to agree on the quickest way to deliver some relief. Why it matters: Voters can't wait until 2029 for life to get cheaper — but any short-term action to meaningfully lower health costs will require Democrats to make deals with President Trump. The big picture: There's already speculation about what a Democratic unity health care agenda would look like, and what progressives' midterms success means for Medicare for All. But that's largely geared toward the 2028 presidential race or a possible Democratic administration. The short-term reality is that any ambitious policies that significantly expand the government's role in health care are almost certain to collide with Trump's veto pen. Strategists say the Democrats' most realistic option is to find piecemeal affordability fixes next year and play the long game when it comes to reshaping the health system. "If you read history, people make the biggest mistakes when they win. That's when they take their eye off the ball and they don't do the right thing," said Zeke Emanuel, an adviser in the Obama White House and a professor of medical ethics and health policy at the University of Pennsylvania. "This is an affordability election. We need to do affordability, but I do agree with the idea that this is a two-step process," he added. "There's going to have to be longer-term reforms." "For those debating whether the new Congress should consider big and bold reforms or pass practical help for people right away, the answer is yes. Voters can and should expect action on multiple fronts," Families USA executive director Anthony Wright said in a statement. Between the lines: Democrats' top priorities for the next Congress are restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and reversing the Medicaid funding cuts in last year's GOP reconciliation law. Their unexpectedly large majorities in each chamber will give them leverage, but no guarantee of a victory, if there's a standoff with Trump. Even if they prevail, it won't help the 157 million Americans with workplace coverage who are feeling the strain of higher premiums, deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs. "Congress thinks of Medicare, Medicaid, and to some extent the exchanges. But they have to remember half the American population and a lot of people complaining about affordability are in the private sector," Emanuel said. What they're saying: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer told MS NOW yesterday that health costs will be a top focus for Democrats. Incoming Senate Finance Committee Chair Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said his committee "will create a new foundation for America's health care system that guarantees health care for all, gives Americans cheaper and better health care, and ends the corporate chokehold on our nation's health care system." And House Energy and Commerce Committee senior Democrat Frank Pallone of New Jersey called for "an agenda that puts working people first and focuses on resolving the outrageous price increases." The intrigue: Drug pricing could be one area ripe for a deal, considering the Trump administration's efforts to get the Republican Congress to write into law the "most favored nation" deals it struck with major manufacturers. "It's very hard for the public to hear both Democrats and the president say they care about this issue and fail to find a way to ... provide greater cost relief for their medications," said Democratic health care consultant Chris Jennings. Emanuel said Democrats should also push for site-neutral hospital payment policies, caps on hospital costs and an end to copays and deductibles for generic drugs in Medicare and ACA markets. The question is whether many Democrats are willing to scale back their ambitions for the sake of striking a deal with a weakened president. Many of those policy options would generate budgetary savings that could instead be used to help pay for sweeping coverage expansions. The bottom line: Voters couldn't have been clearer about how they're being squeezed by the health affordability crisis. Democrats have to figure out how to respond to pressure to act now.

1fc1b5bd0131.text: The AI industry is scrambling to repackage a $10 trillion infrastructure buildout to appease a hostile electorate that overwhelmingly voted to restrict data center construction in ballot measures across the country. It's not just changing the name of data centers to "compute campuses," but offering communities real money, including dividends, benefits for schools or cities, environmental concessions and labor protections. Why it matters: Tuesday's election proved voters won't tolerate unchecked growth, although the market and many analysts see the blue wave slowing — but not stopping — data center construction around the U.S. To prevent an existential threat, the world's biggest companies are working on a rebrand. How well they execute on their promises will determine the pace of the global AI race. What they're saying : Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, compared the turnaround AI must make to the 1996 election, which came shortly after Republicans routed Democrats in a historic midterm election. "A lot happens in two years," he told Axios in an interview. "Smart, talented folks take messages from voters and react and respond to them." Getting community buy-in for data centers will require "really making clear that these can be long-term, durable, economically transformative projects for communities," he said. Driving the news : There's no question about how voters feel about data centers after Election Day, with restrictive measures across 10 states going 43-1 at the ballot box. The margins weren't close, with an average of 75% of people favoring restrictions. In Texas, a new Democratic governor has promised to keep a moratorium in place until the legislature passes comprehensive reforms. Candidates who won in other emerging data center states also favor similar restrictions. Analysts say about 60% of planned 2028 capacity across the U.S. faces a risk of delay. Between the lines : Incoming Democrats aren't going to kill data centers. Virginia, run entirely by Democrats, is the biggest data center hub in the U.S. Unions are also among the buildout's biggest supporters. But many of the new crop of winning candidates have similar demands. Tech companies must pay for infrastructure and bring their own power, ensuring that new strains on the grid from the boom won't hit ratepayers. Tax breaks are dead and face repeal, and the companies will have to show that they will ensure environmental and labor protections. Voters also won't tolerate any more nondisclosure agreements or what look like secret deals. What we're watching: Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and other major data center developers began laying out a new vision for winning public approval before Tuesday's "AI earthquake." Many of their proposals already include efforts to meet these demands, including commitments to ensure data center developers cover their infrastructure and power costs. These concessions may make data centers more costly, but a slower pace could also make it easier to absorb higher costs. Zoom in : Jobs won't be enough, since they are temporary. Look for more payments akin to the $50,000 teacher bonuses that followed the construction of a massive Meta data center in Louisiana. Amazon allocated $1 billion for investing in data center communities over five years, and Microsoft also has its "Datacenter Community Pledge." OpenAI on Thursday unveiled a "Compute Campus Policy Blueprint" and outlined tens of millions of dollars of commitments for free school lunches, parks, first responders and other priorities. Lehane added that renaming data centers to compute campuses—viewed as a gimmick by some policymakers and consumer advocates—was an intentional effort to "provoke that conversation." Yes, but : It's far from clear whether Democrats who are poised to take control of powerful congressional committees in Washington will buy the talking points, and some new state leaders campaigned on the importance of binding agreements. A report last month from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) found that major tech companies aren't covering the full infrastructure costs of their data centers, and companies continue seeking billions in tax breaks as well as using nondisclosure agreements. The bottom line : Data center construction is set to slow, but it won't stop. The race is on to see whether Democrats can translate election momentum into binding restrictions or if the industry tries to head off tougher rules.

d2dc29deadf1.text: It's a de facto motto in the Trump White House: "Somebody's gotta take the fall." Lately, that person looks like Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: From the unpopular war in Iran to his bad bipartisan relations with members of Congress, Hegseth's record has made him the most vulnerable member of Trump's Cabinet after Tuesday night's midterm shellacking. "Hegseth is definitely on thin ice," a Trump adviser told Axios. "It doesn't mean the president forces him out. But there are complications." Driving the news: As early as next week, the House could impeach Hegseth for allegedly defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. The measure is sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a vociferous critic of Israel and foreign wars. Zoom in: Iran is at the center of both Hegseth's possible impeachment and Republicans' midterm collapse. Many voters oppose the war and its byproduct: higher gas prices that spiked after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz. Before Trump attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Hegseth was the most gung-ho about the conflict, and he gave the rosiest projections about how quickly and easily it would be resolved, according to sources familiar with the discussions. By August, a senior administration official said, U.S. Central Command was reportedly soliciting new approaches to pressure Iran, suggesting that military leaders were still reassessing how to achieve strategic results. CentCom was also asking: "At what point did Hegseth recognize that our original strategy wasn't going to produce the outcome he expected and pitched?" Trump stood by Hegseth on Wednesday, telling reporters that the secretary is "doing a very good job." Between the lines: Trump has been known to praise an embattled Cabinet secretary, only to seek their ouster shortly thereafter. With Hegseth, four factors are weighing on Trump: 1. The impeachment threat. Democrats already have tried to impeach Hegseth, and with their new House majority in January, those efforts could intensify. The last thing Trump wants is a series of distracting impeachment hearings focused on Hegseth's rocky tenure — and, inevitably, Trump's decision to attack Iran. "Tonight would have looked very different without the Iran war," one administration official told Axios late Tuesday. "I believe you'll ultimately see POTUS hold Pete Hegseth accountable, and that will play out in the lame duck," a reference to the period between the midterms and the new Congress' first day, Jan. 3. 2. Trump needs a scalp. Presidents have a long history of shaking up their administrations after disastrous midterms. George W. Bush notably ousted Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld after the 2006 elections. It wouldn't be surprising to see Trump make a high-profile personnel change after a defeat of this magnitude. Hegseth, whose tenure has been marked by controversy, is one potential target. "Somebody's gotta take the fall, and Pete is moving to the top of the list," a U.S. official said. 3. The lame-duck window. If Trump is going to replace Hegseth, there's a compelling reason to do it before January. Confirmations in a Democrat-controlled Senate will be impossible. That gives Trump a narrow window to push through a new defense secretary while Republicans still hold the majority. "No one's getting confirmed" in the new Congress, a senior White House official said. "We're operating under that premise." 4. A potential soft landing. There also is a conceivable exit ramp for Hegseth: Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn is about to become that state'e governor, and she will have the power to appoint a replacement to her Senate seat. Hegseth owns a home in Tennessee, giving him a connection there. Trump expressed approval for the idea Wednesday: "I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all." What they're saying: Asked about a possible impeachment vote and efforts to remove Hegseth, a spokesperson said the secretary will "not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists." "The Department of War has followed the law and our secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America." The intrigue: Trump allies in Congress have asked the administration to get rid of Hegseth, but they acknowledge that even if Democrats captured 55 Senate seats, an effort to remove the secretary probably would fail because it would take 12 more votes in the 100-member chamber. "There are some Republican chairs in the Senate who just hate Pete, but that isn't enough," an administration official said. Behind the scenes: Hegseth critics leaked to Politico that the secretary's new financial disclosure report showed his wife worked for a consulting firm with Defense Department ties. One Hegseth ally called the campaign against the secretary "an op." In a statement, Hegseth's department said he's in "full compliance with all ethics laws and regulations ... Any insinuations or claims otherwise are ridiculous slander."

5c6fbd9d42ca.text: Data: Axios research; Map: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Democrats are on track to take control of a majority of legislative chambers, ending 16 years of Republican dominance over America's statehouses. If current leads hold, 75% of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor, and 53% will live in Democratic trifectas. Why it matters: Statehouses are the front line of American federalism, and Tuesday's gains dramatically expand Democrats' power to increase minimum wages, protect abortion access, and set voting rules ahead of 2028 for most Americans. Driving the news: The party is set to flip 12 legislative chambers, dismantle five Republican state trifectas, shatter 11 GOP supermajorities and build 12 of its own, according to AP returns as of 6pm ET on Wednesday. If leads hold, Democrats will control the governor's office and both chambers in five of the seven 2024 presidential battlegrounds: Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. They have also broken Republican one-party rule in the sixth (Georgia) and flipped the House in the seventh (North Carolina). Democrats flipped five GOP-held governorships (Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas) and lead in Alaska. Republicans haven't flipped any, despite targeting Arizona, Michigan, Oregon and Wisconsin. Kansas, where Democrat Cindy Holscher was leading by about half a point Wednesday evening, is uncalled. The big picture: Ever since the 2010 Tea Party wave, Republicans have used their grip on statehouses to reshape American life: banning abortion, loosening gun laws, restricting collective bargaining and expanding private-school vouchers. They drew maps that kept them in power even in years Democrats won more votes statewide. Tuesday's Democratic gains broke that firewall. By the numbers: Republicans entered Election Day with 23 trifectas (control of the governor's office and both chambers) to Democrats' 16. If leads hold, Democrats will have 22 and Republicans 18. 24% of Americans will live under a GOP trifecta, down from 42%. Democrats will control 51 of 99 chambers, up from 39. Republicans will control 46, down from 57. (Minnesota's House was tied, and Alaska's Senate and House have been controlled by a bipartisan coalition.) A combined 5,000-vote swing across six states would have given Democrats control of six more legislative chambers. Data: Axios research; Table: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Zoom in: Democrats won veto-proof majorities against Republican governors in both Vermont chambers and the New Hampshire House, and sit one seat short in the New Hampshire Senate. Republicans lost two-thirds majorities in eight chambers, including the Iowa and Kansas Houses, where Democratic governors' vetoes would now stick. In Kansas, that depends on Holscher winning. Democrats built supermajorities in nine more chambers, including Arizona's Senate and in states they already govern. Policies Democrats could reshape Paychecks: Pennsylvania and Wisconsin still use the $7.25 federal minimum wage. Pennsylvania's House has passed increases before, and the GOP Senate didn't take them up. Wisconsin Democrats can repeal what's left of Act 10, the 2011 law that stripped most public workers of collective bargaining. A judge struck down most of it in 2024, and that ruling is on appeal. Nevada Democrats can revive a paid leave bill the Republican governor vetoed. Abortion: New Democratic attorneys general in Georgia and Texas will decide how hard to defend their states' abortion bans in court and whether Texas keeps pursuing doctors who mail pills from shield-law states. In Iowa and Ohio, and in Kansas if Holscher wins, Democratic governors can veto new restrictions. Schools: Arizona Democrats can cap the state's universal voucher program , which Gov. Katie Hobbs has tried and failed to rein in. Texas' new $1 billion voucher program might survive because the GOP held the state Senate, but now Democrats will have a say in how it's funded. Elections: Pennsylvania and Wisconsin bar officials from processing mail ballots before Election Day. That rule is a big reason both states' counts can drag on for days. Democratic trifectas in both states can change it before 2028. New Democratic secretaries of state in Georgia, Ohio and Indiana will run those states' presidential elections. Yes, but: In Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas, divided government means more vetoes than new laws. Several new majorities are razor-thin. Pennsylvania's Senate is 26-24 and Wisconsin's is 18-15. New Democratic governors also inherit the Medicaid and SNAP cuts in last year's GOP megabill, and backfilling them would come out of state budgets. The bottom line: Republicans spent 16 years building a statehouse majority. Democrats erased it in one night, and now have two years to show voters what they'll do with it.

63aed882ff6e.text:
Midterm Voters Split on Abortion and Trans Healthcare Ballot Questions
ST. LOUIS — Voters’ sweeping support of Democratic candidates in Tuesday’s midterm election didn’t translate into similarly clear outcomes for ballot initiatives on abortion access and transgender issues.
In Missouri, a state that President Donald Trump carried by an 18-point margin in 2024, voters rejected a proposal to ban both abortion and gender-affirming healthcare for transgender minors.
Opponents of the measure celebrated the result with a mix of cheers, tears, hugs, and dancing at an election night watch party in St. Louis — as many of the same people had done only two years earlier when Missouri voters enshrined abortion protections in the state constitution.
But in Washington state, which Trump lost by 18 percentage points in his most recent election, voters appeared to back a measure restricting trans kids’ participation in youth sports, with 60% of votes counted on Wednesday.
Voters also supported proposed restrictions on trans athletes in youth sports in Arizona and Nebraska. And as of Wednesday afternoon, similar restrictions as well as a ban on gender-affirming surgery for minors were leading in Colorado with about 80% of votes counted.
And while voters in Virginia and Nevada backed abortion protections, Idaho voters rejected them.
“Each state also has its own culture,” said Alina Salganicoff, director of Women’s Health Policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
Missouri provides insight into voters’ motivations and thinking about the two separate but related issues. While political messaging in other states, including Virginia and Idaho, tied abortion and trans issues together, Missouri was the only state where the two were explicitly combined into a single ballot measure.
The measure that Missouri voters rejected Tuesday is part of a years-long battle over abortion access in the state. Missouri was the first state to ban abortion after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal abortion protections with its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving each state to make its own abortion policy.
In 2024, Missouri voters overturned the state ban by passing a ballot measure adding abortion protections to the state constitution. Opponents of that measure argued it would also allow a state ban on gender-affirming care for minors to be overturned. The abortion measure passed by fewer than 100,000 votes while Trump carried the state by over 550,000.
Two years later, the state’s Republican-dominated legislature asked voters to reconsider, with this year’s measure to repeal the 2024 abortion protections.
The initiative also would have barred minors from gender-transition surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy, and puberty blockers. The legislature had already permanently blocked minors’ access to gender-affirming surgeries and temporarily blocked their access to new prescriptions for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones until August 2027. The amendment would have enshrined those bans in the state constitution.
“Tonight is a loss for women, a loss for children, and a loss for life,” James Lawson, campaign manager for Her Health, Her Future, which supported the bans, said in an election night statement. He noted the campaign had built a coalition of doctors, pastors, parents, and volunteers and would continue its advocacy.
A survey of midterm voters by the NORC research organization, with questions from KFF, shows abortion was the stronger motivator of the two issues in Missouri, especially among those opposed to the proposed bans.
Of residents who voted against the measure, 59% said abortion policy was more important to their vote, while 33% said abortion and trans care for minors were equally important. The survey also found that 40% of voters opposed to the combined bans are supportive of restricting gender-affirming care while opposed to repealing abortion rights.
Of the voters who supported the bans, 26% said abortion was more important, 60% weighted the two equally, and 11% said trans care for minors was more important.
“This is the first time we saw these two issues linked,” KFF’s Salganicoff said. And while a sizable minority might be split on the two issues, “it’s not enough to move the needle on abortion rights when you have support in a state.”
Lindsey Dawson, director of LGBTQ Health Policy at KFF, said the Missouri survey data and broader election results across the country also appear to indicate that attempts to politicize trans care may not be as electorally significant as some had thought.
Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, seemed to agree, telling reporters Nov. 4, “I knew Republicans were in trouble when I was reading an overview about what were they running ads on, and they’re spending hundreds of millions of dollars across the country on transgender ads.”
That may have been effective four years ago, DeSantis said, but during this election, it “was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote.”
At the St. Louis watch party for the coalition opposing the proposed Missouri bans, Shira Berkowitz of the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization PROMO Missouri credited the group’s canvassing campaign with helping to sway ambivalent Missouri voters.
The group’s effort included a team of trans Missourians who went door to door to share their personal stories, answer questions, and try to have “transformative” conversations.
“We proved so powerfully that our visibility is not a liability,” Berkowitz said. “We weren’t just running a campaign; we were writing a playbook. What we built here in Missouri, we built to last.”

8a5416d1006d.text:
Federal leaders overseeing a $50 billion rural health fund missed a critical deadline to announce how much they’ll give states next year, alerting state leaders to the delay with a mass email.
A 12-sentence message from Alina Czekai, director of the federal Office of Rural Health Transformation, said officials “discovered an additional administrative process requirement.”
The Rural Health Transformation Program, which President Donald Trump touted as an “unprecedented” investment to “revitalize hospitals in our cherished rural communities,” calls for federal regulators to award states shares of $10 billion a year for five years.
In 2026, each state was awarded between $147 million and $281 million, with allocations determined by a federal scoring process to be revisited each year. State leaders had just over seven weeks last year to write applications as they competed against one another for first-year funds.
A national program of “this size, scope, and complexity” that has operated on a tight timeline is going to have “unforeseen issues in implementation,” said Alan Morgan, chief executive of the National Rural Health Association, which represents rural hospitals and clinics. “It’s just going to happen.”
Since the program launched last summer, state leaders have raised concerns about tight deadlines and burdensome reporting demands. First-year progress reports show state leaders have complied with federal demands to boost rural health technology infrastructure while also sending money to local communities.
Still, the speedy rollout did not “set anybody up for success to make meaningful progress,” said Lori Foley, who leads revenue and compliance advisory at PYA, a national consulting firm that has worked with regional and local health systems over the past year.
For state leaders, the Oct. 30 email has only added to the pressures of the previous months. One called the email funding alert “cryptic.” Another said there have been “plenty of surprises along the way.” One Midwestern state health association leader said her staff was “in the dark over here” about the funding. KFF Health News agreed not to name the state officials because they feared retribution.
On Nov. 2, Kentucky’s Beth Fisher, a spokesperson for the state’s Cabinet for Health and Family Services, confirmed the delay to KFF Health News, even as federal leaders declined to respond to questions. Kentucky won nearly $213 million last year, and Fisher wrote that the rural money was meant to “lessen the impacts” of expected reductions in federal Medicaid funding.
“Team Kentucky believes that healthcare is a basic human right,” Fisher said.
State leaders had expected to hear their 2027 award amount by Oct. 31, as detailed in the original federal notice. The email announcing a delay arrived at 4:05 p.m. Eastern time on Oct. 30, according to one document shared with KFF Health News.
In it, Czekai wrote that each state’s second-year base funding of $100 million was available but that the competitive portion, which varied widely for states last year, is delayed.
“We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible,” wrote Czekai, whose office is part of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. She did not specify when the competitive portion would be announced but wrote that each state’s budget revisions triggered by the new allocations would be “due back to CMS” by Nov. 30.
Czekai did not respond to a request for comment. The CMS press office declined to respond on the record to a list of detailed questions.
Michael Baker, director of healthcare policy at the American Action Forum, a center-right think tank, said he wasn’t surprised that calculating second-year awards “seems to be more complicated than the office anticipated.”
Baker said federal staff had created “ambitious” grading metrics for the funding, awarding points for initiatives such as expanding rural health workforces and policy priorities such as adopting the presidential fitness test for schoolchildren.
At first glance, last year’s awards did not appear to favor states based on the governor’s political party. But one academic data analysis teased out the amount awarded for each state’s competitive score — the discretionary part Czekai said is now delayed. A KFF Health News review of last year’s awards found that states with Republican governors tended to receive more of the competitive funding. Democratic-controlled states crowded the bottom quarter of those awards.
The second-year funding announcement was slated to happen just days before the midterm elections — in which Democrats won majorities in the Senate and House, as well as several governor races. In the weeks before Election Day, Trump officials lauded the rural health program as a Republican success, by visiting battleground states and publishing a flurry of news releases.
Among the stops: In New Hampshire, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced an $11 million grant to support mobile health and emergency care. In Ohio, CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz promoted investments including $30.3 million in one-time funds for rural hospitals.
Program’s Launch
After first-year awards were announced a few days ahead of schedule in late 2025, states had eight months to submit revised budgets, begin spending, and show how they were spending their money.
The first annual progress reports, detailing how each state awarded and spent their money, were due to CMS by the end of August. Officials at CMS have declined repeated requests to release those reports publicly.
KFF Health News gathered more than half the states’ first-year progress reports, through emails and records requests. Together, they reveal that many states hired management and technology consultants, listing them as providing technical assistance, grants management, and “other consulting.”
