If you’ve ever looked for a homegrown replacement for the imported olive, canola and palm oils that typically fill grocery store aisles and home kitchens, there’s a small but growing alternative. A network of sustainability enthusiasts is now making oil from a resource native to Pennsylvania, one of the fastest-growing hubs for this production—bitternut hickory trees.
“We have this staple oil crop on the East Coast of North America that no one looks at as oil,” said Brian Nana-Sinkam, head of product at Third Place Processing in Oley, Pennsylvania, which houses presses that extract edible oil from hickory nuts, “and we import all of the oil that we consume.”
In 2022, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported that American vegetable oil imports cost $10.9 billion, making the U.S. the second-largest global market for cooking oils that year. The global industry relies on mass shipping and other environmentally unsound look to herbicides to profitably grow mass-produced oil.
Meanwhile, across the country, bitternut (otherwise known as yellowbud) hickory trees sit largely untapped for their tasty cooking oil potential—save for this growing group of gatherers, farmers, processors, agroforestry experts and tree breeders determined to make hickory oil a pantry staple. To succeed, they’ll have to overcome low public awareness and limited resources. So they’re starting with one nut-gathering event at a time.
On the Hunt for Hickory Nuts
On a cool, sunny day in mid-October, a group of roughly 25 people of all ages gathered around a picnic table covered in a blue cloth bearing Third Place Processing’s logo in a parking lot at the edge of a roadside forest in Oley, about an hour northeast of Lancaster. A lanky man in an orange Kubota hat passes nuts around so everyone will be able to identify them on the forest floor.
“I didn’t expect so many people…so this is a wonderful thing,” the man, Sam Geesaman, orchard lead at nearby Bloom Farm and expert on yellowbud hickory harvest operations, said. He explained that he stashed buckets where people can dump their nuts among the hickories, whose yellow leaves fan out over the parking lot. “I have a feeling everybody’s going to go Easter egg hunt out there and be like, mine, mine, mine…save some for other folks that are behind you. It’s just about the experience today.”
Experience serves as step one to widening public awareness of hickory nuts as a viable Pennsylvania food source. Attendees disperse into the woods, eyes to the ground, picking out brown-green hulls from fallen leaves, dirt and twigs.
“The flavor profile is similar to olive oil,” Nana-Sinkam said of hickory oil. His colleague at Third Place, processing operations director Matt Holt, calls it “buttery and mellow.” Rich in omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids (good for brain health and reducing inflammation), hickory nut oil has a high smoke point, ideal for cooking. “But the big thing is that it grows vigorously here,” Nana-Sinkam added. “Once people taste it, they’re like, ‘Whoa, I didn’t know I had this in my backyard.’”
In the sustainability movement, backyard access beats importing, which is currently how U.S. consumers get most of their vegetable oil. In 2024, production of these oils (like palm, rapeseed and olive) relied on 364 million hectares of global cropland, close to 20 percent of the world’s total. The demand has harmed biodiversity (forests in Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa have been razed to accommodate palm monocultures), degraded soil health and resulted in significant carbon dioxide and methane emissions.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
To encourage foraging for local tree resources in Pennsylvania, the Keystone Tree Crop Cooperative launched in March 2024. That year, the cooperative collected enough hickory nuts to press between five and six gallons of oil, said director Don English. From last year’s harvest, the group made between 50 and 55 gallons of oil. This year, English says the aim is to produce 300. There’s an urgency to scale production fast. “We’re about the only organization that’s doing it,” he said.
One of the cooperative’s goals is to build out “aggregator hubs” across the state, where those who gather nuts can deposit their hauls in exchange for cash or oil for personal use. To facilitate this, the cooperative recently began hosting hickory nut gathering events like the one organized by Third Place (Nana-Sinkam is also a cooperative member).
In Western Pennsylvania, Andrea Ferich, the cooperative’s marketing director, operates an aggregation hub. She recently led a gathering event in Blair County, where she educated attendees about hickory nuts and worked with them to identify groves of yellowbud hickories.
“I was really interested in developing a stepping stone on the way to Pittsburgh,” Ferich said, “and there was already an existing, thriving community around tree crops in the Blair County area.” She spoke at the county’s Pawpaw Festival in September (harvesting time for the pudding-like pawpaw fruits) to summon attendees for the hickory gathering event. Some traveled from Pittsburgh. Ferich said that people find “meaning” in harvesting local nuts through “connecting with community and having a hobby that can help them produce oil or get paid in cash.”
Amish residents of Pennsylvania have shown particular interest harvesting hickory nuts for income or nutrition. “Within the Amish community, word travels really fast,” she said. Though those she met didn’t have a history of pressing yellowbud hickory nuts for oil (they typically use butter and lard for fat), one Amish woman recalled collecting and eating shagbark hickory nuts when she was young. Democratsâ sweeping midterm victory could give European allies fresh confidence to push back against President Donald Trump, weakening his leverage over countries that have previously accommodated his demands.
After the midterms, âeverybody is now obliged to look toward the post-Trump era,â a European diplomat told Semafor.
âIn the first two years [of Trumpâs presidency], we saw a lot of bending the knee by Europeans,â said Max Bergmann of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
But Bergmann predicted that deference could fade: âWeâre going to see less of that going forward, because thereâs a sense that they donât need to take it.â
Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security, said allies like the United Kingdom and South Korea may also be less inclined to honor billion-dollar trade agreements negotiated under pressure; instead, theyâll have an âincentiveâ to âplay out the clock.â
âPresident Trump has effectively restored American strength on the global stage and strengthened relationships with world leaders,â White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told Semafor.
âThe results speak for themselves: fair trade is restored, investments are pouring in, narcoterrorists are eliminated, detained Americans are home, and our homeland is safer. The President will continue to work with anyone to put America first and improve the livelihoods of families across the country,â she said.

45d94a7ff0dc.text:
Hakeem Jeffries will have the largest House majority in decades next year, and heâs gearing up to use it.
In comments to reporters Wednesday afternoon, Jeffries, set to be the countryâs first Black speaker, said his caucus âmade a promise to the country that we would fight for an affordable America, and we intend to keep it.â
House Democratsâ initial plans involve voting to repeal cuts to Medicaid enacted in Republicansâ megabill, restore lapsed healthcare subsidies, end the Iran war, and sunset tariffs. He and Democratic leaders plan to talk as a caucus about plans to tackle AI and other issues.
The larger-than-expected House majority along with control of the Senate opens more legislative options for Democrats â though President Donald Trump still has veto power. And Democrats have to contend with the Senate filibuster and a new bloc of progressives angling to push for more ambitious policies.
Newly elected House lawmakers are going to quickly face pressure to deliver on their campaign promises to tackle cost-of-living issues.
âWe have to actually start delivering results, and so I think we need to work with anyone to do that,â said Rep.-elect Christina Hines, who flipped a purple seat in Michigan.
In doing so, Democrats will face splits on how much legislating they should attempt with Trump still in the White House and the Senate filibuster intact.
Progressives donât want to be penned in by the threat of a Trump veto. âBig majorities can get big things done,â Progressive Caucus Chair Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, told reporters Wednesday.
On the other hand, many centrist Democrats want to limit their work to what can break a filibuster and be signed into law by Trump â a significantly more limited pool of proposals.
Rep. Adam Gray, D-Calif., a Blue Dog Democrat, told Semafor Democrats should â100%â tailor their agenda to what can become law. âHow about we spend the majority of our time on stuff that we all agree on?â he said.
But some, like Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., are hopeful to even have the option to debate issues in their caucus. âBeing pragmatic does not mean that you canât be bold,â she said.
In a dear-colleague letter to Democratic lawmakers officially kicking off his speakership bid, Jeffries hinted at additional legislative items. He told lawmakers that on top of affordability issues, the caucus would work on âaccountabilityâ concerns like limiting price gouging and restoring âAmerican Values,â like the right to vote.
One major front of House Democratsâ agenda wonât require as many legislative hurdles: their many planned investigations into the Trump administration and the private sector.
âHouse Democrats are going to lead a Congress that does serve as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch,â Jeffries said Wednesday.

Senate Republicans are staring into the abyss. It could be very difficult for them to reclaim the chamber in two years, especially if Democrats win still-uncalled races in Mississippi and Alaska.
Those seats may not be decided for days, and would represent the potential 55th and 56th seats of a Democratic majority â the largest since the first two years of Barack Obamaâs presidency.
Republicansâ top Senate pickup opportunities in 2028 are Arizona, Georgia, Ohio, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. Democrats have solid winning streaks in all of those states except Pennsylvania and Ohio.
It could get even worse for Republicans trying to take the chamber back in two years: Democrats have pickup opportunities of their own in Wisconsin and North Carolina, and GOP-held seats in South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

The News
The new Democratic majority in Congress knows AI is an issue ripe for the taking. A fight is already brewing over how aggressively to regulate it.
Tuesdayâs election results saw more than 40 AI data center-related ballot measures passed that were designed to slow or stop growth outright. Conservative groups said itâs clear that voters are connecting economic woes with the unfettered growth of AI and an overly friendly environment for billionaire CEOs in President Donald Trumpâs Washington.
However, divisions between the more progressive wing of the party and more business-friendly moderates, along with disagreements between the House and the Senate, will make it difficult for the newly empowered party to quickly pass any sweeping AI rules. And of course, Trump, who has thus far embraced a hands-off approach to AI regulation, has threatened to veto bills he doesnât like.
âWe know how important this is, and it is going to be a high priority for Democrats,â Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., a member of the New Democrat Coalition, told reporters on Wednesday. He acknowledged, however, that there is plenty of intra-party debate ahead.
The new Congress will usher in renewed pushes for bills to address AI safety and curb data center growth, as well as the formation of larger coalitions behind banning âsuperintelligence.â
But the lack of agreement around any one legislative policy push will make it difficult for Democrats to accomplish anything, even with larger majorities than they anticipated in both chambers.
âNot that weâve reached a specific agreement on a specific policy,â Stanton said, adding that the caucus understands âhow important it isâ to address cybersecurity risks, protect kids online, and advance worker protections.
party projects optimism
Still, Democrats insist theyâre in a position to deliver on AI guardrails regardless of divisions within their party.
One thing liberals and moderates can agree on: Theyâre already pledging to subpoena tech executives to grill them on safety risks and economic effects stemming from their technology.
âMany Democrats were negotiating with a Republican Party whose main AI policy goal last Congress was to eliminate all AI regulations in all states. Things have shifted drastically, such that even people like JD Vance are admitting they were completely wrong on the issues,â Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, told reporters Wednesday.
âThe Democratic Party coming out of this election can prove to our voters that we are with them, and we are going to call the AI CEOs to testify under oath, not cash their checks,â he said, calling AI regulation a âtop priority.â
Added Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., in a separate conversation with reporters: âTwo things will change next term. We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation and reasonable guardrails on AI.â
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a member of the Problem Solvers Caucus, told Semafor that Democrats are in âsurprisingly broad agreementâ on AI.
âWe agree that this technology is changing how Americans work and live. We also agree that we need commonsense guardrails, so that it works for families, workers, and kids â not against them,â Gottheimer said. âWeâll continue to have constructive discussions on how best to get there. I look forward to working with every member, new and returning, to get it done.â
New progressive voices on Capitol Hill, buoyed by midterm wins and stronger numbers, promise to make a lot of noise about delivering on AI.
âItâs going to take a lot of work to hammer out the details, but failure is not an option. AI poses a real and present danger to our economy and social fabric,â Will Lawrence, a Democrat who just won a House seat in Michigan, told Semafor. âThere is a mandate for action from the American people.â
Room for Disagreement
Democrats see other ways to make an impact with their new power.
One Democratic Capitol Hill staffer told Semafor Democrats can now âsubpoena the hellâ out of Trumpâs executive order on AI from June that has never fully been released publicly, along with using their subpoena power to question the administrationâs use of export controls and the influence of tech players like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on AI policy.
The staffer said he expects Senate leadership to cater to moderates and be reluctant to âgo too far in one direction,â since AI is still a new political issue on which the partyâs platform isnât yet defined. Democrats are shifting left on AI, the staffer argued, but they doubted Democrats in both chambers would broadly support proposals like Casarâs bill to pause the development of advanced AI models.
Notable
- Abdul El-Sayed, the incoming senator from Michigan, has been among the most vocal Democrats raising alarm about AI on the campaign trail.
- Any major AI safety and testing legislation in the Senate would come from the Senate Commerce Committee. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the committeeâs top Democrat, has been pushing for a bill that would mandate independent testing of AI models before their release.
Correction: A previous version of this story misidentified the state where Will Lawrence won election.

24a3cec5264b.text: Democrats of all political stripes won so big on Tuesday that the party didn't settle its long-running civil war between moderates and progressives. Instead, the party's historic victories gave each faction some reasons to claim that its brand of Democrats can defeat the GOP in 2028. Driving the news: Democratic operatives are sure of one thing, though: Tuesday's blowout wins mean that more party leaders will be willing to run for the White House than if the midterms hadn't gone so well. Barack Obama's 2012 campaign manager, Jim Messina, told Bloomberg TV this week that he's already met with 29 potential candidates. Zoom in: On Tuesday, moderate Democrats won. Progressives won. Even one-time socialists won. In Michigan, for example, unapologetic progressive Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed won by 7 points after running on Medicare for All. In the same state , William Lawrence, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America before he let his membership lapse recently, flipped a key swing district. Those results were good news for New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the democratic socialist with a national profile who went all-in on electing El-Sayed — and is considering a run for president in two years. More moderate Senate candidates who frequently talked about their faith on the campaign trail — such as Texas' James Talarico and Kansas' Adam Hamilton — pulled off huge upsets in deep-red states, and in the process created a model for some Democrats to follow. Their mild-mannered, religion-infused campaigns mirrored former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg's 2020 presidential run. For the past year, AOC, Buttigieg and other Democrats eyeing the White House have been laying the groundwork to turn the 2026 elections into a springboard for their potential presidential campaigns. Some put their chips on specific candidates — and virtually all of them succeeded. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a centrist technocrat who campaigned on "getting sh*t done," won reelection by 22 points. His long coattails helped Democrats win four new House seats and a trifecta in his state's government. Former Vice President Kamala Harris , who urged voters to push back against the Supreme Court's ruling threatening Black representation in Congress, saw her efforts to help boost Black turnout across the South pay off. Harris also campaigned with Black gubernatorial candidates in Nevada and Wisconsin who won — and a third Black Senate contender who's on the cusp of flipping a Senate seat in Mississippi in what would be a historic win. Also good for Harris: Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms made history as the first Black woman in the country to win a governor's race. In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff won a second term by 18 points. Because Bottoms as governor would be able to appoint a replacement to a vacated Senate seat, Ossoff — or Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, another potential White House contender in 2028 — wouldn't have to worry about a Republican temporarily filling his position if he were to win the presidency. What they're saying: What happens next for the party is "a big question mark," said Lauren Hitt, a Democratic strategist who advises moderates and progressives. "We're going to spend a year fighting out who actually has the mandate — left/center/populist — and then in 2028 we'll have our answer." Some Democratic operatives believe that the through-line of their wins was simply change — and that the next presidential nominee should represent a new direction more than any policy, identity or ideology. The other side: Some Democrats hope that Tuesday's results signal that the factional warfare that has defined their party for much of the past decade might be coming to an end — or at least entering a new phase. "We've just come to this place as a Democratic Party where it's not one wing — it's all of the wings," said Jane Kleeb, president of the Association of State Democratic Committees. In 2028, "it will be interesting to see which candidates can communicate to the primary voter that they are not only from one wing of the party," she added. "That's going to be the big test."

India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (Â£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.
One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.
Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.
Played by Yash, one of southern India's biggest stars, Ravana is a powerful warrior whose pride leads him into an epic battle with Ram (which will be depicted in part 2, set to release next year).
The film's producer, Namit Malhotra, heads visual-effects company DNEG, which has worked on Hollywood blockbusters including Dune and Interstellar. The music is a collaboration between AR Rahman, the Oscar-winning Indian composer of Slumdog Millionaire, and Hans Zimmer, whose scores for Gladiator, The Dark Knight and Dune have helped define the sound of modern Hollywood.
The film opened days ahead of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights which celebrates Ram's return to Ayodhya after his exile.
But the critical response so far has been mixed.
Saibal Chatterjee of NDTV channel gave it, external three out of five stars, saying its visual spectacle often overshadowed the story. Its enormous scale, he wrote, "remains, for the most part, the only thing that stands out", while the acting remains "wildly inconsistent".
Rishabh Suri of the Hindustan Times newspaper was more enthusiastic, awarding it four stars.
"I am happy to report, all that money shows on screen," he wrote, praising the performances and visual effects, though he found the first half sluggish and the music underwhelming.
Shubhra Gupta, external of The Indian Express, who gave the film three stars, confessed to initial misgivings about its extravagant scale but found herself gradually won over, calling it the "perfect epic".
There was "enough sorcery and thrills and adventure" to sustain the spectacle, she wrote, and the filmmakers had managed to tell a sprawling story without being swallowed by it.
Internationally, too, the film drew contrasting reactions.
Writing in The Guardian, Peter Bradshaw called it a "thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama". He found echoes of Shakespeare in the royal intrigue that sends Rama into exile, and of Homer in his quest to rescue Sita. Its sweeping landscapes and fantastical imagery reminded him of The Lord of the Rings and The Lion King.
"It's a rather amazing adventure," he wrote, external, giving it four stars.
Others were less impressed. Siddhant Adlakha of IGN scored the film four out of 10, describing its action as "clunky" and its computer-generated imagery as an "eye-sore".
Giovanni Lago of Next Best Picture, who gave it, external five out of 10, praised Yash's magnetic Ravana and the score by Rahman and Zimmer. But he felt the film's vast narrative might have been better served by a Game of Thrones-style series.
The use of AI to adjust actors' lip movements for the English-language version also drew criticism. While Tiwari said it was intended to make the film more accessible to international audiences, Adlakha likened the result to "exaggerated mouth movements superimposed on still images for comedy sketches".
In India, the film has invited comparisons with earlier adaptations, particularly Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, which captivated the country nearly four decades ago with simple sets and special effects that now seem quaint.
When the series first aired in 1987, Sunday mornings across India took on an almost devotional stillness.
Streets emptied, shops lowered their shutters and neighbours crowded around TV sets. Some viewers bathed, lit incense and garlanded their screens before the broadcast, preparing for the show much as they might for worship.
Arvind Rajagopal, a media scholar at New York University, told the BBC in 2019 that trains and buses would stop and passengers disembark to watch the show on roadside TVs.
Broadcast on the state-run Doordarshan network, some of the most popular parts of the 78-episode series drew an estimated 80-100 million viewers, astonishing numbers at a time when owning a TV was a luxury in India.
The actors, too, became objects of reverence. Arun Govil, who played Ram, has recalled people weeping at the sight of him and touching his feet. Now, in a casting choice brimming with nostalgia, Govil returns in Tiwari's film as Dasharatha, Ram's father.
Other adaptations found their own ways to reimagine the epic. The 1992 Indo-Japanese animated film Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama brought the tale to life through richly detailed, hand-drawn animation.
Tiwari's Ramayana arrives with technological resources its predecessors could barely have imagined - but also with the expectations of generations who have grown up with the story and its characters.
It also comes at a politically charged moment in India, where Ram has become a powerful symbol of Hindu identity - over the past decade and a half, even popular analyses or retellings of the epic have landed in controversy.

- Published
Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons.
In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff.
"It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service.
In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together.
"My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said.
Democrats say they heard both messages.
"We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe.
But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans.
A message that cut through
The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands.
Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper.
Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump.
In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs.
"They felt betrayed," he said.
This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it?
The affordability plan
Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority.
They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025.
Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials.
They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%.
Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade.
On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children.
It's a long list. But how much of it can they actually deliver?
What can they actually pass?
Investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments, puts it bluntly:
"Congress can't get anything past a presidential veto. President Trump can't get anything he wants."
The result, he says, is likely to be two years of relative quiet on the legislative and regulatory front.
In other words, winning in Congress does not give Democrats a free hand. President Trump can still block legislation, and getting around a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.
For voters hoping for lower bills, that may be a disappointing result. They didn't vote for political deadlock.
Take tariffs. Trump is unlikely to abandon a trade policy that is central to his agenda. Democrats will need Republican support if they want to change it.
Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics, expects the average tariff rate on imports to stay around 10% for the rest of Trump's term.
And there's another complication.
Tariffs are bringing in more money for the government. Import taxes accounted for just over 1% of federal revenue in 2024. This year, they account for more than 5%.
That growing contribution to government income, Yaros argues, will make tariffs "tough for a future administration to fully dismantle."
Still, there are bargains to be struck.
Where the deals might be
President Trump told CNBC he could work with Democrats on "many more things than people understand".
Healthcare might be one of them.
Yaros sees the possibility of a big political trade-off: Democrats agree to extend Republican tax cuts in return for restoring health insurance subsidies. But he doesn't expect a deal until late 2027, with the economic benefits arriving in 2028. That's a long time to wait for anyone struggling with bills today.
Democrats could also turn up the pressure on businesses.
Henrietta Treyz of consultants Veda Partners says Democrats will question companies that passed on the cost of tariffs to customers.
After the Supreme Court ruling in February, she says, the question will be: "Did you turn around, take that tariff rebate, and then lower prices for consumers?"
Companies will also be asked: "What did you get in exchange?"
Democrats, she adds, will "pick and choose very carefully."
In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat set to chair the Finance Committee, has summed up his approach in six words: "affordability for us, accountability for them."
He says he will use the committee to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy. Insurers, drugmakers and banks should expect to be called to explain themselves.
And some of the biggest changes may happen closer to home. State governors and regulators have a say in electricity prices, while local authorities decide where new homes can be built.
Democrats have won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where the rising cost of electricity for data centres is already a concern.
The part they can't control
The hardest test may be something Democrats cannot fix with a new law.
The price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser will depend heavily on what happens in the war with Iran. And forecasters disagree about what comes next.
Oxford Economics warns that with the election over, further escalation "appears more likely," because petrol prices will no longer be as much of a politi

- Published
Major tech firms including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and more than $2 trillion has been wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite stock index in a market rout.
Shares in firms across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors plummeted, partly driven by concerns of tougher regulation following Democratic wins in key data centre states.
Those losses dragged the Nasdaq down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn in market capitalisation, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the onslaught of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400m off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300m off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.
The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%.
The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.
With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

The war on Iran is stripping the western Pacific of US naval forces
“It’s really a big problem. It’s a problem for credibility. It’s a problem for our allies in the Far East,” one expert said.
Half of the U.S. Navy’s Japan-based destroyers are currently supporting the war on Iran, belying Trump-administration strategy documents that called the Pacific theater a top priority and undermining relations with Western Pacific allies.
Five of the 10 destroyers homeported in Yokosuka, along with the Yokosuka-based aircraft carrier George Washington, are deployed to U.S. Central Command’s area of responsibility to help fight a war of choice. Navy officials have told the crews of at least some of those destroyers they won’t return home until 2027.
“It’s really a big problem. It’s a problem for credibility. It’s a problem for our allies in the Far East…who, in a lot of cases, have been planning months in advance for carrier visits and for carrier battle group visits,” said Ralph Cossa, chairman and WSD-Handa chair in peace studies for the Honolulu-based Pacific Forum. And aircraft carriers deploy with several other types of ships, he pointed out.
“That’s all assets that normally would be in the Pacific, that normally would be showing the flag, that normally would be reminding our allies of our commitment. And they’re nowhere to be found.”
This is not what is prescribed by the National Security Strategy, which was released less than a year ago. “Preventing conflict requires a vigilant posture in the Indo-Pacific,” the NSS says. “The days in which the Middle East dominated American foreign policy in both long-term planning and day-to-day execution are thankfully over.” This was echoed in January by the National Defense Strategy, which declared that its top priorities were the U.S. homeland and deterring China.
But five weeks later, President Trump launched a war against Iran. And although Operation Epic Fury officially concluded in June, the Pentagon is keeping a large force in the region, making occasional attacks, and waiting to see whether Trump will order more.
U.S. Pacific Command officials pushed back on the suggestion that they are scaling back the China-deterrence mission.
“Our commitment to the security of the Indo-Pacific and to our allies and partners remains steadfast,” a PACOM spokesperson said, adding that the command “remains focused on deterring aggression and maintaining the readiness required to execute our assigned missions. We continually assess operational requirements and coordinate with the Department of War to ensure our forces have the capabilities and support necessary to meet them.”
Highlighting the recent Keen Sword military exercise, which included participation from the California-based Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, the spokesperson said “continuous training and exercises across the Indo-Pacific strengthen readiness and interoperability, while demonstrating our ability to respond to regional contingencies.”
Last week, at the TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Honolulu, PACOM’s deputy commander, Lt. Gen. George Rowell, underscored that message in a keynote speech.
“Our mandate at U.S. Pacific Command is very clear: deterrence is our highest duty, and our guiding framework is to establish denial defense in the first island chain. We aim to prove that military aggressions will be infeasible, escalation will be catastrophic, and the costs of conflict far outweigh any gains.”
But, said Katherine Kuzminski, vice president of studies at the Center for a New American Security, sending so many of the U.S. Navy warships that are earmarked for patrolling the Pacific to the Middle East—and keeping them there for much longer than traditional Navy deployments—indicates “that our operations currently are not aligning with the administration’s stated national security strategy and national defense strategy, and that makes it really difficult at the service level or at the combatant command level to determine what the requirements are going to be.”
The military must be ready to respond, Kuzminski said, so “if there was some sort of incident that happens in the Indo-Pacific, we would want to be able to shift all of our resources there. But right now we’re kind of treating the [U.S. Central Command area of responsibility] in that way when we’ve committed to not be bogged down in the CENTCOM AOR.”
It’s not the first time the U.S. pivoted on the Pacific.
In 2012, under President Barack Obama, the Pentagon called for a “rebalance to the Indo-Pacific region,” including moving more troops and ships to the area. In 2016, then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter said the rebalance was not transient, but “enduring.” One year later, during the first Trump administration, a State Department official declared the rebalance officially dead.
Chinese president Xi Jinping has reportedly told his military to be prepared to take Taiwan by 2027. Cossa, like other experts, said he doesn’t believe “for a minute” that the Chinese will actually attack Taiwan next year, “but certainly, part of deterrence is convincing Xi that the U.S. has a commitment in this area and that we are going to respond. And when we have a third of our operational fleet out in the Middle East, that just sends the wrong signal.”
Keeping 7th Fleet sailors in the U.S. Navy Central region “for a year is going to be really poor for morale aboard ship and at home,” a Navy officer and expert on Pacific security told Defense One. “Trying to hide the cost by pulling [7th Fleet] away from home is just accounting fraud, and is hurting the fleet’s ability to show up for exercises in the Pacific, which will create its own hangover of damaged credibility, and contributes to the perception that the U.S. isn’t living up to its commitments on security in the region. I’ve heard that the fleet has been told to expect a 17 DDG requirement [in the Middle East] until 2029, which is insane. In terms of deterrent capability, most people I know think this

7fb59ef0aedb.text: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman toppled embattled Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass in a stunning upset, putting South Asian immigrants on course to lead America's two largest cities. Why it matters: With New York's Zohran Mamdani already in office, Raman's win puts democratic socialists on track to run two of America's most powerful city halls — testing whether their promises on affordable housing and better government can survive the pressures of governing. The big picture: Raman's victory marks a historic shift in urban American politics as voters embrace a new generation of immigrant leaders challenging the Democratic establishment. Raman, 45, immigrated from India as a child. Mamdani, New York's mayor, also has South Asian roots and immigrated to the U.S. Both built their political careers around affordability and inequality, giving democratic socialism a powerful foothold in America's largest cities. State of play: The Associated Press called the race for Raman Thursday, making Bass the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose reelection. Raman led Bass 52.1% to 47.9% in unofficial results released Thursday. Ballot counting continues. Bass, who won in 2022, conceded and pledged a smooth transition. Raman takes office Dec. 14. Raman defeated a political heavyweight backed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and much of the City Council. Zoom in: Raman capitalized on growing frustration over homelessness, housing costs and Bass' handling of the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll showed Raman leading Bass 66%-4% among likely voters under 30 and 45%-21% among Latino likely voters. Bass narrowed the gap. The final Berkeley poll showed the candidates tied at 40%, with 19% undecided. Among Latino likely voters, Raman's lead shrank to 43%-40%. Raman launched her challenge in February after previously endorsing Bass, turning former allies into political rivals. Zoom out: Democratic socialism's reach now extends beyond New York and Los Angeles. Washington, D.C., voters also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George Tuesday, delivering another major victory for the movement. The wins raise questions about the Democratic Party's future as younger progressives challenge established leaders. Yes, but: Raman has carved out an independent path that sometimes puts her at odds with fellow socialists. She has repeatedly clashed with the Democratic Socialists of America over Israel, policing and housing. National DSA leaders voted 14-13 Monday against withdrawing her endorsement after a dispute over how the Los Angeles chapter vetted her stance on the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement targeting Israel. The group's Los Angeles chapter previously censured Raman for accepting an endorsement from Democrats for Israel-Los Angeles. She has stressed her political independence. Between the lines: Raman's winning pitch focused less on socialist ideology and more on making City Hall work. She told Axios and Noticias Telemundo at Visionarios that her approach amounts to "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics." "I just want government to work for the people," Raman said. That message could offer progressive candidates a model for building coalitions beyond traditional socialist activists. The bottom line: Winning City Hall may prove easier than running it. Raman faces a homelessness crisis, a housing shortage and the 2028 Olympics — with the nation watching whether democratic socialism can deliver on its promises.

b3bd8c70d856.text: By — Matthew Daly, Associated Press Matthew Daly, Associated Press By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/key-federal-panel-expected-to-approve-trumps-arch-amid-court-challenge Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Key federal panel expected to approve Trump's arch amid court challenge Politics Nov 5, 2026 4:34 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal panel was expected Thursday to approve President Donald Trump's proposed memorial arch in Washington at the end of a meeting that drew dozens of opponents to a key part of the president's push to leave his imprint on the nation's capital. The approval would clear a hurdle on the road to breaking ground on the project, and the administration has said it could launch construction within a day of the vote. But the proposed 250-foot (76-meter) tall gilded arch still faced legal challenges. READ MORE: Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin The remote, call-in hearing — which crashed repeatedly and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section — drew witnesses who gave impassioned, three-minute comments opposing an arch they said will destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington National Cemetery. The Trump-appointed chairman of the commission, however, launched into a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it. "President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments," said Mark Paoletta, the commission's chairman. As Trump has often remarked, "the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London," said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget. In addition to Paoletta, the arch received support during the hearing from Republican lawmakers and a veteran who praised the administration's efforts to build the monument. The commission oversees construction on federal land in the city and began reviewing the arch plan in June. Trump is working to remake Washington The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week. Many of the plans are being challenged in the courts, and three lawsuits have been filed opposing the arch. A judge has been asked to block the construction so long as lawsuits are still being litigated, and she could rule as early as Thursday. Rep. Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal. "This arch would dishonor America," Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch "a tribute to Donald Trump," not veterans as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself. Opponents argue the arch is too big for the skyline and would disrupt carefully designed sight lines between landmarks in and around the capital — most prominently the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — that were meant to symbolize the reunification of the North and the South after the Civil War. But the opposition has done little to influence the members of the commission, which is led by some of Trump's closest allies. Trump appointed Paoletta to chair the 12-member panel. Two other commissioners are also White House aides. Trump wants an arch, but it faces legal challenges Still, a federal judge on Monday complicated Trump's efforts to move quickly on the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who is overseeing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's plans, said she must be told of any decision by the planning commission within an hour. The order set the same time limits for any decision by the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior. Before Thursday's hearing began, attorneys with the Justice Department filed a notice with Chutkan informing her that a contractor had already done site prep work on Oct. 31, with what she said appeared to be no authorization from the National Park Service. The plaintiffs in the three lawsuits are calling for a halt to work on a monument that is set to be built on a patch of grass off a bridge that spans the Potomac River and connects Washington with Arlington National Cemetery, in Arlington, Virginia. When complete, the monument would be 100 feet (30 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal. Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue that the Trump administration must seek congressional approval. The administration maintains that Congress cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle decades ago. Paoletta said it was a "national disgrace" that a memorial arch had not been placed there, despite a 1925 law that designated such a memorial, he said. Last week, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and the west and two mezzanines. Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a fire command center. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national

e2264df5808c.text: Congress returns next week facing a renewed push for transparency over the Jeffrey Epstein files, as a top House Democrat promises new investigations following the party's midterm victories. Why it matters: The Epstein files controversy has been a recurring political issue throughout President Trump's second term and featured prominently in the midterm campaigns . Democrats' incoming House majority could bring fresh scrutiny of his administration's handling of the files. Driving the news: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is harnessing that momentum as lawmakers return, ahead of his January departure from Congress . Massie said in a Thursday post that when the House returns, the effort to force a vote on a second Epstein Files Transparency Act would secure the necessary 218 signatures. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) , who has led the bipartisan effort with Massie, announced in September that they had received sufficient signature commitments for the measure — but House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent the House home early. What's inside: Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II in July, building on their initial legislation that Trump signed in November of last year after previously working to undercut the effort. The bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records. It would also require the attorney general to provide certain unredacted documents to victims upon request. Zoom out: The momentum is unlikely to slow when Democrats take control of Congress in January. With corruption emerging as a top election concern, Democrats ran attack ads accusing the GOP of protecting powerful elites. Candidates from both parties and outside groups aired at least $70 million in TV ads mentioning Epstein, pedophilia and allegations of child sexual abuse between Sept. 1 and Oct. 21, according to AdImpact data reviewed by Axios' Alex Isenstadt . What we're watching: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the committee's ranking Democrat, who formally announced his bid for House Oversight Committee chair, outlined four investigative priorities for the committee under Democratic leadership Wednesday. The fourth will center around Epstein. In his press conference, he argued there has yet to be "real accountability for the co-conspirators and the men who brutally raped, trafficked and abused young women." He lamented the lack of public hearings in the House under Republican leadership, adding he had spoken with multiple survivors who were interested in testifying before Congress. The fact "that so many folks have gotten away with not testifying in front of Congress, I think is shameful," he said. - Published
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
Most of Newsom's action on Thursday will need court approval, CalMatters reported. For the commutations of the nearly 400 prisoners convicted of multiple felonies, at least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court have to sign off.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

AI-funded super PACs saw mixed effectiveness in Tuesdayâs midterm elections, while the newly launched Guardrails Alliance PAC, which promotes AI rules, went 5-0 in its spending. Leading the Future, an AI advocacy group, spent $4.8 million supporting Republican Darline Grahamâs bid to replace her late brother in the Senate. Graham lost; Democratic winner Annie Andrews dubbed her âData Center Darlineâ during the campaign.
Leading the Futureâs other spending in the general helped propel Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., to victory despite redistricting, but Republican House candidates the super PAC supported lost, per Wired.
The other major AI-related and Anthropic-affiliated super PAC, Public First Action, spent $20 million in the general election, somewhat successfully. It backed winners Rep. Valerie Foushee, D-N.C., Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter in Ohio, Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel in Colorado, and Rep.-elect Scott Wiener in California. The Republicans backed by Public Firstâs network lost.
Guardrails Alliance spent more than $3.1 million total opposing five candidates who lost, the group announced. But money could not buy influence on the most salient AI-related outcome of the election: local ballot measures curbing data center development, about 40 of which passed across the country on Tuesday.
The ballot initiatives coincide with hyperscalersâ scramble to figure out a way forward in certain jurisdictions and overhaul their messaging around the projects.
One GOP operative told Semafor that Leading the Future was taken by surprise by the success of the data center ballot measures and had not put any resources into fighting them.
âWeâre proud that many of the pro-innovation champions we supported this cycle won on Tuesday,â Leading the Future spokesman Jesse Hunt said. âOur investments are about building a durable coalition that can advance a national regulatory framework, unleash American innovation, and ensure workers, families, and communities are protected.â
âWe are committed to a multi-cycle effort and 2028 will show who actually cares about passing a national regulatory framework on AI and who wants to politicize an issue thatâs extremely consequential to the future of our country,â he continued.

Scott Colomâs lead against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss., has increased to 1,724 votes but Democrats arenât taking any chances with their nomineeâs campaign.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Elias Law Group are on the ground while Colomâs campaign observes the count across the state, according to a person familiar with the effort.
Senators are lending a hand, too: Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., won her first Senate race on a recount against a GOP incumbent and is also in Mississippi after making multiple visits this fall.
âEvery time we have votes coming in in Mississippi you see Scott Colom getting more and more votes. So I feel confident there,â Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., told Semafor.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee sent letters to county clerks and election commissioners asking them to preserve and set aside provisional ballots. b66453d13d67.text:
Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?
The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.
Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”
Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.
Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.
One, two, three — free!
Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.
Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.
When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.
Out the door on four
When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.
Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.
The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”
Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.
Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

1accc759c7af.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday he plans to commute all 548 of the state's death sentences to life without parole, a sweeping decision that could empty the nation's largest death row. Why it matters: If Newsom follows through, it will be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history , reducing the national death-row population by more than a quarter. The move comes during Newsom's final months as governor and ahead of a potential 2028 bid for president. What he's saying: "I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency," Newsom wrote in a letter to Californians. "Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them." "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims." "This decision is among the most difficult of my career," he wrote. Context: Newsom can commute some sentences on his own, but prisoners with multiple felony convictions need approval from the California Supreme Court before their sentences can be reduced, per the California Constitution . Yes, but: This won't end the death penalty in California. It remains legal even though the state hasn't performed one since 2006 . In fact, California voters rejected ballot measures in 2012 and 2016 to end capital punishment. Flashback: Shortly after taking office, Newsom instituted a moratorium on executions , reprieving 737 prisoners from death row. The ACLU has been pushing Newsom to commute death row sentences since former President Biden did so in 2024 for 37 federal prisoners. Other Democratic governors have similarly commuted death sentences, including North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper , who commuted 15 in 2024. Zoom out: The death penalty faces heavy scrutiny nationwide after Tennessee's failed execution attempt of Christa Pike and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth 's call for a public execution.

e398c4df672f.text: One of the biggest nail-biters of the 2026 election isn't playing out in a purple state, but crimson Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom is trying to pull off a Magnolia State upset. The big picture: It's one of the most remarkable currents of Tuesday's blue wave. The race pitted Colom, a Democratic district attorney powered by grassroots clout, against incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state Trump won by some 23 points in 2024. The big picture: The coalition Colom built with his viral ads and the historic tenor of his candidacy faces the ultimate Deep South test. The race remains too close to call. "The flag has already been planted in Mississippi that a new day has arrived, and whether these final votes carry Scott Colom into that victory column, we will find out," says Nadine Smith, president and CEO of Color Of Change. "But … change has arrived." Follow the money: Colom's was one of the red-state races that drew the attention of Florida attorney Steve Pajcic, whose family-run super PAC New Deal for All sought to boost Dems in under-the-radar races. Mississippi, where they invested around $1.1 million, was ideal "in size and in potential," he tells Axios. That money went far on Mississippi's less-expensive airwaves. The most-aired ad in the closing week featured an Epstein survivor condemning Hyde-Smith, Axios' Donica Phifer reported. New Deal for All paid for the ad, which inundated Mississippi's TV markets. Catch up quick: In October, Axios reported that Senate Republicans were weighing a cash infusion into the race. The GOP Senate Leadership Fund eventually made an investment. Democrats ' Senate Majority PAC announced a $1.2 million ad campaign, and Colom also drew party heavy-hitters like former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Clinton for appearances. Former President Obama also cut an ad. Zoom out: The race's seismic nature is also fueled by history. Colom would be Mississippi's first Black senator elected since Reconstruction, and its first Democrat elected to the Senate since the 1980s. Colom's campaign leaned into the fight for Black Americans' right to vote, producing an ad about civil rights leader Medgar Evers and how his efforts ultimately cost the NAACP's first Mississippi field officer his life. "You can't talk about the struggle for Black freedom without talking about Mississippi, and that is why the symbolism of this moment is so powerful," Smith says. Flashback: Hyde-Smith set the stage for her dragged-out drama with Colom in 2023: She blocked former President Joe Biden's nomination of Colom to be a U.S. District Court Judge for the Northern District of Mississippi — despite fellow Republican Sen. Roger Wicker backing him. Black Mississippians favored Colom 91% to Hyde-Smith's 7% per New York Times voter trend estimates , something political analysts have said was key for a Democrat to win: strong Black turnout, combined with a quarter of white Mississippians' support. The Supreme Court's ruling limiting the Voting Rights Act , empowering Republican redistricting and diluting Black votes, also pushed Black voters to the polls, Smith said. The SCOTUS ruling awoke "a giant," Smith said. "People were not going to be discouraged; they were going to be galvanized." What we're watching: Pajcic tells Axios that the 2026 vote is a door to historic moments. "It's a new Mississippi, and it goes with a new South Carolina, a new Georgia, a new North Carolina, new Texas," Pajcic says. "We've got a new South." Go deeper: Democrats poised to break GOP's 16-year grip on statehouses

Inside Mississippi's ballot counting in tight Senate race
The BBC's Carl Nasman takes us inside a county election commission building as ballots get counted in the surprisingly tight race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.

PHOENIX—Two years after President Donald Trump won Arizona with 52 percent of the vote, Democrats are poised to win a trifecta in the state House, Senate and governor’s office, and could potentially win every statewide elected position. The battleground state’s blue wave could fundamentally alter how it responds to increasingly deadly heat and persistent drought brought on by climate change.
Central to the Democrats’ wins, party members and candidates said, was their focus on addressing the state’s growing energy demand and declining water resources, which are increasingly top issues for Arizonans.
Attorney General Kris Mayes, who has made protecting the state’s water resources and fighting rising energy costs her top two priorities, won her bid for reelection. Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill took two seats on the state’s currently all-Republican commission that regulates utilities. And, for the first time since 1966, Democrats are almost guaranteed to have a trifecta with incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs winning her reelection bid against Republican-candidate Rep. Andy Biggs. Even the party’s candidate for state mine inspector, Brian Matlock, leads in the polls, with his potential win marking the first time that seat has gone to a Democrat since 1976.
Taken together, the Democrats’ wins present an opportunity for major changes to how the state approaches climate change and energy policy, potentially paving the way for new renewable energy development and groundwater regulations. The latter has proven to be one of the state’s stickiest policy debates over the last decade, and an issue where Hobbs has attempted to make strides but been stopped from enacting reform by the Republican-controlled legislature.
“What we’ve seen is data centers have brought [energy and water] issues to the forefront,” Priya Sundareshan, Democratic leader in the state Senate, told Inside Climate News at the Arizona Democrats watch party Tuesday night. “The bipartisan response to data centers that we know voters have is around their energy use and their water use, and those are fundamentally questions that we have failed to address at the state level, and we continue to fail to address because of Republican control of the legislature.”
Arizona knows extreme weather well, she said, from record-hot summers to flooding that left communities evacuated over the last week to dwindling water supplies.
“All of that is directly tied to the changing climate, and that’s something where we can tie that picture together and be able to show voters that we can see the big picture,” Sundareshan said. “We can work toward a future that makes sure that we can all live here.”
In an interview with Inside Climate News, Mayes, the attorney general, said focusing her office and campaign on energy and water issues “were pivotal” to her victory. During her first four years, Mayes sued Fondomonte Arizona, a subsidiary of a Saudi Arabian company, which was pumping an unlimited amount of water from a groundwater basin on state trust land to irrigate alfalfa that was eventually fed to cattle in Saudi Arabia. She also challenged the Arizona Corporation Commission—of which she was once an elected member—over its decisions to roll back renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. And she has called for a statewide moratorium on new data center development until a plan for them can be developed.

“I did 70 town halls all over Arizona, many of them about water and data centers,” she said. “I think that resonated with Arizonans. People are worried about our water supplies, and they didn’t think that they had politicians working hard enough on those issues, and they saw in me somebody that was willing to stick my neck out against powerful entities and I will continue to do that.”
Many of the state’s races are far from a done deal, with only a fraction of the votes counted so far. But Democrats hold overwhelming leads for many seats that put them out of reach for Republicans. The final count for the state Senate and House remain undecided, though it is clear Democrats will have a majority in both.
Democrats flipped Scottsdale’s Congressional District 1 in one of the country’s most contested races, with Dr. Amish Shah winning the seat he failed to take in 2024. They also beat incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani in southern Arizona’s Congressional District 6, with Democrat JoAnna Mendoza flipping the seat.
But it’s too early to call some of the state’s other races for the U.S. House of Representatives. Democrats are maintaining close races in three other Republican-held districts. Only one Arizona Republican, Paul Gosar, has won his reelection for his House seat so far.
Polling has consistently shown energy and water issues were top of mind for voters. The Center for the Future of Arizona found 69 percent of voters don’t have confidence that the state will have enough water in the long-term, and that water was the top issue for its voters. Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. More than 60 percent said their summer power bills are difficult to afford.
“The people of Arizona deserve leaders who are looking out for us and ensuring that we can afford to fill our gas tank and keep our lights on, and that’s why they re-elected Governor Hobbs,” said Climate Power’s Arizona State Director Diali Avila in a statement. “Andy Biggs and his fellow Republicans rubber-stamped Trump’s agenda at every turn, and now they’re paying the price. Arizonans need relief from skyrocketing costs, and Governor Hobbs will work to bring down costs for Arizonans—not enrich oil and gas billionai
