High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.
While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.
Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.
However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.
What is the polar vortex?
The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.
Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.
Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.
In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.
It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.
Unknown territory
Most SSW events tend to occur from mid-winter but we are currently witnessing a dramatic weakening of the strong winds with some forecasts even showing a reversal of the polar vortex winds by mid-November.
Due to this weakening, the vortex has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations around the Arctic.
If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.
Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observingâ¦with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."
The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.
Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.
But we also know in a "normal" El NiÃ±o year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.
While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El NiÃ±o directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.
These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.
With the current record El NiÃ±o taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".
A link between a strong El NiÃ±o and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.
Will the UK see snow?
Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El NiÃ±o pattern.
However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.
Professor Andrew Perez-Charlton, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."
"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."
One reason is the timing.
The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.
Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.
And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.
Continuation of drought conditions "more concerning"
Long-term forecasts are based on large-scale climate signals and how they have affected weather patterns in previous years.
Much of the forecast for this autumn and winter has been focused around the influence of the exceptionally strong El NiÃ±o, pointing to a stormier start to winter, with the potential to be followed by colder and drier conditions from January.
But this unusually early disruption of the polar vortex and SSW presents meteorologists with a situation for which there are few modern comparisons.
For Perez-Charlton, the "concerning thing would be if this event ends up bringing the typical drier weather pattern and lack of rain" associated with a sudden stratospheric warming over the coming months.
With most of England and Wales still in drought, we need to rely on a wetter winter to fill up extremely low reservoirs.
For now, experts stress that it is too early to know whether recent changes in the polar vortex will change the winter outlook.

US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
Trump, a former real estate mogul, has altered the president's official office during his second term, most notably by adding many gold features to its walls.
"So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.
Thursday's executive order declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms.
The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".
"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said.
The president has the power to create national monuments, which are similar to national parks.
Trump's order calls on the office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".
The entire building is already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.
Trump's proclamation notes the existing protection, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".
Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.
Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".
"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he tells BBC News.
Werkheiser argues that the Trump administration has shown extreme disregard for other historic sites in Washington, and through lawsuits has attempted to undermine the laws that require preservation.
Trump has undertaken a massive beautification project in Washington and has held three events in the past week to boast of the construction, even as his Republican party was trounced by Democrats in the midterm elections.
"The hypocrisy is that on the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."
Werkheiser notes Trump's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center in Washington DC, to build a new triumphal arch in the city, and to paint the granite exterior of the historic executive office building. His firm has filed lawsuits to block two of the projects.
In October, the president suggested in an interview with Time, external magazine that the Oval Office would need to be torn down due to security concerns from the US Secret Service.
"I said, 'My ass, you can't build a new one. This is a special place,'" Trump said at the time.
During the midterm election campaign Democrats criticised Trump's redesigns, with former President Barack Obama saying that his golden tweaks have "got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory".

93ab760674bd.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been asked by three House Republican committee chairs to brief Congress behind closed doors about his reported ties to a woman accused of spying for China. Why it matters: The request escalates the scrutiny of the Nvidia CEO over his alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China. Catch up quick: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang purportedly had a "close" relationship, per reporting from The New York Times . The Times also reported that President Trump was briefed by intelligence officials about their relationship and the allegations that Alice Huang was a spy, but chose not to act. The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that officials in at least three countries had concerns that Alice Huang was passing information to the Chinese government, potentially including sensitive details on Nvidia chips. Nvidia has denied the allegations, saying Jensen Huang and Alice Huang's contacts were just routine business interactions. The Chinese government previously called the allegations it was spying on Nvidia "groundless speculation." Zoom out: Reps. Brian J. Mast (R-Fla.), John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Jensen Huang Thursday, requesting he sit for a joint briefing with the respective House committees that they chair: Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the Select Committee on Intelligence. They are seeking answers on Nvidia's protocols to protect itself from foreign adversaries and his interactions with Alice Huang, according to the letter. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People's Republic of China] access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter reads. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the letter continues. The other side: "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," Nvidia said in a statement. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the company said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," it added. Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Nvidia.

fe8f3288ecce.text: By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/alabama-executes-man-for-1991-killings-in-last-of-3-u-s-executions-carried-out-the-same-day Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alabama executes man for 1991 killings in last of 3 U.S. executions carried out the same day Nation Nov 5, 2026 7:49 PM EST Florida carried out a record-tying 19th execution of the year in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day. Jesse Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke. He had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing. Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010, and in Alabama, a man received the last lethal injection of the day for his conviction in the killing of an elderly man and woman in a home robbery. The executions were taking place the same day California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values." WATCH: Newsom plans to commute all of California's death sentences That was in sharp contrast to Florida's outgoing governor, Republican Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 35 executions so far this year in the U.S., where capital punishment has come under renewed scrutiny following Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September. It is the second time since August that three states had conducted executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010. Florida inmate apologized before receiving lethal injection Guardado, 64, was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain went up promptly at 6:00 p.m. Asked if he had a last statement, he replied, "I would like to once again apologize for the pain and suffering I've caused to the victim's family and my own family as well." The drugs began flowing immediately afterward. About a minute later, Guardado began breathing heavily, followed by some sputtering and twitching. As the twitching subsided, a warden shook Guardado and shouted his name, but got no response. A medic soon after pronounced him dead. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wants to bring justice to victims' families who have often waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a state record of 19 executions in 2025. The state will set a new record if two more executions are carried out as planned later this year. The victim's son, Patrick Malone, spoke briefly to media witnesses after the execution. Instead of discussing his mother or her murder, he questioned those who oppose the death penalty. "Do such people ever think about what happened to the victim or consider the unending aftermath the victim's family endures and relives every time that terrible event comes up?" Malone said. Alabama man drew the death penalty for a double killing In neighboring Alabama, Michael Taylor, 54, received a lethal injection and was pronounced dead at 6:10 p.m. local time. The execution got underway shortly before 6 p.m. as Taylor replied "no sir" when asked if he had any final words. He appeared to mouth "thank you" toward his attorneys seated in the witness room. Taylor's spiritual adviser approached and prayed with him, and he then closed his eyes, never opening them again. In 1991, Taylor, then 19, fatally beat two people, ages 83 and 79, with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden, Alabama, home. Police arrested him with the victims' Cadillac an hour away in Birmingham. Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time. She declined. Ivey issued a statement immediately afterward calling his actions "reprehensible" and saying, "35 years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry." The state changed the execution method after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. Taylor's attorneys had objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor. Lawyers had asked for a life sentence for Indiana man In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the Department of Correction. He had no final words. Weisheit had publicly acknowledged killing his girlfriend's two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped Gov. Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined. Lawyers failed to persuade Braun, a Republican, to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that should prevent execution. Weisheit's last objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Supreme Court declined to intervene Wednesday night, though two of the five justices wanted a 10-day stay for more information about the drugs' expiration and storage. f698c8b9d564.text: Tuesday's blue tsunami is poised to sweep an unusually large cohort of House Democrats into office who are virtually unknown outside of their districts. Why it matters: Obscure though these incoming lawmakers may be on Capitol Hill, they are poised to play a major role in determining the direction of the Democratic Party. House Democrats' progressive and centrist wings are both looking to recruit as many of these so-called "wave babies" as possible to grow their strength for the ideological fights ahead, Axios reported on Wednesday . Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), a co-chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus' PAC, told Axios some of these candidates applied for her group's endorsement but didn't get it because "honestly.... the districts looked so tough." "We will definitely be reaching out to them," she said. What we're hearing: Several Democratic operatives told Axios they had to Google many of the candidates who won upset victories in North Carolina, Tennessee and elsewhere on Election Day. "Never heard of them," a senior House Democrat, who was involved in battleground House races, told Axios. Said another House Democrat: "I don't think they were on my radar, and they were not on any of the DCCC's targeted lists from what I am aware." Tennessee 4th: Victoria Broderick Photo courtesy of the Victoria Broderick campaign Perhaps the most stunning result of the night was Broderick's upset over longtime Rep. Scott DesJarlais in a seat President Trump carried by 24 percentage points in 2024. Broderick leads DesJarlais by just 280 votes but told Axios in an interview she is "100% confident" of victory and is "ready to be a representative." "There's a little shock, and there's almost a beauty in that. It's beautiful, it's poetic, for the district," said Broderick, a local activist and tech support worker. DesJarlais had regularly won in landslides since he was first elected in 2010, despite a history of scandals . GOP state legislators drew Republican voters out of his Trump+43 district this year and replaced them with Democrats to make neighboring seats more favorable. That opened the door for Broderick, who previously lost to DesJarlais by more than 40 points when she challenged him in 2024. Broderick had spent just $90,000 to DesJarlais' $500,000 as of Oct. 14, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Neither national party spent on the race. "I'm a progressive," Broderick told Axios. "I ran the most progressive race they've ever had in that district. ... I ran on safety, affordability, freedom and equity." Broderick said she supports universal health care and that "every working person deserves affordable living." Asked if she would vote for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker, she said: "We are still waiting to get our feet wet and understand where we're going with everything, so I am not going to say 'yes' or 'no' to that question." North Carolina 5th: Chuck Hubbard Photo: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Like several others , Hubbard benefited from a combination of a Republican "dummy-mander" and strong coattails from Democratic Senate candidate Roy Cooper. The retired local newspaper journalist and publisher has declared victory over Rep. Virginia Foxx, the chair of the powerful House Rules Committee. Hubbard leads by 100 votes in a district Trump carried by 17 points in 2024. (AP has not called this race, and there are provisional ballots still to be counted.) The seat was made less Republican-leaning in 2024 when GOP legislators redrew North Carolina's maps to turn their evenly split U.S. House delegation into a 10-4 Republican one. Now it's likely to be 10-4 Democratic. Like Broderick, Hubbard previously challenged Foxx in 2024 but lost by 19 percentage points. Foxx had a more than 2-to-1 spending advantage this year, with $1.6 million in disbursements as of Oct. 14 to Hubbard's $700,000, per FEC filings. The only national party ad spending was $175,000 from the Democratic group American Bridge, according to AdImpact. Cook Political Report rated the race as "likely Republican." "I know it wasn't on anybody's radar, but that's not required to win the race," Hubbard said in an interview. "The person who has to believe in winning the race is me." Hubbard described himself as "probably center-left," saying he "might rate conservative, even, financially" but that "when it comes to social issues, I probably skew to the left." On health care: "I'm in favor of public choice in health care. You can call it universal health care, you can call it Medicare-for-All." On Israel aid: "We're going to have to find a way to exert some control on Netanyahu." On voting for Jeffries as speaker: "I have nothing against Hakeem Jeffries at all, but I think it's unwise to say ... before talking to him." North Carolina 6th: Cyril Jefferson Photo courtesy of the Cyril Jefferson campaign Another beneficiary of Cooper's performance and 2024 redistricting, Jefferson unseated freshman Rep. Addison McDowell in a district Trump carried by 16 points. Jefferson, the mayor of High Point, N.C., spent just $225,000 to McDowell's $1.3 million, per FEC filings. Neither national party invested in this race. The only ads were from McDowell, who launched a $230,000 campaign ad buy and spent another $40,000 on franked ads , according to AdImpact. "What they kept saying was, 'Your seat's just nowhere on our radar, we don't think it's going to get on our radar until something happens,'" Jefferson said of his meetings with national groups to solicit their support. Jefferson said they consistently laid out three criteria that he needed to meet to be taken seriously: Strong fundraising, competitive polling, and grassroots enthusiasm on the ground. "I'll tell you, the fundraising part is really tough," he said, telling Axios his de facto campaign manager used to be one of his students when he was a high school teacher. "There are examples where me and progressives may not be on the same sid

5d973da28a69.text: By — Sarah El Deeb, Associated Press Sarah El Deeb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/jd-habibi-arabs-celebrate-el-sayeds-use-of-a-term-of-affection-in-his-victory-speech Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'JD, habibi.' Arabs celebrate El-Sayed's use of a term of affection in his victory speech Politics Nov 5, 2026 7:42 PM EST BEIRUT (AP) — From Michigan to the Middle East, Arabs are celebrating Abdul El-Sayed's Senate win and delighting in his introduction of Arabic terms like "habibi" and "inshallah" to the American political lexicon. After being the target of Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, the rising political star who will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator has mocked his critics on the right while championing the Palestinian cause and leaning into his faith and Egyptian heritage. READ MORE: The election brought a wave of historic firsts. Here are some groundbreaking winners "JD, habibi," El-Sayed said in his victory speech, addressing U.S. Vice President JD Vance, who had warned that the candidate would lead rioters in burning down Detroit. "There is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January." 'Habibi' is a term of affection "Habibi" literally translates to "my beloved" and is peppered through Arab pop songs. In everyday speech, it often means "buddy," "pal," or "bro." El-Sayed's supporters have sported shirts reading "Habibi for Abdul." El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, said his campaign had turned "inshallah" — "God willing" — into "hamdulillah," which means "thank God." Arabs thrilled to the gentle ribbing of the vice president, with many posting music video clips featuring "habibi" to social media. It was a rare outpouring of joy in a region traumatized by past and present conflicts — which have also fueled negative stereotypes in the West. One user on X posted a video of Egyptian diva Shireen Abd El-Wahab dancing to one of her most popular songs, joking that El-Sayed would make it the new national anthem. Egyptians are renowned in the Arab world for their sense of humor and are known for cracking jokes in the face of life's difficulties, a spirit that has been popularized in films and by famous comedic actors. Riffing off El-Sayed's victory speech, some shared a meme from an Egyptian film in which a man attends a funeral while high and is unable to stop laughing. "I came here to crack jokes," read the caption, quoting a line from the film. An Egyptian academic, Khalil al-Anani, praised El-Sayed on X, saying: "'Habibi' is the sweetest word." He thanked the senator-elect for bringing joy to Egyptians. Signs of change after decades of prejudice Arab and Muslim Americans have faced prejudice for decades, with popular films depicting them as terrorists and politicians on the right fanning baseless fears about the imposition of sharia, or Islamic law. During the campaign, U.S. President Donald Trump referred to El-Sayed as a "jihadist," evoked the Sept. 11 attacks and deliberately misstated the candidate's name. On social media, users responded to such attacks by posting light-hearted videos, including of Lebanese diva Haifa Wehbe belly dancing and young veiled women breakdancing in the streets. "Donald, look, I know you've struggled with my name," El-Sayed said in his victory speech. "So after JD swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me 'senator.'" 39072f0f45d9.text:
Republicans in Florida narrowly held off a nationwide repudiation Tuesday of their party and President Donald Trump, eking out slim victories in statewide races. But the GOP failed to flip congressional seats Democrats held and lost seats in the Legislature.
Voters elected Republican Byron Donalds as governor over Democrat David Jolly by a margin of a little over 1 percentage point and Republican Ashley Moody for the U.S. Senate over Democrat Angie Nixon by less than 3 percentage points. Both GOP candidates raised significantly more money than their Democratic challengers. Republicans also held onto three cabinet positions in similarly close races.
“Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red!” Donalds, a Trump-endorsed congressman representing the 19th district in southwest Florida, announced Tuesday night to cheering supporters gathered to celebrate his victory. Donalds is the first Black governor elected in Florida and first Black Republican governor in the nation.
It was possible but perhaps unlikely Republicans might take a more moderate approach on issues such as climate change after Democrats’ gains in Florida, said Aubrey Jewett, associate director of the School of Politics, Security and International Affairs at the University of Central Florida.
“They didn’t win, and so that stings. But on another level I think it gives perhaps Democrats a little bit of hope after all, because it really seemed that Florida had become a red state to such a degree that Democrats just didn’t really have any hope,” he said. “I emphasize though, a loss is a loss, and it stings. And I’m sure they’re disappointed that they lost, and they don’t have control of the executive branch. And they actually, in some ways, they came so close and didn’t win, it perhaps stings a little more.”
Democrats did maintain seats in four congressional districts where the boundaries were redrawn to favor Republicans, as part of a controversial redistricting effort this spring directed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican, and the GOP-controlled Legislature. Among the winning Democrats were Rep. Darren Soto, whose Hispanic-majority district in central Florida was redrawn to include conservative-leaning areas as far south as Lake Okeechobee.
Susannah Randolph, director of the Florida chapter of the Sierra Club, said the redistricting effort failed.
“That was very inspiring,” she said. “I think folks kind of saw through that scheme.”
Democrats also made gains in the Legislature, where Republicans maintained majorities in the Senate and House but lost super-majorities in both chambers, Jewett said. Democrats now will wield more influence as bills are shaped and voted on.
“Still the big picture is the Republicans have the majority, and they are in charge,” he said.
Republicans benefited from an infusion of campaign contributions and boast 1.5 million more registered voters in the state than Democrats. But for many years Florida was a must-win swing state, opting six times in a row for the prevailing presidential candidate, from Bill Clinton in 1996 to Trump in 2016. For much of the 20th century Democrats ruled the state. Randolph said Tuesday’s results suggest Florida could be a swing state again.
“That’s kind of up to the Florida Democratic Party,” she said. “If I were them I would be looking at the fact that Angie [Nixon] and Jolly got wildly outspent and had just hardly any resources and came as close as they did with a giant voter registration gap.”
DeSantis as governor dismissed the role of climate change in intensifying hurricanes and flooding and did little to address the emissions exacerbating the problem or hold polluters accountable. He focused his environmental policy instead on the Everglades and water quality.
Some voting locations in Florida were closed early this week because of heavy rain and flooding. Rachel Cleetus, climate program director for the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the situation demonstrated the urgency of the issue of climate change in the state.
“Florida is almost one of the most acute manifestations of this fossil fuel energy crisis affecting costs, as well as climate change is causing so much damage and the threats are growing for the state,” she said. “It’s just unmistakable that these issues are top-of-mind for voters.”

We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. 41fe8ea2b5fb.text: President Trump said Thursday night that voters had themselves to blame for the stock market's historic sell-off . Why it matters: Two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections in historic fashion, the president is lashing out at the voters who rejected his candidates and message. Driving the news: Stocks plunged Thursday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq sinking more than 5% as AI-linked stocks sold off. Investors are skittish about the future for AI development — and the data centers that power the technology — after Tuesday's blue wave ushered in candidates who campaigned on restricting AI. What he's saying: " The Stock Market crashed today because the Dumocrats had a big Tuesday — So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" Trump posted to Truth Social. The intrigue: Thursday's plunge was an unusually delayed reaction — the market actually had a massive rally Wednesday as the initial election results became apparent. Trump was quick to claim credit at the time for the conditions that led to those market highs. What to watch: Stock futures were down again in pre-market trading late Thursday, and Asian markets were broadly lower as well, pointing to the potential for another rough day Friday.

86a37e45b7f9.text: By — David McHugh, Associated Press David McHugh, Associated Press By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/tankers-carrying-russian-diesel-change-course-raising-doubts-about-shipments-to-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Tankers carrying Russian diesel change course, raising doubts about shipments to U.S. World Nov 5, 2026 7:17 PM EST FRANKFURT, Germany (AP) — President Donald Trump's plan to allow imports of Russian diesel appeared to falter this week after state and federal officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences and two tankers initially bound for the United States changed course. Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 9 to make more than 300,000 metric tons of Russia's diesel available immediately to U.S. and global markets, with larger shipments to follow. The U.S. banned Russian energy imports after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the deal angered some lawmakers and foreign allies. WATCH: First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials. Trump met with Putin's envoy The arrangement has yet to produce a confirmed U.S. delivery. Analysts have said the imports were unlikely to do much to lower U.S. diesel prices, which have reached record highs during the U.S. war with Iran. Two sanctioned tankers that departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month originally declared their destinations as the U.S. East Coast. As of Thursday, both had changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com. A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the U.S. but changed its destination from New York to "for orders," which leaves the unloading point open. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin have disclosed whether the agreement was put in writing or revealed the price, payment terms or participating companies. Although the Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions that would ordinarily be subject to U.S. sanctions, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill advised port and terminal operators in her state to turn away ships carrying the fuel, warning in a letter dated Monday that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties." Sherrill argued that the Trump administration lacked authority to override the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago and said New Jersey would use its legal and regulatory powers to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel. A bipartisan group of senators has urged Trump to negate the deal, saying the U.S. "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline." Lawmakers also have warned major banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that facilitating the imports could expose companies to civil or criminal liability and future congressional investigations. The administration maintains its authorization was lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute. In response to a request for comment Thursday, the Treasury Department issued a statement saying the sanctions exemption its Office of Foreign Assets Control issued for the sale, delivery, unloading and importing of Russian diesel until April 7 was consistent with previous actions and "in compliance with all applicable laws." A Trump administration official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity said en route Russian diesel shipments would reduce price pressures for Americans. The official said increasing shipments was in keeping with Putin and Trump's agreement but did not specify whether any Russian fuel would reach the U.S. directly. Expensive diesel can have wide-ranging economic effects, including on consumer prices, since the trucking industry and many farmers use the fuel to produce and transport goods. Trump has tried blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for this year's diesel spikes. He has pressed Ukraine to halt drone attacks that damaged Russian refineries and curbed production of the fuel. The Financial Times first reported the diverted courses of the two sanctioned vessels, the Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo. Kpler analyst Matt Smith said it was not clear if Russian diesel shipments had U.S. buyers yet and that the third tanker in the North Atlantic also might change course. "Because of regulatory, sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the U.S. Atlantic coast," Smith said. "It's clear there's hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said details were not available about commercial shipments but that "all the diesel will find its buyers." Putin's special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, dismissed the Financial Times report. "Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev posted on X. Wiseman reported from Washington. - Published
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

d5ce8d81a94d.text: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and Republicans grapple with stunning losses, every remaining race matters. Some races are still too close to call, including Senate battles in both Alaska and Mississippi. Congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins reports. Amna Nawaz: As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and Republicans grapple with stunning losses, every remaining race matters. And some races are still too close to call. That includes tight Senate contests in both Alaska and Mississippi. Our congressional correspondent, Lisa Desjardins, starts us off tonight. Lisa Desjardins: In a diner in Mississippi, Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom displayed the energy that got him here, saying hello to all and joining a morning prayer. He and his Republican opponent, Cindy Hyde-Smith, are in a razor-thin race, but Colom gained several hundred votes overnight. Both parties are carefully watching the counting of provisional ballots now. Hyde-Smith did not appear today, but Mississippi's Republican Party chairman held a news conference. Mike Hurst: Any time you have an election that's this close and any time we want to make sure that our laws are being followed, we want to make sure that there's nothing untoward done. Lisa Desjardins: But Colom was confident of a win and a message from it. Scott Colom: We're going to show the country that Mississippi matters, right? We have great people that are full of great values, and we have a vision for our country that really people could learn something from. Lisa Desjardins: Alaska is the other state where a key Senate race still hangs by a razor's edge. A sizable amount of votes are yet to be counted, some from such remote areas, they must be flown in by plane. Mike Zoske, Alaska Voter: Now, there's a lot of votes that still have to come in from the bush, a lot of votes out there. And they typically vote Democratic, but I don't know how they're going to vote. Lisa Desjardins: Amidst the blue tsunami, there has been one Republican flip of a current blue House seat in Maine. Democrat Matt Dunlap conceded to the state's former Governor Paul LePage in a race that almost went to a ranked-choice count. And in a stunning upset in Los Angeles, Democratic Socialist Nithya Raman will be the city's new mayor after young voters surged for her and incumbent Karen Bass conceded. Raman will be L.A.'s first Asian American mayor. The margin is to be determined, but control of Congress is set for Democrats. And every part of the country is digesting the results, from an Iowa bar, where some drowned out their shock. Man: I woke up to my daughter saying: "The liberals are taking over." I turned it on, and I saw it as, like, surely not. Lisa Desjardins: And others chewed on understanding. Kelia Rice, Iowa Voter: With prices going up and the war and things just building on everybody, they finally decided that maybe we'll give it a chance to the Democratic Party and we'll switch our views for a moment and maybe they will help us. Lisa Desjardins: To a farmers market near Austin, where voters reckoned with the state's new blue tone. Carol Belk, Texas Voter: Disillusionment with what Trump has been doing or not doing. So we voted for Trump the last three times. So that really surprised me, the switch. the complete switch-over. Lisa Desjardins: That swing toward a new team of Democrats in Texas came largely from a new coalition of young voters and Latinos, like this college student. Sophia Flores, Texas Voter: It's the party that votes for the underdog, I like to say. Like, they vote for the little man. They try for the little man. They fight for us, rather than big corporations, big money, stuff like that. Lisa Desjardins: The range of Democratic voters was sweeping, including this cattle rancher in Kansas, who had a more watchful message for the party. Tom Holmquist, Kansas Voter: I was telling my wife this morning, I said, OK, they won. The Democrats won. They have taken 54 seats and 250 House seats. Don't blow it. Don't fall into that same trap, and actually do the things that for us. Amna Nawaz: As ballots are still being counted, Lisa Desjardins is back at the Super Screen to break down the numbers. So, Lisa, two days out post-election, what are the numbers when it comes to control of Congress? Lisa Desjardins: It really is hour by hour. Let's start with the Senate and those two big races a lot of folks are watching. What's going on in Alaska? It is exactly where it was when I talked to you one night ago. We are still waiting for ballots potentially to fly in by mail. This could be at least 10 days, maybe more, depending on how things go, with a possible look at ranked-choice. But since I have this magical screen, let's fly 3,000 miles away and go to Mississippi. Where is that race? Also where it was last night. We have Scott Colom ahead just by about 1,800 votes. We are waiting for Hinds County still, which looks like it still has 10 percent of its votes out. So this will be a waiting game, but we will keep you updated. Let's fly to the top of the country and look at the House of Representatives, where we have -- actually had quite a lot of news in the last day. Democrats now are up 40 seats. That is the net number of seats they have flipped. They only needed to flip three in order to get the House into their control. And as the races I'm watching start closing, there are still seven seats that Democrats right now are poised to flip. So that would be, right, a tremendous gain for them, potentially 47 seats. Republicans are having a couple of flips. There are two in particular. One is here just outside of Dallas in Texas 32, and also in Tennessee's Ninth District right there. But, Amna, both of these were redistricted specifically to give Republicans an advantage. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, Lisa, that unprecedented mid-decade redistricting effort led by Republicans. You have been tracking the results. What do we know? Lisa Desjardins

c7dd1e9c5b75.text: In our news wrap Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon is stepping down as head of the Justice Department's civil rights division, Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials to mark a localized ceasefire and European authorities are investigating a series of bomb threats that targeted more than a dozen flights. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines with a high-level departure at the Justice Department. Harmeet Dhillon is stepping down as head of the agency's Civil Rights Division. The conservative attorney oversaw a massive overhaul of the office, shifting its focus from protecting the rights of minorities to pursuing President Trump's agenda. That included lawsuits against elite universities, scrapping police reform efforts, and pushing dozens of states for their voter registration lists. In a statement, Dhillon said the job has been -- quote -- "the honor of a lifetime." Her departure comes just two days after massive Republican losses in the midterm elections. First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House today to mark a localized cease-fire she helped broker last month. Mrs. Trump said she hopes the deal in Oleshky, the Ukrainian city captured by Russia early on in the war -- quote -- "inspires greater peace." First Lady Melania Trump: We have chosen humanity over war. Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. Amna Nawaz: Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also spoke at the event and presented the first lady with an award. And in a sight rarely seen in the White House, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin took to the podium. Kirill Dmitriev, a U.S.-sanctioned Russian financier, thanked Mrs. Trump and Putin for the peace deal. Kirill Dmitriev, Russian Special Envoy: President Putin personally gave all of the necessary instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the local cease-fire in Oleshky. Ukrainian side abided by cease-fire. And this humanitarian mission shows what can be achieved when compassion, determination and cooperation come together. Amna Nawaz: Speaking later in the Oval Office, President Trump said he met with Dmitriev, but not with the visiting Ukrainian officials. And he told reporters that a -- quote -- "big agreement" is in the works aimed at ending the war. Meanwhile, on the ground, both countries carried out strikes today. Authorities in Ukraine's Kyiv region say a Russian attack sparked a fire that injured at least one person. And in a Russian-controlled area of Eastern Ukraine, officials say a Ukrainian attack on a bus killed at least five people and wounded 13 others. In Europe, authorities are investigating a series of bomb threats that targeted more than a dozen flights, prompting emergency landings and even military escorts. From Spain to Poland, planes were forced to land, disrupting travel across the region. No suspicious materials were found, and one British official described these as malicious hoaxes. The threats follow similar incidents earlier this week. No explosives were found in those instances either. Passengers on affected flights today described their experience. Elena Pala, Threatened Flight Passenger (through interpreter): When we landed, I commented on how good the flight had been. But the moment I stepped off the plane, I saw fire trucks. The aircraft was surrounded. Woman (through interpreter): They inspected the luggage, had us get off, lined three of us up, told us to step aside and checked the luggage with dogs. Amna Nawaz: Authorities haven't determined who issued the threats, but they come as European officials have warned about a rise in Russian sabotage and so-called hybrid attacks. In France, officials say more than 600,000 people took to the streets nationwide today, demanding higher wages and more funding for education. There were some clashes between protesters and police, though most of the demonstrations were peaceful. Today's included both public and private sector workers and were part of a general strike that disrupted some public transportation and other services. It follows weeks of student-led protests that have sometimes turned violent. The unrest has pressured the nation's government ahead of presidential elections next year. British comedian Russell Brand was found guilty today of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. Photographers swarmed a police van carrying Brand as it left a London court. He was also found not guilty of three other charges. The case stems from the late 1990s and 2000s, when Brand became known for his suggestive humor and promiscuity. Prosecutors say he was a manipulative predator, though Brand has denied the charges. The 51-year-old was denied bail and will be sentenced on Monday, with the judge saying he faces significant time in prison. Turning now to sports news, Cristiano Ronaldo is retiring from international football after more than two decades playing for Portugal. He shared the news today on social media. Cristiano Ronaldo, (through interpreter): It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart. Amna Nawaz: The striker's career spans six World Cups, and he holds the men's international scoring record with 146 goals. The decision follows a series of public disputes with Portugal's new manager. In a statement, the Portuguese Football Federation expressed its deep gratitude, calling him -- quote -- "the greatest player of all time." The 41-year-old will continue to play at the club level in Saudi Arabia, where he's aiming for his 1,000th career goal. And the biggest night in fashion has a new theme for 2027. The Metropolitan Museum of Art announced today that it will showcase ordinary items and materials like jeans or plastic and how designers transform them into fashion. The show is called "extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday." And it replaces a planned exhibit focused on th

fae1702af4ac.text: By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press By — Linley Sanders, Associated Press Linley Sanders, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/after-midterms-trump-is-left-to-weigh-his-next-move-in-iran-war-that-contributed-to-gop-loss Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter After midterms, Trump is left to weigh his next move in Iran war that contributed to GOP loss Politics Nov 5, 2026 6:46 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — As he takes stock of his Republican Party's midterm drubbing, President Donald Trump now faces the difficult question of what to do about his unpopular 8-month-old war against Iran. For weeks, Trump has threatened to return to a full-scale bombardment of Iran once the U.S. elections were in the rearview mirror if Tehran did not come to a settlement under terms acceptable to him. READ MORE: Iranian leaders say midterm results show U.S. voters have rejected Trump's war In his first comments on Wednesday after Democrats' resounding election victory — a wave powered in part by the American electorate's dissatisfaction with the war — Trump largely agreed with Vice President JD Vance, who publicly ruminated on the war being a catastrophe for Republicans. And in an Oval Office exchange with reporters Thursday, Trump suggested that the election losses aren't weighing on his calculations. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in," Trump said. The strikes, and counterstrikes, have caused tens of billions of dollars of damage in the region. And the conflict has reached into the pocketbook of families around the globe with elevated gas prices and rising costs in just about every sector. Now, as Trump ponders his next move, the stakes couldn't be higher for Iran, the Middle East and the global economy writ large. Trump may be less restrained, but the conflict is now more complicated While oil is flowing again from the Strait of Hormuz with the help of U.S. Navy escorts for international tankers, the conflict has spread to the Red Sea with Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi Arabia -led coalition fighting it out. The situation in the Red Sea remains particularly volatile. The Houthis are attacking Yemeni civilians and Saudi infrastructure, and are looking to bolster ties with militant groups across the Horn of Africa. The attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on areas controlled by the internationally recognized Yemeni government have also worsened a growing humanitarian crisis. The threat that the region faces from Iran and its proxy groups, noted a senior Yemeni government official, "did not change overnight" with the U.S. elections, urging Washington to avoid hasty decisions. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the basis of anonymity. "There's reason to suspect that Trump may feel less restrained given that the political damage is done," said Brian Haggerty, a former senior analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency who focused on Middle East security issues. "At the same time, the strategic calculus or the strategic logic of what you hope to achieve through an escalation of strikes against Iran is no different today than it was a week ago or a month ago." Trump has at least a few options, analysts say Haggerty, who now works with Defense Priorities, a Washington think tank, said Trump could choose to maintain something close to the current posture, with the U.S. military carrying out what it calls "defensive strikes" while continuing its naval blockade to restrict the flow of Iranian oil to the global market. Another option is striking Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to its nuclear program that is buried deep underground in central Iran, said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for Near Eastern affairs in Trump's first term. Trump has repeatedly suggested he was considering targeting the site. Schenker said Trump could then walk away and contend he had done sufficient damage to Iran's nuclear program — and perhaps try to pursue a "fig leaf agreement" that restores freedom of navigation to the Strait of Hormuz, offers Iran some degree of sanctions relief, and punts additional nuclear talks to the future. Yet another option would be to follow up on threats Trump made earlier in the war to launch massive attacks on Iranian infrastructure. "The Iranians may believe the president is wounded and constrained by Congress, but the opposite can also be true," Schenker said. But such escalation would likely exacerbate the oil and energy price problem that many voters cited as a reason for supporting Democrats on Tuesday, Schenker said. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil tumbled below $95 on Wednesday after the election, touching its lowest level in two months, a signal that markets do not expect major strikes. Iran, of course, also has a say, analysts note. "Once you start a fistfight, you can stop throwing punches. That doesn't mean the other combatant will stop throwing punches," said Bradley Bowman, an analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "We can try to end the war, but what do we do if the Islamic Republic of Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz?" Regional officials are on high alert for what Trump does next Middle East officials had been hanging on Trump's every word in the weeks leading up to the U.S. elections, looking for clues on how the Republican leader was weighing his next steps. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed for renewed strikes on Iran during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it. Three Middle Eastern government officials said on Wednesday that Trump and his administration had seemed to be signaling to Iran that its leve

d48a36390bf5.text: Tuesday's election results were not just closely watched in the U.S. American elections, in many ways, have become global events and the Democratic wave led to an extraordinary outpouring. Nick Schifrin gauges that reaction. Amna Nawaz: Well, Tuesday's election results weren't just closely watched here at home. American elections in many ways become global events. And this Democratic wave has led to an extraordinary outpouring. Nick Schifrin gauges that reaction, beginning with Iran. Nick Schifrin: On the darkened streets of Iran overnight, the regime put President Donald Trump in jail. This fake lockup followed Democrats locking down Election Day victories. Iranian leaders resisted a preelection agreement and believe they helped hand President Trump electoral defeat. Iran's chief negotiator relished the rebuke and said it should end the war. But Iran's supreme leader, warned divided American government will not lead to American concessions, a sentiment echoed on the streets of Tehran. Ali Akbar Mashayekhi, Iranian Demonstrator (through interpreter): It's always the same cycle, negotiations, then war, then back to negotiations, then war again. We're not afraid of war. If they want to fight, we will fight back. Nick Schifrin: Trump agreed with his vice president that the war in Iran, now entering its ninth month, triggered a blue tsunami. President Donald Trump: It's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term. Nick Schifrin: But the war has only brought Iran closer to its allies, including Russia. Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin welcomed Iran's National Security Council Chief Mohsen Rezaei. Iranian weapon designs have helped Russia target Ukraine. And so it was again today when Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv. Ukrainian officials tell "PBS News Hour" they are skeptical the new Congress can shift U.S. policy. But some European leaders hope a new Democratic Congress can make a difference. Kaja Kallas, Foreign Affairs High Representative, European Commission: I hope that the new Congress and the new Senate will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia. Man: Today, democracy won in America. Nick Schifrin: Across Europe, some officials publicly breathe a sigh of relief and described Democrats as kindred spirits. And in the Global South, some leaders said the midterms could result in a reset. Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President: I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations, really. Nick Schifrin: But one country's current leaders do not welcome that new era. President Donald Trump: We have already agreed that, by the end of this year, we won't be paying Israel. Nick Schifrin: On FOX News earlier this week, President Trump announced the U.S. would stop giving Israel grants to buy American jets and weapons. Israel will now have to use its own money. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan Senator-Elect: I think the fact that we're fighting the war in Iran is a function of what the prime minister of Israel wanted. Nick Schifrin: And this election produced what may prove the most hostile U.S. Congress to Israel in history. Democrats now face a choice, whether to go further and try to block weapons sales to Israel and whether to end funding for the war in Iran. Amna Nawaz: And Nick is here with me now. Nick, let's begin with that war in Iran. Where are negotiations to end it? Nick Schifrin: A senior regional and senior American official both tell me that, before the elections, the two sides were close to a deal that would have returned them to the memorandum of understanding earlier this year. One official, in fact, Amna, told me it was 80 percent there. And that deal would have included an agreement for Iran to downblend its highly enriched uranium. Now, before the June 2025 strikes, the U.N.'s nuclear agency reported Iran had nearly 1,000 pounds of 60 percent enriched uranium, a small step away from weapons-grade. Iran's agreeing to downblend its stockpile would be a significant concession on their part. It would also mean the U.S. would accept some Iranian-enriched uranium, at least for now, Amna. The agreement would also include the U.S. is lifting sanctions and unfreezing some Iranian assets, and it would have reopened the strait without any kind of tolls, according to these officials. Now, Vice President Vance during this time even wrote a letter to the man we just showed was in Moscow today, the head of Iran's supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei. Now, simultaneously is all that, Amna, a senior U.S. official told me President Trump told regional allies that the U.S. would start bombing Iran again with a short, intense campaign. And then he said, well, that campaign was postponed, but he has not said that was canceled. And, today, the president said this still could come soon. Today, in the Oval Office, the president said -- quote -- "And now we will make a decision. Do we want to go further and certify it? By certifying it, meaning it will never happen again. I think it will take 25 years to rebuild the country." He concluded, "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You will know soon enough." Amna Nawaz: So the big question is how, if at all, do these midterm election results play into all of this? Nick Schifrin: So, interestingly, regional officials tell me that they are worried that actually it will take Iran's calculus and change it. The regime has used rallies this week to celebrate the Democrats' win. And regional and U.S. officials tell me Iran has been gloating in private and public it didn't give the president the deal he wanted, and therefore helped deliver that Republican defeat. And these regional officials fear Iran will now drive a harder bargain now that it feels like it in some ways won the midterm elections. Now, on the U.S. side, we saw this extraordinary post on X by Vice President Vance, right? He listed the war and the U.S. re

9344591304b2.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted the state’s entire death row population to life in prison without parole. The decision could grant clemency to 548 people. Newsom had previously put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, but left hundreds on death row. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Robin Maher of the Death Penalty Information Center. Amna Nawaz: California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the largest mass commutation in the country's history, changing the state's entire death row population sentences to life in prison without parole. The decision could grant clemency to 548 people. Newsom, who is considering a run for the presidency, wrote in a letter to constituents that -- quote -- "State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." Newsom had previously put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, but left hundreds on death row. For more on all of this, I'm joined by Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Welcome back, and thanks for joining us. So, the largest such commutation in the nation's history. We should point out, though, California has not executed anyone since 2006. Does this decision have a real impact or is it more about sending a message? Robin Maher: Oh, I think it does. I mean, both historically and symbolically, this decision carries real significance. I mean, this mass commutation will remove more than 500 people from death row. That's 30 percent of the total number of people on death rows throughout the United States. And Governor Newsom very publicly wrestled with this decision, taking the time to first consult with victims' family members and corrections officials, judges, lawyers, and many others. He also looked to the research and the evidence that revealed that the death penalty in California was a very costly, deeply flawed policy choice. And I think all of that careful work and consultation led to today's decision. Amna Nawaz: And yet it's not a decision being supported by all. Some families who lost loved ones in these crimes are not backing it, Marc Klaas among them, as I'm sure you know, the father of Polly Klaas, who was 12 years old when she was kidnapped from her home and murdered in 1993. He told The New York Times today, "We're talking about serial killers, spree killers, cop killers, baby killers, talking about the absolute worst people in our society without a doubt. And he's putting his energy into commuting these characters?"" The head of Crime Victims United said: "Families were asked to trust the justice system through trials, appeals, and decades of anguish. Their loved ones deserve more than a blanket decision that sweeps aside individual judgments." What do you say to that, Robin? Robin Maher: Right. Well, I'm not surprised. I am sure that some victims' family members are disappointed, just as others feel a sense of relief that these sentences are now final, and the sense of uncertainty and retraumatization that so many family members feel during these lengthy appeals is now over. I mean, one important thing to consider is that the money, the tremendous amount of money that has been necessary to prop up the death penalty in California can now be reinvested in meaningful solutions to prevent violent crime from occurring and also to support family members who are still grieving from these terrible losses. Amna Nawaz: There are some groups already talking about potentially suing Newsom to stop that. Could this move be stalled? Robin Maher: I don't think so. The California Constitution is very clear that Governor Newsom's authority to make these decisions is absolute and final. There are a number of people on the row whose sentences the commutation will need to be reviewed by the California Supreme Court. Anyone who has two felony convictions will need the court to first approve of this recommendation to commute their sentences. But his decision regarding the other commutations is final. Amna Nawaz: Robin, in the minute or so I have left, we should point out both Indiana and Florida carried out executions in their states today. Alabama plans to do one later this evening. And, of course, we have seen this national debate after the botched execution of Christa Pike. When it comes to that debate, where are most Americans on this issue? Robin Maher: Well, public support for the death penalty has been declining, pretty steadily declining over the last several years. Now barely a majority of people support use of the death penalty, and the largest number ever have very serious concerns about its reliability and its fairness. So things have certainly changed quite a bit in the last few years. We're expecting a new poll to be released later this month. Amna Nawaz: All right, that is Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Robin, thank you for your time. Robin Maher: My pleasure.

b5bde5de974b.text: With Democrats set to take control of the House, they are making plans to use their majority not only to advance legislation but also to ramp up congressional oversight. California Rep. Robert Garcia is expected to become the new chairman of the House Oversight Committee. He says Democrats have plans to move quickly with a series of investigations. Garcia joined Liz Landers to discuss more. Amna Nawaz: With Democrats set to take control of the House, they're making plans to use their majority not only to advance legislation, but also ramp up congressional oversight. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, has more. Liz Landers: California Congressman Robert Garcia, who is expected to become the new chairman of the House Oversight Committee, says Democrats have plans to move quickly with a series of investigations when the new Congress takes office in January. These could include reviews into the Jeffrey Epstein files, the Trump family financial dealings, and immigration enforcement. Congressman Garcia joins us now. Congressman, welcome back to the program. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA): Sure. Happy to be here. Liz Landers: On election night, you posted this two-word statement on X: "Lawyer up." Do you think the election results have given Democrats a mandate to investigate the Trump administration? Rep. Robert Garcia: I think they have, and especially because, right now, when you think about the key issue, which is affordability, in large part, the reason why people can't afford to pay the gas, the groceries, they're struggling with the rent or the mortgage is because the Trump family continues to enrich themselves, steal people's wealth, and enrich their billionaire friends and donors. They continue to support companies and CEOs that are ripping off the American public. And so we have to, of course, focus on affordability, but there also has to be accountability and there has to be justice. There has to be justice for families that are being picked up by ICE agents and that are removing due process from the system. There has to be justice for the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein. So there's a lot of work to do, but I think there's definitely a mandate to ensure we have accountability and affordability. Liz Landers: You have said that you have been preparing for these investigations for months and you're not starting from scratch here. What is the first thing you expect to investigate and how quickly will those subpoenas go out? Rep. Robert Garcia: Look, the first issue for us is going to be around the Trump family and the clear corruption. This is the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States. When you have the president making billions from these crypto schemes, you have Jared Kushner getting $2 billion from the Saudis for his investment firm just after leaving the White House. Don Jr., his entire wedding being paid for by a Russian oligarch, him sitting on boards of companies that get contracts from the Pentagon, I mean, this is really serious stuff. And the American public are looking at their own bills and seeing costs go up when they go to the supermarket, yet they're seeing the Trumps get richer. And so that's a real contrast, and that's a real issue for us to take on. People want solutions. They want accountability. Liz Landers: When it comes to the Epstein files, what more is there to learn and what documents have not been released? Rep. Robert Garcia: Look, I think, first, we want to center our work on justice for the survivors. Half of the Epstein documents, of the files have not been released to the public, even though Trump -- even though we know that Trump has tried to create confusion, calling this a hoax, and Todd Blanche saying they're going to release documents, and then they don't. So we still have half of the files have not been released. We need more information from the Epstein estate. We need -- the co-conspirators that were involved with Jeffrey Epstein, there needs to be real accountability for them. If you abused, trafficked, raped women and children, and you're walking around with no sort of justice, that has to end. There has not been a single, not one public hearing on the Epstein investigation in the Congress. And that's going to end when we take over the Oversight Committee. Liz Landers: Are you going to investigate Elon Musk and his role in DOGE? Rep. Robert Garcia: I think Elon Musk and his companies is something that are of interest to committees across the Congress. And so I think especially you're going to hear a lot from Armed Services and others around how these contracts happen. And certainly for us in Oversight, issues around DOGE are really important. Like, were people's data stolen? Where is their data? Who had access to it? All these federal workers that were fired and let go. I mean, what's happening to our federal work force and our agencies because of the loss of talent is really serious. And so absolutely we have questions for Mr. Musk, but we also have questions for those that were engaged in that work. There was a group of data folks running around taking people's data. Where is that information? So those are serious questions that deserve answers. Liz Landers: Leader Jeffries has said that Democrats are focused on affordability and accountability. Do you think that impeaching President Trump again would be a mistake? Rep. Robert Garcia: Look, I don't think that that's an agenda item for House Democrats as we're coming in. Let's be really clear. Donald Trump's been impeached twice. He commits probably an impeachable offense every week. The Senate has not convicted him.
