a86099ab2928.text: There are few places where the consequences of the Trump administration's cuts to global aid programs are more apparent than South Sudan. With a raging civil war in Sudan to its north, South Sudan is contending not just with its own underserved people, but with more than a million Sudanese refugees. Special correspondent Anna Conkling of Noosphere, a new journalism app, reports. Amna Nawaz: There are few places where the consequences of the Trump administration's cuts to global aid programs are more apparent than South Sudan. With a raging civil war in Sudan to its north, South Sudan, also still racked by conflict, is contending with its own underserved population and more than a million Sudanese refugees. Special correspondent Anna Conkling of Noosphere, a new journalism app, reports from Renk in South Sudan. Anna Conkling: Those raspy, labored breaths are Kalia's. She spent 15 days in the pediatric ward of this hospital in Renk just south of the Sudan border. She is just 11 months old. And like so many of the babies here, she is starving. Woman: So we are giving for bed two, which is 90. Anna Conkling: Nurse Shadiya is preparing formula for them all. In addition to the breathing trouble, Kalia has severe fever and she's lost too much weight. Doctors are trying to formulate treatment for her. Kout Kout, Clinical Officer, Renk Civil Hospital: of recent weight loss, we suspect T.B. And we are treating it now. Anna Conkling: T.B. is... Kout Kout: Yes. Anna Conkling: ... tuberculosis. Kout Kout: Yes, tuberculosis. And it is meningitis. Meningitis T.B. is in the brain. But the good thing for this girl is not coughing. There's no cough. Yes, that's the good thing of it. Anna Conkling: Is she expected to survive? Kout Kout: Actually, we are monitoring it over 24 hours. Now we will see. Anna Conkling: A few beds down is Azma, a 1.5-year-old Sudanese refugee who has been sick for five months. Doctors told me that her hair fell out from malnutrition. And she's now being treated for pneumonia and sepsis, likely resulting from the malnutrition. Her mother, Fatima, says she was referred here from another hospital. Kalia and Azma are just two of the more than 500 patients that arrive here needing help every day. But as international aid cuts decimate South Sudan's health care system, hospitals like this one are struggling to carry on. Much of that is because of the war to the north in Sudan, from which South Sudan gained independence 15 years ago. It is the world's worst humanitarian crisis. Millions have been displaced internally. Millions more are now refugees, and the war has no end in sight. In Renk, the refugee influx has strained the hospital beyond a breaking point. They try to treat local cases like Kalia's, while helping some of the up to 3,000 refugees that flee Sudan each week. The hospital's pharmacy plays a vital role in its ability to continue to operate. But it's running low on medication and has no way to refill them. Dr. Suhier told us she faces the challenges of devastating aid cuts every day. The pharmacy is completely funded by international partners. And one of the medication that they're running critically low on are malaria tablets. And it's the rainy season here in Renk, which means that there's a lot more mosquitoes out and a lot more infections. Suhier watches her supply of medication diminish with little hope that they will be replaced. Cuts to foreign programs like USAID are not only causing shortages. They're also costing lives. Relief International, a global human rights organization based in Washington, D.C., is one of the main partners here. But the hospital said the agency reduced its presence at the end of September. I asked Dr. Suhier what their absence will mean for the hospital. Suhier Ahmed Deng, Pharmacist, Renk Civil Hospital: Until now, even today, if you look to my eyes, they are so red because of thinking. We think a lot to have the solution, but we cannot tell anyone that to come and to walk in a state that we don't have money. Here, if there is not any support, they will die without medicine, without food, so better for them to go again to work to Sudan, to die there. Man: So this is the OPD site. Anna Conkling: Throughout the hospital, evidence of the gutting of foreign assistance is everywhere. We learned that doctors are forced to decide each day which ward most needs generator power. So, over here is another part of the ward. And you can see that there's not really any electricity, there's no lights on, and when we were here on Saturday, the staff told us that this ward doesn't really have a lot of electricity because the generator isn't being used as a priority here. The intensive care unit had no power at all the day we were there. It was also running low on most of the medication it needed to help its 12 patients. Despite the shortages, the hospital still hopes to serve as a stabilization point for the refugees who stream into Renk each week. For those who need it, surgery is still being scheduled on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. The patients recover in urine-soaked rooms filled with flies and an inescapable heat. But this is the desperate state of health care today in South Sudan. Back in the pediatric ward, one bed is now completely empty. We are told that Kalia, the 11-month-old girl who was having trouble breathing, died eight hours after our visit. The official cause was malnutrition. The nurse said that Kalia's death deeply saddened the parents of other patients here. Once hopeful for their child's recovery, they now fear death. But, as we were leaving, we found baby Azma sitting up and playing with her mom. Doctors say she's recovering from her illness and is expected to make a full recovery. "Alhamdulillah," says Fatima, "Praise be to God." For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Anna Conkling with Noosphere in Renk, South Sudan.

0400bccd5222.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/hegseth-allows-national-guard-to-boost-dc-patrols-with-military-vehicles-boats-and-patrol-cars Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hegseth allows National Guard to boost DC patrols with military vehicles, boats and patrol cars Politics Nov 5, 2026 6:31 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has signed off on the National Guard ramping up its presence in the nation's capital in military vehicles and boats as troops deepen their integration with local law enforcement. WATCH: The effectiveness and cost of the National Guard deployment in D.C. In two memos signed Oct. 29 and obtained by The Associated Press, Hegseth approved the National Guard to use 60 military police cars as well as tactical vehicles, patrol boats and portable light towers during increased patrols around Washington. Troops will also be able to carry rifles during some operations but not in Metro rail stations. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The sight of vehicles that look more at home on a battlefield than a city street will harken back to when President Donald Trump first deployed the National Guard in August 2025 for what he called a crime-fighting mission. Tactical vehicles and troops carrying guns initially were seen at some Washington landmarks. National Guard members have supported law enforcement operations, patrolled neighborhoods, dispersed homeless camps and helped with citywide cleanup efforts. READ MORE: Trump wants to clear homeless encampments. Here's what usually happens, according to experts A boost in troop presence comes amid increased issues involving Guard members assigned to the city, including the arrest of a Georgia serviceman for pulling a gun on a fellow Guard member, the arrest of a Guard member for carrying an unauthorized firearm, and the shooting of a Guardsman while trying to break up a fight. The memos say "visibility patrols," a mainstay of the Guard's mission in Washington, are going to be expanded and 20 light towers will be employed to "enhance force protection in patrol zones." But Hegseth says the maximum number of deployed Guard members would stay at 3,500, lower than a summertime peak of about 5,000 during America's 250th anniversary celebrations. Hegseth signed off on the National Guard using patrol cars and tactical vehicles to support law enforcement operations, though the memos stressed that the patrol cars need to be marked as "National Guard" and troops need to be in uniform. Two National Guard patrol boats will also be used "to provide operational maritime support." The memos forbid troops from conducting high-speed chases. The memos suggest that troops will play a greater role in taking on "gangs and drug traffickers." Hegseth is continuing to provide six analysts "to address organized drug distribution within D.C.," and troops who are supporting anti-gang and drug operations will now be able to carry rifles in addition to their traditional pistols. One of the memos grants the U.S. Marshals Service the use of the D.C. National Guard's 260th Special Purpose Brigade — a unit that functioned as a "quick reaction force" — to help protect "key federal leaders" and help secure and defend "key federal facilities." A Marshals Service request for National Guard helicopters or the use of troops "to clean up abandoned tires in specific areas of D.C." was denied in a Nov. 4 memo, however. When asked about the memos, the Pentagon confirmed that Hegseth "authorized the continued use of National Guard personnel and capabilities in support of the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission." The District of Columbia, which sued in September 2025 over the National Guard deployment, has argued that the mobilization is an illegal use of the military for domestic law enforcement. A federal appeals court panel heard arguments Oct. 14 after a lower court sided with the city. Nearly 3,100 Guard members from various states are in Washington, including more than 500 from Georgia, the largest contingent behind the District of Columbia, which had 514 members involved as of Monday. 6477aa142612.text: President Trump said after meeting with his national security advisers Thursday that he'll soon decide whether to resume all-out war in Iran now that the midterms are over. Why it matters: The election was seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a new wave of bombing to try to bring the war to an end. The president, at least for now, is considering three options: launch new strikes, continue to strangle Iran's regime economically, or cut a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians. On Thursday, Trump and his top national security advisers met on Iran for the first time since the election, as part of his weekly intelligence briefing, two U.S. officials said. What he's saying: "Now we will make a decision," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "Do we want to go further" with strikes to ensure Iran's nuclear program is dead and that "it will never happen again?" he added. "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough." State of play: As Trump was weighing his next move, there was a flurry of diplomatic activity Thursday, including multiple phone calls between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and regional mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt. The Qatari mediators continued discussions with the Iranians and the White House about a draft proposal calling for the two sides to take a series of steps over two days to build mutual confidence toward a broader deal. On the first day, the U.S. would lift its naval blockade and release some of Iran's frozen funds. In return, Iran would issue an official invitation to the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to bombed nuclear sites, based on an agreement reached in Cairo a year ago, regional sources said. On the second day, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen, after which nuclear talks would resume, focusing on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The big picture: The secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei — a key player in indirect negotiations with the U.S. — met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Thursday. The meeting took place several days after a call between Putin and Rezaei and proposals by the Russian president to mediate between the U.S. and Iran. Rezaei said he delivered a message to Putin from Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He added that Putin stressed he is ready to try to help end the war. "We told Mr. Putin that we announced seven conditions to the Americans regarding diplomacy, and that until the Americans fulfill our seven conditions, neither the Strait of Hormuz will be opened nor will there be any negotiations," Rezaei said after the meeting. What to watch: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) is finalizing preparations to potentially resume major combat operations in Iran, though it hasn't received a new directive from Washington, a U.S. official said. One signal that the U.S. plans renewed strikes could be the arrival of a third U.S. Navy aircraft carrier strike group in the Middle East. A U.S. official said the USS Theodore Roosevelt and its strike group will spend a few days in Singapore starting Friday for a port call. It won't reach CENTCOM's area of responsibility before mid-November.

There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.
Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?
This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.
Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.
This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.
For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.
The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.
Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.
Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.
"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.
"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."
Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.
"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."
Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.
In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".
On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.
The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

521e5c15ffbc.text: By — Isabel DeBre, Associated Press Isabel DeBre, Associated Press By — Emilio Sanabria, Associated Press Emilio Sanabria, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/paraguay-prosecutor-will-seek-charges-against-embattled-president-after-bank-collapse Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Paraguay prosecutor will seek charges against embattled president after bank collapse World Nov 5, 2026 6:16 PM EST ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay (AP) — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña is under criminal investigation following the collapse of a major digital bank, prosecutors announced, hours after the South American leader's resignation and impeachment Thursday. The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration. READ MORE: How the digital era helped speed up bank runs Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders will continue voting Friday on whether to accept Peña's resignation, which would clear the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial. Opposition senators are continuing to demand that Peña be removed from office, arguing that allowing him to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution, should Paraguay's Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández opt to file charges. Rolón has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Peña and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor's office said Thursday. The investigations will examine authorities' oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender. Peña said he would cooperate with investigators. "Whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution," he said on X. Earlier Thursday, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions." Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations, but the Trump administration lifted the sanctions last year. Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages. "I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me." From star lender to seized bank Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living.
"That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday.
"It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish."
The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing.
The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War.
Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; Â£27bn), with no path to balance.
Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact.
The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year.
But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian.
And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment.
Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget.
A plan to end homelessness within a decade
One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness.
This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment.
Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime.
The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year.
Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues.
There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs.
The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver.
And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive.
No boost to immigration levels any time soon
After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly.
This includes a cap on international students and temporary foreign workers, which have been relied on by companies to ease labour shortages.
The Carney government has previously said it will keep its permanent resident admission target to 380,000 people annually until 2028.
Meanwhile, it will gradually reduce its temporary resident arrivals to 370,000.
There has been pressure on Carney to increase some of those numbers. A report from the Royal Bank of Canada in September, external warned that "without immigration, the country's population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century".
On the other hand, the Conservative opposition has called on the government to further lower its targets.
In the new budget, Carney has opted to keep immigration levels flat.
Helping businesses through US tariff dispute
A big focus of the Carney government has been reducing Canada's reliance on the US as a trade partner, while also helping cushion the blow from Trump's tariffs on its key sectors.
Last year, it promised millions in backing for businesses working to develop new export markets. It also lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate in a bid to stop businesses from moving to the US to escape tariff pains.
This budget builds on that, including plans to support specific sectors hit by US tariffs like steel and forestry.
The new funding was welcome by Canada's forestry sector, with the BC Council of Forest Industries saying in a statement that the support "comes at a critical time for workers".
Since March 2025, the Carney government has set aside nearly C$44bn in support for workers and businesses hit by US tariffs, the budget notes.
The budget states that "diversification will take time, given the scale and depth of Canada's economic relationship with the United States. But the shift is underway".
Sovereignty through arts - and rockets
Sovereignty is a big theme in Carney's second budget, which proposes funding different measures to strengthen Canadian identity - whether it be through the arts or in space.
Canada is the only G7 country that does not have the capability to launch its own rockets. A line item in the budget looks to change that, with C$2.7bn earmarked to developing Canadian space technology and launch infrastructure.
On arts and culture, Carney is promising a tax exemption on income that is made through "original and creative artistic works".
The budget also sets aside C$32.2m over four years to establish a free national digital library for Canadians. It will launch with at least 200 titles with plans to expand in coming years.
Carney had previously pledged to significantly boost defence spending to meet the Nato target of 5% of annual GDP by 2035.

World Nov 5, 2026 5:31 PM EST LONDON (AP) — Hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts this week after a series of bomb threats that officials have said were malicious hoaxes. READ MORE: Flights across Europe face disruption after false bomb threats It was not immediately known who was behind the threats, which came at a time of rising tensions with Russia and warnings that it may be ramping up so-called hybrid attacks in Europe. Here's what happens when airlines receive bomb threats. Threats are assessed and then relayed to pilots Assessors determine whether a threat is credible, partially credible or not credible, according to Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation for the British Airline Pilots' Association. If deemed credible, the flight crew is informed right away and the captain makes all the decisions, guided by a safety checklist, said Waites. If the aircraft is on the ground, that would mean evacuation. If already in flight, the priority would be to land as soon and as safely as possible. "Pilots are highly trained and skilled professionals. Their expertise is invaluable in ensuring passenger safety and keeping aviation one of the safest forms of transport there is," Waites said. Airlines, airport operators and law enforcement generally follow guidelines developed by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency and the International Civil Aviation Organization, which conducts audits to ensure compliance. Flight crew training includes live situational exercises covering various threats, including how to search for explosives that may have been smuggled on board. Diverting and inspecting flights is costly When threats are called in, airline employees are instructed to keep the caller on the line and to gather as much information as possible, according to aviation security expert Philip Baum. Many of the threats received this week were sent by email, with enough information for authorities to determine that aircraft needed inspection. That can be costly for airlines. Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England, said diverting a flight because of an unruly passenger or a bomb threat can cost up to $250,000. The costs may be lower in this case because most of the disrupted flights were short-haul, where there is less likelihood of overnight delays, he said. Empty threats could test defenses The intent with these threats "appears to be to sow chaos, uncertainty, about the reliability of air traffic across Europe," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, senior fellow at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels. The threats could also be testing the relative response time and level of coordination among authorities in different countries, with the aim of identifying weaknesses for future attacks. "Do the authorities in Poland respond at the same speed and with the same urgency, et cetera, as the authorities of Italy, for instance?" Kirkegaard said, comparing such threats to a "stress test" of the system. Carlson reported from Brussels and Hadjicostis from Nicosia, Cyprus. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of incitement and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, was charged over remarks he made while campaigning for electoral reforms ahead of the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said the incitement case stemmed from his campaign over his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election."
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu has been on trial on charges of treason and says this is the first time he has heard of the separate charge of incitement.
"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," said Lissu, when he was given a chance to address the judges.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
- Electoral commissioners should be independently appointed (not by the president)
- Police should allow all parties to campaign free of intimidation
- Government-appointed district chiefs should no longer act as returning officers
- Party agents should be able to observe counting without harassment
- It should be possible to challenge presidential election results in court.
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years outside Tanzania.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, rights group Amnesty International accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.

52f6d6104e5e.text: Voters were unambiguous on Tuesday: Don't B.S. us. Don't say you'll lower prices and end wars and corruption, then do the opposite. It's really that simple. This isn't so different from when Americans told Democrats not to B.S. them about Joe Biden's health, or about the words they should use, or social behaviors they should adopt. Why it matters: Most Americans agree broadly on most things, most of the time. They want competent politicians to focus on issues that meaningfully impact their lives. Like clockwork, every two years, Americans feel the party in power fails to deliver this — so they punish the incumbents at the polls. Politicians and some journalists tend to treat the American people as dopes and dupes who don't get what's happening in front of their faces. Tuesday's midterms, which will live in history as a Watergate-level reset for democracy, show that voters were paying attention and hit a boiling point. They didn't hide it. Polls consistently showed that all they really care about is rising inflation, job insecurity, ending the war, and stopping the rampant corruption. This was a repudiation of overreach, incompetence and corruption. People will tolerate it in small doses, but eventually reject it. In an age when people trust institutions less all the time , our institutions held. Courts restrained executive-branch excess. The press kept doing its job. Voters did theirs. But for all the hand-wringing that America is crumbling, that democracy is fading, or elections are eroding, the system worked. Remember: most Americans are normal and resilient. We should celebrate that. Despite it all, America works. For years, we've been reminding you about the power of Normal America : The vast majority of people — including our siblings, who are scattered from Oshkosh to Oregon — don't marinate in cable news, obsess about X or wake up thinking about Washington. They volunteer, they give to good causes, they'll help you in a pinch. They're good, they're fair ... and they're smart. Between the lines: That's Normal America. Sometimes when we're making a tough call about journalism or business, we ask ourselves: "What would the person at the bar think?" It's a useful, clarifying proxy for: What would seem on the level through the lens of common sense and plain fairness? The person at the bar, and the voter in the booth, didn't want their soccer coach deported, didn't want their business to crumble because of a war of choice that's dragging on and on, didn't want the president's family and friends to enrich themselves while Normal America was wheezing. What we're watching: Democrats will be tempted and pressured to overreach. If they overinterpret their mandate the way Republicans did, they'll be punished, like clockwork. Here's what Republicans and Democrats will do if they're smart: Watch Texas. A seemingly impenetrable red state turned all blue, from the U.S. Senate to the governor's office to the state legislature. If Democrats can keep Texas, Republicans have no path to the presidency. Look at what happened in those southern border counties in Texas. These were the people who demanded tighter borders and punished Democrats when they wouldn't listen. But they're the same people who are saying stop with the thuggery and targeting of nonviolent people. Republicans were obliterated in those areas for not listening. Then look to the Texas suburbs, where you have many more traditional Republicans and moderate Democrats. They looked at Ken Paxton and said he's simply not on the level, even if they might agree with him on a lot of ideas. Corruption is never a good look. Enabling it and elevating it is even worse. The bottom line: This remains a 50-50 nation — a simple fact that every party and power instantly, constantly ignores. Once again, Normal Americans spoke: Ignore or B.S. them at your peril.

- Published
One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.
The driver is reported to have been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.
Earlier, French education minister Ãdouard Geffray said the crash involved students.
He told reporters it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
French Transport minister Philippe Tabarot, who was on his way to the area, said more than 100 firefighters had also been sent.
The local town hall has been opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

The News
Republicansâ stunning midterm defeat is forcing them to confront a question that will shape their 2028 primary: Can their next standard-bearer come from inside the Trump administration?
Vice President JD Vance remains the most prominent potential successor to President Donald Trump, but his blunt X post pinning the partyâs Tuesday collapse on the Iran war showed heâs aware that itâs a political liability for all Republicans heading into 2028. And concerns about Vanceâs viability are brewing in some corners of the GOP.
âThe biggest loser Tuesday night, heading into 2028, was JD Vance,â one Republican strategist argued. â2028 shifted from a conversation about who could carry the torch of Trumpism, to who can rebuild the movement from shambles.â
Vance isnât the only prospective candidate tied to Trump with new problems after the midterms. While former Speaker Newt Gingrich suggested that Tuesday night might have opened a 2028 lane for Secretary of State Marco Rubio â whoâs indicated that he has no plans to run â anyone in Trumpâs circle could face similar headwinds.
That includes administration officials who are occasionally whispered about as harboring presidential ambitions, like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Semafor spoke with more than a half-dozen Republicans, inside and close to the administration, who are starting to doubt that voters will embrace Trumpâs chosen successor.
âItâs an open race, no question about it,â one person close to the White House said of the looming 2028 debate.
Others in the party are focused on an even touchier topic: Are Republicans doomed for 2028, particularly if the war drags on and voters continue feeling the economic effects?
âThere are a lot of Republicans who desperately do not want Donald Trump to be the conversation in 2028. But theyâre living in a fantasy world â and the reality is, Donald Trump will always be a big part of the Republican conversation,â said a second person close to the White House. âThe actual question is: Can any Republican win?â
Outsiders See An Opening
Democratsâ huge margin of victory in Tuesdayâs popular vote for the House, estimated at 13 points, stemmed in large part from fury over Trumpâs handling of the economy. Exit polls showed nearly nine out of 10 voters considered the cost of living as a big factor in their vote, while the majority of voters expressed dissatisfaction with the direction of the country.
As one Trump ally put it, the night was a âdisasterâ for the GOP.
Thatâs creating opportunities for Republicans who have kept separate political identities during Trumpâs second term. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who lost to Trump in the 2024 primary, acknowledged that the midterms were a ârebukeâ of the president. He also amplified Floridaâs GOP successes, a rare bright spot for the party on Tuesday.
Some Republicans who were critical of DeSantis during his 2024 run suggested to Semafor this week that they and other doubters would be quieter in 2028 if he chose to run.
Others are more skeptical that Trump defenders (and Trump himself) could resist the temptation to attack DeSantis, particularly if he campaigns with more direct criticism of the president.
Walking a more middle road when it comes to anti-Trump sentiment is Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who has long previewed a potential run. Cruz described the midterm results as âa Watergate-level repudiation,â blaming Trumpâs tariffs and the dragging war â both of which he voted to affirm â as well as a disconnect between extreme wealth and everyday Americans.
Vanceâs Theory of the Case
The vice presidentâs social media postmortem showcased his balancing act: supporting Trump while looking toward his own political future.
âThe reason we lost is the war,â Vance wrote on X. âThe president himself said so last night.â
Vanceâs allies argue that, if he decides to run, he might be the only candidate close enough to Trump to break from the president without paying harsh consequences. One of those allies described it as creating space to be âhis own man without criticizing or alienating the president.â
Trump seemed unbothered by the vice presidentâs assessment of the midterms, telling reporters âitâs largely trueâ while standing by his decision to go to war.
Yet Vance has declined to clearly oppose the conflict since it began; his views have emerged in subtle gestures, like taking the lead on negotiations with Tehran. As Gingrich put it, âa good bit of the luster has come off the bloomâ for Vance 2028, thanks to the âgo-slow strategy blowing up in Iran.â
The View From Trump
Trump is in no rush to focus on 2028, or issue any sort of endorsement. Asked about the topic earlier this week, he told reporters that he speaks with Vance âabout a lot of thingsâ and emphasized that anyone could ultimately jump into the race.
âYou donât know whoâs talking about running,â Trump said. âYouâre going to have people running â¦ maybe a lot of people running. Maybe nobodyâs going to run. Maybe [Vance] wonât run. I donât know whoâs going to run.â
Shelbyâs view
Electoral catastrophes, like the ones Republicans just experienced, are bound to prompt panic and hand-wringing about the future. But the midterms have surfaced a question that I hear a lot: Can anyone successfully lead this party for the years after Trump leaves the stage?
The GOPâs 2028 hopefuls are damned if they do, damned if they donât. Running as an anti-Trump figure will carry risks; running on loyalty to him will pose separate problems.
The biggest unknown is Trump himself. If he can find a way to wind down the war and refocus on earning back Americansâ trust over the next two years, he could leave his successor with a clearer path.

- Democratic Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen as a potential 2028 candidate as well, is already trying to tie Vance closely to Trump: He told CNN this week Vance âis out promotingâ the policies that have turned off voters.

db55ea156274.text: Talk of subpoenas and warnings to "lawyer up" hint at the extent of the health care investigations and oversight hearings that Democrats are expected to launch once they take control of Congress. Why it matters: Democrats have been building a paper trail for months to probe instances of political interference in vaccine policies, whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. benefited financially from vaccine litigation and more. But the early efforts will more likely be directed at making a case for changes to federal Medicaid cuts, showcasing health affordability problems and examining whether federal health agencies are sufficiently funded and staffed. "You don't just do oversight to raise hell," said Tim Stretton, director of the Congressional Oversight Initiative at the Project On Government Oversight. "Trying to create some systematic change is arguably more important." What we're hearing: The House Oversight, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees will be focal points of early activity, along with the Senate health and Finance committees. Some law firms already are advising their corporate clients to cooperate with committee staffs and minimize their exposure to possible negative headlines from hearings. One prominent player will be the likely new House Oversight chair, Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) — the one who publicly warned Republicans to "lawyer up" on Tuesday after Democrats flipped control of the House. The former Long Beach mayor lost his mother, a frontline health worker, and stepfather to COVID and has publicly assailed Kennedy for undermining public health and preventing or delaying needed cures. Bernie Sanders' expected return to chair the Senate health committee will give the Vermont independent another chance to harness public outrage on drug prices and spar with Kennedy over his tenure as health secretary. Zoom in: The power shift in Congress gives Democrats the ability to subpoena witnesses, demand records and hold officials and individuals in contempt if they don't comply. Hearings and investigations into problems with Affordable Care Act markets, drug pricing or hospital billing will likely be bipartisan in nature and feature ordinary citizens, to put a face on the problem. But Democrats will surely blame Trump administration policies and the conduct of officials for making Americans worse off. Garcia has said corruption within the administration is responsible for affordability woes. Along similar lines, likely Senate Finance Chair Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) has suggested that President Trump's drug pricing agreements amount to "sweetheart deals" with the pharmaceutical industry that won't help the vast majority of Americans. What we're watching: Kennedy's tenure as secretary may constitute its own category of oversight and consume committees in both houses. Sanders is expected to bring up internal communications that the health committee's Democrats obtained from former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention chief medical officer Debra Houry. Democrats say they show Kennedy changed vaccine recommendations without expert review and directed a federal vaccine advisory panel's actions to undermine access to vaccines. Some of the activity took place around the time former CDC director Susan Monarez was ousted over vaccine recommendations and could shed light on whether officials misrepresented the rationale for revising recommendations. Another group of senators, including Wyden and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), has questioned whether Kennedy personally benefited from a $50 million settlement around Merck's Gardasil human papillomavirus vaccine. Kennedy, a prominent vaccine critic, said during his confirmation process that he divested a contingency-fee interest in certain Gardasil lawsuits, but the senators want to know whether his ethics agreement correctly described the arrangement or whether there were conflicts of interest. On the House side, Energy and Commerce Committee Democrats have focused on activities like the Food and Drug Administration blocking the publication of studies showing COVID and shingles vaccines were safe and what they contend is a trend of suppressing data that doesn't sync with his views. The other side: "Secretary Kennedy has delivered the most sweeping public health reforms in modern history. Oversight hearings will not distract him from serving the American people. He will continue to put prevention at the center of health care to end the chronic disease epidemic and Make America Healthy Again," said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. David Mansdoerfer, a senior health official in the first Trump administration, said he expects DOGE cuts to be a key focus of Democrats' oversight, followed by decision-making around vaccines, research grants and health agency budgets. "Outside of some minor procedural issues, I don't see a ton of substantive areas that are anything more than just an oversight hearing YouTube highlight clip," Mansdoerfer wrote on X. The bottom line: For all the confrontational rhetoric, the administration and Democrats will pick and choose their battles, per a client alert from law firm Morrison Foerster. It notes the White House has added legal staff to prepare for oversight, and that the administration may assert executive privilege over certain presidential communications with private parties.

abed5b7e7bce.text: President Trump has told advisers that he plans to keep raising money for his political operation — a move aimed at salvaging his clout after the GOP's midterm debacle. Why it matters: Maintaining a political organization — either his existing MAGA Inc. super PAC or one to be created — would give Trump a vehicle to try to influence elections in 2028 and beyond, including the next presidential contest. It also would give Trump a way to pressure GOP lawmakers who consider breaking with him as the unpopular president enters his lame-duck era and Democrats prepare congressional investigations into his administration. Trump's MAGA Inc. enforced party discipline during the 2026 primary campaigns when it helped defeat Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R), an outspoken Trump critic. Zoom in: MAGA Inc. has been the centerpiece of Trump's political operation during his second term, raising nearly $450 million since the beginning of 2025. The group received massive checks from cryptocurrency and AI industry donors, along with Republican megadonors such as Elon Musk and Miriam Adelson. Trump has hosted high-dollar fundraising dinners at Mar-a-Lago and his golf club in Sterling, Va., drawing business leaders eager to curry favor with the president. Some donors subsequently benefited from administration decisions. The New York Times reported that a medical products company whose executives and affiliates gave $5 million to MAGA Inc. benefited from an administration decision to delay Medicare reimbursement restrictions, for example. By the numbers: MAGA Inc. spent more than $400 million on the midterms, making it one of the election's biggest spending forces, according to a source familiar with the totals. The massive investment failed to prevent Republicans from losing control of Congress amid voter anger over Trump's war on Iran, high prices and corruption concerns. As of Oct. 14, MAGA Inc. had more than $164 million in the bank, though it spent tens of millions more on TV and digital advertising in the campaign's final weeks so it's unclear how much remains. The group invested aggressively in traditionally safe GOP seats that had become competitive, helping some Republicans survive, according to party operatives. Yes, but: Raising money could become much harder with Democrats controlling Congress and major donors beginning to look turning their attention toward 2028. Republicans say Trump's diminished political clout will make it harder to attract the enormous checks that have flowed into MAGA Inc. The prospect of congressional investigations into alleged pay-for-play arrangements involving donors to Trump's political operation could further discourage contributions. Technology executives who contributed heavily to the group may increasingly turn to Democrats, while major Republican donors shift their attention to prospective 2028 presidential candidates. What they're saying: A MAGA Inc. spokesperson declined to comment. White House spokespeople didn't respond to a request for comment.

737babbd2885.text: Democrats have made climate change a centerpiece of their campaigns for years — but this year they barely mentioned it. Why it matters: The midterms showed just how far the topic has fallen down the political priority list, even within the party most committed to addressing it — and suggest affordability will shape how Democrats govern next year. Driving the news: Democrats up and down the ballot campaigned overwhelmingly on affordability, including fuel prices surging amid President Trump's Iran war and rising electricity bills, accentuated by the AI boom. The big picture: The relative absence of climate change is striking considering that Democrats of all political stripes won big. Zoom in: Even some of the party's most prominent climate advocates emphasized affordability over climate change — or reconsidered ambitious climate policies in response to rising costs. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who previously championed the state's ambitious climate agenda, pushed to weaken parts of its landmark climate law this year, citing affordability concerns. Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who co-authored the Green New Deal, played down the proposal during his reelection campaign, emphasizing affordability and other priorities instead. Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico, who has previously warned about fossil fuels' impact on the planet, campaigned on protecting oil and gas jobs alongside expanding renewable energy and lowering electricity bills. Flashback: The political shift has been underway since the 2024 presidential election, when even climate-focused groups began de-emphasizing climate change in their political advertising, a trend that persisted through the midterms. State of play: On a call with reporters the day after the election, leading environmental groups celebrated Democrats' victories as a rejection of Trump's energy policies, arguing that his attacks on clean energy contributed to higher electricity bills. "Trump's energy agenda was an economic disaster for families and a political disaster for Republicans, and voters sent a very loud message," said Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power, an advocacy group that spent heavily on the election. Yes, but: While the Green New Deal-era approach of campaigning explicitly on climate change is mostly gone, Democrats are repositioning clean energy as one part of a broader focus on affordability and the economy. "There's no question that climate change is going to be a more vocal part of the agenda under Democrat leadership," said Jason Grumet, head of the American Clean Power Association, this week. "And I think that people recognize that the solution flows more from an abundance premise than a restrictive premise." Zoom out: The affordability-first approach reflects a broader reckoning within the climate movement. "We have to find the limited spaces for progress in a world where climate is even more deprioritized than it was a couple years ago," Armond Cohen, executive director of Clean Air Task Force, told Axios in an interview before the election. Cohen's organization recently unveiled a revised strategy focused on climate solutions that governments can more realistically afford and that can attract support across political lines. What we're watching: The election of Democrats in traditionally Republican, fossil-fuel-producing states like Texas could reinforce the party's emphasis on affordable energy and economic development rather than an explicit transition away from fossil fuels. Reality check: Even though climate change has faded as a top political priority, its physical impacts — and mounting economic costs — aren't going away. The intrigue: As Axios' Ben Geman pointed out earlier this week, Democrats are unlikely to revive the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis , though no decision has been announced. A current-day version could instead focus on energy affordability, building on efforts like the existing Gas and Utilities Affordability Working Group . What's next: Next week will offer a split-screen reality. The Senate is poised to begin debate on a wonky but important bill aimed at expediting energy projects of all kinds, whose impact on climate change could be significant — or not. Meanwhile, some Democratic lawmakers plan to attend the annual United Nations climate conference beginning Monday in Antalya, Turkey.

The News
READING, Pa. â A few days before he won re-election by 22 points, Gov. Josh Shapiro was barely mentioning his Republican opponent anymore. Heâd share his stages with local Democratic candidates, ask for a Democratic majority in the state Senate, and explain what it could do.
âIâm going to the good people of Pennsylvania, saying: I want to raise your minimum wage,â Shapiro told Semafor. âI want to have a big housing and critical infrastructure fund. Thatâs the stuff they can expect to see from us, and Iâm going to stay true to that.â
Tuesdayâs Democratic landslides gave the party full control of multiple swing states â not just Shapiroâs Pennsylvania, but Wisconsin, Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, and Minnesota. Democrats won legislative trifectas big enough to pass progressive bills that had gathered dust and lint under Republican control.
Instead, swing-state governors plan to focus on popular economic proposals that won over voters ââ lowering living costs, taxes, and healthcare â and not the left-wing agenda items demonized in billions of dollars in GOP ads.
After their biggest wins in decades, Democratic state leaders are coalescing around moderation, rather than the progressive politics that shaped the party in Trumpâs first term and during Joe Bidenâs presidency.
âIâm committed to moving our state forward,â Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., told reporters at her first press conference as governor-elect. âNot to the left, not to the right, but forward.â
In Wisconsin, where Democrats won their first governing trifecta since 2008, Gov.-elect David Crowley ran on expanding Medicaid, which Republicans in Madison refused to do for eight years under retiring Gov. Tony Evers.
âWeâre going to expand access to quality affordable healthcare that offers real options for families, our children, our seniors, and people with disabilities,â Crowley said after beating GOP Rep. Tom Tiffany.
Medicaid expansion was also top of mind for Democratic winners in Georgia and Texas, where the party elected governors and won control of the lower house of their state legislatures. In DC, Democrats plan to fight next year to restore Medicaid funding that was cut or restricted by Republicans in 2025; in states, Democrats are confident that Republicans, chastened by their losses, might be willing to expand health care coverage.
âI truly believe that this is an issue we can get bipartisan support with,â Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said on Wednesday.
Not on the agenda: progressive bills focused on crime and social issues.
In New York state, the passage of cash bail reform during Trumpâs presidency became a target for Republicans who over-performed in 2022 and 2024, blaming Democrats for a temporary rise in crime.
In Minnesota, Gov. Tim Walzâs 2022 sweep helped Democrats pass a pile of bills that were halted by Republicans. That made him a surprising star among left-leaning Democrats â and gave Republicans a number of attack points against his party in 2024, such as when they mocked âTampon Timâ for making sanitary products available in boysâ restrooms in public schools.
Democrats are talking more cautiously now, and the party is rooting them on from DC. At a Thursday post-election conference organized by the Center for American Progress, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said that the people whoâd beaten invincible-looking Republicans needed space to vote and govern their way. That, he said, could help the whole party.
âInstead of letting Fox News define what a Democrat is, our Democrats in these states will define what a Democrat is,â said Schumer.
Even some Democrats who had endorsed more progressive policies in the past were urging the party to focus on economic needs first, and convince the voters who broke from the GOP this year that the party deserved a long-term mandate.
In a memo shared with supporters of the Democracy Alliance, a progressive donor collective, the group urged Democrats with trifectas to âpass structural reforms that make it easier for everyone to participate in our democracy, and to improve the lives of working families â setting a model for whatâs possible nationwide.â
It would be a mistake, it said, for the party to âtake any of this cycleâs demographic swings for granted.â
Davidâs view
The slow-moving Democratic story of the last two years has been the end of the old ârising American electorateâ theory. After their 2018 wins, many influential Democrats and their donors suggested that a new, more progressive majority was forming as a reaction to Donald Trump. That confidence decreased after their 2020 victory, which was narrower than they expected, and it was shredded in 2024.
This time, Democrats generally agree that âeconomic populismâ won everywhere, that voters gave them a chance because prices were too high, and that they had defused the power of some cultural issues by telling voters they would not act on them. That is going to be tested next year, but itâs the plan right now.
Room for Disagreement
Kelley Robinson, the president of the LGBTQ+ advocacy group the Human Rights Campaign, told Semafor that the âfirst thing that weâre going to ask [Democrats] to deliver on is showing how they can make life more affordable for all Americans, including the LGBTQ+ community.â
If Democrats believed that they could pass economic bills and not pass the Equality Act, which would enshrine civil rights protections based on sexual orientation and gender identity, they were mistaken, she said.
âI would just remind folks that advocating for the LGBTQ+ community is an affordability issue,â said Robinson. âLook, if I can get fired at work because of my sexual orientation or gender identity, that is an economic issue. If Iâm not allowed to shop in certain stores because of my sexual orientation or gender identity, that is an economic issue. If my kids cannot go to a school because they are the children of LGBTQ+ parents, please believe that is an economic issue thatâs going to be hitting

The News
House Democrats are debating the future of the chamberâs select panel on US-China competition.
One option for overhauling the committee, according to people familiar with the situation, is broadening its focus beyond China to explore issues related to other bad foreign actors.
But the decisions on the select panel are ultimately up to Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, whoâs said the caucus will discuss future steps.
A Jeffries spokesperson said oversight of China-related matters will be an important priority next Congress regardless of committee structure.
One complication for the future of the panel: Its current top Democrat, Rep. Ro Khanna of California, likely plans to run for president. If he runs, that would mean Democrats might have to switch chairs midway through Congress.
The last Democrat to serve as its ranking member, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., stepped down when he launched his unsuccessful Senate bid.
The bipartisan panel, established in 2023 under GOP House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, examines US competition with China, including issues involving technology transfers and export controls.

00b5af24ac5b.text:
Midterm Wave Sets a Course for ‘Medicare for All’ Fight
LANSING, Mich. — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over.
Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can’t afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once.
That’s why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city’s Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who made “Medicare for All” a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect.
But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn’t mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. “Nobody expected that,” Bogan said.
Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms, the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats.
“Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn’t vote to have the government take over health insurance,” said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.
Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon, are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems.
The affordability crisis “dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that,” Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said.
But more moderate Democrats may see the idea’s growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. “If Democrats want to hold those seats, which were very difficult to win, they’re probably not interested in passing Medicare for All,” Oberlander said. “That’s a huge political risk in red-leaning states. So just because Democrats have a majority doesn’t mean it’s a majority for Medicare for All.”
Previous Medicare for All proposals would have required getting millions of people to willingly give up their existing coverage, fueling unprecedented opposition from the healthcare industry, said Michael Cannon, a healthcare economist at the libertarian Cato Institute and a Medicare for All opponent.
“If Medicare for All actually had the price levels that Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed envision, the industry would tear it to shreds,” he said.
And even as voters say they support Medicare for All in greater numbers than in nearly a decade, support falters when they’re presented with common arguments against it — like it could lead to higher taxes or delays in treatment — according to a recent KFF poll.
Jaime Bardenhagen said she feels a little guilty about the idea of getting her healthcare coverage from the government. A former nurse in rural Leelanau County in northern Michigan, Bardenhagen has Parkinson’s and sialidosis, a rare genetic disease that can cause seizures.
Yet she “feels bad” about qualifying for disability benefits next year. Such programs were something she “didn’t believe in” while growing up on a farm, she said. You were supposed to work for what you needed, she said, not rely on government support. “And I did work as hard as I could, for as long as I could.”
But like millions of Americans, Bardenhagen and her husband saw their health insurance costs skyrocket this year, after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired.
Their monthly premiums went from $700 to $1,300, with a deductible of $7,500. They started putting off medical tests her doctor wanted, she said. “We couldn’t afford that,” she said.
Her husband voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Bardenhagen said. This time, he stayed home. Bardenhagen, a Democrat, also considered sitting out the midterms. “I just don’t trust either party anymore,” she said.
Despite those misgivings, she says she supports Medicare for All. Her years as a nurse left her disillusioned with the current healthcare system, she said.
She felt the insurance companies, not doctors, were calling the shots, determining which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive. Wouldn’t it be fairer, she figured, if “good people” in government were making those calls? “So, absolutely, the government should take it over.”
That takeover is Cannon’s worst-case scenario. The libertarian economist said giving the federal government greater control over the healthcare system would only backfire. Patients would be left “in even more vulnerable positions, because they would be relying for their access to healthcare on government spending that is just not sustainable.”
Medicare for All supporters are naive to think the government could negotiate lower drug and healthcare prices by replacing private plans with a public one, he said. “Everyone knows that the industry is going to end up running the show, and that has been the case since they passed Medicare,” Cannon said.
For Bardenhagen, the message she wants Democrats to take from the midterms is simple: “Do something,” the former nurse said.
