'Permanent, serious' dialogue needed with China on AI: tech-focused lawmaker
“The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do,” Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., said Thursday.
Rep. James Walkinshaw’s vision for artificial intelligence regulation includes maintaining “permanent, serious” dialogue with China to mitigate the risk that powerful AI models pose.
That won’t be easy, but if the U.S. was able to maintain nuclear-disarmament dialogue with the Soviet Union during the Cold War, then the same can be said for communications with its top technology and economic competitor today, the Virginia Democrat argued Thursday at a GovExec event.
Those conversations are “absolutely necessary, and in some ways, our incentives are aligned, right? The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do, so we have to have that permanent dialogue and reach some agreements,” he said.
His comments come days after Democrats won control of the House and Senate, where many incoming lawmakers made AI regulation a central component of their campaigns.
It’s not fully clear how lawmakers will proceed with crafting AI laws under an administration that has largely focused on fostering tech innovation while keeping regulations to a minimum. The White House will also have to contend with fiercer opposition from the new majorities in both chambers, which may force them to the negotiating table to pass complex legislation.
Walkinshaw is hardly the first member of Congress to advocate for U.S.-China AI dialogue, though his position gives the comments added weight. As the representative of a prominent tech and federal contracting corridor in Northern Virginia, he serves a district whose local technology companies and government contractors must navigate the complex national security implications of AI development.
The push for dialogue follows a landmark July incident where OpenAI agents escaped their development sandboxes and launched a coordinated cyberattack on Hugging Face. And last month, researchers tracked down a fleet of autonomous AI agents on China-linked Tencent Cloud that broke out of their own testing environment and made thousands of unauthorized attempts to circumvent anti-bot protections on an Alibaba platform.
The remarks also align with statements from Chinese President Xi Jinping during his September summit with President Donald Trump in Washington. Acknowledging that both superpowers share a “responsibility” to manage the technology, Xi agreed to establish the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue and a crisis “hotline” for severe AI incidents.
Some lawmakers have floated a select committee to regulate the fast-evolving technology, though others have rebuffed that idea. Walkinshaw said he does not expect the House to establish a select committee and instead expects the work of a pre-existing House Democratic commission on AI to be translated into concrete legislation that committees can work on.
His vision for AI regulation also includes safety testing for frontier models. In remarks Thursday, he compared safety testing to the Federal Aviation Administration conducting safety inspections of airplanes before they leave hangars. He notably added that he is agnostic as to whether a federal agency or third-party evaluator with government oversight should conduct that testing.

European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds, external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close SÃ¡nchez ally Ãscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that SÃ¡nchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.
The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
How to spot the Leonids
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
What is the forecast on Saturday and Sunday evenings?
This weekend's forecast will not necessarily be great news for those hoping to catch the start of the shower.
While the weather will often be dry, large amounts of cloud are expected to fill the sky in many areas with the chance of a few spots of rain or drizzle.
At the moment the best opportunities for clear skies appear to be in southern and western areas of England and Wales on Friday and Saturday nights, with more cloud in northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
By Sunday night it is likely that more parts of the UK will be clear.
However, fog could be an additional issue, forming in any areas where skies remain clear for any length of time, obscuring the view.
Overnight temperatures will drop into single figures with the chance of a touch of frost in a few locations so if you are looking at the night sky for any length of time you will want to wrap up warmly.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.
And if you miss them this weekend then take heart that viewing conditions look particularly good around their peak in the middle of November. This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma entered the U.S. Senate to fill a vacancy in March with a clear priority: pass permitting reform that he argued was necessary based on his experience leading a major natural gas pipeline company.
Now, as he prepares to leave office, that goal is within reach—with big potential benefits for the company and him personally.
The bipartisan permitting bill slated for a vote next week would overhaul regulations for building all kinds of projects. But it also includes provisions Armstrong promoted that could push through a disputed pipeline that the Williams Companies, his former employer, has tried to build through New York for more than a decade.
When state regulators denied a water quality permit for the Constitution pipeline in 2016, it was a rare rebuke for an industry unaccustomed to having government officials block its projects. Provisions in the new bill would limit New York’s authority to deny it again.
Williams is now asking federal regulators to revive their approval of the pipeline from more than a decade ago.
Armstrong continued to hold at least tens of millions of dollars in Williams stock as of Oct. 22, according to his most recent financial disclosures. He also hired three former Williams colleagues to his staff, one of whom maintained his role as senior vice president and general counsel at the company while temporarily serving as Armstrong’s chief of staff in the Senate.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would greatly restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to deny or place conditions on water quality certifications. The bill would also make other changes to accelerate approval of Constitution and other pipelines, including restricting judicial review and scaling back certain environmental reviews.
Environmental lawyers say changes to what’s known as a Section 401 certification of the federal Clean Water Act appear tailored to help a small number of gas pipeline projects. One of the companies that would benefit most is Williams, where Armstrong served as chief executive and chairman for 15 years until his appointment in March by Oklahoma’s governor to fill a vacated U.S. Senate seat.
Williams has already received extraordinary support from the Trump administration.
President Donald Trump claimed he made a deal with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to get the Constitution pipeline built, which she denies. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin has pledged support for the pipeline, and his agency is finalizing a rule change that would restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to condition permits in order to safeguard water quality, similar to the permitting bill.
In October, the U.S. Department of Energy said it would devote up to $42 million under the Defense Production Act to pay permitting costs for the project.
Armstrong’s office did not respond to questions for this article, though he has frequently criticized what he calls a broken regulatory system that drives up costs.
“When every pipeline, transmission line, power plant and industrial project is treated as something to stop rather than something to build responsibly, the costs do not disappear,” Armstrong said in a Senate speech in July. “They accumulate slowly, until families are paying more, reliability is deteriorating, and investment is moving elsewhere.”
Williams spokesperson Blake Jackson said the company supports the permitting bill “and all its provisions to provide a tech-neutral and level-playing field for all energy infrastructure.”
Some residents of upstate New York see things differently.
A Threat to State Waters
Anne Marie Garti, a lawyer who owns a home near the Constitution pipeline route, fought the project the first time around. From the start, “there was a huge amount of opposition,” Garti said, “and skepticism.”
The Constitution project would run 125 miles from the Pennsylvania shale gas fields across upstate New York, eventually connecting to other interstate pipelines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, also known as FERC, oversees interstate gas pipelines. But states retain authority under the Clean Water Act, which requires energy companies like Williams to apply for water quality certifications.
Garti called these permits the “weak link” in the regulatory process. Taking inspiration from an earlier permit denial in Connecticut, she and other residents focused their fight on the pipeline’s potential effects on 251 streams along its route. State regulators said 87 of those streams provided trout habitat.
Building the pipeline would require digging trenches across streams, diverting their flow and clearing trees and brush along their banks. The work would send sediment into clear waters, raise temperatures and temporarily damage habitat for trout and other species, according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s 2016 denial.
State regulators rarely reject water quality permits, which are needed not only for pipelines but many federally regulated projects. In a recent survey of 24 states by the Association of Clean Water Administrators, no state reported a denial rate higher than 3.5 percent—most said they’d never denied a permit.
New York denied the certification for Constitution in 2016, saying the company had failed to address the project’s water quality impacts and had not provided sufficient proof that Williams would comply with state standards. The denial kicked off years of legal wrangling. In 2020, Williams said it would not pursue the pipeline and a federal appeals court ruling later vacated the federal permit.
Another permit denial followed in 2019 for a second Williams project: the Northeast Supply Enhancement (NESE) pipeline that would have run from New Jersey across the New York harbor. A few other pipeline proposals in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic faced similar fates, while in some cases regulators imposed conditions to protect waterways.

f4d70379f40b.text: In our news wrap Friday, Trump’s plans to build a massive triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery have been put on hold, two more top officials resigned from the Justice Department, residents along the Georgia-Tennessee border are returning home after record floodwaters receded, Pope Leo started his 12-day tour of Latin America, and Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck. Geoff Bennett: And we start today's other headlines in Washington, D.C. President Trump's plans to build a massive Triumphal Arch near Arlington National Cemetery are on hold, at least for now. Late yesterday, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the monument for two weeks, citing concerns about disruptions to traffic and emergency services. The ruling came just hours after a federal panel, including several Trump appointees, gave final approval to the project. Despite the setback, the administration launched a new Web site today promoting the proposed monument. Some veterans have objected to its placement near Arlington National Cemetery, arguing that it detracts from the solemnity of the site. Two more top officials have resigned from the Justice Department just days after Democrats won back control of Congress. John Eisenberg led the DOJ's National Security Division, where he oversaw cases involving terrorism, leak investigations, and espionage. And Jason Reding Quinones helped lead the so-called grand conspiracy investigation into President Trump's political opponents. Attorney General Todd Blanche thanked both men for their service, but did not provide additional details on their departures. Just a day earlier, Harmeet Dhillon left her post as head of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division. Along the Georgia-Tennessee border, waters have receded and residents are returning home after record flooding submerged local towns. As much as 10 inches of rain fell in just six hours Thursday, turning the Toccoa River into raging rapids. Floodwaters surged through roads, rising as high as street signs and reaching the rooftops of some homes. First responders deployed helicopters, drones, and swift water boats to conduct dozens of rescues. In McCaysville, Georgia, businesses were swamped by mud and debris. One owner said he likely suffered hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost inventory, but said others were even worse off. Hugh Rogers, Business Owner: It's a little bit heartbreaking, but there's a lot of people that's lost their homes and everything they have, so it's -- we're not in such bad shape here. And I would a lot rather be doing this than lose a home. So... Geoff Bennett: Both McCaysville and neighboring Copperhill, Tennessee, had just recently finished cleaning up from a separate flood back in August. Senator Chris Murphy says he will miss several weeks of votes on Capitol Hill while he recovers from a recent stroke. The Democrat from Connecticut says he was released from the hospital today and will spend the coming weeks at a rehabilitation center. His doctor says Murphy suffered a small stroke last weekend and that he's shown tremendous improvement. Murphy is expected to make a full recovery. The longtime manager of the late country music legend Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew. The suit accused Bryan Seaver, who once served as Parton's bodyguard and announced her death on social media, of threatening to damage her business empire in an effort to extract money from her estate. Seaver denied the allegations, saying he was simply seeking payments owed to his security company. Parton died back in August after a brief battle with cancer. The reason for the lawsuit's dismissal was not disclosed. Pope Leo touched down in Uruguay today to kick off a three-country tour of Latin America. The 71-year-old pontiff was welcomed by the nation's president in Montevideo this afternoon. His 12-day tour comes just three weeks after he underwent lung cancer surgery, which put the entire trip in doubt. After Uruguay, Leo will head to Argentina and then Peru, where he will enjoy a homecoming of sorts. He served as a missionary and bishop there for more than two decades and even became a naturalized citizen before being elected pope last year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk says the company will wind down production of its Cybertruck by the middle of next year. Musk says the Texas factory that produces the electric pickup will shift its focus to Tesla's new Cybercab Robotaxi. The Cybertruck has struggled to gain traction since its 2023 debut. Sales fell short of expectations. The vehicle faced multiple recalls. And Musk's political activities also alienated some potential buyers. Tesla shares closed more than 4 percent higher today following yesterday's sell-off. Elsewhere on Wall Street today, stocks steadied a bit to close out the week. The Dow Jones industrial average slipped nearly 240 points, but the Nasdaq managed a gain of more than 1 percent. The S&P 500 also ended in positive territory.

3db1c09ba17b.text: Employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, according to a new government report. Job gains for August and September were revised upward as well, by a combined 84,000 jobs. That makes the last three months of the job market look better than expected, but it comes as questions grow about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amna Nawaz speaks with Diane Swonk, chief economist for KPMG, for more. Amna Nawaz: Well, hiring was much stronger than expected last month. Employers added 165,000 new jobs, according to a new government report out today. Job gains for August and September were revised upward as well by a combined 84,000 jobs. That makes the last three months of the job market look better than we thought, an average of 137,000 new jobs per month. But it all comes during a week when questions grew about the sustainability of the AI boom and its impact on the economy. Markets had a wild ride, losing more than $2.5 trillion in value yesterday before rebounding today. For some insight, I'm joined now by Diane Swonk. She's chief economist for KPMG. That's one of the world's largest firms for professional and tax services. Diane, welcome back. Thanks for joining us. Diane Swonk, Chief Economist, KPMG: Good to be here. Amna Nawaz: So, stronger-than-expected jobs report, upward revisions for August and September, what does all of this tell you about the labor market right now? Diane Swonk: Well, it tells us that we're generating a lot more paychecks, which is great. That is what's helping to keep aggregate consumer spending afloat, along with wealth effects tied to AI. The downside is, of course, that even though the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent, average hourly earnings rose only 3.1 percent from a year ago. That's yet another month it will fall short of overall inflation. That's why it's not resonating to most individuals, because they're actually losing purchasing power out there. And I think that's important. We also know the underemployment rate, which includes discouraged workers, those unemployed for a very long time, over 27 weeks, and those forced to take on part-time, instead of full-time work, when they were looking for a full-time job, that rose to 7.9 percent in the unemployment rate. That's the highest since July and well above anything we saw pre-pandemic. One more notable issue is that the New York Fed updated the unemployment rate for new college grads, which fell over the summer, but, again, for not the best reasons. And that is underemployment for new college grads is at its highest level since 2020, during the pandemic. Amna Nawaz: That's concerning news there. But we also saw that big drop in the markets yesterday that I mentioned, part of a massive tech- and AI-driven sell-off. We saw the president kind of refer to that drop today. He attributed to the midterm elections on Tuesday. Is that what you saw? Tell us more about that. Diane Swonk: Well, what we saw is, first of all, we have been tracking the backlash to AI since the beginning of the year, which has really grown to a crescendo. It crosses every age, income strata, and party affiliation. There's just nothing more galvanizing than the fears of job loss due to AI, along with the concerns that people have about a data center in their backyard, their higher electricity costs. So it collides with the concerns about inflation out there. And we had already seen market jitters in the month of October, which is why we started modeling both bear case, a bear market scenario, along with a base case where we're able to sort of muddle through and keep the wealth effects going. But when you're sitting on something that's a one-legged stool, which is the AI boom and the wealth that it generates propelling the economy forward and adding to inflation, that's precarious at best. At worst, it can tip over fairly easily. Amna Nawaz: So what kind of concerns are investors expressing with those kinds of sell-offs? How real are the concerns that we're hearing about an AI bubble? Everyone arguing that, like, housing and, like, the Internet, the investments and spending into AI, are -- gotten way ahead now of profit expectations. What if it bursts? What are you hearing? Diane Swonk: Well, that's exactly -- it is. This is not uncommon with the technological innovation. Innovation requires technology. Productivity requires trust. There isn't trust out there. And the returns on those investments are far in the future. It takes a long time to scale these innovations to make them as powerful and tap the productivity growth. But you have also got to make sure that you include human beings and people's lives and livelihoods in the center of that innovation. People have to see a place for themselves where their fortunes rise with the tide, instead of recede with the shoreline. Amna Nawaz: All right, that is Diane Swonk, chief economist for KPMG, joining us tonight. Diane, thank you. It's always great to talk to you. Diane Swonk: Thank you.

8d89932a8268.text: Democrats’ midterm wins have reached red states across the country, including Kansas, which has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932. That will soon change after Rev. Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist church in the country, defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall Tuesday night. Amna Nawaz speaks with Sen.-elect Hamilton for more. Amna Nawaz: Democrats' midterm election wins have reached red states throughout the country. That includes Kansas, a state that hadn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932. That will soon change after Reverend Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist Church in the country, defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall on Tuesday night. And Senator-Elect Hamilton joins us now. Congratulations, Reverend. Thanks so much for joining us. Adam Hamilton: Oh, it's a joy to be with you today. Thank you. Amna Nawaz: So, 94 years since Kansans have sent a Democrat to the Senate. Why do you think they chose to do so this year? Adam Hamilton: I think there was a lot of frustration with what's happening in Washington. Across the state of Kansas, there were people who had voted Republican all their lives and yet looked at what was happening in Washington and felt like things were happening there that were -- that were not kind, they were cruel, they were immoral, they were corrupt, and policies that were hurting people in our state. And I think there was a lot of folks who said, this is not OK. This is not who we are. Amna Nawaz: You put messages of decency, of morality right at the center of your campaign. You said that those are rooted in your faith. How does your time at the pulpit translate to how you talk to voters in this campaign? Adam Hamilton: Sure. Well, first of all, I have spent my life communicating with people. That is what I do. And so every Sunday you're asking the question, how does this -- how does our sacred text, the old New Testament, how does it speak to people's daily lives? And part of that is trying to understand where are people, what are they struggling with, what's happening in their lives. So, when you go out, and, as a pastor, I will just tell you I deeply care about people. I tell folks I don't have very many remarkable gifts. My superpowers are that I listen carefully, I care deeply, and I fight for people. And so, when I traveled across the state, listening to people, hearing their stories, hearing their pain, their frustrations, their disappointments, and then imagining with them what a better future looks like comes naturally as a pastor. And then communicating on the campaign trail is a lot of fun for me. And -- but the biggest thing is, I have spent 38 years trying to ask, what should the world look like? And Jesus talks about this in the Sermon on the Mount in the Lord's Prayer. He asks us to pray, thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. And I tell people who have no particular religious faith, I say, if you think about that, this is like, what is the world supposed to look like? And we're hoping to see that happen. And as a -- as somebody who's running for office, you're imagining what that world should look like, and then you are willing to go fight to see it happen. Amna Nawaz: One of the first big decisions you're going to have to make is what you want your leadership to look like when you get to the Senate. You said you're not going to support Chuck Schumer to be majority leader. So who do you think should lead the party in the Senate at this point in time? Adam Hamilton: Sure. And I mean no disrespect by saying that about Chuck Schumer. He's had a long and distinguished career. I just -- I think we need leaders who are going to bring people together, Republicans and Democrats together, centrists, moderates, and progressives bringing people together, conservatives. And I would like to see... (CROSSTALK) Amna Nawaz: And you don't think Chuck Schumer can do that? Adam Hamilton: I'm not saying he can't. I'm just saying, in my mind, I don't know Chuck very well. I'm just saying that I feel like we need to have people who are determined to do that. I also think it's time for fresh ideas, young newer ideas, newer people coming in, and folks -- I hear that a lot from people in Kansas as well, both Democrats and Republicans, saying, I think we have got to have fresh ideas. We have got to have people who are bringing folks together. And I think the perception, at least here in Kansas, is that maybe that doesn't happen as much as it could in the United States Senate. Amna Nawaz: Can I ask you about some news? We heard just today about President Trump naming Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. What kind of message does that send to you as an incoming member of the Democratic majority that he has promised to work with? Adam Hamilton: Yes. Well, I would say I think, for many of us, Stephen Miller seems to be the author, the person who has put together so many of the things that the president has done that we don't actually like. So, whether it's about immigration and how we talk about immigrants, or it's the war in Iran, it's policies related to tariffs, in all of these ways, dismantling so many of the important agencies in the federal government, if he is in fact the person who is -- who's behind these ideas, placing him as the chief of staff seems -- it just seems difficult and challenging, I think, for many of us. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you about something else voters made clear in this election, which was something like 90 percent of them said government corruption was a crucial factor for them in how they voted. The likely new chairman of the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, told us yesterday that the first issue for them will be investigating the Trump family and what he called clear corruption. Do you agree with that approach? Adam Hamilton: Well, look, I want to stop the corruption, and I do think there has been a lot of corruption happeni

a3f0e277cdf9.text: Georgia voters made history this week, electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as the state’s first Democratic senator in more than two decades and the first-ever Black woman governor in the country. The former Atlanta mayor campaigned on lowering costs, expanding healthcare access and pushing back against the Trump administration. Geoff Bennett speaks with Gov.-elect Bottoms for more. Geoff Bennett: Georgia voters made history this week, electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as the state's first Democratic governor in more than two decades and the first Black woman ever elected governor in the country. The former Atlanta mayor campaigned on lowering costs, expanding access to health care, and pushing back against the Trump administration. But she will face the challenge of advancing that agenda in a state where Republicans still control the Senate. I spoke with the governor-elect earlier today. Governor-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, welcome to the "News Hour." Keisha Lance Bottoms: Oh, thank you for having me. Geoff Bennett: You have, of course, made history as the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history. What does this moment mean to you personally? And what message did Georgia voters send with your victory? Keisha Lance Bottoms: It's deeply personal for me. My family goes back at least five generations in Georgia. We are able to trace our roots to a plantation in Crawfordville, Georgia, where my great-great-grandparents were once enslaved. So just on a personal level, to have come from people who had to toil the soul of Georgia, and to now be elected governor has exceeded every dream that I ever had for my life. So I'm grateful for that. And just for the people of Georgia, for us to have had the blue wave, or the blue tsunami, as it's being described in this state, really represents a shift in Georgia, throughout the South, I believe, that's going to reshape who we are as a party, as a state for many years to come. Geoff Bennett: I wonder, have you spoken with Stacey Abrams since your victory? As our viewers will know, she ran for governor herself and spent years rebuilding the political infrastructure that allowed for Georgia to be competitive for Democrats. What do you think this moment means for the movement that she helped build? Keisha Lance Bottoms: Yes, I haven't spoken with her, but for so many of us across the state, it's been about building on progress that's been made. And we take all the lessons from elections passed, we keep all the great things that were done, and then we make corrections where necessary. And this has been decades of work in Georgia. We haven't had a governor, a Democrat governor, elected since 1998. And there have been so many elections since then, so much work that's been done, not just from groups that Stacey has worked with, but a lot of groups across the state, names who never get called on national news, but people who've been deeply committed to building a true grassroots movement in this state. And it's finally all come together in the way that we have hoped that it would for a very long time. Geoff Bennett: What lessons should the national Democratic Party take from your winning campaign? Keisha Lance Bottoms: I think, across America, hopefully, everyone realizes that you have got to listen to people and those issues that matter to them and focus on those things that impact their daily lives. Throughout the course of this campaign, it's been about the cost of living and people asking me directly, what can you do, what will you do as governor to address these issues, and then going back and delivering plans to do just that? And, hopefully, Democrats across the nation -- and just based on the results, it appears that we all had the same takeaways, that we needed to focus on the things that mattered to people and not get distracted and not get pulled into fights that weren't productive for us to be able to deliver. Geoff Bennett: Affordability, as you mentioned, was central to your campaign. You have promised to raise the minimum wage. How do you plan to deliver on promises like that, given that Republicans still control the state Senate? How quickly can Georgians realistically expect to see your agenda put into action? Keisha Lance Bottoms: Well, we were able to take the House this time, and we are really one seat away from controlling the Senate. So we're going to try and find those things that we can get bipartisan agreement on, those things we can get done immediately. And if minimum wage, for example, is one of those things, then we're going to move forward with it. But it may be something that we have to wait until we have control of the Senate. But I do believe things like health care and education funding are things that we can cross party lines to find consensus on immediately. Geoff Bennett: Finally, there is enormous symbolism in your election, especially for the Black women who have been so central to the Democratic Party's success over the years. Symbolism also creates enormous expectation. I wonder, do you feel additional responsibility to deliver, knowing how many people see themselves in your victory? Keisha Lance Bottoms: You know, for me, it is just the responsibility to deliver. I moved around this state, and I asked people to support our campaign and to believe in the vision that I was setting forth for the state of Georgia. And I want to make sure that I'm true to my word. So it is -- it's beyond who I am and the symbolism, representation of who I am. It is just about being an effective leader on behalf of all Georgians. Geoff Bennett: Georgia's Governor-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, thanks again for your time. We appreciate it. And congratulations. Keisha Lance Bottoms: Thank you. Thank you.

Texas Democrats Swept Statewide Races. Now Comes the Hard Part of Solving Healthcare Angst.
Texas Democrats spent three decades trying to regain control of the governor’s mansion and other top state leadership positions. This Election Day, they pulled off a decisive upset, taking statewide offices and the state House, partly due to voter anger over healthcare costs and the difficulty of getting care.
Now the state’s newly elected leaders have two months before the next legislative session to figure out how to deliver on their promises on healthcare affordability and other thorny issues, such as abortion. And they need to do it in the face of bruising political opposition over a frenetic 140-day legislative session that begins Jan. 12.
“Democrats are still putting together something of an agenda in essentially what is a ‘dog catches car’ scenario,” said James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project, a polling and political analysis group at the University of Texas-Austin.
Texas was at the crest of the nationwide blue wave that flipped control of Congress. The traditionally deep-red state elected James Talarico to the U.S. Senate, and Democrats picked up a seat in the U.S. House, despite efforts by Republicans to draw districts in their favor and at least $225 million spent by Elon Musk to elect Texas GOP candidates.
But the biggest changes for Texans could come from the state-level elections that Democrats also dominated on Nov. 3. And the stakes are high: Texas routinely ranks among the lowest in the nation in health outcomes and has the most uninsured people in the country.
Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin, both state lawmakers, are scheduled to be sworn in on Jan. 19, a week after the legislative session opens. Hinojosa will become the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since Ann Richards moved out in 1995. Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, a popular, well-funded incumbent who had never lost an election before this one.
For three terms, Abbott, along with Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, fought against expanding Medicaid, contested the Affordable Care Act, oversaw the gutting of abortion rights, and weakened vaccine mandates.
While campaigning, Hinojosa and Goodwin said their top health priorities were expanding coverage, bringing down healthcare costs, and improving women’s health. Goodwin has proposed creating a state health insurance plan, funded through Texas’ $24 billion “rainy day fund.”
As state House members, Goodwin filed bills to expand Medicaid and restore abortion rights and Hinojosa filed or signed on to bills to broaden exemptions to abortion bans and add doulas to the state’s maternal mortality review committee. Few of those bills got floor votes.
Political watchers and lobbyists in Austin, Texas’ capital, say it’s too early to tell how Hinojosa, Goodwin, and other newly elected top Democrats will shape legislation for the upcoming session, whom they will appoint to top agency leadership positions, and how they will maneuver around opposition from Republicans who will still hold the majority in the state Senate.
This may be the new leaders’ best shot to figure things out. After the legislative session is over at the end of May, Texas’ legislative schedule doesn’t call for another regular session until 2029 — following the 2028 presidential election, when the entire state House will again be up for reelection.
The State of the State’s Health
About 5 million of Texas’ nearly 32 million residents lack health coverage. That includes 1 million children without insurance. Texas is one of 10 states that didn’t expand Medicaid to cover more low-income adults. New moms in Texas continue to die at higher rates than they do nationally. And healthcare costs topped lists of voter concerns in the state, according to polls in recent months.
On the federal level, Congress didn’t renew enhanced subsidies for Affordable Care Act premiums last year, passed a budget bill with new restrictions on food and healthcare assistance, and cut the federal health budget.
Because of rising costs and enrollment glitches, hundreds of thousands of Texans recently lost health coverage, said Lynn Cowles, director of health and food justice at the policy group Every Texan.
Rachel Elsberry, an insurance broker in Austin who has clients in more than a dozen states, witnessed the challenges people faced with affordability.
“Whether you voted red or blue, every client I talk to, regardless of where they are on the political spectrum, says healthcare costs are too high,” she said. She said she routinely turns away Texas clients who don’t qualify for subsidies on ACA plans or low-cost or free federal health programs.
“It’s heartbreaking,” she said.
Cowles has already met with Hinojosa’s staffers, who she said were receptive to more than a dozen steps her group suggested the governor take to make it easier for people to sign up and stay covered under state health programs.
“It’s an incredibly different world,” Cowles said. “It’s amazing to say these things out loud.”
About 1 million Texans would be newly eligible for Medicaid coverage if state leaders expanded the program. Even though the federal government would foot 90% of the bill for those enrollees, Democratic state leadership still faces steep odds.
“To thread that needle even after dramatic changes like last night is going to be challenging,” John Henderson, president and CEO of the Texas Organization of Rural & Community Hospitals, said the day after the election.
Legislators have a very narrow window to pass bills in the Texas Statehouse, said Charles Miller, director of health and economic mobility at Texas 2036, a nonpartisan policy research and advocacy group. And few measures succeed: During the state’s last regular session, in 2025, of 11,503 bills filed, 3,534 went into effect.
“The clock is ticking,” Miller said.

Jeff Flake, one of the most outspoken Republican critics of Trump during his first administration and the author of the 2017 book “The Conscience of a Conservative.” Amna Nawaz: As Democrats celebrate their historic gains, Republicans are beginning to take stock of major upsets and what comes next for their party. Here with us now is former Arizona Senator Jeff Flake, one of the most outspoken Republican critics of President Donald Trump during his first term and the author of the 2017 book "Conscience of a Conservative." Senator Flake, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake (R-AZ): Thanks for having me on. Amna Nawaz: I want to begin with that piece of news today that President Trump has elevated Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff. This is the man who's the architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, so many other policies. What does that decision, just days after huge Republican losses in the midterms, say to you? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Well, it suggests that the president is doubling down. I had hoped that, on that issue to immigration, that that's one area where the president might reach an agreement on certain issues revolving around immigration. I know, when I was in the Senate and the president was in his first term, he seemed willing to do that, but he was always pulled back by people like Stephen Miller. And so I'm a little discouraged to see that, because, on some issues, he might be inclined to work with the Democrats, but not so much now. Amna Nawaz: Does that tell you anything about what we should expect to see these next two years? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Yes, I -- unfortunately, I think it does. I think the president would not have elevated Stephen Miller if he expected to reach some deals with Democrats on certain issues. I hope I'm wrong on that, but that's kind of been the history. Amna Nawaz: We know that there are still a few races left to be called from this election, but the picture's very clear. We're talking about generational losses for the Republicans. Extinction level is how Florida Governor Ron DeSantis put it. And I'm sure you have seen President Trump, Vice President Vance have basically said this was all about the Iran war. Do you agree with that? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: No. Certainly, that played a big role, but on the economy and affordability, obviously, was the biggest issue for voters. The original sin for this administration economically were tariffs. Tariffs raised prices for everyone. And that was long before the war started. So, no, it wasn't just the war. And then it wasn't just policy as well. It was just style, Republicans referring to Democrats or anybody they didn't agree with as socialists or communists or pedophiles or jihadists, that just hope -- gratefully ran its course, and people are tired of it. Amna Nawaz: And it was reported late today that Arizona Democrats gained a trifecta to control the state house, Senate, and governor's office for the first time in 60 years. What does that tell you about what's going on in your state? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Yes, it's been huge. One anecdote to let you know how it is for a clerk of the superior court in Maricopa County -- Maricopa County is the fourth largest county in the country with about nearly four million residents -- a Democrat, a 19-year-old, won that seat from a former state legislator Republican who wasn't scandal-ridden. It was just a Republican. And a 19-year-old Democrat won that seat by about 100,000 votes. That's kind of how it went in Arizona, and I think was replicated elsewhere in the country. Amna Nawaz: So, back in 2019, you wrote this in a tweet. You said: "One day in the not-too-distant future, Republicans will wake up and say, we did this for this man?" Has that day come? What are you hearing from other Republicans? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Well, I think so, from some other Republicans, yes, but then you hear some of the talking heads or those who have closely aligned themselves with the president, whether it's think tanks or other advocacy groups, and you see they're sticking with it. So I hope that Republicans, certainly elected officials, those who are left, will realize that this is not a winning ticket here, and that we're in a cul-de-sac as a party unless we change course. Amna Nawaz: But when you decided not to run for reelection, like so many others who opposed and publicly spoke out against President Trump, you left office, and now the party is almost entirely the party of Donald Trump. Where does it go from here? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Well, nothing focuses the mind like a huge election loss, and we underwent that. And we have to now get a nominee for president. And I can tell you, I don't think it's going to be somebody who is in lockstep with the current president. We have got to chart a different course and in some ways regain and go back to some of the principles that have animated the party for generations, limited government, economic freedom, some modicum of free trade, American leadership abroad, recognizing our allies from our adversaries. 9fcf1fd4a133.text: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Geoff Bennett to discuss the week in politics, including Trump shaking up his White House leadership, deep divisions in the Republican Party and how Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress. Geoff Bennett: Well, President Trump is shaking up his White House leadership, Republicans are confronting deep divisions within their party, and Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress. For more on what comes next, we turn to Brooks and Capehart. That's David Brooks of "The Atlantic" and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW. What a week, gentlemen. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: And we end it with President Trump announcing that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. After one of the most devastating midterm defeats in modern history, the president is elevating one of the architects of his most hard-line policy. David, your reaction. How's it all strike you? David Brooks: Stunning. Stunning. He's going for the wartime consigliere, which is what Stephen Miller is. I guess they're going to the mattresses, as they would say. I spent a week in Sicily, so I got a lot of "Godfather" references. (LAUGHTER) David Brooks: I just think he's going with the guy who's the ultimate loyalist. And he's I think sending Susie Wiles over to help pick the nominee for the next Republican, on the illusion that he has going to have much of a say in who's the next nominee. I have really been struck by how so many Republicans are unleashed, not all in public. The one who's been most public is Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor. After the election, he was unleashed, and he was just furious about what's happened to the party, how it's been destroyed. He called this election a near-extinction event for the Republican Party. And a lot of Republicans feel that. A lot of other Republicans, I would say, are just quiet. They have gone sullen. And so how that shakes out, but I don't think there's going to be much flavor for more of the same, which is what Stephen Miller is, doubling down on the same. Geoff Bennett: Our Liz Landers reports that Susie Wiles submitted her resignation last night. And there's other reporting that President Trump was angry with Wiles after the GOP's shellacking in this week's midterm election. Is Stephen Miller's elevation, Jonathan, the clearest signal yet that President Trump has no intention of changing course? Jonathan Capehart: Yes. I mean, I think, pardon the imagery I'm about to present, Stephen Miller's elevation is a big middle finger to the American voters, what they had to say through their votes on Tuesday, to the incoming Democratic majorities. How are they going to -- it just seems to me this is the clearest indication that the president has even -- has given up even pretending that he wants to govern. My hope is that -- to pick up on what David was saying about Republicans, is that the behavior of the Republicans who come back to Washington in the 120th Congress, that their behavior will change. And I'm particularly looking at Republican senators. Lisa Murkowski is going to need some other moderates to join her in working with Democrats to get things done. I mean, Democrats have a lot on their plate, given the results of the election. But so do -- but so do Republicans. And I would hope that there are some moderates within the Republican Party, because I do know that there are some, will start to assert themselves, especially if they're thinking of running for president themselves in '28. Geoff Bennett: In order for that to happen, Republicans would have to believe that MAGA is no longer a potent political force. Tucker Carlson said last night on his show that the Trump era is over. Is he right? David Brooks: Yes, absolutely. For this election, people don't -- in 2010, when Barack Obama suffered that shellacking, he -- the Republicans had an advantage of 7 percentage points up in the total House race. This time, the Democrats had a total House race advantage of 13 points. So it was twice as big as 2010, which we considered this massive midterm setback for the president. This was twice as big. I still am stunned by the margins. On election night, we weren't quite clear on how big these margins is, Jon Ossoff 18 points, Talarico 12 points, El-Sayed, who was kind of one of the weaker candidates, seven points, just huge margins. And so the Republican -- he's suffered setbacks before, but never when he's two years away from ending his term. And so I think this was such a comprehensive, existential setback, and he's got so little left in his term in office, I think people are -- this is the end of MAGA. He will still do stuff. But, as a movement, as a force, there's the end. Geoff Bennett: Let's talk about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his future, because Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, he's forcing a confrontation and will introduce this measure to launch what would be an impeachment vote potentially as early as next week -- excuse me -- given the controversy surrounding Hegseth's leadership and the deeply unpopular war with Iran. How do you see this playing out, Jonathan? In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.
One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.
He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.
He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.
He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.
Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.
The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats â and some Republicans.
"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.
Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.
On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.
Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.
"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.
At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.
Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

0dcc6baa3a46.text: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and longtime U.S. senator, has died at age 89. Born into one of America's wealthiest and most prominent families, Rockefeller forged his own path in politics and became a leading voice on healthcare, education and the needs of working families. Lisa Desjardins looks back at Rockefeller’s life and impact. Geoff Bennett: And now we remember Jay Rockefeller, the former West Virginia governor and longtime U.S. senator, who devoted more than half-a-century to public service. Born into one of America's wealthiest and most prominent families, Rockefeller forged his own path in politics, becoming a leading voice on health care, education, and the needs of working families. Amna Nawaz: Across five terms in the Senate, he earned a reputation for putting the interests of his constituents ahead of partisan politics. He was also the husband of Sharon Rockefeller, president and CEO of WETA, the public television station that produces the "PBS News Hour." Lisa Desjardins looks back now at Senator Rockefeller's life and impact. I love the Senate. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller (D-WV): I love the intensity of the work, the gravity of the issues. I love fighting for West Virginia here. Lisa Desjardins: A son of one of the country's wealthiest families... Man: Senator Rockefeller. Lisa Desjardins: ... John D. Rockefeller IV, known As jay, dedicated his career to one of the nation's poorest states. Rockefeller was born in New York in 1937, a month after the death of his great grandfather of the same name, who co-founded the Standard Oil Company. His great-grandson charted a maverick path. His early jobs were at the Peace Corps' offices in Washington, but Rockefeller wanted a more hands-on position tackling poverty. That drive took him to rural Emmons, West Virginia, where he worked to improve the lives of young people in the community. From there, Rockefeller quickly decided to enter politics. He switched from Republican to Democrat, breaking from his family's longstanding affiliation with the Republican Party. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Since 1960, I have really felt myself to be a Democrat, although I realized that public image would probably be different. Lisa Desjardins: And in 1966, he won a seat in the state's House of delegates. In 1968, following the assassination of Robert F. Kennedy, Rockefeller's uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller, offered him the then vacant Senate seat if he would become a Republican again. Rockefeller said no. Over the next decade, he instead rose up the West Virginia political ladder. He also met and married his wife, Sharon Percy. Their wedding was featured on the cover of "LIFE" magazine. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: I run for governor. Lisa Desjardins: The '70s brought one setback, a defeat for governor in 1972, and then a comeback in 1976. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Today, we leave behind the defeatism of the past. Starting here, starting now, you and I together step out into the rising sun of a new day for West Virginia. Lisa Desjardins: His time as governor saw many challenges, from natural disasters to strikes and economic downturn. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: I have a tremendous sense of what our future can be and how I can help as your United States senator. Lisa Desjardins: In 1985, Rockefeller moved on to the U.S. Senate, where he would represent West Virginia for 30 years. His largest impact was on health care. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Our problem is that we treat potential solutions in health care on like a short-term basis. Lisa Desjardins: Rockefeller fought to keep and expand Medicare and Medicaid. And he authored the Children's Health Insurance Program, CHIP, which still provides low-cost health coverage to millions of children annually. Rockefeller also created a bill securing lifetime benefits for retired coal miners, often referred to as the Rockefeller Coal Act. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Saddam's existing biological and chemical weapons capabilities pose real threats to America today. Lisa Desjardins: Senator Rockefeller voted to authorize the invasion of Iraq. He later started an investigation into the evidence for the war. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: We haven't found any weapons of mass destruction. The al-Qaida/Iraq connection has not been found to be very real. Lisa Desjardins: Then, in 2013, the West Virginia senator announced his retirement. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: I will miss the Senate. Lisa Desjardins: He addressed the chamber for the last time on December 4, 2014. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: To West Virginia, thank you for placing your faith in me, I know it was hard at first, and giving me the greatest reward, the chance to fight for meaningful and lasting opportunity for those who are too often forgotten, but absolutely deserve the best. Lisa Desjardins: He was committed to philanthropy, along with his wife. They founded the Blanchette Rockefeller Neuroscience Institute for Alzheimer's Research, dedicated to his mother, who lived with the disease. Rockefeller leaves behind his wife, Sharon, four children and his grandchildren. He was 89 years old. Amna Nawaz: Of course, our thoughts are with Sharon and the entire Rockefeller family.

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering with U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman.
Congressional committees originate legislation and oversight investigations, and under the seniority system—as Democrats take control and their senior members presumably become chairs—many House committees have broad subpoena powers.
U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman has represented northern California’s second district since 2013 and is an environmental lawyer in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
STEVE CURWOOD: Representative Huffman, what can we expect to be a top priority from you and your committee when it comes to energy?
JARED HUFFMAN: On all of the subjects before our committee within our jurisdiction, it’s going to be a two-part agenda. We’re going to have to do oversight and investigations to make up for the fact that we haven’t really had a Congress for the last two years. There haven’t been checks and balances. So we will be digging into and investigating so many different things on energy and other subjects that we oversee.
But then we’ve got to move an affirmative policy agenda as well. And we can’t, in my opinion, constrain ourselves to just what Donald Trump might sign into law. I think we’ve got to advance an agenda that reflects our values and our priorities, even if we draw some vetoes from this president. There’s enormous value in drawing that contrast.
JENNI DOERING: Just how important do you think energy and access to affordable energy was in these midterm elections?
HUFFMAN: It was part of the affordability backlash that I think helped shape this blue wave, for sure. The fact that electricity bills, utility bills have been skyrocketing as Donald Trump pays offshore wind developers to walk away from projects that could bring cheap, reliable, clean energy onto the grid, as he does everything he can to strangle clean energy—the cheapest, fastest form of energy that can help lower utility bills.
I think people connected those dots, and they also put together the connection with the corruption, with just the fact that the fossil fuel industry was so programmed with Donald Trump on all of this and was making money hand over fist, war profiteering. Donald Trump boasted, in his words, “We are making a killing on the war in Iran” while people were struggling to afford fuel. All of that helped shape the election in a big way.
CURWOOD: I think it’s fair to say that in many campaigns we didn’t hear the words “climate change” or “climate emergency,” and yet, to what extent do you think the concern about the climate is part of this blue wave?
HUFFMAN: Climate is part of it, even if it wasn’t articulated with that specific phrase. When you look at the inability to get [home] insurance or the inability to afford insurance. When you look at skyrocketing food costs. When you look at the fact that American consumers found themselves stuck on the fossil fuel roller coaster once again because Donald Trump had burned the bridge to clean electric vehicles—or at least tried to do so—while the rest of the world is moving forward in a way that will liberate them from that fossil fuel roller coaster. These were significant elements, and climate was on the agenda, whether folks realized it or talked about it as such or not.
DOERING: How is the climate crisis affecting your district and your constituents? What are you hearing from them?
HUFFMAN: I’m hearing them kind of stunned that in the middle of sunny days, at high tide, we have coastal areas underwater because of what’s called a Kelvin wave—this pulse of warm water that’s moving up the West Coast due to El Niño, which is more intense because of human-caused climate change. The reality really comes home when you’re in the middle of a sunny day, there’s been no storm and you have roads and bike paths and trails and coastal buildings underwater.
CURWOOD: You’ll become chair, in a few weeks, of the House Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Looking at your newfound power, what’s at the very top of your list to get done while you have this opportunity to influence things?
HUFFMAN: We need to do a permitting reform bill on our terms. That’s going to be high on my priority list, if I’m allowed to do it. When we get back to Washington, everybody’s going to be consumed with this fight over the Senate permitting reform deal, a deal that was cut behind closed doors by four people—two of whom are coal-state Republicans—a deal that was written largely by the oil and gas industry. I think waking up after that profoundly huge blue-wave statement by the American people, people—I hope—are going to question why we would constrain our permitting reform ambition to this, which was negotiated with zero leverage for Democrats.
Why wouldn’t we give Democrats a chance to use this newfound power to cut a better deal that doesn’t throw the Endangered Species Act and Native American tribes and the Clean Water Act and all of these other core values under the bus, and a deal that ends the war on clean energy, so that we can give the next president a chance to lead on climate action instead of tying his hands, which is one of the things that this bill would do.
CURWOOD: To what extent is that going to move ahead, though, in a lame duck session?
HUFFMAN: They’re going to try to jam it [through]. That’s very clear. This deal is premised on a very rapid, no-hearings push through the Senate and the House. A lot of the votes have already been lined up, and it is just a good old-fashioned jam job that is going to hit us as soon as we get back to town next week.
DOERING: Part of this permitting bill fight that you’re referring to is public lands. When it comes to the lands that all Americans hold as a public trust, what are your priorities with the Natural Resources Committee?
HUFFMAN: Our public lands are an intergenerational trust.

As global climate negotiators and government officials convene for the annual United Nations climate summit, the scientific organization they rely on to guide their decisions is mired in gridlock and short on funds.
Since 1990, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has produced influential global reports in cycles. Its 2013 and 2014 reports provided the scientific foundation for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, which continues to shape international climate policy. But the IPCC suspended its mid-October meeting without approving a budget for next year or agreeing on a timetable for publishing upcoming reports.
The political disputes that derailed the meeting rattled many of the scientists who devote hundreds of hours, often without pay, to assess the latest climate research across dozens of disciplines, from ice sheets and glaciers to forests and agriculture. Their work not only tracks the science of a changing climate, it also identifies ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions and helps communities adapt to increasingly severe climate impacts.
More than 100 IPCC scientists expressed their concern about the future of the panel in an Oct. 19 open letter, asking political leaders to provide it with adequate resources. The scientists reaffirmed their commitment to the work, but warned that, as climate impacts intensify, governments must ensure the panel can produce timely assessments of climate risks and potential solutions when they are needed. They also called for a process that gives all countries an equitable voice, rather than allowing wealthy, industrialized nations to dominate.
The IPCC will resume its session online in December, after the annual COP, the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year’s event, COP31, begins next week in Antalya, Turkey. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change continually informs the negotiations with science updates, but political tensions have affected its budget and timelines for upcoming reports.
Governments decide voluntarily each year how much to contribute to the panel’s annual budget of $9.7 million, about the cost of producing a major movie. That pays to keep the meetings running, covering travel, scientific support and workshops, especially for developing countries.
Next year’s budget remains uncertain, but a concerted push by nations to increase funding at the upcoming climate summit in Turkey could be effective, history shows. In 1999, at COP5, an urgent funding appeal in the meeting’s final decision document helped the IPCC maintain momentum for its third and fourth cycles of updated climate reports.
Repeated reminders from the annual climate COPs helped sustain funding through the early 2010s, leading up to the landmark Fifth Assessment Report that is the scientific basis of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit human-caused warming as close to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5C) as possible.
Scientists Speak
The United States has, at times, contributed as much as one-third of the IPCC’s annual budget. The Trump administration’s withdrawal of funding over the last two years, along with the U.S. government’s withdrawal from the panel, likely contributed to stalling the IPCC process, said Bob Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University, who signed the Oct. 19 letter and has worked on several of the panel’s reports.
Despite the loss of federal support, the United States still has a significant scientific presence in the current assessment cycle, Kopp said. The U.S. Academic Alliance for the IPCC was formed in 2025 by the American Geophysical Union, bringing together colleges and universities to help ensure continued U.S. scientist participation without federal support. He said the U.S. has the largest percentage of contributing authors of any country, about 7.5 percent, and that the alliance nominated more authors for the current cycle than the U.S. government did for the previous one.
“I’m very pleased that civil society in the U.S. has managed to fill some of this gap,” he said. “But we can also see from what’s happening among the governments and the IPCC budget that there’s only so much civil society can do on its own.”

Key IPCC reports are scheduled to track whether countries are living up to what they promised in the Paris Agreement, said Carl Schleussner, a climate scientist with Climate Analytics and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. Without a timeline for those reports, scientists can’t plan their IPCC-related work schedule, he said.
The delay in the IPCC’s process reflects a range of complex factors, against a backdrop of deteriorating international cooperation. Among them are concerns raised by a group known as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, including India and China. They are questioning whether the panel’s scenarios fairly represent the range of possible climate pathways for all countries, according to reports by observers with the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s Earth Negotiations Bulletin.
Weaponized Science?
Davide Faranda, another IPCC author who signed the letter, said he’s concerned that a breakdown of international collaboration could lead to climate information being weaponized.
If the IPCC fails to provide that timely, widely available knowledge, major powers like the United States or Russia could try to keep climate assessments private to gain strategic advantages through knowledge of climate impacts on agriculture, natural resources, national security and other sectors, he said.

The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.
The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.
Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."
In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."
"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.
Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.
Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.
Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.
He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , external
Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.
The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.
Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.
Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.
The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.
